In the Second Temple period, the praises sung in the temple (particularly by the Levitical choir) were understood as creating a sacred space in which God's presence was especially concentrated. The idea that God 'dwells' (yosheb) on the praises suggests that corporate worship creates the locus of God's sovereignty. This is not mere metaphor in ancient Jewish thought; the praises literally constituted the throne room. In Mesopotamian religious thought, a deity's throne was a physical reality within the temple, and the rituals and songs performed there were understood to activate the god's presence. Israel's theology transfers this to the corporate, vocal act of praise itself.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: Helaman 12:13-15 portrays the Nephites in covenant fidelity, recognizing God's greatness despite their struggles: 'O then, why will not our hearts be turned unto the Lord our God... we may know of a surety that he is with us, and has made known unto us the things which we have received.' The pivot in Psalm 22:4 from individual suffering to affirmation of God's nature parallels this corporate recognition.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 109:77 (from the dedication of the Kirtland Temple) contains the phrase 'that thy glory may rest down upon thy people,' expressing the same theology of God enthroned in the worship of the covenant community. Also, D&C 88:62 speaks of the voice of God's power in nature and in the hearts of the faithful, suggesting that God's presence is realized through the obedience and praise of the people.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The temple is the house of God, the place where God's holiness dwells and where the covenant people gather to praise. Psalm 22:4's image of God enthroned on praises directly applies to temple worship, where the congregation's collective voice creates a sacred space.

commentary.christological_typology: Christ is the ultimate 'praise of Israel'—the embodiment of perfect worship, perfect obedience, perfect gratitude to the Father. God is enthroned not only on the people's praises but supremely on Christ, who is the 'Lamb worthy to receive power, and riches, and wisdom, and strength, and honour, and glory, and blessing' (Revelation 5:12). Jesus' passion itself becomes the ultimate prayer of praise—a total offering of will and life to the Father. The shift in Psalm 22 from the sufferer's cry to affirmation of God's holiness finds its fullest expression in Christ's ultimate prayer on the cross, which (as later verses reveal) becomes vindication and exaltation.
commentary.application: Verse 4 teaches that our experience of God's presence is not the measure of God's reality. When we feel abandoned or unheard, we can confess as the sufferer does: 'Yet you are holy.' This confession is not denial of our pain but contextualization of it within a larger theological reality. God's nature is not contingent on our experience. Additionally, the image of God enthroned on the praises of the community suggests that our corporate worship has cosmic significance. When we gather with the covenant community to praise, we are creating the throne room of God. Our individual suffering and individual prayers, while important, participate in a much larger prayer ecology. We are never praying alone; we pray as part of Israel, as part of the Church, as part of a community whose praises sustain God's presence and sovereignty.

text_kjv: Our fathers trusted in thee: they trusted, and thou didst deliver them.

commentary.narrative: Verse 5 continues the pivot begun in verse 4, but now shifts from God's nature (holiness) to God's actions (deliverance). The sufferer constructs a historical argument: God delivered the ancestors; therefore, God must deliver the present sufferer. The threefold repetition of trust (batchu... batchu... tefalletemo) creates a rhythmic hammer-blow of logic. The ancestors trusted. They continued trusting. And God rescued them. The argument is entirely reasonable: if God is faithful to the covenant, and if the ancestors embodied covenant fidelity, then the covenant promise should hold for their descendants. Yet this historical argument, while rhetorically powerful, will prove insufficient. Later in the psalm (vv. 7-9), the sufferer will describe being mocked and despised despite this heritage. The argument from precedent will collapse before the reality of continued suffering. But at this moment in the psalm, the sufferer appeals to memory: God's character was established in saving acts toward the fathers; why should that character change? The naming of the forefathers (implied in 'our fathers') creates a link across generations—the sufferer is part of a chain of covenant faith stretching backward through history and (as the psalm will reveal) forward toward future generations.

word_study.meaning: To trust, to rely on, to have confidence in. The root suggests a security rooted in dependence. To batach in God is to commit oneself entirely to God's character and promises.
word_study.significance: The triple repetition (batchu... batchu) emphasizes that trust was not a momentary feeling but a sustained, continual posture. The ancestors did not trust once and abandon faith; they trusted persistently. This becomes a model for the sufferer's own continuous prayer.

word_study.meaning: To escape, to be delivered, to be rescued. The verb carries the sense of swift, complete rescue from danger. Used often of God snatching the righteous from peril.
word_study.significance: Palat is a dynamic, action-oriented word. God does not merely promise; God rescues. The word emphasizes that the ancestors' trust was vindicated by concrete action. The sufferer appeals to this pattern of divine action.

word_study.meaning: Fathers, ancestors, patriarchs. In covenant theology, the fathers are the bearers of promise—Abraham, Isaac, Jacob—and later, King David. The term carries covenantal weight.
word_study.significance: The sufferer's claim to be part of the 'our fathers' lineage establishes a covenantal identity. He is not a lone individual but an heir of covenant promises. This inheritance should obligate God to sustain covenant fidelity.

cross_references.connection: The Shema passage teaches each generation to recount to their children how God delivered Israel from Egypt, establishing the pattern of historical memory as the foundation of covenant fidelity.
Joshua's covenant renewal ceremony explicitly recounts God's acts toward Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, using historical memory to bind the people to ongoing covenant obligation.
The entire 'Hall of Faith' chapter recounts the trust of ancestors (Abel, Enoch, Noah, Abraham, Sarah, Isaac, Jacob) as exemplars whose faith should inspire modern believers.

A long didactic psalm that teaches each generation about God's mighty acts and commands them not to hide the truth 'from their children,' establishing the intergenerational transmission of covenant memory.
Nephi opens his record by noting that his father, Lehi, came from Jerusalem, establishing lineage and hereditary covenant obligation—a parallel structure to Psalm 22:5's appeal to the fathers.

commentary.historical_context: In ancient Israel, historical memory was not mere nostalgia but a covenantal tool. The recitation of God's mighty acts (particularly the exodus from Egypt) was central to festival liturgy and was understood to renew the covenant and obligate God's future faithfulness. The theology embedded in Psalm 22:5 reflects the widespread ancient Near Eastern practice of invoking a deity's past acts as a warrant for present intervention. Egyptian prayers often appealed to a god's demonstrated benevolence in order to petition for new acts of deliverance. The ancestral connection was also crucial: in ANE thought, a person's standing before the gods was partly determined by family lineage and family religious precedent. A family with a history of favors from the gods could appeal to that history.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: 1 Nephi 3:15-16 shows Nephi's brothers doubting God's ability to deliver them from Laban, while Nephi appeals to the covenant promises made to their father Lehi and to Abraham before him. Nephi embodies the principle of Psalm 22:5—trusting in God based on the precedent of ancestral faithfulness.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 21:4-5 contains the Lord's promise to Oliver Cowdery and Joseph Smith, invoking covenant fidelity in generational terms: 'Wherefore, meaning the church, thou shalt give heed unto all his words and commandments which he shall give unto you as he receiveth them, walking in all holiness before me.' The Restoration renews and extends the covenantal inheritance of the fathers.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: Temple ordinances explicitly connect the living to ancestors and to lineage covenants. Sealing work is based on the principle that covenant fidelity extends across generations—a liturgical enactment of the principle in Psalm 22:5.

commentary.christological_typology: Jesus is the ultimate heir and inheritor of the ancestral covenant promises. Matthew 1:1 opens with 'The book of the generation of Jesus Christ, the son of David, the son of Abraham,' anchoring Jesus in the covenantal lineage. Christ's trust in the Father (exemplified in Gethsemane and at Calvary) is the ultimate expression of batach. And Christ's resurrection becomes the ultimate palat—the supreme deliverance that vindicates both his own faith and the faith of all ancestors who trusted in future redemption.
commentary.application: For modern Latter-day Saints, Psalm 22:5 invokes both genealogy and spiritual inheritance. We stand in the line of a long covenant tradition stretching back through Joseph Smith and the prophets to the patriarchs. When we struggle with doubt or unanswered prayer, we can appeal to this history: the God who delivered Abraham, Moses, David, and Joseph Smith remains bound by covenant to deliver us. Our ancestors' faith becomes a foundation for our own. Additionally, we bear responsibility to transmit this covenant legacy to the next generation, ensuring that the chain of trust remains unbroken. We are not praying alone; we pray as heirs of a vast company of faithful witnesses.

text_kjv: They cried unto thee, and were delivered: they trusted in thee, and were not confounded.

commentary.narrative: Verse 6 completes the historical argument begun in verse 5, now adding a crucial theological element: shame or vindication. The ancestors cried out (zaaku, the same verb as in v. 2 for the sufferer's own cry), and they were delivered. Moreover—and this is the theological clincher—they were not put to shame (voshu, to be ashamed, to be humiliated, to be publicly exposed as a fool). The logic is devastating in its clarity: those who trust in God are not shamed by that trust. Shame (bosh) in Hebrew is public exposure of one's folly; it is the social consequence of backing the wrong horse. If you trust in something and it fails you, you are bosh—humiliated, disgraced. But the ancestors trusted and were not bosh; their faith was vindicated. Yet the sufferer himself experiences precisely the opposite (vv. 7-9): he is despised, mocked, surrounded by those who ridicule him. The ancestors' pattern (trust leads to deliverance, deliverance leads to vindication, vindication means no shame) is being broken in his case. This creates the theological crisis that propels the entire psalm: How can God's pattern of faithfulness to the trusting be interrupted? The verse thus accomplishes two things: it strengthens the sufferer's historical argument while simultaneously setting up the confrontation with inexplicable suffering that follows.

word_study.meaning: To cry out, to shout, to appeal urgently. More forceful than qara (used in v. 2), suggesting loud, desperate vocalization.
word_study.significance: The sufferer uses the same urgent vocabulary ('I cry out') and now recalls that the ancestors also cried urgently, and their urgent cries were heard. The implied lesson: urgent, faithful prayer receives response.

word_study.meaning: To escape, to be delivered, to be rescued. Similar to palat in v. 5, emphasizing swift, complete rescue.
word_study.significance: The doubling of rescue vocabulary (palat in v. 5, malat in v. 6) creates emphasis. God does not merely help; God rescues. Complete deliverance is God's pattern.

word_study.meaning: To be ashamed, to be confounded, to be put to shame. Shame in Hebrew is not merely internal guilt but public humiliation—exposure as someone whose trust or judgment was foolish.
word_study.significance: This is the theological crux. Trusting in God and then being publicly humiliated would suggest that trust in God was misplaced. The absence of bosh for the ancestors proves that their faith was rational, justified, vindicated. The sufferer's experience of being mocked (vv. 7-9) becomes incomprehensible against this background.

cross_references.connection: The servant song declares: 'Therefore have I set my face like a flint, and I know that I shall not be ashamed.' Like Psalm 22:6, this passage connects trust to freedom from shame, anticipating the innocent sufferer's ultimate vindication.
Paul quotes Isaiah, establishing that no one who believes in Christ will be ashamed (put to shame). The theological pattern of Psalm 22:6 becomes a New Testament promise.
Similar structure: 'Unto thee, O Lord, do I lift up my soul... Let me not be ashamed, let not mine enemies triumph over me... neither shall any that wait on thee be ashamed.'
God promises to those who trust in him: 'Fear not; for thou shalt not be ashamed... for the Lord has called thee as a woman forsaken and grieved in spirit.' Ultimate deliverance dissolves shame.

commentary.historical_context: In ancient Israel, shame was a deeply social phenomenon. To be exposed as someone whose trust was misplaced meant public ridicule, loss of social standing, and exclusion from community. Conversely, those whose trust in God was vindicated through deliverance gained social honor and standing. The ancestors' freedom from shame was thus not merely personal or internal; it was socially validated. This makes the contrast in Psalm 22 particularly acute: the sufferer, following the same covenant pattern (trust → cry → ?) finds himself experiencing the opposite outcome (trust → cry → shame and mockery). In ancient Near Eastern texts, shame was often the prerogative of the enemy; to overcome an enemy without shaming them was incomplete victory. The promise in Psalm 22:6 is that trusting God results in the enemy's shame, not the believer's.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: Alma 36:27-30 describes how Alma, having repented and come to faith, now experiences divine protection and vindication: 'And I have been supported under trials and troubles of every kind, yea, and in all manner of afflictions... and I do not fear death; for I am conscious of my sins having been forgiven me.' The movement from shame (his previous state) to vindication (his present peace) mirrors the pattern affirmed in Psalm 22:6.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 76:50-60 describes the celestial kingdom as a place where the faithful inherit exaltation and vindication—the ultimate removal of shame. Also, D&C 132:49 promises that those faithful in their covenants will be exalted and will not be ashamed before the Lord.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: Temple progression moves from symbolic shame (the fig aprons representing loss of innocence) to exaltation and honour. The ordinance enacts the principle of Psalm 22:6: faithful covenant keepers are not put to shame but are clothed in honour.

commentary.christological_typology: Christ's crucifixion was designed by his enemies to produce maximum shame: public execution as a condemned criminal, nakedness on the cross, mockery by passersby. Yet Psalm 22:6's promise—that those who trust in God are not put to shame—finds its ultimate vindication in Christ's resurrection. The shame of the cross is overwhelmed by the vindication of the resurrection. Romans 1:16 captures this: 'I am not ashamed of the gospel of Christ: for it is the power of God unto salvation.' Christ's resurrection proves that his trust in the Father was not misplaced, and extends that vindication to all who believe in him.
commentary.application: Modern believers often fear that public identification with Christ or covenant commitment will result in shame—social ridicule, professional consequences, or loss of standing. Psalm 22:6 offers historical and theological warrant: the pattern established by the ancestors is that trust in God does not issue in lasting shame. Ultimate vindication belongs to the faithful, not to those who mock them. This does not mean we will never experience social discomfort for our faith; rather, it means that our trust is not misplaced, and that final vindication—the removal of all shame in God's sight—is assured. We can endure temporary mockery knowing that the ancestors' experience of vindication is our inheritance.

text_kjv: But I am a worm, and no man; a reproach of men, and despised of the people.

commentary.narrative: The psalmist's self-description as a worm rather than a human being marks the emotional and social nadir of the poem. This is not figurative language meant to convey humility—it is a statement of complete dehumanization. The sufferer has been stripped of dignity to the point where the very category of "humanity" no longer applies. The parallel construction (worm/man; reproach/despised) intensifies the degradation: not only is he less than human, but he is actively scorned and rejected by his community. The Covenant Rendering's attention to tolaath (the crimson worm used to produce scarlet dye) adds a layer of meaning—this particular insect is crushed to yield its color, suggesting not merely insignificance but destruction itself as the mechanism of the sufferer's condition.
commentary.narrative_continued: The movement from verse 1 ("My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me?") to verse 7 shows the progression of abandonment. The initial cry was directed upward to God; now the sufferer turns his gaze to those around him and experiences their contempt. Yet even in this statement of absolute rejection, there is an implicit claim: he still has enough agency to declare his own condition. The worm has a voice. This paradox—that the utterly degraded one still speaks—becomes the foundation for everything that follows.

word_study.meaning: Specifically the crimson worm (tola'at shani) from which scarlet dye was extracted. The creature was crushed to release its color. The Hebrew choice here is precise: not just any worm, but the one associated with destruction and the production of color through suffering.
word_study.significance: The image carries overtones of being pressed, squeezed, annihilated—yet yielding something of value in the process. Later Christian theology saw in this verse a prefiguring of Christ's blood-stained sacrifice, though the psalmist's original context was simply extreme social degradation. The specificity of tolaath rather than a generic insect suggests deep humiliation: even the mechanism of the degradation is public and well-known.

word_study.meaning: Shame, disgrace, insult—the condition of being scorned or mocked. It implies public shaming, not private shame.
word_study.significance: This is not internal guilt but external contempt. The sufferer's pain is not his alone but a spectacle witnessed and participated in by others. Cherpah appears throughout the Psalms as the experience of being abandoned to mockery (cf. Psalm 69:7, 79:4). The Restoration adds weight to this: D&C 76:35 uses 'reproach' to describe the condition of those separated from God's presence.

word_study.meaning: Scorned, held in contempt, regarded as worthless. The root bazah means to despise or treat with disdain.
word_study.significance: Unlike cherpah (active shaming), bazui carries the sense of being regarded as inherently worthless. The community's response is not even heated—it is cold dismissal. The sufferer is beneath anger; he is simply beneath notice.

cross_references.connection: Another lament where the psalmist is 'become a stranger unto my brethren' and the reproach of those who mock him. The pattern of social isolation and public shame is repeated across lament psalms.
The Suffering Servant is 'despised and rejected of men; a man of sorrows, and acquainted with grief.' The language parallels Psalm 22:7 in describing total social rejection and dehumanization.
The crucifixion narrative records those who passed by 'wagging their heads' and deriding Jesus, directly mirroring the mockery described in Psalm 22:7-8 and fulfilling it typologically.
Nephi quotes Isaiah 53 in the context of recognizing that the Messiah would suffer rejection and shame. The Book of Mormon explicitly connects the suffering servant passages to Christ's experience.
Angel declares that Christ would be 'despised and rejected by his people' and would 'suffer temptations,' echoing the pattern of absolute social dehumanization.

commentary.historical_context: In ancient Israelite society, social status was tied to membership in the community and family. Complete isolation or rejection was not merely emotional pain—it was existential annihilation. The Hebrew social world understood identity as relational and public. To be despised was to be outside the covenant community, without protection, without honor, without standing. The specific mention of being despised 'by the people' (am, the covenant community itself, not foreigners) intensifies the betrayal. This was not rejection by enemies but by one's own.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: Alma 7:11-13 clarifies that Christ's suffering included 'pains and afflictions and temptations of every kind' including the emotional and social agony of rejection. The Book of Mormon emphasizes that Christ's suffering was not merely physical but included bearing the weight of human shame and isolation.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 76:36 describes those separated from God's presence as experiencing 'their shame and condemnation.' The doctrine of degrees of glory in the Restoration acknowledges that separation from God's presence carries emotional and social consequences that are real and devastating.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The temple teaches that the path to exaltation involves being 'proven' through trials and rejection. The Savior's passage through mockery and shame represents the archetypal pattern that all covenant keepers must follow in some form. The suffering of the Atonement includes bearing the full weight of human contempt.

commentary.christological_typology: Psalm 22:7 prefigures Christ's crucifixion in multiple ways. Jesus was stripped of dignity (literally of his garments), mocked by the crowd, and reduced to an object of contempt. The mockers at Golgotha 'wagged their heads' exactly as Psalm 22:8 describes. Yet beneath this typology is a deeper truth: Christ's willingness to accept complete social dehumanization—to become 'a worm, and no man'—is the mechanism of redemption. In taking upon himself the full weight of human shame and rejection, Christ sanctifies suffering itself. The Savior does not remain a worm; his resurrection transforms the meaning of the degradation.
commentary.application: Modern covenant members often experience a subtler form of the degradation described in Psalm 22:7. Social mockery, professional marginalization, or family rejection for living gospel standards can feel like being reduced to something less than fully human in the eyes of others. This verse validates the reality of that pain—it does not minimize it as merely emotional or subjective. At the same time, it teaches that claiming one's identity before God (verse 11: 'you are my God') takes precedence over claiming identity before the world. The sufferer's confession that God drew him from the womb (verses 10-11) becomes his foundation when everything else is stripped away. In covenant life, this means that no amount of worldly contempt can diminish the relationship established between the soul and God before time began.

text_kjv: All they that see me laugh me to scorn: they shoot out the lip, they shake the head, saying,

commentary.narrative: If verse 7 established the sufferer's degraded condition, verse 8 dramatizes the public participation in that degradation. The sufferer is not merely passively rejected; he is actively mocked by all who see him. The translation 'laugh me to scorn' (yalgiyu li) carries the sense of open mockery, derision that is vocal and visible. The Hebrew verb yaltgiyu comes from lg', meaning to mock, deride, make sport of. This is not subtle contempt but theatrical scorn—the kind that includes gestures and performance. The Covenant Rendering emphasizes the physical details: they 'curl their lips' and 'shake their heads.' These are not random gestures but ritualized expressions of contempt well understood in the ancient world.
commentary.narrative_continued: The phrase 'they shoot out the lip' (yaftiru be-safah) is anatomically specific and deliberately insulting. Pushing out the lower lip in a sneer is a gesture of contempt that communicates dismissal and disgust. When combined with shaking the head (yaniu rosh), it creates a full tableau of mockery. The verse is vivid because the psalmist is not merely describing emotional pain but recording the exact physicality of public humiliation—the spectacle of his suffering. The final phrase 'saying' introduces the specific words that accompany these gestures (developed in the next clause), suggesting that the mockers are not acting silently but narrating their contempt aloud.

word_study.meaning: To mock, deride, make sport of. The root lg' carries overtones of both derision and physical mockery.
word_study.significance: This is not mere disagreement or criticism but organized social derision. The verb suggests a coordinated action: 'all who see me' participate together in mocking, creating a communal experience of contempt that isolates the sufferer further.

word_study.meaning: Literally, 'they open wide with the lip' or 'they gape with the lip.' The verb ptir means to open wide; the body part is specifically the lip (safah), suggesting a sneering gesture.
word_study.significance: The Covenant Rendering's term 'curl their lips' captures the gesture more clearly than the KJV. This is not accidental grimacing but deliberate mimicry of disgust. In many ancient cultures, the curled lip signaled contamination or aversion. The mockers are performing the gesture of someone recoiling from something unclean.

word_study.meaning: To shake, wave, or swing the head back and forth. The verb nia' means to shake or sway; rosh is the head.
word_study.significance: This gesture appears throughout the ancient Near East as a sign of rejection, dismissal, or judgment. In Lamentations 2:15, those who pass by 'clap their hands at thee, and hiss and wag their head.' It is the physical embodiment of 'I reject you.'

cross_references.connection: The fulfillment: 'And they that passed by reviled him, wagging their heads.' The exact gestures of Psalm 22:8 are recorded at the crucifixion, showing that Christ experienced the typological fulfillment of this verse in precise detail.

In the destruction of Jerusalem, 'All that pass by clap their hands at thee; they hiss and wag their head at the daughter of Jerusalem.' The pattern of public mockery as judgment appears across lament literature.

Job also describes how others would mock him, creating an archetype of the innocent sufferer subjected to public derision. The pattern of the suffering righteous mocked by the community appears in wisdom literature.

The Gospel accounts add the detail that mockers 'wagging their heads' said, 'Ah, thou that destroyest the temple and buildest it in three days, save thyself.' The words that accompany the gestures in Psalm 22:8 parallel the content of the mockery at Golgotha.

Peter reflects on Christ's passion: 'Who, when he was reviled, reviled not again; when he suffered, he threatened not.' This captures the profound difference between the mockers in Psalm 22:8 and the silent endurance of Christ.

commentary.historical_context: In the ancient Near Eastern honor-shame culture, public mockery was not merely insulting; it was a mechanism of social annihilation. The mocking crowd created a ritual of rejection that literally unmade a person's social identity. The coordinated gestures—the lip-curling, the head-shaking, the laughter—were choreographed forms of contempt. Archaeological evidence and artistic depictions from Egypt and Mesopotamia show that such gestures of derision were well-established and recognized. The phrase 'all they that see me' suggests that the sufferer is in a public space, likely the temple precincts or a place where many would gather. The mockery is not private but performed before witnesses, which amplified its social devastation.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: Mosiah 3:9 and 12:7 describe how the Messiah would be mocked and despised. The Book of Mormon presents Christ's mockery not as an incidental suffering but as a central element of his atoning work. King Benjamin explicitly prepares his people for the reality that the Messiah would face organized public contempt.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 122:5-8 addresses Joseph Smith in Liberty Jail with language echoing Psalm 22, telling him that 'all these things shall give thee experience' and that 'the Son of Man hath descended below them all.' The Doctrine and Covenants makes explicit that following Christ includes experiencing forms of public rejection and ridicule.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The temple teaches that the path to exaltation involves being 'proven' and even 'broken' before being renewed. The degree of suffering in Psalm 22:8 represents the depth of the Savior's submission to the will of the Father and to human contempt as part of the Atonement.

commentary.christological_typology: The crucifixion accounts in the Gospels are structured to show Christ's literal fulfillment of Psalm 22:8. Matthew, Mark, and Luke all record that those passing by the cross 'wagged their heads' at Jesus, using the exact physical gestures the psalm describes. The Gospel writers were clearly conscious that Christ's passion was the historical realization of this psalm's imagery. Yet the typology goes deeper: just as the psalmist responds to mockery not by defending himself but by reaffirming trust in God (verses 9-11), so Jesus does not answer his mockers with recrimination but with 'Father, into thy hands I commend my spirit.' The suffering of mockery becomes, in Christ, a form of submission rather than defeat.
commentary.application: In a culture that increasingly emphasizes public performance and social media presence, Psalm 22:8 speaks to the terror of public humiliation. Modern covenant members may experience mockery not in a physical crowd but in comments, shares, and reactions online—which can feel even more dehumanizing because the audience is invisible and vast. This verse validates the deep pain of organized public contempt. It also teaches that such mockery, however real and damaging, is not the final word. The sufferer in this psalm does not attempt to defend himself to the mockers; instead, he turns to God (verse 9) and to his foundational identity established before birth (verses 10-11). The covenant application is this: when facing public ridicule for living gospel standards, the response is not to fight for vindication in the court of public opinion but to strengthen one's grip on the identity given by God. The mockers are numerous, but God is the audience that matters.

text_kjv: He trusted on the LORD that he would deliver him: let him deliver him, seeing he delighted in him.

commentary.narrative: Verse 9 is a turning point—the mockers now speak, and their words are crucial. They are not merely deriding the sufferer's condition; they are specifically attacking his faith. The mockers quote back to the sufferer his own trust in God, turning it into evidence of his delusion. In the Hebrew, they are saying: 'He rolled himself onto the LORD—let the LORD rescue him! Let him deliver him, since he delights in him!' The Covenant Rendering makes clear that gol ('he rolled') is an imperative verb form, but the mockers are quoting it as a past action—'he rolled his burden to the LORD.' This is a precise theological attack: the mockers are saying that the sufferer's trust in God is now being put to the test, and God is apparently failing.
commentary.narrative_continued: The word 'delighted' (chafatz) carries the sense of being pleased with, taking delight in, or having a preference for someone. The mockers are therefore saying, 'If God truly delights in this man, why is he suffering? Why is he being mocked? Why is God not rescuing him?' This is the ancient version of the problem of theodicy—how can a good God allow innocent suffering? The mockery is not merely personal but theological: it challenges the sufferer's foundational claim that God loves and cares for him. Yet notice what the mockers are actually doing: they are tacitly acknowledging that the sufferer does trust in God. Their attack would have no force if there were nothing to attack. In quoting the sufferer's faith back to him mockingly, they are inadvertently testifying to the reality of his trust.

word_study.meaning: To roll, cast, or throw a burden onto someone. The verb gol implies shifting weight, like rolling a heavy stone. The preposition el indicates direction—'toward' or 'onto' someone.
word_study.significance: This verb choice is theologically rich. Trust (in this image) is not intellectual assent but a physical act of transferring weight, of making oneself dependent. The mockers' use of this image suggests a complete, weight-bearing commitment to God. The sufferer has made himself vulnerable by placing his entire burden on God. This makes the apparent silence of God all the more painful—the sufferer has nowhere else to turn.

word_study.meaning: To delight in, take pleasure in, prefer, have a preference for someone or something. It implies active, positive regard.
word_study.significance: The mockers use this word to expose the contradiction they perceive: if God is genuinely pleased with this man, the present suffering proves that either God does not actually delight in him (contradicting his faith) or God is unable to help him (contradicting God's power). The word chafatz appears in the Psalms as an expression of God's delight in the righteous (e.g., Psalm 18:19, 'The Lord delighted in me'). The mockers are weaponizing this very language to challenge the sufferer's confidence in God's favor.

cross_references.connection: The chief priests, scribes, and elders mock Jesus with words echoing Psalm 22:9: 'He trusted in God; let him deliver him now, if he will have him.' Matthew explicitly connects the crucifixion mockery to this verse, showing that Christ experienced the exact theological attack described in the psalm.
Job also laments being mocked for his piety: 'I am as one mocked of his neighbour, who calleth upon God, and he answereth him.' Those who trust God sometimes become objects of contempt to others.

The Epistle quotes Psalm 22:8 ('I will put my trust in him') in the context of Christ's perfection through suffering, showing that the Psalm's theme of tested faith is central to understanding Christ's work.

Alma testifies, 'I have trusted in [God] with all my heart,' echoing the language of trust (gol el) that the mockers attack in Psalm 22:9. The Book of Mormon affirms that trust in God, even when challenged, is the core covenant virtue.

commentary.historical_context: The ancient Near Eastern understanding of divine favor was that it should manifest in visible blessing, prosperity, and protection. A righteous person who suffered was therefore considered problematic—either they were not truly righteous, or their god was not truly powerful or interested in them. The Book of Job explores this exact tension. The mockers in Psalm 22:9 are not inventing a new argument; they are drawing on common cultural assumptions about what divine favor should look like. The fact that the sufferer is mocked rather than vindicated by miraculous deliverance suggests that God operates on a different principle—that trust can be refined through testing, and that faith persisting through apparent abandonment is the highest form of devotion.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: Alma 36:27-29 presents a man of faith (Alma the Younger) crying out from spiritual despair while maintaining trust in the Savior: 'I cried within my heart: O Jesus, thou Son of God, have mercy on me.' Like the mockers' challenge in Psalm 22:9, Alma's spiritual trial attacks his faith precisely when he feels abandoned, yet he persists in crying unto God.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 76:58-60 teaches that exaltation requires the capacity to endure when God's presence seems withdrawn, when enemies mock the sufferer's faith, and when deliverance is delayed. The Doctrine and Covenants affirms that tested faith—faith that persists despite apparent divine silence—is the faith that inherits all things.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The temple covenant includes the teaching that the righteous may be tried and mocked (the 'telestial world') but that their trust in God will be vindicated when the veil is parted. The temple teaches that present suffering and public contempt do not negate divine favor but may actually be the mechanism through which it is refined.

commentary.christological_typology: The mockers' words in Psalm 22:9 become the exact words spoken at the crucifixion, making this verse a precise prophetic prefiguring of Christ's passion. Jesus hung on the cross while the chief priests and scribes said, 'He trusted in God; let him deliver him now.' Like the psalmist, Jesus had rolled his burden completely onto God (John 12:27, 'Father, save me from this hour... Father, glorify thy name'). The mockery attacks the very foundation of Christ's trust. Yet in Christ's case, the mockery becomes the moment of greatest trust—the surrender so complete that he cries out in abandonment (Psalm 22:1) and yet continues to address God as Father (Luke 23:46, 'Father, into thy hands I commend my spirit'). Christ's response to the mockers is not vindication but persistent trust—he does not come down from the cross to prove the mockers wrong. This is the pattern: faith tested by mockery, refined through silent seeming-abandonment, perfected in trust that depends on nothing but the character of God.
commentary.application: Covenant members who face testing of their faith—whether through doubt, delayed answers to prayer, unanswered questions, or public mockery—experience the exact dynamic of Psalm 22:9. The world (and sometimes our own doubts) mocks the claim that God cares for us: 'Where is your God? Why isn't he answering your prayers? Why are you still suffering if he delights in you?' This verse teaches that such testing is not evidence that faith is misplaced but that faith is real and is being refined. The sufferer's response is not to stop trusting but to persist in trust precisely when it is most tested. In covenant life, this means that periods of felt divine absence are not periods to abandon the covenant but periods to strengthen it. The ability to say, 'I trust in God even when I cannot see his hand' is the trust that the Atonement was designed to create.

text_kjv: But thou art he that took me out of the womb: thou didst make me hope when I was upon my mother's breasts.

commentary.narrative: The sufferer now responds to the mockers' attack on his faith not with argumentation but with a statement of original fact: before there were mockers, before there was suffering, before there was doubt, God was there at the beginning. The response is radical in its simplicity—it bypasses all theological debate and returns to the foundational moment of human experience: birth. The sufferer does not defend his faith with reasons; he defends it by going back to its source. The Hebrew verb gochah ('drew me from the womb') makes God the midwife, the one who was present at the most vulnerable moment of human emergence. The Covenant Rendering captures this clearly: 'you who drew me from the womb.'
commentary.narrative_continued: The second line moves from birth to infancy: 'thou didst make me hope when I was upon my mother's breasts.' The Hebrew mavtiachi (from the root btch, meaning to trust or seek refuge) suggests that the sufferer learned trust before he could speak, before he had a choice about it. God taught him to trust in the most primal way—by being the source of security at the mother's breast, the only world an infant knows. This is profound: the sufferer's claim that he trusts God is not a choice made at some moment in adulthood; it is woven into the fabric of his existence from before his conscious memory. It is the most foundational relationship of his life. In responding to the mockers this way, the sufferer is saying: 'Your mockery cannot undo what God did at my beginning. You can mock my faith, but you cannot mock my birth. You can mock my trust, but you cannot mock my infancy.'

word_study.meaning: The verb gachah means to draw, extract, or pull out; baten is womb or belly. The image is of pulling a newborn from the mother's body at birth.
word_study.significance: The choice of God as the one who 'drew' the sufferer from the womb makes God the agent of life itself, the midwife. This language appears elsewhere in the Bible when God is described as the creator and sustainer of life (Isaiah 46:3, 'hearken unto me... I am he, from the womb I will save you'). The sufferer is claiming not merely that God exists, but that God's relationship to him predates his own existence.

word_study.meaning: From the root btch (to trust, be confident, seek refuge). The causative form 'made me' suggests that someone instilled confidence in the sufferer. It is not something he chose but something that was taught to him.
word_study.significance: The sufferer learned trust (btach) before he could reflect on it or choose it. It was implanted in his very first experience of the world—the experience of being fed, held, and secured at his mother's breast. This suggests that trust in God is not a reasoned conclusion but a primal, embodied knowledge that comes from being cared for from the beginning. The Covenant Rendering's 'who made me secure' captures this sense of foundational safety.

word_study.meaning: Breasts, specifically the mother's breasts. The term emphasizes the most intimate, vulnerable moment of early human care and bonding.
word_study.significance: This is not metaphorical language but literal: the sufferer is remembering the moment when he was most dependent, most vulnerable, and most completely cared for. At the mother's breast, there is no question of trust—the infant does not reason about whether to trust; trust is implicit in the relationship. By returning to this image, the sufferer is recovering the pre-rational foundation of all trust. The specific choice of 'breasts' rather than, say, 'arms' or 'care' emphasizes the total bodily dependency and the primal security of the bond.

cross_references.connection: God declares: 'I am he... I am he; even to your old age I am he... and to hoar hairs will I carry you.' The promise echoes Psalm 22:10 by emphasizing God's presence from birth to old age, the entire arc of human life.
God tells Jeremiah, 'Before thou camest forth out of the womb I sanctified thee.' Like Psalm 22:10, this verse emphasizes that God's relationship to the prophet precedes even birth itself.

Elizabeth experiences the unborn John the Baptist 'leaping in her womb' at the voice of Mary. The passage suggests that relationship with God and response to God's presence can occur in the womb itself, earlier than birth.

The psalmist declares, 'I am fearfully and wonderfully made... my substance was not hid from thee, when I was made in secret.' This verse echoes Psalm 22:10's claim that God was present and active at the very origins of human existence.

The revelation teaches that 'the light and the Spirit of truth' proceeding from God 'enlighten the eyes of the understanding of all those who believe.' This echoes the idea that God's presence and influence are foundational to human existence and consciousness.

commentary.historical_context: In ancient Israel, the moment of birth was understood as a critical threshold where the infant's survival was uncertain. High infant mortality meant that birth was not guaranteed to lead to life. The fact that the sufferer made it from the womb to his mother's breast to childhood was understood as the result of divine providence. The mother's breast was the symbol of nurture, security, and the first relationship of care. To recall this in the context of present suffering is to say: 'God proved himself faithful when I was most vulnerable; he will not abandon me now.' The imagery also connects to the covenantal relationship: Israel is sometimes described as having been nursed at the breast of God (Isaiah 66:10-13), suggesting that God's care for his people follows the pattern of maternal nurture.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: 1 Nephi 1:20 presents Nephi's statement of trust based on God's ancient covenants with his father—a similar movement back to foundational commitments before present trials. The Book of Mormon teaches that when present suffering seems to shake faith, the solution is to return to the original covenant made with ancestors and with God.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 93:29-30 teaches that 'all truth is independent in that sphere in which God has placed it,' and that intelligence was 'not created or made... but is coequal with God himself.' This suggests that the sufferer's spirit, like all spirits, had existence and relationship with God before the womb. Psalm 22:10 thus points to pre-mortal relationship renewed at birth.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The temple covenant restores and emphasizes the relationship between the individual and God that was established pre-mortally. The temple teaches that the bonds created at the beginning (pre-mortal and birth) are eternal and cannot be severed by the trials and mockery of mortality. The sufferer's recourse is to remember that original covenant.

commentary.christological_typology: Christ's descent into mortality, like all human descent into flesh, involved passage through the womb and dependence on a mother's care. Luke 2 depicts the infant Jesus 'lying in a manger,' an image of vulnerability and dependence. This specificity—that God became an infant dependent on maternal care—is central to the Incarnation's meaning. Christ experienced the same foundational moment of human vulnerability and trust that Psalm 22:10 describes. Yet Christ's experience carried eternal significance: his emergence from Mary's womb was not merely his beginning but the beginning of redemption. The psychological implication is profound: when Christ later cries out in abandonment (Psalm 22:1), he does so as one who has experienced the full spectrum of human existence—from infant dependence to adult suffering. This makes his trust in the Father, even in apparent abandonment, the fullest expression of covenant faithfulness.
commentary.application: In times of testing, when the mockers (whether external critics or internal doubt) attack our faith, Psalm 22:10 teaches a radical response: return to the origins of trust. For modern covenant members, this might mean remembering one's own spiritual birth—a moment of confirmation, a personal revelation, a time when the presence of God became undeniable. It might also mean meditating on how God has sustained us from childhood, how prayers were answered in small ways, how we were 'made secure' in faith long before we faced present trials. The covenant practice is not to defend faith through abstract argument but to strengthen it by remembering God's faithfulness at the foundations of our spiritual life. When suffering makes God seem distant, returning to the memory of his nearness at the beginning restores perspective. This is why bearing testimony of foundational spiritual experiences—the moment one came to know God—is so powerful. It is Psalm 22:10 in practice: I know God loves me because I experienced his care at my spiritual birth.

text_kjv: I was cast upon thee from the womb: thou art my God from my mother's belly.

commentary.narrative: If verse 10 looked back to God as the source of life, verse 11 makes the more audacious claim: the sufferer was not merely born but was cast or thrown 'onto' God. The Hebrew hoshlakhti (from the root shlk, to cast, throw, or fling) is in the passive voice—the sufferer did not choose to be cast onto God; he was placed there by the very act of coming into existence. This is a stunning theological claim: the covenant relationship is not something the sufferer entered into by choice or volition, but something woven into his existence at its origin. He was not placed gently but 'cast'—suggesting force, purpose, and inevitability. The second line drives the point home: 'thou art my God from my mother's belly.' The preposition 'from' (min) indicates that this relationship began even before birth, in the womb itself.
commentary.narrative_continued: The phrase 'thou art my God' (eli attah) echoes the opening of the entire psalm (verse 1: 'My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me?'). This repetition creates a structural frame: despite the cry of abandonment that began the psalm, and despite all the suffering, mockery, and anguish that follows, the sufferer returns to the foundational claim—'you are my God.' This is not a reasoned argument but a confession, a reassertion of identity and relationship. The sufferer's identity is not determined by present circumstances (dehumanization, mocking, abandonment) but by this original relationship. In the flow of the psalm, verse 11 is where the sufferer takes his stand: no matter what happens, regardless of whether God seems present or absent, the sufferer will not relinquish the claim that God is his God.

word_study.meaning: The verb shlk means to throw, cast, or fling. The preposition al means 'upon' or 'onto.' The combination creates an image of being forcefully placed onto someone else.
word_study.significance: The Covenant Rendering's 'I was cast from birth' captures the sense of inevitability and divine purpose. The sufferer did not negotiate or consent; he was placed by divine action onto dependence on God. This is stronger than verse 10's 'you drew me from the womb.' Here, the action is more forceful—a 'casting' that establishes relationship not by gentleness but by sovereign appointment. The passive voice is crucial: the sufferer is not acting; God is. The relationship is not optional.

word_study.meaning: Beten is womb or belly; immi is 'my mother.' The phrase emphasizes the earliest possible moment of human existence.
word_study.significance: By placing this claim at the opening of the mother's womb, the sufferer is claiming that the covenant relationship predates conscious memory, rational choice, or any ability to object or consent. It is as original as consciousness itself. This teaching aligns with latter-day revelation about the pre-mortal existence and covenant-making (e.g., Abraham 3, where spirits made covenants with God before coming to earth).

cross_references.connection: The psalmist declares, 'By thee have I been holden up ever since the womb.' Like Psalm 22:11, this verse emphasizes lifelong divine sustenance from the moment of birth.

God tells Israel: 'Ye have seen what I did unto the Egyptians, and how I bare you on eagles' wings, and brought you unto myself.' The image of being 'cast' onto God parallels this covenantal language of being chosen and carried by God.

Jeremiah laments that God 'deceived' him, that God was 'stronger' than him and 'prevailed.' Like Psalm 22:11, Jeremiah acknowledges that his relationship to God was established not by his choice but by God's sovereign action.

Abraham's vision shows that spirits made covenants with God in the pre-mortal existence: 'We will go down, for there is space there... and we will make an earth.' This suggests that the 'casting' onto God in Psalm 22:11 reflects a pre-mortal covenant antecedent.

Joseph F. Smith's vision teaches that righteous spirits in the pre-mortal world were chosen for specific purposes. The 'casting' onto God in Psalm 22:11 reflects this doctrine of covenantal pre-mortal appointment.

commentary.historical_context: In the ancient Near Eastern understanding, birth was the moment of covenant establishment between an individual and their god. The child was understood to belong to the deity from that moment forward. The language of being 'cast' or 'placed' reflects the ancient understanding that a newborn was not free to choose allegiance but was bound to the deity by the fact of birth itself. In Israel, circumcision at eight days established the male child in the Abrahamic covenant, but the spiritual principle is already present at birth: the child belongs to the covenant people and the covenant God from the womb. This understanding would have been normative to the psalmist's audience.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: Alma 26:16-17 presents Alma testifying of his pre-mortal covenant: 'And I have been supported under trials and troubles of every kind, yea, and in all manner of afflictions; yea, God has granted unto me that I might be an instrument in his hands in bringing so many of you to a knowledge of his truth.' Alma understands his existence as covenantal from the beginning.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 138:56 teaches that 'from among the great and mighty ones who were assembled' in the pre-mortal world, the Lord 'chose... his son Jesus Christ.' This doctrine of pre-mortal covenant choice is the Restoration framework for understanding Psalm 22:11. Every covenant member was 'cast' onto God not at birth merely, but in the pre-mortal covenant.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The endowment covenant reestablishes the relationship between the individual and God that was original and pre-mortal. The temple teaches that the covenants made in the pre-mortal world are renewed and ratified in mortality through the ordinances. Psalm 22:11 thus points to the eternal nature of covenant relationship.

commentary.christological_typology: Christ's incarnation represents the ultimate 'casting' onto God—the Word made flesh, fully placed within human existence and human vulnerability. Christ was literally cast into the womb of Mary, subject to the full trajectory of human birth and development. Unlike other humans, Christ entered mortality with full consciousness of the pre-mortal covenant, making his submission to the human condition an act of infinite condescension and love. When Christ later cries out in Psalm 22:1, 'My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me,' he does so as the one who was 'cast' onto God at his incarnation. The abandonment he experiences is real, yet it does not negate the foundational covenant relationship. This is the deeper typological meaning: Christ's willingness to be 'cast' onto the Father—to make himself utterly dependent, utterly vulnerable—is what makes the Atonement efficacious.
commentary.application: Psalm 22:11 teaches that the covenant relationship is not something the individual negotiated or chose but something woven into the fabric of existence from the beginning. For modern covenant members, this principle has profound implications. When facing trials that make us question whether we want to continue in the covenant, verse 11 teaches that the covenant is not contingent on feeling good about it or understanding it. We were 'cast' onto God before we had the faculty to choose or refuse. The covenant is original, prior to consciousness, inescapable. This is not meant to sound coercive but liberating: if the covenant is original and not dependent on our present emotional state, then we can endure trials without losing the covenant. We cannot unmake ourselves. We cannot undo the fact that 'from the mother's womb,' God is our God. The application is this: when doubt or despair tempts us to relinquish the covenant, remember that you do not have that option. You were cast onto God before you could choose it. You can only choose whether to live in awareness of that relationship or in denial of it. The covenant stands regardless.

text_kjv: Be not far from me; for trouble is near; for there is none to help.

commentary.narrative: After the sufferer has reasserted his foundational identity and covenant relationship with God (verses 10-11), he now returns to the present crisis with an urgent petition. Despite the consolation of remembering his origins, the sufferer faces immediate danger. The spatial language is precise and devastating: God is far (rachaq), trouble is near (qerovah), and help is absent (ein ozer). The sufferer is caught in a terrible geometry—alone between a distant God and a close enemy. The Hebrew construction emphasizes the contrast: 'Do not be far from me / for trouble is near.' The parallel structure creates a pressure: the absence of God (even if only apparent) combined with the approach of trouble creates an unbearable tension. The final phrase 'for there is none to help' shifts the issue from the cosmic (Is God distant?) to the earthly (Is there anyone here who will defend me?).
commentary.narrative_continued: The movement in the psalm has been to establish the sufferer's identity (worm, not man) and his foundational covenant with God (cast upon you from the womb), then to name the present crisis in its starkest terms. This is not an abstract theological crisis but a concrete, immediate danger. The word 'trouble' (tzarah) can mean distress, affliction, anguish, or literally enemies pressing in. In the context of verses 7-9 (mockery and public derision), tzarah likely refers to active enemies or at least the acute stress of present persecution. The phrase 'there is none to help' suggests that the sufferer has looked around and found no human ally, no human support. This combination—divine distance, present danger, and human isolation—creates the context for the violent imagery that follows in verses 13-18.

word_study.meaning: The imperative 'do not' (al) plus the verb rachaq (to be far, go far, distance oneself) plus the preposition min (from) and first-person possessive (me/from me). The request is spatial: do not increase the distance between God and the sufferer.
word_study.significance: The use of spatial language for the covenant relationship is consistent with Hebrew theology: God's presence is near to those in covenant; his absence or distance is a form of abandonment. The sufferer is not arguing that God is literally far away but that God seems withdrawn, not responsive. The plea is for God to draw near, to restore the sense of presence that was foundational in verse 11.

word_study.meaning: Tzarah means distress, trouble, affliction, or pressure; qerovah means near, close, approaching. The proximity is urgent and immediate.
word_study.significance: The parallel structure (God far / trouble near) creates a devastating spatial image: the sufferer feels pinched between a withdrawn God and approaching danger. In the context of verses 7-9, tzarah likely refers to the human enemies who mock and attack. The word suggests not merely sadness or loss but active threat.

word_study.meaning: Ein means there is not, there is none; ozer means helper, one who aids or rescues. The phrase is absolute: no help exists in the sufferer's immediate context.
word_study.significance: The Covenant Rendering's phrasing 'there is no one to help' emphasizes the personal isolation. The sufferer has looked for human allies—for someone to defend him, to speak on his behalf, to offer protection—and found no one. This is not a theoretical statement but a lived experience: the sufferer stands alone, with no human support and (apparently) no divine presence. This is the nadir of desolation: cosmic abandonment and earthly isolation.

cross_references.connection: The psalmist laments, 'When my father and my mother forsake me, then the Lord will take me up.' Like Psalm 22:12, this verse addresses the anguish of human abandonment and appeals to God as the only remaining hope.

At the arrest of Jesus: 'All the disciples forsook him, and fled.' The fulfillment of Psalm 22:11-12 includes both the divine seeming-absence and the human abandonment. Every ally fled; Christ faced his trial alone.

God declares, 'I looked, and there was none to help; and I wondered that there was none to uphold.' The language of searching for help and finding none appears in the context of God's saving action. Help is absent from humans but comes from God.

Jerusalem laments, 'All her people sigh, they seek bread; they have given their pleasant things for meat to relieve the soul: see, O Lord, and consider; for I am become vile.' Like Psalm 22:12, Lamentations combines the sense of abandonment with active suffering and the absence of human helpers.

The revelation addresses Joseph Smith in his isolation: 'Verily, thus saith the Lord unto you who have assembled yourselves together to receive my word... I say unto you, I am in your midst.' This resonates with the sufferer's plea for God to 'not be far from me' in the midst of trouble.

commentary.historical_context: In ancient Israel, survival often depended on being part of a community, a tribe, or a patron-client relationship. A person without allies was in extreme danger. The phrase 'there is none to help' would have invoked concrete fear—the fear of being cut off from social protection, without witnesses or defenders, vulnerable to violence or theft. The cry 'Do not be far from me' reflects the ancient understanding that God's presence was a form of protection. When God was near, one was defended; when God withdrew, one was exposed. The spatial language is not merely metaphorical but reflects ancient theology: God's nearness meant victory and protection; God's distance meant vulnerability and defeat.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: Mosiah 24:15 presents a similar pattern: 'And now the Lord said unto Alma: Hast thou believed on his words? And Alma said: Yea, I have.' Despite oppression and the nearness of enemies, Alma finds relief through God's nearness. The sufferer's plea in Psalm 22:12 is answered in Mosiah's narrative when God's presence becomes immediately felt.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 121:1-6 presents Joseph Smith in Liberty Jail crying out in anguish: 'O God, where art thou?... Why art thou absent from the eyes of those who have loved thee?' Joseph Smith experienced the exact desolation of Psalm 22:12. The revelation that followed (D&C 121:7-46) is God's answer: 'All these things shall give thee experience, and shall be for thy good.' Psalm 22:12 is thus the template for understanding Joseph Smith's experience.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The endowment teaches that the individual, while passing through mortality (represented by the terrestrial room), is not finally abandoned but is brought into God's presence (represented by the celestial room). Psalm 22:12 represents the sufferer in the terrestrial condition—troubled, seemingly alone, awaiting rescue. The temple's progression from isolation to presence enacts the theological answer to this verse.

commentary.christological_typology: In the crucifixion, Christ experienced the full force of Psalm 22:12. Every disciple had fled (Matthew 26:56). The crowd mocked. The authorities condemned. Human help was utterly absent. And Christ's own cry on the cross—'My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me?' (Psalm 22:1)—expresses the sense of divine distance. Yet in Christ's experience, the distance is not final or actually separating; it is the form that radical obedience takes. Christ endures the full desolation of being alone, between a withdrawn God (seemingly) and advancing enemies (the powers of death and hell), with no human helper, no escaping angel, no miraculous deliverance. This is the depth of Christ's descent into suffering. The typology teaches that Christ did not demand rescue or vindication; he surrendered to the desolation completely. This surrender becomes the mechanism of redemption.
commentary.application: Modern covenant members in times of severe trial—whether depression, persecution, loss, or spiritual darkness—may experience the exact desolation of Psalm 22:12. The feeling that God is far off, that enemies are pressing close, and that no human helper is available. This verse validates that experience. It does not minimize it as merely emotional or tell the sufferer to 'just have faith.' Instead, it gives voice to the desolation and, crucially, addresses it with prayer. The application is this: in your most isolated moments, when it feels as though God is absent and you are alone, cry out. Use the words of this verse. Do not internalize the desolation as evidence that you have been rejected by God; rather, give voice to the pain and appeal to God to draw near. The verse teaches that the sufferer's job is not to solve the situation or to find help on his own, but to persist in calling upon God despite the seeming distance. The act of prayer itself—the refusal to despair—is the beginning of rescue.

text_kjv: Many bulls have compassed me: strong bulls of Bashan have beset me round.

commentary.narrative: The psalmist begins a vivid descent into violent suffering, using animal imagery to describe enemies closing in with overwhelming force. The 'bulls of Bashan' was a proverbial expression in ancient Israel for creatures of unmatched power and danger. Bashan (the Golan Heights region) was renowned throughout the ancient Near East for its rich pastureland, which produced the largest and most powerful cattle known to the biblical world. The psalmist chooses this specific image deliberately—not merely enemies, but enemies as massive, unstoppable forces. The verbs 'surround' (sevavuni) and 'beset' (kitteruni) describe a tightening circle with no escape route. The enemy is not scattered or distant; they encircle the sufferer completely.

word_study.meaning: Young bulls, cattle—the strongest and most dangerous bovine. The root pel- relates to bearing or carrying, suggesting strength and power. In ancient Near Eastern texts, bulls represented raw, unstoppable force.
word_study.significance: The choice of 'bulls' rather than lions or other predators emphasizes overwhelming numerical and physical superiority rather than cunning. This is brutish, crushable force.

word_study.meaning: Abbir means 'mighty one' or 'strong one' (from a root meaning 'to be mighty'). Bashan's bulls were legendary for their size and power (also mentioned in Amos 4:1 regarding wealthy women, and Ezekiel 39:18 regarding restoration). This phrase became synonymous with unstoppable adversarial force.
word_study.significance: For the original Hebrew audience, 'bulls of Bashan' would immediately conjure the image of the most powerful, most dangerous cattle in the known world. The psalmist is saying his enemies possess not merely strength but the archetypal strength recognized across the ancient Near East.

word_study.meaning: Root sbb means 'to turn around, encircle, surround.' The word describes a complete circle with no exit. It is used in military contexts (enemies surrounding a city) and in worship contexts (circling the altar).
word_study.significance: The tense is perfect—the action is complete. The sufferer is not being surrounded; he is surrounded. The encirclement is already accomplished, the trap already sprung.

word_study.meaning: Root ktr means 'to surround, enclose, hem in.' It is a stronger, more constrictive word than sevavuni—it suggests being pressed in, crowded, contained. The noun ketret (crown) shares the root, suggesting a circular constraint.
word_study.significance: Where sevavuni establishes the circle, kitteruni describes the pressure of that circle tightening. The enemies are not merely present; they are actively pressing inward. The Covenant Rendering captures this distinction: 'surround' followed by 'encircle.'

cross_references.connection: Amos uses 'cows of Bashan' as a symbol of oppressive power and luxury, parallel to the psalmist's use of 'bulls of Bashan' to represent overwhelming adversarial force.
The psalmist uses similar animal imagery: 'evildoers came upon me to eat up my flesh,' establishing a pattern in the Psalms of describing enemies as predatory creatures.
Peter uses the lion as an image of the adversary prowling for victims, continuing the NT tradition of depicting spiritual opposition through animal metaphor.
Ezekiel references the bulls of Bashan in eschatological context, reinforcing their status as symbols of supreme earthly power within biblical tradition.

commentary.historical_context: Bashan was a region east of the Jordan, known from Egyptian and Assyrian sources as exceptionally fertile pastureland. Archaeological and ancient textual evidence confirms that cattle raised in Bashan were prized throughout the Levantine world for their size and strength. The Masoretic Text, supported by the Dead Sea Scrolls, preserves this geographical and zoological specificity. In the context of the psalmist's distress, invoking the 'bulls of Bashan' would have immediately conveyed to any Hebrew listener: the most powerful, most unstoppable force known to their world. This is not hyperbole born of desperation; this is precise, culturally-calibrated language. The enemy possesses the kind of overwhelming force that no ordinary resistance could withstand.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: Alma 26:27 uses similar imagery: 'Yea, they were encircled about with a most firm barrier of fire,' describing how the Lord surrounds and contains enemies. The distinction here is crucial: in Alma, the believers are protected within a barrier; in Psalm 22:13, the sufferer is pressed inward by enemies.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 76:28 describes enemies of God as those who 'rebelled against the light.' The progressively tightening rings of adversity in Psalm 22 prefigure the spiritual opposition that covenant keepers face. D&C 121:7 promises 'thy God shall stand by thee,' a direct answer to the encirclement described here.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The imagery of encirclement recalls the temple's architecture of concentric circles of holiness—yet here inverted. Instead of sacred geometry protecting the righteous within, enemies form profane circles pressing inward. This inversion is significant to understanding the psalm's theology of abandonment.

commentary.christological_typology: In Christian interpretation, the bulls of Bashan prefigure the massed Roman forces at Calvary—soldiers, priests, and crowds encircling the crucified Christ. The overwhelming, unstoppable force they represent corresponds to the political and religious machinery arrayed against Jesus. Jesus's suffering is not the suffering of a lone individual but of one surrounded by institutional power seeking his destruction.
commentary.application: When facing circumstances where opposition seems overwhelming and escape appears impossible—when our own 'bulls of Bashan' encircle us—this verse invites us to name the reality of our distress without spiritual platitude. The psalmist does not deny the encirclement or pretend the enemies are weak. He states the facts as they are. For modern covenant keepers, this is permission to acknowledge genuine adversity, systemic opposition, and circumstances where the forces arrayed against us possess real power. The faithfulness comes not in denying these realities but in continuing to address them to God, as the psalmist does in the verses that follow.

text_kjv: They gaped upon me with their mouths, as a ravening and a roaring lion.

commentary.narrative: The animal imagery shifts from the slow, encircling pressure of bulls to the sudden, violent attack of a predator. The psalmist moves from being surrounded to being actively assailed. The gaping mouths—both literal and metaphorical—represent the enemies' hunger to devour and their verbal mockery. This verse presents a dual threat: the physical attack of a lion tearing into flesh and the verbal assault of mockers hurling insults and curses. The image of an open mouth serves both functions in ancient literature—it is the mouth of the predator and the mouth of the insulter simultaneously. The lion 'tearing and roaring' is described in its moment of kill, not merely circling prey. The ferocity is immediate and final.

word_study.meaning: Patsu means 'they opened wide, they gaped.' The preposition alai means 'against me, upon me.' Pihem means 'their mouths.' Combined, this describes mouths opened wide against the sufferer—the literal gaping jaws of a lion and the metaphorical gaping mouths of those who mock and curse.
word_study.significance: The verb patsu (open wide) is used for mouths in contexts of appetite, mockery, and predatory readiness. It conveys simultaneity of action—at the moment of the psalmist's speech, mouths are gaping against him.

word_study.meaning: Lion. The root arye- is used throughout biblical literature for the king of beasts, the ultimate predator. Unlike 'bulls' which represent overwhelming force through mass and strength, the lion represents predatory intelligence and killing precision.
word_study.significance: In biblical symbolism, the lion often represents divine judgment (Hosea 5:14, Amos 3:8) or satanic opposition (1 Peter 5:8). Here it is the enemy in his most violent, consumptive aspect.

word_study.meaning: Toref means 'tearing, rending flesh' (from the root tr-p). Shoeg means 'roaring, growling' (from the root sh-a-g). The participles describe simultaneous actions—the lion is tearing while roaring, killing while vocalizing. This is predatory behavior at its peak intensity.
word_study.significance: The combination of these two participles emphasizes that the attack is active and ongoing. This is not a threat of violence but violence in the act. The roaring serves both to terrify and to signal dominance. The Covenant Rendering 'a lion tearing and roaring' captures the simultaneity and the crescendo effect.

cross_references.connection: David uses nearly identical language: 'Lest he tear my soul like a lion, rending it in pieces, while there is none to deliver.' The pattern of lion-predation appears throughout David's psalms as a symbol of acute danger.
The lion's roar becomes the voice of divine judgment: 'The lion hath roared, who will not fear?' linking the lion's voice to both human enmity and divine authority.
Peter describes the devil as 'a roaring lion, walking about, seeking whom he may devour,' applying the Psalmic imagery of predatory opposition to spiritual warfare.
In contrast to the devouring lion, Jesus is called 'the Lamb of God which taketh away the sin of the world'—a reversal of predator and prey that is central to Christian interpretation of Psalm 22.

commentary.historical_context: In the ancient Near East, the lion was the most feared and most revered predator known to Israel and her neighbors. Egyptian, Hittite, and Mesopotamian texts all feature the lion as an image of supreme predatory power and royal authority. Lions were present in the Levantine region during the biblical period (they were exterminated only in more recent centuries). To invoke the image of a lion 'tearing and roaring' would be to invoke the most vivid, most terrifying predatory scenario known to ancient listeners. The combination of tearing flesh and roaring—the dual sensory assault of witnessing and hearing an attack—makes this perhaps the most intense image of violence in the psalm. The psalmist is not exaggerating; he is using the most accurate language available to describe extremity.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: Mormon 6:10-11 describes the Nephites and Lamanites as 'as a lion raging in the midst of a fold of lambs.' This reversal—the wicked as devouring predators, the righteous as vulnerable prey—parallels the psalmist's position. Yet in the Book of Mormon, the carnage is finite and leads to redemption; in Psalm 22, the devouring seems total.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 97:25 warns that the Lord's judgments come 'as a whirlwind upon the wicked, and they shall be taken down into captivity.' The lion's roar in Psalm 22 is the roar of judgment; the psalmist is experiencing not only human enmity but what feels like divine wrath.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The temple's imagery of protection—the sanctuary as a refuge from predators (Psalm 27:5)—is entirely absent from Psalm 22. The sufferer has no fortress, no inner sanctum. He is exposed to the lion's attack. This absence of sanctuary is theologically significant.

commentary.christological_typology: In Matthew 27:39-44, the crucifixion account, the chief priests, scribes, and elders 'gaped upon him'—using identical language to Psalm 22:14—mocking and deriding Jesus on the cross. The historical convergence between the Psalmist's metaphor and the Gospel's literal account (the soldiers piercing his hands and feet, the mockers surrounding him) has led Christian interpreters for two millennia to read Psalm 22 as a passion prophecy. Whether the psalmist intended such specificity remains debated, but the typological correspondence is undeniable in Christian tradition.
commentary.application: This verse names both the physical and verbal assault of mockery. Modern believers facing ridicule, public shame, or coordinated opposition will recognize the psalmist's description of having multiple sources of attack converging simultaneously: those who assault through action and those who assault through words. The sufferer is being torn apart and laughed at. The psalmist gives us language to articulate this dual assault. There is spiritual power in naming what is happening without euphemism: this is predatory, this is consuming, this is aimed at annihilation.

text_kjv: I am poured out like water, and all my bones are out of joint: my heart is like wax; it is melted in the midst of my bowels.

commentary.narrative: The psalmist now turns from describing external enemies to describing his own bodily dissolution. This is the pivot point where the suffering becomes not merely about external assault but about internal disintegration. The language moves through three progressive images of loss of coherence: liquefaction (water poured out), skeletal displacement (bones pulled apart), and cardiac collapse (heart melted like wax). Each image represents a deeper level of bodily integrity—the whole body, then the structural system, then the vital organ. The psalmist is not describing pain in the sense of sensation; he is describing the systematic unraveling of the body's ability to hold itself together. This is medical observation of someone dying, and it is presented with startling specificity. The sufferer is aware of his own dissolution and able to articulate it precisely. The verbs convey irreversible processes: 'poured out' (shapakh) cannot be recovered, 'melts' (namas) cannot be reversed.

word_study.meaning: Shapakh (שׁפך) means 'to pour out, spill, shed.' The passive form nishpakti ('I am poured out') describes an action done to the subject rather than by the subject. Mayim means 'water.' The image is of liquid spilled onto the ground, irretrievable and dispersing.
