word_study.significance: Water, the most essential sustenance, becomes the metaphor for the dissolution of the self. The sufferer is being emptied—drained of vitality. In Genesis 9:6, blood 'poured out' represents life taken. Here, the sufferer's very being is being spilled forth like water on thirsty ground. The Covenant Rendering's 'I am poured out like water' preserves the passive voice, which is theologically crucial: the sufferer is not emptying himself; something is emptying him.

word_study.term_english: all my bones are out of joint
word_study.meaning: Hitpardu is the reflexive form of parad (פרד), meaning 'to separate, scatter, divide.' Atsmotai means 'my bones.' The image is of the skeletal structure—the very framework that holds the body together—coming undone, separating from one another.
word_study.significance: The KJV renders 'out of joint,' but the Hebrew is more radical: the bones are not merely dislocated, they are separating from one another. The entire skeletal architecture is coming apart. This is the body losing its structural integrity. In Joshua 2:11, namas ('melted') describes the hearts of the Canaanites at news of Israel's might; here the psalmist's own body is melting in despair.

word_study.meaning: Donag (דונג) is beeswax, the most useful metaphor for something that holds firm until heated, then loses all shape and coherence. Leb (לב) means 'heart,' the seat of courage, will, and vitality in biblical usage.
word_study.significance: The heart—the command center of courage and resolve—is now losing all capacity to resist or endure. Wax that melts returns to formlessness. The imagery suggests not pain but the loss of the self's structural integrity at every level: the body becomes liquid, the skeleton scatters, the heart—the very core of personhood—loses form. The Covenant Rendering captures this: 'it melts within me,' emphasizing the interior collapse.

word_study.term_english: melted in the midst of my bowels
word_study.meaning: Namas (נמס) means 'to melt, dissolve.' Mea'im (מעים) refers to the bowels, the interior organs. The preposition betokh means 'in the midst of' or 'within.'
word_study.significance: The heart melting happens 'within' the bowels—the deepest, most hidden part of the body. The dissolution is not external or visible to others; it is happening at the core, in the most intimate interior space. The sufferer alone knows the extent of this dissolution. This progression from external (water poured out) to structural (bones separated) to intimate (heart melting inside) traces a journey into the body's very center—and finds only dissolution there.

cross_references.connection: Rahab says the hearts of the Canaanites 'melted' (namas) at news of Israel's strength, using the same verb that describes the psalmist's heart melting in despair—the same word describes loss of courage in the face of overwhelming power.

David again uses water imagery: 'My life is spent with grief, and my years with sighing: my strength faileth because of mine iniquity, and my bones are consumed.' The same progression—bodily dissolution through sorrow.

The foundational statement: 'dust thou art, and unto dust shalt thou return.' The psalmist's dissolution is the beginning of that return—the body coming apart, the minerals of the body returning to the earth's elements.
Jesus on the cross declares 'I thirst,' the extreme dehydration that accompanies the loss of bodily fluids and life force described here in Psalm 22.

Jeremiah describes Jerusalem's devastation in nearly identical terms: 'Mine eyes do fail with tears, my bowels are troubled, my liver is poured upon the earth' —the same vocabulary of bodily dissolution applied to corporate suffering.

commentary.historical_context: The medical specificity of verse 15 suggests either direct experience of severe suffering (whether literal or imaginative) or the psalmist's knowledge of what crucifixion, torture, or extreme dehydration does to the human body. The progression from dehydration (the drying of strength and clinging of tongue in verse 16) through to full dissolution makes physiological sense: a sufferer losing blood loses fluid and becomes like water poured out; the skeletal system becomes prominent as flesh is lost, with joints separating as the body loses elasticity; the heart loses capacity to pump and maintain circulation. Whether the psalmist witnessed such suffering, experienced it, or imaginatively constructed it from observations of the dying is uncertain, but the accuracy of the progression is remarkable. Ancient medical understanding was sufficient to recognize these stages.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: Alma 36:21 describes Alma in spiritual despair: 'the very thought of coming into the presence of my God did rack my soul with inexpressible horror.' While Alma's suffering is spiritual rather than physical, the language of bodily anguish ('rack my soul') is parallel. Both the psalmist and Alma experience an interior dissolution that is simultaneously spiritual and corporeal.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 19:16-18 describes Jesus taking upon himself the sufferings of all men: 'For behold, I, God, have suffered these things for all, that they might not suffer if they would repent...Which suffering caused myself, even God the greatest of all, to tremble because of pain, and to bleed at every pore, and to suffer both body and spirit.' The Doctrine and Covenants explicitly connects Jesus to the bodily and spiritual dissolution described in Psalm 22:15.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: In the temple's drama of the Fall and Atonement, the sufferer in Psalm 22 anticipates the Savior's redemptive suffering. The complete dissolution of the body in Psalm 22 prefigures the complete self-emptying of Christ in the Atonement.

commentary.christological_typology: In Christian interpretation, verse 15 is read as a direct prophecy of Christ's passion—his body becoming like water poured out (his blood shed), his bones separating (his crucifixion positioning pulling him apart), his heart melting in despair as he experiences the full weight of human sin. Matthew, Mark, and Luke all record details of the crucifixion that correspond to these images: the piercing of Jesus's side (from which blood and water flowed, John 19:34), the visibility of his skeletal frame as he hung exposed, the moment of abandonment ('My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me?') when Jesus experienced the dissolution of connection to the Father. The typological reading does not require that the original psalmist intended a prophecy of the cross; rather, it observes that the suffering described in Psalm 22 is precisely the suffering experienced at Calvary.
commentary.application: For modern believers, verse 15 gives language to spiritual despair and bodily anguish that cannot be minimized or spiritualized away. Some experiences of suffering do feel like complete dissolution—the loss of strength, coherence, and interior stability simultaneously. The psalmist does not offer comfort here; he offers witness. His testimony is that even in such dissolution, he continued to speak, to lament, to address God. For those experiencing severe depression, chronic illness, or trauma-induced despair, this verse validates the experience without requiring premature resolution. The faithful response is not to deny the dissolution but to continue speaking it forth to God, as the psalmist does.

text_kjv: My strength is dried up like a potsherd; and my tongue cleaveth to my jaws; and thou hast brought me into the dust of death.

commentary.narrative: The psalmist descends further into the specifics of dying. The first image—strength dried up like a potsherd—is particularly telling: not merely dried, but shattered, broken into useless fragments. A potsherd is a piece of broken pottery, utterly without function or value. The second image—tongue clinging to jaws—describes extreme dehydration, where the mouth's interior has dried so completely that the tongue adheres to the palate and jawbone. The third image—brought into the dust of death—moves the focus from the psalmist's body to his positioning. Crucially, in this line, the address shifts directly to God: 'thou hast brought me.' The enemies may surround and attack, but it is God who is laying the sufferer into death. This is the heart of the psalm's theology of abandonment: not that God is absent, but that God is present in the act of bringing the sufferer to death. This is accusation as much as lament. The dust of death is not merely metaphorical; it is the grave, the return to the earth of Genesis 3:19.

word_study.term_english: strength is dried up like a potsherd
word_study.meaning: Yabesh (יבש) means 'to dry up, wither.' Cheres (חרש) specifically means 'a potsherd'—a broken piece of earthenware pottery, utterly without use or value. Koach (כח) means 'strength, power, vigor.'
word_study.significance: The comparison is not merely to something dry (like a dried branch that might still have structure), but to a broken, shattered fragment. The psalmist's strength is not merely diminished; it is broken into fragments, scattered, useless. A potsherd has archaeological value only; in the moment, it is refuse. The Covenant Rendering's rendering makes this clear: strength 'dried up like a potsherd' is radical deterioration and fragmentation, not merely desiccation.

word_study.meaning: Leshon (לשון) means 'tongue.' Mudbaq (מדבק) is the passive form of dabak (דבק), meaning 'to stick, to cling.' Malqoach (מלקוח) means 'jaws' or 'palate' (from a root meaning 'to take, seize').
word_study.significance: This is the image of extreme dehydration: the tongue loses moisture and adheres to the roof of the mouth and jawbone. In living persons, this indicates severe fluid loss and approaches to death from dehydration. John 19:28 records Jesus saying 'I thirst' from the cross, and the Gospels record that a sponge soaked in vinegar was offered to him—a detail that aligns with this specific experience of terminal dehydration. The adhesion of tongue to palate is a medical marker of the dying process.

word_study.meaning: Afar (עפר) means 'dust, earth, soil.' Mavet (מות) means 'death.' The construct form 'dust of death' suggests not merely ordinary earth but the dust of the grave, the specific earth where death occurs.
word_study.significance: This phrase echoes Genesis 3:19: 'dust thou art, and unto dust shalt thou return.' The sufferer is being brought to the point of bodily dissolution, the return to the elemental earth. But the remarkable shift in this line is the direct address to God: 'thou hast brought me into the dust of death.' It is not enemies who are accomplishing this; it is God. This is the core theological problem the psalm articulates: the sufferer is not merely abandoned by God; he is being actively brought to death by God.

cross_references.connection: The foundational pronouncement of death: 'dust thou art, and unto dust shalt thou return.' The psalmist invokes the original curse—he is returning to dust, as all humanity must, but he is doing so at God's direct hand.

Jesus cries out 'I thirst' from the cross, the precise symptom of the extreme dehydration and tongue-adhesion described in Psalm 22:16. Matthew and Mark both record this detail, directly paralleling the psalmist's suffering.

Another psalm of suffering using identical imagery: 'For my days are consumed like smoke, and my bones are burned as an hearth. My heart is smitten, and withered like grass; so that I forget to eat my bread.' The same pattern of bodily wasting.

The Gospel account: 'And straightway one of them ran, and took a spunge, and filled it with vinegar, and put it on a reed, and gave him to drink.' The offering of vinegar-soaked sponge directly addresses the thirst and mouth-drying described in Psalm 22:16.

The NT applies Psalm 8 to Christ's suffering: 'But now we see not yet all things put under him. But we see Jesus...made a little lower than the angels for the suffering of death.' Psalm 22:16 provides the specific physiological details of that suffering.

commentary.historical_context: The symptoms described—extreme dehydration (tongue adhering to palate), loss of strength (broken like pottery), approaching death—correspond precisely to what medical literature describes in cases of crucifixion, severe dehydration, or blood loss. Ancient Near Eastern texts provide fewer specific descriptions of dying, but Egyptian mummification texts and medical papyri describe the progressive dehydration of the body. The psalmist's specificity here (not merely 'I am weak' but 'my strength is dried like a potsherd,' not merely 'my mouth is dry' but 'my tongue cleaves to my jaws') suggests either direct observation or medical knowledge. The phrase 'dust of death' is consistent with ancient Near Eastern burial practices, where the body returns to the earth of the grave, but the Hebrew specifically invokes the covenant theology of Genesis 3:19.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: Alma 36:16-19 describes Alma's spiritual suffering: 'And behold, the Spirit said unto me: This is damnation; nevertheless, raise up thy head and take courage...And now the change of heart which I have experienced is such as I have never before known.' Where Alma experiences spiritual dissolution and then restoration, the psalmist in Psalm 22:16 articulates the dissolution while the restoration remains absent—creating a stark contrast that heightens the psalm's theology of abandonment.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 19:18 applies Psalm 22's suffering directly to Christ: 'Which suffering caused myself, even God the greatest of all, to tremble because of pain, and to bleed at every pore, and to suffer both body and spirit.' The Doctrine and Covenants explicitly identifies Jesus as the one who experiences the dust-of-death suffering described in Psalm 22. The psalmist's accusation—'thou hast brought me into the dust of death'—becomes, in LDS theology, the Father bringing the Son to the suffering necessary for universal redemption.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The temple endowment presents the complete cycle: the fall into dust, the covenant with God, and the redemption through Christ. Psalm 22:16 articulates the 'dust of death' portion of this cycle—the consequence of sin and the path all humanity must walk.

commentary.christological_typology: In Christian interpretation, Psalm 22:16 is the verse most directly prophetic of crucifixion. The concentration of dying's symptoms—dehydration, loss of strength, positioning in the dust (dust suggesting the ground near the crucifixion site at Golgotha, 'the place of the skull')—all align with what the Gospels record at Calvary. The shift in address to God ('thou hast brought me') is theologically crucial: in Christian reading, the Father allows the Son to be brought to this death for the salvation of the world. The cross is not an abandonment of Jesus but a divinely orchestrated redemptive act. The psalmist's accusatory tone ('thou hast brought me') becomes, in Christian theology, the moment of ultimate faithfulness: Jesus accepting the Father's will even unto death.
commentary.application: Verse 16's direct accusation—'thou hast brought me'—gives permission to name the ways God's providential hand seems, in the moment of suffering, to be the hand that is causing suffering. This is not heresy; it is biblical lament. When we face circumstances that feel divinely ordained (the 'dust of death'), the psalm permits us to address God directly with the accusation: 'This is you.' Paradoxically, this direct address to God acknowledges God's power and presence even in the moment of deepest anguish. The sufferer is not claiming God is absent; he is claiming God is present in the act of bringing him to death. For modern believers, this means we can voice our accusations to God without fear—God is capable of hearing our anger, our confusion, our sense that He has brought us to a place we did not choose to go. The faithful response is not to suppress this accusation but to voice it, as the psalmist does.

text_kjv: For dogs have compassed me: the assembly of the wicked have inclosed me: they pierced my hands and my feet.

commentary.narrative: Verse 17 contains what is perhaps the most textually and theologically complex moment in all of Psalm 22. The psalmist returns to animal imagery, now invoking dogs—the most contemptible creatures in the ancient Near East—rather than the bulls and lion of verses 13-14. But the central crisis of this verse is the rendering of the Hebrew word that may mean either 'like a lion' (kaari, כָּאֲרִי) or 'they pierced' (kaaru, כָּאֲרוּ). The difference hinges on a single letter: the difference between yod (י) and vav (ו). In the Masoretic Text, which was standardized in the medieval period, the word is kaari ('like a lion'). But the Septuagint, translated in the 3rd century BCE, reads oryxan ('they pierced'). A Dead Sea Scrolls fragment from Nahal Hever (5/6HevPs), dated to the 1st century CE, also supports kaaru ('they pierced'). If kaaru is correct, the verse describes the piercing of hands and feet—a detail that corresponds precisely to crucifixion, a Roman execution method unknown in David's time but standard by the first century. If kaari is correct, the verse is grammatically incomplete (there is no verb: 'like a lion [what?] my hands and my feet' does not parse). The Covenant Rendering, following the ancient versional evidence and the Dead Sea Scrolls, renders 'they pierce my hands and my feet.' This choice is defensible textually but must be noted as controversial.

word_study.meaning: Dogs (plural of kelev). In the biblical world, dogs were not domesticated companions but feral scavengers, pack animals that fed on garbage and corpses. They are consistently portrayed as unclean and contemptible (1 Kings 14:11, 21:23-24).
word_study.significance: After the bulls and lion, the dog represents the ultimate debasement. A pack of dogs feeding on a corpse is the final indignity. To be 'surrounded by dogs' in biblical metaphor means to be treated as carrion, already dead. The descent in animal imagery (powerful bulls > fierce lion > feral dogs) traces a descent in dignity.

word_study.term_english: assembly of the wicked / pack of evildoers
word_study.meaning: Adat (עדה) means 'assembly, congregation, community'—the same word used for the assembly of Israel (adat Yisrael). Mere'im (מרעים) means 'those who do harm/evil,' from the root r-a-a (to harm, to pasture). The word 'pasture' in the root is ironic: where the good shepherd pastures his flock, the assembly of evildoers hunts.
word_study.significance: The term 'assembly' (adat) is significant: this is not mere individual enemies but an organized, corporative opposition. The use of this term invokes the congregation of Israel turned against the psalmist. In Christian interpretation, this becomes the assembled religious and political authorities: the Sanhedrin, the Roman garrison, the crowds at Calvary.

word_study.meaning: If kaaru (from root k-r-a, 'to dig, to pierce'): 'they pierced.' If kaari: 'like a lion.' The Masoretic Text preserves kaari. The Septuagint (3rd century BCE) and the Dead Sea Scroll 5/6HevPs (1st century CE) support kaaru.
word_study.significance: This is the single most important textual decision in Psalm 22. The Covenant Rendering notes that kaaru yields 'a grammatically complete and contextually coherent clause,' while kaari requires supplying a missing verb. The rendering 'they pierce my hands and my feet' has no parallel in non-crucifixion contexts in ancient literature, making it difficult to explain if the original psalmist invented it. However, if early Jewish scribes (those who produced the Septuagint and the Dead Sea Scrolls) knew of crucifixion as a Roman practice and recognized in the kaari reading an incomplete or inadequate reference to the piercing of hands and feet, they may have emended to kaaru. The textual evidence favors kaaru; the Masoretic tradition preserves kaari. For commentary purposes, The Covenant Rendering's choice to render 'they pierce' is defensible, following ancient witnesses, while acknowledging the Masoretic kaari reading in the main historical tradition.

cross_references.connection: Moses uses 'dogs' to describe instruments of divine judgment: 'I will also send the teeth of beasts upon them, with the poison of serpents of the dust.' Dogs as judgmental instruments appear throughout Scripture.
Goliath's insult to David: 'Am I a dog, that thou comest to me with staves?' The comparison to a dog in biblical usage is a comparison to something contemptible, unworthy.
Paul uses 'dogs' to describe Jewish legalists: 'Beware of dogs, beware of evil workers.' The term retains its biblical connotation of contempt and exclusion.

The piercing of Jesus's side on the cross: 'But one of the soldiers with a spear pierced his side, and forthwith came there out blood and water.' In Christian reading, this verse fulfills the piercing of hands and feet described (or believed to be described) in Psalm 22:17.

The Gospels record that at the crucifixion the soldiers 'parted his garments, casting lots' — a detail that connects to the next verse (Psalm 22:18) and suggests the psalmist's foreknowledge of crucifixion details.

commentary.historical_context: Dogs were present throughout the ancient Near East, and remains of dogs appear in archaeological contexts from biblical periods. They were not domesticated companions as they are in modern Western societies but feral pack animals. The language of 'surrounding dogs' conjures the image of a dying or dead animal being set upon by a pack of scavengers. This would be the ultimate indignity in ancient understanding. The textual problem regarding kaaru vs. kaari is one of the most discussed issues in biblical scholarship. If kaaru is correct and refers to piercing of hands and feet, it is the closest thing in the Hebrew Bible to a specific reference to crucifixion, an execution method that becomes standard Roman practice only in the intertestamental period. If kaari is correct, the verse is grammatically problematic. The Dead Sea Scrolls evidence (5/6HevPs) is particularly significant because it is dated to the late 1st century BCE to early 1st century CE—the period immediately preceding Jesus's ministry. Whatever the original reading, scribal transmission shows that by the Second Temple period, both readings were known and preserved.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: 1 Nephi 19:10-12 contains Nephi's direct citation of Psalm 22: 'Wherefore the Jews must needs reject the Messiah, and stain their hands in his blood, and cast him out from among them...and after he should be lifted up upon the cross, that he should be risen from the dead and should ascend into heaven.' Nephi's interpretation of Psalm 22 is explicitly Christological and identifies the piercing of hands and feet as a detail of the Messiah's death. Nephi's reading suggests that by the time of the Book of Mormon narrative (6th century BCE), the interpretation of Psalm 22 as messianic prophecy was established LDS doctrine.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 45:52-53 describes the Lord gathering his people: 'And they shall go out from all nations, and they shall not go out in haste, nor go by flight; for I will go before them, saith the Father. And I will be their rearguard. And then shall they fall down and be crowned with glory, even in Zion, by the hands of the servants of the Lord, even the children of Zion.' In contrast, Psalm 22:17 describes gathering for judgment and piercing. The Doctrine and Covenants presents the inverse scenario: gathering for salvation rather than damnation.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The temple endowment presents Christ's descent into mortality and suffering, culminating in his resurrection and exaltation. Psalm 22:17's piercing corresponds to the crucifixion in that redemptive narrative. The piercing of hands and feet, whether original or textually emended, becomes in the temple tradition the sign of Christ's willingness to suffer for humanity's redemption.

commentary.christological_typology: Verse 17 is the most directly Christological verse in Psalm 22. Whether the original psalmist intended a reference to crucifixion remains debated, but in the Christian reading, which is normative in the LDS tradition (as evidenced by Nephi's citation in 1 Nephi 19:10-12), the verse prophesies the piercing of Jesus's hands and feet on the cross. Matthew 27:35, Mark 15:24, Luke 23:34, and John 19:23-24 all record the crucifixion and the soldiers dividing Jesus's garments. John 19:34 records the piercing of his side. If kaaru is the correct reading, then Psalm 22:17 contains a specific prophecy of crucifixion details centuries or centuries before the Romans standardized that execution method. If kaari is correct, the verse is less specific but still describes the ultimate indignity of the psalmist's suffering. In either case, Christian interpreters have found in Psalm 22:17 a prophecy of Calvary.
commentary.application: Modern believers face varying degrees of social ostracism, contempt, and indignity—being treated, metaphorically, like scavengers' carrion. This verse names that experience: the gathered opposition of an assembly of evildoers, the reduction of the sufferer to the status of something contemptible and worth destroying. For those who suffer from religious persecution, social contempt, or concerted opposition, verse 17 validates the reality of such treatment. The piercing detail—whether original or textually emended—adds a dimension of physical violation and vulnerability. For modern believers, the application is this: faithful suffering is not merely deprivation or disappointment; it can include direct harm, violation, and the active malice of an organized opposition. The psalm gives permission to name this as it is, without pretending it is anything less than what it is.

text_kjv: I may tell all my bones: they look and stare upon me.

commentary.narrative: The psalmist reaches what appears to be the nadir of the psalm's descent. Extreme emaciation—so severe that every bone of the body is visible and countable—becomes the mark of the sufferer's condition. This is not metaphorical thinness but the skeletal visibility of someone who is dying or nearing death. The verb 'asapper' ('I can tell/count') suggests that the sufferer, in an act of horrifying self-awareness, is able to enumerate his own bones as though cataloging the remains of a corpse. But crucially, verse 18 is not merely about the sufferer's bodily condition; it is about the watched condition. The sufferer is not dying in private but being observed. The pronoun 'they' shifts to spectators—'they look and stare upon me' (hemmah yabbitu yiru bi). The double verbs 'look and stare' (yabbitu + yiru) suggest a fixed, fascinated gaze, possibly a mixture of contempt and morbid curiosity. The sufferer is a spectacle, a public dying, a visible disintegration. The verse marks a transition: the sufferer has moved from describing the violence inflicted upon him (enemies, predators) and his own bodily dissolution to describing his awareness of being watched. This awareness adds a psychological dimension to the suffering. He is not alone in his death; he is an audience.

word_study.term_english: I can tell all my bones
word_study.meaning: Asapper is the first-person singular imperfect of spr (ספר), meaning 'to tell, to count, to recount.' Atsmotai means 'my bones.' The verb suggests both the ability to enumerate (literally count) and to speak forth, to testify about.
word_study.significance: This is a haunting image: the sufferer's body has become so wasted that he can account for every bone. The verb 'count' suggests a kind of inventory of one's own remains. In ancient literature, the ability to 'tell' or 'count' one's bones is a marker of extreme emaciation. This is the body at the point of disintegration into its component elements. The Covenant Rendering's 'I can count all my bones' preserves this sense of both visibility and enumeration.

word_study.term_original: הֵמָּה יַבִּיטוּ יִרְאוּ־בִי (hemmah yabbitu yiru bi)
word_study.meaning: Hemmah means 'they' (the spectators, contrasted with the sufferer's 'I'). Yabbitu (from nbh, to look at, to gaze) means 'they look at, they gaze upon.' Yiru (from ra'ah, to see, to perceive) means 'they see' or 'they stare.' The preposition bi means 'at me, upon me.'
word_study.significance: The doubling of the verbs (look + stare) creates a sense of fixed, fascinated attention. This is not a glance but a sustained, intentional gazing. The use of two different verbs may suggest looking with intent to see details, to absorb the spectacle. In a public execution context (crucifixion, for instance), onlookers would indeed look and stare at the dying. The verse names the psychological agony of being the object of this collective gaze. The Covenant Rendering's 'they stare and gaze at me' captures the dual verbs and their sense of fixed attention.

cross_references.connection: David describes similar public shame: 'I was a reproach among all mine enemies, but especially among my neighbours, and a fear to mine acquaintance: they that did see me without fled from me.' The visible degradation that causes others to flee.

The prophet describes the visible wasting of Zion's people: 'Her Nazarites were purer than snow, they were whiter than milk...their visage is blacker than a coal; they are not known in the streets.' The visible transformation through suffering that makes the sufferer unrecognizable.

At the crucifixion: 'And the people stood beholding. And the rulers also with them derided him, saying, He saved others; let him save himself.' The spectators look and stare, divided between fascination and derision.

At the cross, 'Jesus therefore seeing his mother, and the disciple standing by, whom he loved, saith unto his mother, Woman, behold thy son!' Jesus, in his emaciated and dying state, remains aware of and responsive to the witnesses present.

The author describes running 'the race that is set before us, Looking unto Jesus the author and finisher of our faith; who for the joy that was set before him endured the cross, despising the shame.' This inverts Psalm 22:18: where the psalmist is stared at in shame, Jesus endured the cross with the Father's approval as witness.

commentary.historical_context: Public executions in the ancient world were intentionally visible spectacles. The crucifixion, which Roman texts describe in detail, was a death designed to be observed and prolonged, taking hours or even days. The visibility of the sufferer's degradation was part of the punishment. Archaeological evidence and Roman historical texts (Josephus, Tacitus) confirm that crucified persons could remain suspended for extended periods, visible to passersby, crowds, and family members. The extreme emaciation described in verse 18—where every bone is visible—corresponds to the point of advanced suffering on the cross, when the body has lost massive amounts of fluid and tissue has wasted away. The awareness of being watched, of being a spectacle, adds a psychological dimension to the physical suffering. The sufferer's awareness that he is being observed while dying is not incidental; it is part of the torment.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: Mormon 3:8-12 describes the gathering of the wicked against the righteous: 'And they came forth to battle against us...And it came to pass that the judgments of God were in the midst of the wicked.' The Nephites, like the psalmist, experience the gathered opposition and public nature of their destruction. Yet in the Book of Mormon, the righteous can repent and return to the Lord; in Psalm 22, the psalmist seems to have no such option.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 127:2 promises that the righteous will not be forgotten: 'And again, when the Lord shall see fit to make known his secrets unto his servants, they shall know them, and a knowledge of them shall be of great worth to them.' Where Psalm 22:18 describes the sufferer as a spectacle of shame, the Doctrine and Covenants promises that the righteous acts will be known and valued by God. The hidden faithfulness will be revealed.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The temple drama presents Christ's suffering as witnessed not only by enemies but by the Father. In the temple understanding, Jesus's suffering is observed by a heavenly witness who approves the sacrifice. Psalm 22:18's description of being watched during death becomes, in temple theology, a moment where the Father observes the Son's redemptive suffering.

commentary.christological_typology: In Matthew 27:35-39, the crucifixion account explicitly invokes Psalm 22:18: 'And they crucified him, and parted his garments, casting lots...And they that passed by reviled him, wagging their heads.' The visible, watched nature of Jesus's death corresponds precisely to the psalmist's experience of being stared at while dying. The next verse in Matthew (27:39) records those 'wagging their heads' while looking at Jesus—a perfect parallel to Psalm 22:18's 'they look and stare upon me.' In John 19:26-27, Jesus is aware of the witnesses present ('Jesus therefore seeing his mother...') despite his bodily extremity. The correspondence between Psalm 22:18 and the Gospel accounts of the crucifixion is precise and sustained across all four Gospels.
commentary.application: For modern believers facing public shame, humiliation, or the sense of being watched and judged during a time of personal crisis or suffering, verse 18 names the particular agony of private suffering made public. The awareness of being observed—whether literally in a courtroom, hospital, or congregation, or metaphorically through social media or community knowledge—adds a layer of psychological suffering to physical or spiritual pain. The psalmist validates this experience as real and significant. He does not deny the watching, does not minimize it, does not reframe it as good. He names it: 'they look and stare upon me.' For those whose suffering has become public spectacle, this verse affirms the legitimacy of the pain of being observed while broken. The faithful response is not to hide or deny the observation but to continue speaking forth the truth of one's condition, as the psalmist does.

text_kjv: They part my garments among them, and cast lots upon my vesture.

commentary.narrative: This verse marks the continuation of the psalmist's graphic description of physical suffering and humiliation. The enemies do not merely wound the sufferer—they strip him bare and redistribute his clothing. This is not incidental detail; it represents the ultimate violation of dignity. In the ancient world, a person's garments were extensions of identity and honor. To have them divided among enemies was to be utterly exposed, vulnerable, and dishonored. The TCR rendering clarifies a critical distinction between begadai ('garments'—plural, divisible outer clothing) and levushi ('clothing'—singular, suggesting one inner garment)—suggesting that the outer garments are divided into portions while a single inner garment is awarded by lot as an undivided prize. This specificity becomes electrifying when read against John 19:23–24, where the Roman soldiers divide Jesus's outer garments but cast lots for the seamless tunic, matching the exact structure described here centuries earlier.
commentary.narrative_2: The casting of lots introduces an element of chance and mockery—the enemies are not methodically distributing belongings but gambling over them, treating the sufferer's possessions as spoils of victory at his own execution. The verb יַפִּילוּ (yappilu, 'cast' or 'fall down') suggests the lots are thrown to the ground like dice. This adds to the indignity: not only are the garments taken, but their disposition is left to fate rather than deliberate division. The psalmist is forced to witness the consumption of his own property while unable to stop it—a helplessness that compounds the physical suffering described in earlier verses.

word_study.meaning: outer garments, clothing worn on the outside; from a root suggesting 'to separate' or 'cover'
word_study.significance: The plural form indicates multiple pieces or the divisibility of outer layers. In contrast to levushi, begadim are the everyday, replaceable outer coverings.

word_study.meaning: clothing, garment; root לבש (labash, 'to wear, put on'); carries connotation of an integral covering, often a tunic or inner garment
word_study.significance: The singular form suggests a single, unified garment—possibly the undertunic or inner robe. The distinction between begadai and levushi is theologically and typologically significant, preserved precisely in the Gospel account of the crucifixion.

word_study.meaning: literally 'they cause to fall/cast the lot'; from פיל (fall/cast) and גורל (lot, portion by chance, or sometimes 'my adversary')
word_study.significance: The verb conveys an action of throwing—the lots are not carefully divided but scattered. Goral can mean both 'lot' (as in casting lots) and 'portion' or even 'adversary,' creating a semantic richness that underscores the randomness and hostility of the action.

cross_references.connection: The Gospels record that soldiers cast lots for Jesus's garments at the crucifixion, dividing the outer garments and casting lots for the seamless tunic—an exact parallel to the distinction made here between begadai and levushi, suggesting this psalm was understood as a messianic prophecy of the crucifixion.
Part of the same lament section describing mockery and humiliation; the stripping of garments continues the pattern of shame and exposure begun in the earlier verses.
Describes the priestly garments (begadim) given by God; the division and loss of garments here stands in sharp contrast to God-ordained, sacred clothing.

Uses similar language of exposure and shame—'I will cast abominable filth upon thee, and make thee vile'—connecting the stripping of dignity to divine judgment against enemies (though in opposite direction here).
Records Jesus's response to those who cast lots for his garments—'Father, forgive them'—transforming the humiliation of Psalm 22:19 into an act of redemptive intercession.

commentary.historical_context: In the ancient Near East and Mediterranean world, the loss of clothing was a recognized form of shaming and degradation. Egyptian and Mesopotamian texts describe the stripping of defeated enemies and slaves as part of the conquest narrative. Roman crucifixion practice included the crucifixion of naked victims as an additional form of humiliation. The specific practice of casting lots for property was common in both Greek and Roman contexts—soldiers would gamble over the spoils of war or execution. The psalmist's awareness of these practices suggests a familiarity with the brutal realities of ancient warfare and execution, or possibly the institutional practices of Roman occupation in the Second Temple period.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: Alma 11:26–27 reflects on the paradox of salvation purchased through shame and nakedness—the clothing of immortality purchased through the stripping away of mortal defenses. The principle of exaltation through abasement appears throughout Book of Mormon Christology.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 19:16–19 describes the sufferings of Christ, who 'trembled because of pain' and 'would that [he] might not drink the bitter cup'—the physical humiliation of Psalm 22:19 is contextualized within the infinite scope of Christ's suffering as taught in modern revelation.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The stripping of garments here prefigures the temple initiatory, where candidates are ritually unclothed and reclothed as part of the covenant process. The psalmist's loss of clothing becomes, in the Christian tradition, the necessary precondition for receiving the white robes of salvation (Revelation 3:5; 7:9).

commentary.christological_typology: Psalm 22:19 is recognized in Christian tradition as a direct messianic prophecy of the crucifixion of Jesus Christ. The division of garments and casting of lots is not merely descriptive suffering—it is the precise mechanism by which the psalmist's innocence and vulnerability are exposed before God and witnesses. In the Gospel account, this humiliation becomes the moment of Christ's complete self-emptying, the stripping away of all earthly authority and dignity. The psalmist's nakedness foreshadows the nakedness of Christ on the cross, the ultimate exposure of the sinless before the sin-bearing God. The randomness of the lot—suggesting that even this humiliation is not directed but allowed—points to Christ's acceptance of the Father's will in all things.
commentary.application: Modern covenant members can reflect on what it means to be spiritually stripped before God. The psalmist's experience of losing all earthly protection and dignity parallels the spiritual 'nakedness' required for genuine repentance and entry into covenant. Just as the psalmist cannot prevent the division of garments, we cannot control how others perceive or treat us when we stand for truth. The application is not to seek humiliation, but to recognize that standing in covenant sometimes requires vulnerability and exposure—and that God's presence does not depend on our social standing, possessions, or the respect others grant us. The verse calls us to release attachment to reputation and outward signs of worth, trusting that God sees and honors what cannot be taken away.

text_kjv: But be not thou far from me, O LORD: O my strength, haste thee to help me.

commentary.narrative: After describing the sufferer's enemies and their violent actions, the psalmist turns sharply from lament to direct address with God. The Hebrew structure emphasizes urgency and intimacy: 'But you, O LORD'—the shift from describing enemies to addressing God is itself an act of faith and re-orientation. This verse echoes the opening complaint in verse 1 ('My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me? why art thou so far from helping me?'), but with a crucial difference: now the sufferer is not asking why God is far, but demanding that God not be far. The plea al-tirchaq ('do not be far') is an imperative, not a question—it is the voice of someone who has already endured enough waiting and explanation.
commentary.narrative_2: The psalmist calls God eyaluti ('my strength'), a rare word possibly derived from ayyal ('ram' or 'deer'), suggesting both swiftness and power. This is not a weak call for comfort but a demand for urgent, violent intervention. The final imperative chushah ('hurry!' or 'haste') is the language of emergency—the sufferer's life is measured in moments, and every second of God's silence is lethal. The verse moves from spatial concern (do not be far) to temporal concern (come quickly), creating a double urgency: God must be present and must act now. This is the voice of someone at the absolute edge of survival, not someone asking politely for eventual help.

word_study.meaning: distant, far, remote; describes both spatial and relational distance
word_study.significance: The root recurs from verse 1 and verse 12, creating a motif of God's apparent absence. The sufferer's complaint that God is 'far' (rachoq) is answered here with a demand that God not be 'far'—suggesting that spatial metaphors are being used to describe spiritual or covenantal distance.

word_study.meaning: strength, power, might; possibly from אַיִּל (ayyal, 'ram' or 'deer'), animals known for swiftness and muscular power; the feminine form eyalah appears in Isaiah 35:6
word_study.significance: This is a rare term, appearing only here in the Hebrew Bible. The Covenant Rendering notes that it may carry connotations of swift, muscular power—the kind of strength that moves quickly. It is not God's abstract omnipotence the sufferer calls upon, but God's swift, embodied, kinetic strength.

word_study.meaning: to haste, hurry, move with speed; from חוש (chush, 'to feel, sense, or move quickly')
word_study.significance: An imperative in the second person—a direct command to God to move with urgency. The verb conveys desperation and immediacy. This is not a patient prayer but an urgent plea that brooks no delay.

word_study.meaning: help, aid, assistance; often describes active intervention or rescue
word_study.significance: The noun is concrete and directional—not abstract comfort or spiritual presence, but specific, active help that changes circumstances.

cross_references.connection: The opening verse asks 'why art thou so far from helping me?'—this verse transforms that question into a demand: 'do not be far.' The movement from question to command shows the progression of faith within the psalm itself.
Also uses the language of God being 'far' in the face of approaching enemies; verse 20 marks the turning point where the sufferer stops accepting distance and demands God's presence.
A parallel plea: 'Be pleased, O LORD, to deliver me: O LORD, make haste to help me'—similar structure of demanding speed and intervention from God.
Describes renewal of strength (koach) and those who 'mount up with wings as eagles'—God's swift strength contrasts with human weakness and weariness, echoing the appeal to God's swiftness here.

Quotes from Habakkuk with urgency language similar to chushah: 'yet a little while, and he that shall come will come, and will not tarry'—connecting the Old Testament cry for God's swift intervention to New Testament eschatology.

commentary.historical_context: In the ancient Near East, appeals to divine urgency often appear in Mesopotamian lament psalms and Egyptian mortuary texts, where the supplicant begs the gods to act quickly against enemies or death. The structure of verse 20—turning from description of enemies to direct address of God—reflects a recognized pattern in ancient lament liturgy, where the psalmist would shift from lament (describing suffering) to petition (addressing the deity). The terminology of 'strength' and 'swiftness' echoes the language used of warriors and divine beings in Ugaritic and Mesopotamian texts. The urgency conveyed by chushah reflects the brutal reality of ancient execution and warfare—delays meant death.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: Alma 34:21 teaches the principle of 'crying unto the Lord with all your heart' without ceasing—Psalm 22:20 exemplifies this kind of unceasing, urgent prayer. The Book of Mormon also emphasizes the necessity of acting with urgency in righteousness (D&C 38:27: 'I say unto you, be one; and prepare yourselves, and be ye ready for all things').
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 88:63 teaches 'Therefore, cease from all your light speeches, from all laughter, from all your lustful desires, from all your pride, all your anger, all your abuse'—the urgency of Psalm 22:20 reflects a spirituality that recognizes the reality of immediate spiritual danger and the need for swift divine intervention, not delayed complacency.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The call for God's swift strength and presence echoes the temple prayer circle tradition, where members repeat the plea 'O God, hear the words of my mouth' with emphasis on God's immediate presence and active participation in the covenant transaction.

commentary.christological_typology: In Christian tradition, Psalm 22:20 is read as Christ's final, urgent cry to the Father during the crucifixion. The shift from describing enemies to addressing God directly mirrors the Gospel account of Jesus crying out on the cross. The appeal to God's 'strength' prefigures the Resurrection, where God's power is demonstrated through the raising of Christ. The demand for swiftness ('haste') finds its answer in the rapid triumph of the Resurrection three days later. The verse encapsulates the paradox of the crucifixion: Jesus endures complete abandonment while simultaneously trusting God's ultimate intervention—he is the one who speaks both 'why hast thou forsaken me?' (verse 1) and 'do not be far from me' (verse 20).
commentary.application: In moments of acute spiritual or personal crisis, covenant members face the question this verse asks: Do we continue to accept distance from God, or do we demand His presence? The psalmist's shift from complaint to direct command reflects a mature spirituality that does not wait for God's explanation but claims the covenant relationship directly. Modern application involves recognizing when we have settled into passive acceptance of spiritual distance—through worldliness, compromise, or discouragement—and actively calling ourselves back to urgent communion with God. The term eyaluti ('my strength') invites the question: Are we drawing on God's swift, muscular intervention, or relying only on our own depleted resources? The verse calls us to pray not as supplicants begging for crumbs, but as covenant partners claiming promised help.

text_kjv: Deliver my soul from the sword; my darling from the power of the dog.

commentary.narrative: This verse continues the urgent plea begun in verse 20, but with heightened specificity: the psalmist names two threats and calls them by names that demean the enemies. The 'sword' (cherev) is the instrument of violent death—execution, military slaughter, or assassination. But alongside the sword stands 'the dog' (kelev, singular and definite—'the dog,' not 'a dog'), which appears to reference the contemptuous enemy mentioned in verse 17 ('they pierced my hands and my feet, I may tell all my bones: they look and stare upon me; they part my garments among them, and cast lots upon my vesture.'). The reference to 'the dog' uses a term of extreme contempt in ancient Israelite culture. To call someone a 'dog' was to strip them of human dignity and rank them among the basest creatures. Yet here, paradoxically, it is the psalmist who uses 'dog' to describe an enemy of greater social power and position.
commentary.narrative_2: The parallelism between 'my soul' (nafshi) and 'my only one' (yechidati) is striking. Both refer to the same reality—the psalmist's life—but the second term adds a theological weight that the first does not carry. Yechidah means 'only, unique, solitary'—it emphasizes that the psalmist has only one life, only one existence, and it is uniquely precious and irreplaceable. The TCR rendering, 'my only life from the power of the dog,' captures this better than the KJV's 'my darling from the power of the dog.' The psalmist is not asking for comfort or the preservation of a pet, but for the deliverance of his singular, irreplaceable life from the contemptible enemy described as 'the dog.' The verse is a cry for basic survival: protect my one and only life.

word_study.meaning: to rescue, deliver, snatch away from danger; a verb of sudden, forceful removal
word_study.significance: Not a gentle salvation, but a violent rescue—God is asked to snatch the psalmist away from death as one snatches a child from the jaws of danger. The verb conveys urgency and physical removal.

word_study.meaning: soul, life, self, person, breath; the seat of desire, emotion, and vitality
word_study.significance: In Hebrew thought, nafshi is not a disembodied spirit but the whole living self. To save one's nafshi is to save one's life in its totality.

word_study.meaning: only one, unique one, solitary; from a root meaning 'to be alone' or 'to be unique'
word_study.significance: This term appears only a handful of times in the Hebrew Bible (Psalm 25:16; Jeremiah 6:26; Amos 8:10). It emphasizes not merely 'life' but 'my only life,' 'my unique existence'—irreplaceable and singularly precious. The KJV's 'darling' misses this emphasis on singularity and uniqueness.

word_study.meaning: sword, blade, weapon; instrument of violence and death; metonym for violence and warfare
word_study.significance: In Hebrew poetry, the sword is the supreme instrument of fatal violence. To be delivered 'from the sword' is to be delivered from death itself.

word_study.meaning: dog, a creature; in Hebrew usage, an insult and term of contempt (compare 2 Samuel 3:8; 1 Kings 14:11)
word_study.significance: To call someone or something 'the dog' is to place it at the lowest level of contempt. The singular, definite form 'the dog' suggests a specific, identifiable enemy who is contemned as subhuman. Paradoxically, it is the powerful enemy who is named as 'the dog'—the psalmist claims the right to demean the one who threatens his life.

word_study.meaning: hand, power, authority; metonym for strength and control
word_study.significance: The 'hand' of the dog is its power, grasp, and authority. To be delivered from the hand of the dog is to escape its controlling power.

cross_references.connection: References the enemies as dogs: 'For dogs have compassed me: the assembly of the wicked have inclosed me'—verse 21 links to this earlier reference and names 'the dog' specifically, suggesting a continuation of the same threat.

Goliath's insult to David: 'Am I a dog, that thou comest to me with staves?'—reversing the dynamic where the powerful speaker claims to demean the weaker, whereas in Psalm 22:21 the weak speaker names the powerful enemy as 'the dog.'
Uses the image of the dog as a metaphor for one who returns to sin: 'the dog is turned to his own vomit'—connecting the contempt language to spiritual degradation.

In the Revelation description of those outside the eternal city: 'without are dogs'—connecting the image of the dog to those separated from God's presence, reinforcing the contempt language of Psalm 22:21.

While not directly quoting verse 21, the Gospel account of Jesus praying for those crucifying him ('Father, forgive them') demonstrates the transformation of Psalm 22's enemies—from 'dogs' to be condemned to sinners to be forgiven.

commentary.historical_context: In ancient Near Eastern culture, dogs were not domestic pets as in modern Western societies, but scavenging animals associated with uncleanness and death. In Egyptian and Mesopotamian texts, to be left unburied meant one's body would be eaten by dogs—the ultimate desecration. In Hebrew Scripture, dogs are rarely portrayed positively (exceptions like Job 30:1 are sarcastic). To call someone 'a dog' was to strip them of human status entirely. Significantly, in the Roman crucifixion context (the likely historical setting of the psalm's pesher application), crucified victims were sometimes left exposed for scavengers—the threat of being devoured by animals was real and culturally significant. The 'sword' reference may also point to Roman military execution, as swords were the primary weapons of Roman soldiers.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: Alma 5:26 contrasts those who can 'withstand the justice of God' with those who cannot—Psalm 22:21 pleads for deliverance precisely because the psalmist cannot withstand the power arrayed against him. The Book of Mormon's emphasis on the need for divine grace and rescue from death through Christ parallels the psalmist's plea.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 76:36–37 describes those who are 'thrust down to hell' and overcome by enemies—standing in contrast to those delivered by God's power. Psalm 22:21's plea for deliverance from 'the power of the dog' finds its answer in D&C 76's vision of those raised to exaltation through Christ.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The phrase 'my only one' (yechidati) recalls the temple concept of the Only Begotten Son—Jesus is God's 'only one,' unique and irreplaceable. In the temple context, covenant members are taught to become 'sons and daughters of God' (D&C 76:24), receiving an identity similar to Christ's uniqueness.

commentary.christological_typology: Psalm 22:21 is read in Christian tradition as Christ's plea for deliverance from death during his crucifixion. The 'sword' represents the violence of crucifixion; the 'dog' represents the contemptuous enemies (soldiers, religious authorities, the crowd) who mock and execute him. Yet the typology contains paradox: Christ does not in fact escape the sword and the dogs. Rather, he is delivered not from death, but through death and into resurrection. The verse's fulfillment is not in avoiding the cross, but in the Resurrection that transforms the execution into the means of salvation. Christ's yechidati ('only one') existence—his unique status as the Son of God—is what makes his sacrifice infinitely efficacious. Where the psalmist pleads for deliverance from contempt, Christ transforms contempt into the source of eternal honor.
commentary.application: Modern covenant members experience moments when enemies—whether literal opponents, sickness, poverty, or spiritual opposition—threaten to overwhelm. The psalmist's plea in verse 21 offers several applications: First, it validates the reality of threat and the appropriateness of crying out to God for rescue. Second, it demonstrates the language of specificity—naming the threat ('the sword,' 'the dog') rather than speaking in vague generalities. Third, it emphasizes the preciousness of one's 'only life' (yechidati)—not in a selfish sense, but recognizing that each individual existence is unique and valuable before God. Fourth, it models the reversal of contempt: the psalmist claims the right to demean the enemy as 'the dog,' asserting a spiritual hierarchy over circumstances that temporarily appear to dominate. Covenant members are invited to claim their own yechidati—their unique, irreplaceable identity as children of God—in the face of enemies that would strip that identity away.

text_kjv: Save me from the lion's mouth: for thou hast heard me from the horns of the unicorns.

commentary.narrative: This verse is the hinge upon which the entire Psalm turns—arguably the most dramatic transition in all of Hebrew poetry. The first half continues the plea: 'Save me from the lion's mouth!'—a straightforward petition for deliverance from a supremely dangerous enemy. But then, without explanation, warning, or narrative transition, the psalmist abruptly shifts: 'and from the horns of the wild oxen—you have answered me!' The shift from plea to praise is instantaneous and unexplained. The psalmist was crying out for rescue, and suddenly, without describing how, he declares that God has already answered. The verb anah ('to answer, respond') is in the perfect tense—completed action. Something has happened between verses 22a and 22b that the psalm does not narrate. The text offers no mechanism, no transition, no explanation—only the astonished fact of God's response.
commentary.narrative_2: The TCR rendering and translator notes highlight the scholarly discussion: Some scholars propose that during liturgical performance, a priestly oracle of salvation was spoken between these two halves—a voice of the priest declaring on God's behalf that the prayer had been heard. Others see this as an act of pure faith—the sufferer, in the midst of crying out, suddenly grasps with certainty that God has heard, and that certainty becomes its own transformation. Whatever the mechanism, the theological and emotional reality is unmistakable: the psalmist moves from petition to thanksgiving without any external cause being narrated. This is faith operating at its highest intensity—not faith as belief, but faith as the sudden knowledge that God is present and responsive, even when circumstances have not visibly changed. From this point forward, the psalm does not look back at the lament. Every remaining verse is thanksgiving, vow, and praise.
commentary.narrative_3: The imagery shifts from the 'lion's mouth' (the most fearsome predator of the ancient Near East) to the 'horns of the wild oxen' (remim—the massive, now-extinct aurochs, the largest bovine creature known). Both are images of overwhelming power and danger, yet they are also the backdrop against which God's answering becomes visible. The sufferer has not escaped the danger; he has not been transported to safety. Rather, surrounded by lion and wild ox, he testifies that God has answered. This is a declaration of faith and trust made in the very presence of mortal threat, not after the threat has passed.

word_study.transliteration: yasha (imperative, meaning 'to save, deliver, make wide space for')
word_study.meaning: to save, rescue, deliver; literally 'to make wide,' suggesting creating space for escape or safety
word_study.significance: The root suggests not merely rescue but the active creation of deliverance—God opening a way where there was none. It is an active, kinetic verb.

word_study.meaning: lion, the supreme predator of the ancient Levantine wilderness; symbol of power, ferocity, and divine strength
word_study.significance: In Hebrew poetry, the lion is the ultimate image of threatening power. To be in the lion's mouth is to be at the absolute edge of death—no escape is possible.

word_study.meaning: horns, rays of light, rays of power; from a root suggesting 'strength' and 'exaltation'
word_study.significance: Horns in ancient Near Eastern iconography represent power, authority, and aggression. The 'horns of the wild oxen' are weapons of impalement—instruments of death.

word_study.meaning: wild oxen, the Bos primigenius or aurochs—a massive, powerful bovine now extinct; the largest land animals known to the ancient Near East
word_study.significance: The KJV translated this as 'unicorns' following the Septuagint's monokeros (one-horned), but the remim were two-horned wild oxen. They were larger and more dangerous than domesticated cattle. To be threatened by the horns of remim was to face an almost incomprehensible force of nature.

word_study.meaning: to answer, respond, testify, declare; to make a response that is audible and effective
word_study.significance: The verb is in the perfect tense—completed action. God has answered. The tense does not indicate future response or hoped-for deliverance, but present reality of God's responsive presence. This is the hinge-verb of the entire psalm.

cross_references.connection: Also expresses sudden confidence: 'I cried unto the LORD with my voice, and he heard me out of his holy hill'—similar structure of cry followed by assurance of God's hearing.

Another example of sudden shift from distress to confidence: 'I called upon the LORD in distress: the LORD answered me, and set me in a large place'—the same pattern of prayer answered, space created, enemies overcome.
God's promise: 'When thou passest through the waters, I will be with thee'—the assurance that God's presence in danger is the answer to prayer, not escape from danger.

Describes Christ 'in the days of his flesh, when he had offered up prayers and supplications with strong crying and tears unto him that was able to save him from death: and was heard in that he feared'—applied to Jesus's prayers in Gethsemane and on the cross, identifying this psalm with Christ's experience.
Promises deliverance from 'the snare of the fowler' and protection from 'the terror by night'—another psalm that emphasizes God's protective response to those who call.

commentary.historical_context: The structure of verse 22—lament followed by sudden assurance—appears in Mesopotamian lament psalms and some Egyptian mortuary texts, where the supplicant's cry is met with a divine response, often delivered through a priest or oracle. The literary pattern suggests a liturgical practice where lament and response were incorporated into worship—possibly the individual lamented, and a priestly voice declared on God's behalf that the prayer was heard. The terminology of 'lion' and 'wild oxen' reflects a cultural familiarity with dangerous predators and wild animals that were part of the wilderness experience. The aurochs (remim) were known from ancient Near Eastern royal inscriptions and are depicted in surviving reliefs; they were prized as royal hunt prey and symbols of power. The shift from petition to thanksgiving is so abrupt that some scholars propose a Gattung (form-critical) boundary here, suggesting two originally separate poems, though the theological and emotional coherence argues against this fragmentation.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: Alma 36:3–4 describes Alma's sudden transformation from despair to assurance: 'And it came to pass that as I was thus racked with torment, while I was harrowed up by the memory of my sins, behold, I remembered also to have heard my father prophesy unto the people...And as I was thus racked with torment, the Spirit of the Lord began to withdraw from before me'—the Book of Mormon portrays spiritual crisis resolved by sudden, unexplained assurance of God's presence.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 121:7–8 addresses Joseph Smith in prison: 'My son, peace be unto thy soul; thine adversity and thine afflictions shall be but a small moment; And then, if thou endure it well, God shall exalt thee on high'—demonstrating the same pattern of assurance given in the midst of trial, not after deliverance from it.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The sudden shift in Psalm 22:22 from lament to praise mirrors the temple endowment pattern, where the initiate moves from trials and temptations to the veil and exaltation. The assurance that 'you have answered me' reflects the temple theme that God's covenants are secure and His responses are certain, even in the face of threatening powers.

commentary.christological_typology: Hebrews 5:7 applies Psalm 22 directly to Christ: 'Who in the days of his flesh, when he had offered up prayers and supplications with strong crying and tears unto him that was able to save him from death: and was heard in that he feared.' The writer identifies Jesus with the sufferer of Psalm 22, and identifies the answering of prayer with the Resurrection. The 'lion's mouth' and 'horns of wild oxen' represent the forces of death and evil arrayed against Christ—and yet, in the Resurrection, God's answer is revealed. Christ does not escape death, but is answered through death, in the Resurrection. The verse's theology of answered prayer is not that danger ceases, but that God's responsive presence is confirmed even in the midst of danger. For Christ, the answer is the Resurrection; for the psalmist, the answer is the testimony, in verse 22, that God has heard. The perfect tense ('you have answered me') in the mouth of one still surrounded by lions and wild oxen is the highest expression of faith—not faith that circumstances will change, but faith that God's responsiveness is already established fact.
commentary.application: The most challenging and transformative application of Psalm 22:22 is the possibility that God answers prayer not always by removing the threat, but by confirming His presence within the threat. Modern covenant members facing ongoing crises—terminal illness, financial ruin, relational breakdown, spiritual doubt—are sometimes disappointed when prayer does not remove the burden. Verse 22 invites a different understanding: The answer may be the sudden, inexplicable assurance that God hears and is present, even while the 'lion's mouth' and 'horns of wild oxen' remain. This assurance is not a placebo or distraction; it is the fundamental change that transforms the meaning of suffering from meaningless cruelty to redemptive trial. The application is to listen for God's 'answering' not as external deliverance, but as the confirmation of His presence and responsiveness. It also invites practitioners to identify the moment in their own lives when prayer shifted from petition to praise—when asking shifted to thanking—and to understand that shift as evidence of God's having answered.

text_kjv: I will declare thy name unto my brethren: in the midst of the congregation will I praise thee.

commentary.narrative: Immediately following the pivot point of verse 22—where God's answer is asserted without narration—the psalmist vows to declare God's name publicly. This is not private relief or personal satisfaction, but a public testimony made 'in the midst of the congregation' (betok qahal). The vow is made with urgency and certainty: 'I will declare' (asaprah—future tense of commitment and promised action). The sufferer, who was isolated and surrounded by enemies in verses 1–21, now envisions a return to the assembly of the covenant people. The restoration is not merely personal but relational—he will stand again among his 'brethren' (achai) and testify to them of God's name.
commentary.narrative_2: The verb 'declare' (asaprah, from saphar, 'to count, number, tell, narrate') carries the sense of making a full report or recounting a story. The psalmist will not merely mention God's name in passing; he will narrate what God has done. The 'name' (shem) in Hebrew theology represents God's character, reputation, and revealed identity. To declare God's name is to make known who God is. This vow transforms private suffering into public testimony. What the individual endured becomes the occasion for the community to know God more fully.
commentary.narrative_3: Hebrews 2:12 quotes this verse and applies it directly to Jesus Christ: 'Saying, I will declare thy name unto my brethren, in the midst of the church will I sing praise unto thee.' The New Testament writer sees in the psalmist's vow to declare God's name to the brethren the prototype of Christ's role as mediator and revealer of the Father to the Church. For the original psalmist, the declaration to 'brethren' means restoration to the community of Israel. For Christ, the declaration to 'brethren' (literally, 'brothers') is the Church—all those united in His name. The assembly (qahal) becomes in the Christian reading the ekklesia, the called-out ones.

word_study.transliteration: saphar (imperfect/future tense, meaning 'to recount, narrate, declare')
word_study.meaning: to tell, count, number, narrate; to recount a story or sequence of events
word_study.significance: The verb suggests not a one-time mention but a full narrative recounting. It is the verb used of testifying to God's deeds and character. This is not casual speech but deliberate proclamation.

word_study.meaning: name, reputation, character, authority; in Hebrew theology, the name represents the full identity and presence of the person
word_study.significance: To declare God's name is not to repeat a word but to make known God's character and works. The 'name' is God's revealed identity—His justice, mercy, power, and covenant faithfulness.

word_study.transliteration: ach (masculine plural construct with pronominal suffix)
word_study.meaning: brothers, kinfolk, members of the covenant community
word_study.significance: The term emphasizes not merely family relations but covenant kinship. To address the congregation as 'brethren' is to emphasize the bonds of mutual obligation and shared identity in the covenant.

word_study.meaning: in the middle, among, surrounded by
word_study.significance: The location shifts from the isolation of verses 1–21 to the center of the assembly. The psalmist is no longer on the periphery or outside, but in the visible, public center of the congregation.

word_study.meaning: assembly, congregation, community gathered for worship or deliberation
word_study.significance: The qahal is the assembled covenant people—those gathered in the name of God. To praise God in the qahal is to make one's testimony part of the community's witness.

word_study.meaning: to praise, celebrate, exalt, magnify
word_study.significance: The verb suggests joyful, exuberant celebration. This is not mere acknowledgment but celebratory worship.

cross_references.connection: Directly quotes this verse and applies it to Jesus Christ declaring God's name to the Church—establishing this as a messianic prophecy fulfilled in Christ's role as revealer of the Father.
Uses similar language of public testimony: 'Let the redeemed of the LORD say so, whom he hath redeemed from the hand of the enemy'—the pattern of private suffering followed by public proclamation.
Describes restoration to the assembly: 'Thou preparest a table before me...I will dwell in the house of the LORD forever'—another shift from threat to restoration and community.
Jesus says, 'I have manifested thy name unto the men which thou gavest me'—Christ's declaration of the Father's name parallels the psalmist's vow.
Describes the apostolic testimony: 'That which we have seen and heard declare we unto you'—the pattern of personal experience of God followed by public declaration continues in the New Testament.

commentary.historical_context: The vow to testify publicly in the sanctuary was part of ancient Israelite practice. Psalm 116:14–15 and 116:19 describe a similar vow: 'I will pay my vows unto the LORD now in the presence of all his people...I will pay my vows unto the LORD now in the presence of all his people.' The custom of public thanksgiving after deliverance from illness or danger was part of Second Temple practice. The sufferer would appear in the temple or synagogue and recount their deliverance to the assembled community. This transformed private suffering into communal edification and deepened the community's faith in God's power. The naming of God (declaring His name and attributes) was a central act of worship in ancient Israelite religion, not merely recitation but proclamation of God's revealed character.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: Alma 26:9–16 contains Ammon's declaration to his brethren: 'Now when our hearts were depressed, and we were about to turn back, behold, the Lord comforted us, and said: Go amongst thy brethren, the Lamanites, and bear with patience thine afflictions...now when I think of the success of these my brethren I cannot but praise and thank him.'—The Book of Mormon pattern of individual redemption leading to public testimony parallels Psalm 22:23.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 60:2 teaches: 'Now, I say unto you, that ye ought to open your hearts, even to listen to the voice of the Lord your God, whose word is quick and powerful, sharper than a two-edged sword'—the instruction to declare God's name is connected to the obligation to bear testimony in the gathering of the Saints (D&C 84:102).
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The vow to 'declare thy name' in the congregation parallels the temple recommend phrase and the emphasis throughout temple worship on making and keeping covenants publicly before witnesses. The restoration to the qahal (congregation) reflects the temple theology of restoration to God's presence through covenant.

commentary.christological_typology: Hebrews 2:12 explicitly identifies Psalm 22:23 with Christ declaring God's name to His 'brethren,' which the New Testament identifies as the Church. The typology works in multiple directions: First, the psalmist's restoration to the assembly prefigures Christ's restoration (resurrection) and return to the Father. Second, the psalmist's declaration to brethren in the congregation prefigures Christ's ongoing intercession for the Church (Hebrews 7:25) and His revelation of the Father to all believers. Third, the vow to declare God's name in the midst of the assembly anticipates the Church's continuation of this role—believers declaring God's works to others. The shift from verse 22 (God's answer in the midst of danger) to verse 23 (testimony in the congregation) mirrors the pattern of Christ's resurrection and the Church's subsequent witness.
commentary.application: The application of Psalm 22:23 for covenant members involves recognizing that personal spiritual experiences—answers to prayer, deliverances from crisis, encounters with God's presence—are not meant to remain private. The verse invites a specific action: to declare God's name and works within the congregation. This can take forms as simple as bearing testimony in sacrament meeting, as intentional as teaching a lesson on God's character, or as involved as one-on-one testimony with a friend or family member. The verse teaches that the sufferer who has cried out to God in isolation has a covenantal obligation to return and testify publicly—not for personal glory, but to strengthen the faith of others and to declare God's name. Importantly, the verse also implies restoration: the one who felt isolated and abandoned in verses 1–21 now stands 'in the midst of the congregation' (betok qahal)—not on the margins, but in the visible center. The application invites modern covenant members to recognize both the privilege of declaring God's name and the restoration that comes through bearing testimony within the covenant community.

text_kjv: Ye that fear the LORD, praise him; all ye the seed of Jacob, glorify him; and fear him, all ye the seed of Israel.

commentary.narrative: The scope of the psalm expands dramatically in its final verse. The psalmist, who was isolated and surrounded by enemies, now addresses not merely the congregation but calls all who fear the LORD to join in the praise. The verse moves from singular ('I will declare' in verse 23) to universal call ('Ye that fear the LORD'). Three times the verse addresses a specific group and issues a specific command: 'You who fear the LORD, praise him!'; 'All you seed of Jacob, glorify him!'; 'All you seed of Israel, stand in awe of him!' The parallelism suggests an expanding circle: from those who fear God, to all descendants of Jacob, to all descendants of Israel. This is not the same as the 'congregation' of verse 23—this is the entire covenant people, and implicitly, all people who are willing to enter into the covenant relationship with God.
commentary.narrative_2: The structure of the verse—three groups, three commands—is intentional and mirrors liturgical call-and-response patterns. Each group is addressed and given a verb of praise: hallelahu ('praise him'), kabbeduhu ('glorify/honor him'), guru mimmennu ('stand in awe of him'). The progression moves from praise to glorification to reverent awe—an escalation of response. The final phrase, 'all ye the seed of Israel,' returns to the specific covenant people, but the trajectory has been expansive: from the individual sufferer to the congregation to the entire covenant people to the implied nations that might listen and join. This is the voice of someone who has moved from isolation to the conviction that God's work extends beyond the individual to all creation.
commentary.narrative_3: The use of 'seed of Jacob' and 'seed of Israel' (two names for the same people, given as synonyms in parallel lines) emphasizes the unity of God's people. Jacob/Israel was the patriarch who wrestled with God and received a new name—the name Israel itself means 'he who struggles with God' or 'God prevails.' To be called 'seed of Israel' is to be part of the covenant people, those who bear God's name and engage in the struggle of faith. The final verse uses the name 'Israel' rather than 'Jacob' to emphasize not genealogy alone but the covenant identity of the people.

word_study.meaning: to fear, revere, respect; in religious context, to stand in awe of God and recognize His authority
word_study.significance: The phrase 'you who fear the LORD' (yirei YHWH) is a title for the faithful covenant people. To 'fear' God is not to be terrified but to recognize God's majesty and respond with obedience and worship. This is the same root as 'stand in awe of him' (guru mimmennu) in the final phrase.

word_study.meaning: to praise, laud, exalt, celebrate; to make much of, magnify
word_study.significance: This is the Hebrew root of 'Hallelujah' ('Praise God!'). The imperative form commands active, joyful celebration.

word_study.transliteration: kabad (imperative, meaning 'to honor, glorify, make heavy/weighty')
