word_study.meaning: to honor, glorify, esteem; from a root meaning 'to be heavy' or 'weighty,' suggesting 'to give weight to' or 'to magnify'
word_study.significance: The TCR translator notes indicate that kavad shares the root of kavod ('glory' or 'weight'). To glorify God is to 'add weight to God's reputation,' to make God's honor and authority weighty and significant in the world. The verb suggests intentional action to build up and establish God's reputation.

word_study.transliteration: gur min (meaning literally 'to fear from' or 'to stand back in awe of')
word_study.meaning: to fear, be afraid, stand in awe; to reverence
word_study.significance: The phrase 'stand in awe of him' (guru mimmennu) combines the verb 'to fear' with the preposition 'from,' suggesting a response of trembling respect and reverent distance. This is the climax of the three commands—moving from external praise to internal transformation.

word_study.meaning: seed, offspring, descendants, posterity; used both literally and metaphorically for all who descend from an ancestor
word_study.significance: The term 'seed of Jacob' and 'seed of Israel' links the present community to the patriarchal covenant. All who are 'seed of Israel' inherit the promises and obligations of the covenant made with Jacob.

cross_references.connection: Similar expansive praise: 'For as the heaven is high above the earth, so great is his mercy toward them that fear him'—addressing 'those who fear the Lord' as the audience for God's mercies.
Also uses the imperative form with expansion: 'Praise ye the LORD. Praise, O ye servants of the LORD, praise the name of the LORD'—repeating the command to praise with increasing scope.

God's call to all nations: 'Look unto me, and be ye saved, all the ends of the earth...unto me every knee shall bow, every tongue shall swear'—similar expansion from specific covenant people to universal scope.

The heavenly chorus: 'And they sung a new song, saying...Worthy is the Lamb...And every creature which is in heaven, and on the earth, and under the earth...heard I saying, Blessing, and honour, and glory, and power, be unto him that sitteth upon the throne'—the ultimate expansion of the psalmist's vision to all creation praising God.
Paul's promise: 'And so all Israel shall be saved'—the New Testament's application of 'all ye the seed of Israel' to the future redemption of the covenant people.

commentary.historical_context: The call to 'all ye the seed of Jacob...all ye the seed of Israel' reflects the way covenant identity was understood in ancient Israel. The 'seed' was not merely genealogical (DNA), but covenantal—those who accepted the God of Israel and lived under the covenant. In post-exilic Judaism, the definition of 'seed of Israel' expanded to include proselytes and those who joined the covenant community. The threefold call (praise, glorify, stand in awe) mirrors the structure of ancient Near Eastern hymnic literature, where congregational worship often involved responsive patterns of praise. The expansion of scope from individual to community to all nations represents the theological trajectory visible in the latter prophets (Isaiah 40–66), where Israel's restoration is connected to the redemption of all nations. The use of parallelism with slight variation (Jacob/Israel, praise/glorify/fear) is characteristic of Hebrew poetry's technique of developing ideas through repeated structures.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: Alma 36:22–23 describes Alma's expanded vision: 'And now I can join with you in the hope of the Lord'—the pattern of personal redemption expanding to include the whole covenant people appears throughout the Book of Mormon. Also, Mosiah 4:28 emphasizes the covenant people's responsibility to 'teach [the commandments] diligently unto your children, and...speak them when thou sittest in thine house, and when thou walkest by the way'—the obligation to declare God's works to the seed of Jacob.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 35:8 teaches: 'Wherefore, be faithful, stand in the office which I have appointed unto you; succor the weak, lift up the hands which hang down, and strengthen the feeble knees'—the instruction to the individual is connected to the work of strengthening the whole covenant people. Also, D&C 121:45 promises that the faithful shall have 'power over all things in this world, and all things are given him of the Father.'
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The final verse's expansion to 'all ye the seed of Jacob...all ye the seed of Israel' reflects the temple theology that covenants made in the temple are not private benefits but are meant to extend to the salvation of all humanity. The temple recommend emphasizes that one's covenants are made 'in behalf of' the living and the dead—an expansion of individual covenant to include the whole of God's people.

commentary.christological_typology: The expansion in verse 24 from the individual psalmist to 'all ye the seed of Jacob...all ye the seed of Israel' prefigures the universal scope of Christ's redemption. Just as the psalmist's experience of deliverance becomes the occasion for the entire covenant people to praise God, so Christ's redemption is extended to all who will believe. In Hebrews 2:12–13, where Psalm 22:23 is quoted in application to Christ, the passage continues: 'Saying, I will declare thy name unto my brethren' and 'Here am I and the children which God hath given me.' The 'children' (brethren, seed) represent the Church, all those who are gathered into God's covenant through Christ. The progression from individual sufferer (Psalm 22:1–22) to individual declaration (verse 23) to universal call (verse 24) mirrors the pattern of Christ's redemptive work: personal suffering, resurrection and declaration, and the gathering of all nations into God's kingdom.
commentary.application: The final verse of Psalm 22 invites covenant members to recognize that personal spiritual experience has corporate implications. The psalmist's individual deliverance becomes the occasion for calling others to praise God. Similarly, modern covenant members' experiences of God's power—answers to prayer, miracles, deliverances from danger or doubt—are not private possessions but testimonies meant to strengthen the entire covenant community. The verse also invites reflection on what it means to be 'seed of Jacob' or 'seed of Israel' in modern context: not merely genealogical or cultural identity, but covenantal identity—those who have made covenants with God and live in response to those covenants. The threefold command—praise, glorify, stand in awe—suggests that different forms of response are appropriate: active celebration (praise), intentional reputation-building (glorify), and reverent respect (stand in awe). The application is both personal and communal: each covenant member is called to these responses, and each carries responsibility for calling others to join in the praise of God. The expansion of the psalm's scope from the individual's isolated cry to the universal call to all nations suggests that the individual's faith, when rooted in covenant with God, becomes part of a transformative work that extends to all humanity.

text_kjv: For he hath not despised nor abhorred the affliction of the afflicted; neither hath he hid his face from him; but when he cried unto him, he heard.

commentary.narrative:
This verse marks a decisive theological turning point in Psalm 22. The psalmist has moved from lament and abandonment (verses 1-24) to proclamation of vindication. The verse declares that God did not treat the sufferer's affliction as abhorrent or unclean — a radical statement in ancient Israelite theology, where physical suffering was commonly interpreted as divine judgment or contamination. The sufferer was desperate, abandoned, mocked, and dying; yet God did not hide his face (a idiom for divine rejection) but rather heard his cry. The structure moves from what God did not do (despise, abhor, hide) to what he did do (hear). This is the foundation for everything that follows: God's character is such that he neither abandons the afflicted nor treats their suffering as repulsive to him.

The phrase 'affliction of the afflicted' (through the Hebrew enuwt anee) emphasizes the depth of suffering — not merely circumstantial hardship but existential misery. The psalmist insists that this very suffering, which seemed to separate him from God, became instead the occasion of God's deepest compassion. This reframes suffering not as evidence of divine abandonment but as the context in which God's hesed (faithful love) is most fully revealed.

word_study.meaning: To regard as worthless, to scorn, to treat with contempt. The root carries the sense of making light of something or dismissing it as valueless.
word_study.significance: God's refusal to bazah the sufferer's affliction means he does not dismiss or minimize it. The sufferer's pain has worth and dignity before God, unlike the mockery he endures from human enemies.

word_study.meaning: To detest, to find abominable; the verb form of sheqets ('abomination'). Used in the Torah for unclean animals and idolatrous practices — things that are ritually repulsive and must be avoided.
word_study.significance: As the TCR notes, this is a radical claim: God does not find the sufferer's affliction sheqets (abominable, unclean, repulsive). In a world where suffering was often read as punishment or contamination, this declaration asserts that affliction does not make a person ritually or morally repugnant to God. The sufferer's agony is not detestable in God's sight.

word_study.meaning: To conceal one's face; used idiomatically for divine rejection, abandonment, or the withdrawal of God's protective presence. When God hides his face, his people experience desolation (Psalm 27:9, 44:24).
word_study.significance: The psalmist affirms that God did not hide his face — meaning he did not truly abandon the sufferer, even though the abandonment felt total in verses 1-3. God's presence remained, even in the darkness.

word_study.meaning: When he cried out, from the root שׁוּע (shua), meaning to cry for help, to call out in distress. This is the cry of the desperate, the prayer of the afflicted.
word_study.significance: The sufferer's cry — the raw, urgent plea from agony — was heard. God responds to the authentic cry of pain, not because the sufferer earned it or deserved it, but because he is the God who hears.

cross_references.connection: The psalmist declares that when God says 'Seek my face,' he will not hide his face but will welcome the seeker. This verse answers that promise — God indeed does not hide his face from those who cry out.

The suffering servant is 'despised and rejected of men,' yet God does not despise him. The Messiah's affliction, like the psalmist's, is not treated as abhorrent by God but as the vehicle of redemption.
The righteous cry out and the Lord hears them and delivers them from all troubles. This verse affirms the same pattern: authentic cry + God's hearing = deliverance.
In the New Testament, Christ's affliction (his bearing our sins on the cross) is not treated as abhorrent but as redemptive, echoing this psalm's claim that God does not despise the sufferer's pain.

The Savior takes upon himself the afflictions and infirmities of his people so he might know how to succor them. Like this verse, the Book of Mormon teaches that God does not despise or hide from our afflictions but enters into them.

commentary.historical_context: In ancient Near Eastern thought, suffering and disease were often read as signs of divine disfavor or ritual impurity. The sufferer was not merely physically afflicted but socially and religiously contaminated. Temples and clean spaces were not accessible to the diseased or disabled. This psalm's assertion that God does not find the affliction sheqets (abominable) fundamentally challenges that worldview. It insists that the deepest divine compassion — not contempt — meets the suffering. This was countercultural in the ancient world and remains theologically revolutionary: God's character is defined by his refusal to abandon or despise those who suffer.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: In Alma 7:11-12, Alma teaches that Christ will 'go forth, suffering pains and afflictions and temptations of every kind... that he may know according to the flesh how to succor his people according to their infirmities.' Like this verse, the Savior does not despise or hide from our afflictions; instead, he enters into them to understand and alleviate them. The suffering becomes the context of divine love, not rejection.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 121:7-8 addresses Joseph Smith in the midst of his affliction in Liberty Jail: 'My son, peace be unto thy soul; thine adversity and thine afflictions shall be but a small moment; And then, if thou endure it well, God shall exalt thee on high.' Like Psalm 22, the Doctrine and Covenants refuses to interpret affliction as divine abandonment; rather, it becomes the crucible of exaltation.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: In temple symbolism, the veil represents the boundary between God and his people. This verse affirms that God does not keep the veil closed against the afflicted; his face is revealed to those who cry out in deepest need. The temple teaches that suffering, honestly brought before God, opens access to his presence.

commentary.christological_typology: This verse prophetically describes Christ's suffering on the cross. Jesus experienced total abandonment (crying 'My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me?'), yet God did not truly despise or hide his face. The Father's silence was not rejection but the mysterious completion of the redemptive work. As the suffering servant of Isaiah 53, Christ knew that his affliction would not be treated as abhorrent but as the means of salvation for all people. This verse is the voice of Christ in his extremity, declaring the truth that sustained him: God hears; God does not despise; God is near.
commentary.application: When we face profound affliction, doubt, or the sense that God has abandoned us, this verse calls us to cling to the core truth: God does not despise our suffering, and he is not hiding his face. Our cry, however inarticulate or desperate, is heard. The modern temptation is to interpret affliction as punishment or as evidence of God's indifference. This verse insists otherwise. Our suffering has dignity before God. He is attentive to our cry. We are invited to move from the lament of verses 1-3 to the proclamation of verse 25: God has heard, God does not hide, and deliverance is real.

text_kjv: My praise shall be of thee in the great congregation: I will pay my vows before them that fear him.

commentary.narrative:
The sufferer has moved from isolation to communal worship. Verse 26 describes the public fulfillment of a vow made in crisis — an ancient Israelite practice where someone in desperate circumstances promised an offering or dedication to God if he would grant deliverance. Now, delivered, the sufferer stands before the great congregation (qahel rab) to publicly pay (fulfill) that vow. The phrase 'my praise shall be of thee' (me-ittekha tehillati) carries the crucial meaning that the praise itself originates in God, not the sufferer. The psalmist does not generate worship from his own resources; God supplies both the deliverance and the capacity to praise it. This is not pride in personal survival but gratitude for unmerited rescue.

The 'great congregation' is Israel assembled for worship, likely in the temple. This is a complete reversal from the isolation of the early verses, where the sufferer was mocked and despised. Now he stands in the midst of the faithful (those who fear the Lord) and publicly testifies to God's saving work. The vow-payment often included a todah (thanksgiving sacrifice) and a communal meal, which anticipates verse 27. This verse establishes the structure: personal deliverance leads to public testimony, which draws others into worship.

word_study.meaning: Praise, glory, renown; often used for the praises sung to God. The root תהל carries the sense of 'shining forth' or 'making bright.' A psalm is a tehillim — a song that makes God's glory shine forth.
word_study.significance: The sufferer's tehillah does not glorify himself but God. His praise is the vehicle through which God's glory becomes visible to the congregation. This is the entire point of deliverance — not personal vindication but the revelation of God's character.

word_study.meaning: From you, from your side, originating in you. This phrase indicates source and origin.
word_study.significance: As the TCR notes, this is theologically crucial: the praise originates in God, not the sufferer. God provides both the deliverance and the responsive worship. The sufferer is the instrument through which God's praise is voiced, not the author of it. This humbles the worshipper and exalts God.

word_study.meaning: Assembly, congregation, community gathered together. In biblical context, often refers to Israel assembled for worship or covenant renewal. This is the same root from which qahal Elohim ('the assembly of God') derives — the gathered people of God.
word_study.significance: The solitary sufferer now stands within the qahal — the covenanted community. His individual deliverance has meaning only as it is witnessed and celebrated communally. The congregation is not merely an audience but a community that shares in and is sanctified by his testimony.

word_study.meaning: Vows, solemn promises made to God, typically in time of distress, promising an offering or service in exchange for deliverance. Vow-payment (nedar ashleim, 'I will fulfill my vow') is a binding obligation.
word_study.significance: Vows are not casual promises but covenantal commitments. The sufferer promised God something if he would be saved, and now, saved, he must publicly and fully keep that promise. This models the integrity expected of God's people — we cannot make light of promises made in covenant.

word_study.meaning: Those who fear, from the root יראה (yara), meaning to fear, revere, respect with awe. In biblical idiom, 'the fear of the Lord' is not terror but reverent obedience and awe.
word_study.significance: The sufferer pays his vows 'before those who fear him' — in the presence of the truly devoted community. This is not performance for the sake of reputation but testimony offered to those who already worship. The vow-payment strengthens the faith of the fearers of God.

cross_references.connection: Another thanksgiving psalm describing the fulfillment of vows after deliverance: 'What shall I render unto the Lord for all his benefits toward me? I will take the cup of salvation, and call upon the name of the Lord. I will pay my vows unto the Lord now in the presence of all his people.'

Hannah brings young Samuel to the temple to fulfill the vow she made when she cried out for a child. Her vow-payment, like the psalmist's, is public and communal, offering the fruit of her deliverance to God's service.

The todah (thanksgiving offering) is described in the Torah, including the requirement to offer it with unleavened bread and the communal meal that follows. This verse presupposes that legal framework.
God commands: 'Offer unto God thanksgiving; and pay thy vows unto the most High.' This verse shows that vow-fulfillment is not merely personal obligation but part of covenant worship.

In modern revelation, the Lord teaches about the thanksgiving offering: 'And in nothing doth man offend God, or against none is his wrath kindled, save those who confess not his hand in all things, and obey not his commandments.' The thanksgiving vow is part of this confessing God's hand and obedience.

commentary.historical_context: In ancient Israelite worship, vow-making was a standard response to crisis. When death seemed imminent, individuals would vow offerings, pilgrimages, or dedications to God in exchange for rescue. Upon deliverance, these vows were publicly fulfilled, typically in the temple during pilgrimage festivals when the great congregation assembled. The vow-payment often took the form of a todah (thanksgiving sacrifice), which differed from other sacrifices in that it included a communal meal — the meat was shared among priests and the worshipping community. This meal was not merely celebratory but covenantal, binding the community together in witness to God's saving work. The public nature of vow-fulfillment served multiple functions: it honored the God who delivered, it strengthened the faith of other worshippers, and it integrated the formerly isolated sufferer back into covenant community.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: In Helaman 8:23-24, Nephi testifies publicly before the congregation about the Lord's deliverance and the signs that confirm God's word. Like the psalmist, Nephi's testimony is offered before 'them that fear him' — the covenant community gathered to strengthen their faith.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 19:37 teaches: 'Pray always, that you may come off conqueror; yea, that you may conquer Satan, and that you may escape the hands of the servants of Satan that do uphold his work.' When delivered, we are to testify of that deliverance. Section 42:61 emphasizes thanksgiving: 'Now I give unto you a commandment that ye shall teach one another the doctrine of the kingdom.' Part of that teaching is testimony to God's delivering power.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The temple is the place where vows are made and paid. In modern temple worship, we renew covenants made, offer our devotion publicly before the covenant community, and participate in the ritual meal/sacrament that parallels the ancient todah meal. The gathering in the temple courtyard is our 'great congregation.'

commentary.christological_typology: Christ is the ultimate fulfiller of the vow. In Hebrews 10:7, the Father says to the Son, 'Then said I, Lo, I come (in the volume of the book it is written of me,) to do thy will, O God.' Christ made the ultimate vow at the foundation of the world to pay the price of redemption. After his resurrection, he stands before the great congregation of the redeemed and offers his praise to the Father. This verse is Christ's voice, giving thanks before those who fear the Lord for his deliverance through death and resurrection.
commentary.application: In modern covenant life, we similarly make vows — in baptism, in the temple, in our daily commitments to serve God. This verse invites us to fulfill those vows publicly and authentically, not for pride but as testimony to God's faithfulness. When we have experienced deliverance (from addiction, from despair, from sin), we are called to stand before the community and let our praise originate from God, not from self-congratulation. The congregation strengthens their own faith by witnessing our honesty about God's saving work. Are we willing to pay our vows openly, to give testimony that makes God's glory visible to those who fear him?

text_kjv: The meek shall eat and be satisfied: they shall praise the LORD that seek him: your heart shall live for ever.

commentary.narrative:
Verse 27 expands the circle of blessing outward from the individual sufferer to the entire community of the humble (anavim). The 'eating and being satisfied' (yochlu, yisba'u) refers specifically to the todah meal — the communal thanksgiving feast that followed vow-fulfillment. In the ancient temple economy, when a person brought a thanksgiving offering, the meat was not consumed by priests alone but shared with the worshipper and the gathered community. This meal was not merely food for the hungry; it was a sacramental experience where the saved person and the faithful community together experienced God's provision and grace. The phrase 'they shall praise the Lord that seek him' shifts focus to the larger congregation — those who seek God are themselves satisfied and strengthened through participation in the testimony of deliverance.

The final clause, 'your heart shall live for ever,' is extraordinary. The sufferer's deepest cry in verse 21 was for life (chasai — save my life). Now that petition is answered not only for him but extended to the entire worshipping community: their hearts live forever. This is not merely individual immortality but the perpetual vitality of the covenant community. The Hebrew yachi levavkhem la-ad carries the sense of lasting renewal, of continuous life flowing through the hearts of the faithful. The todah meal thus becomes a type of the eschatological feast, the eternal communion of God's people where all are nourished and all hearts live forever.

word_study.meaning: The humble, the afflicted, the poor; those without power or status in the world. The root ענה carries connotations of being bowed down, afflicted, lowly. These are the aniyim — the poor in spirit.
word_study.significance: The anavim are not the strong or the wealthy but those who, like the psalmist, have no resources except God. The todah meal feeds them — not as charity but as participation in God's covenant mercy. The inclusion of the anavim in the feast affirms that deliverance is not reserved for the powerful but especially for the powerless.

word_study.meaning: To eat, to consume food; in the context of the todah, to participate in the sacrificial meal.
word_study.significance: This is not mere physical eating but sacramental participation. To eat at the todah meal is to enter into covenant communion with God and the community. The body is nourished, yes, but the soul is sanctified.

word_study.meaning: And they will be satisfied, full, sated. The root שׂבע (saba) means to have one's fill, to be satisfied completely.
word_study.significance: Not merely fed but satisfied — their deepest hunger is answered. In biblical imagination, satisfaction is both physical and spiritual. To eat at the todah is to experience complete sustenance, the meeting of every hunger.

word_study.meaning: Those who seek, inquire after, search for. The root דרש (darash) means to seek with intentionality and devotion.
word_study.significance: The seekers of God are those who actively pursue him, who make him the object of their search. They are not passive but devoted. The praise they offer is the fruit of their seeking.

word_study.meaning: Heart, the seat of intellect, will, emotion, and moral decision. The heart is where covenant commitment is made (all your heart, all your soul, all your might).
word_study.significance: When hearts live forever, it means the inner life of the community — its commitment, its worship, its covenant devotion — is perpetually renewed. The heart is not the organ that stops but the spiritual center that endures eternally in communion with God.

cross_references.connection: The eschatological feast where the Lord spreads a feast for all peoples: 'And in this mountain shall the LORD of hosts make unto all people a feast of fat things... And he will destroy in this mountain the face of the covering cast over all people, and the vail that is spread over all nations.' The todah meal is a type of this ultimate feast.
The marriage supper of the Lamb, where the blessed are called: 'Blessed are they which are called unto the marriage supper of the Lamb.' The todah anticipates this eternal communion.
The ancient wisdom tradition teaches: 'A man's pride shall bring him low: but honour shall uphold the humble.' The anavim (humble) who eat at the todah are exalted by God.
In Nephi's dream, the tree of life bears white fruit that is desirable and most sweet, and those who eat it are filled. The todah meal is the historical reality that types this eternal satisfaction.

Joseph Smith received revelation about the sacrament: 'For, behold, I say unto you, that it mattereth not what ye shall eat or what ye shall drink when ye partake of the sacrament, if it so be that ye do it with an eye single to my glory.' The sacrament perpetuates the pattern of the todah — communal eating in remembrance of deliverance.

commentary.historical_context: The todah (thanksgiving offering) was central to Israelite worship and differed significantly from other sacrifices. While burnt offerings and sin offerings benefited primarily the priests, the todah was a communal meal. The animals offered (cattle, sheep, or goats) were butchered, portions given to priests, and the remainder shared among the worshipper and their guests. The meal had to be eaten the same day it was offered (it could not be stored), enforcing the immediate, communal nature of the celebration. The poor and the sojourners were specifically invited to participate. This meal was not optional politeness but legal requirement (Leviticus 7:15-18). In a society where the poor had little access to meat, the todah meal was a profound act of redistribution — the wealthy sufferer, having been saved, fed the hungry as part of their covenant gratitude. The satisfaction described in this verse is thus both spiritual and concrete: the anavim are literally filled because the covenant community shares in the delivered one's blessing.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: In Mosiah 18, King Benjamin's people gather and are filled with joy and gladness, satisfied by God's word. When Benjamin teaches them that Jesus Christ will redeem them, 'the Spirit of the Lord came upon them, and they were filled with joy, having received a remission of their sins, and having peace of conscience, because of the exceeding faith which they had in Jesus Christ.' This is the spiritual equivalent of the todah meal — communal satisfaction found in God's deliverance.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 65:5 teaches about God's eternal kingdom: 'Wherefore, may the kingdom of God go forth, that the kingdom of heaven may come, that thou, O God, mayest be glorified in heaven so on earth, that thine enemies may be subdued; for thine is the honor, power, and glory, forever and ever.' The eternal satisfaction of verse 27 is the goal of all history — God's kingdom spreading and all peoples being fed by his bounty.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The sacrament continues the tradition of the todah meal. In the temple, members eat and drink together in remembrance of Christ's deliverance. The satisfaction promised here is fulfilled in the temple experience, where individuals and communities are spiritually nourished and their hearts are strengthened in covenant devotion.

commentary.christological_typology: The verse prophetically describes Christ as the ultimate source of eternal satisfaction. Jesus taught, 'I am the bread of life: he that cometh to me shall never hunger; and he that believeth on me shall never thirst' (John 6:35). The todah meal, where the saved one feeds the hungry community, is a type of the Atonement, where Christ's sacrifice nourishes all humanity. The 'hearts living forever' is the resurrection — eternal life made possible through Christ's deliverance. This verse is the promise that in Christ's kingdom, all the anavim (humble, afflicted, poor) will be satisfied eternally.
commentary.application: This verse calls us to both receive and share the satisfaction of God's deliverance. First, to allow our own hearts to be nourished by participation in the community of the saved — to eat at the table of the Lord's covenant community, strengthened by the testimonies of others who have been delivered. Second, to ensure that the todah meal of our own deliverance includes the anavim — to use our salvation as an occasion to feed the hungry, to welcome the poor and afflicted, to redistribute blessing. The satisfaction promised is not for the proud or the self-sufficient but for those who seek God with genuine devotion. We are invited to both partake and to share the feast.

text_kjv: All the ends of the world shall remember and turn unto the LORD: and all the kindreds of the nations shall worship before thee.

commentary.narrative:
The scope of Psalm 22 suddenly explodes from the local and national to the universal and cosmic. From one afflicted individual, to the congregation of Israel, to the todah meal of the humble — now to all the ends of the earth and all the nations of the world. This is a missionary vision of staggering scope. The phrase 'all the ends of the world will remember and turn' (yizkeru ve-yashuvu) suggests that the nations once knew God (or ought to have known him) and will return to that knowledge. The verb 'remember' (zakhar) implies not creating new knowledge but recovering what was lost or forgotten. The verb 'turn' (shuv) is the language of repentance (teshuvah) — a complete reorientation of heart and allegiance back toward God.

The sufferer's individual story — abandoned, mocked, dying — becomes the occasion for this universal turning. The logic seems to be: when one person experiences utter dereliction followed by vindication, when death is followed by life, this becomes a sign to all nations of God's power and mercy. The 'kindreds of the nations' (mishpechot goyim) will bow down before God. This vision echoes the Abrahamic covenant in Genesis 12:3 ('in you all the families of the earth will be blessed') and asserts that the afflicted sufferer is somehow the vehicle through which that universal blessing flows. The God who did not despise one person's affliction reveals his character to the whole world. One person's deliverance becomes the hinge of cosmic salvation history.

word_study.meaning: They will remember, recall, bring to mind. The root זכר (zachar) means to remember with intentionality, to bring something into active consciousness, sometimes with the sense of 'make mention of' or 'recall in order to act.'
word_study.significance: This is not passive forgetting and then accidental recollection but active remembrance. The nations will deliberately bring God to mind. The sense is that God was known or knowable, and this remembrance is a return to that knowledge. The deliverance of the afflicted one triggers this remembrance.

word_study.meaning: And they will turn, return, repent. The root שׁוב (shuv) is the fundamental verb of repentance in Hebrew, meaning to turn around, to change direction, to return to the right path.
word_study.significance: This is teshuvah — the comprehensive reorientation of the nations from whatever false gods or idolatries they have pursued back to the true God. The singular deed of salvation becomes the catalyst for universal moral and spiritual revolution.

word_study.meaning: All the ends of the earth, the farthest reaches, the distant places. Afsei carries the sense of boundary or extremity.
word_study.significance: No corner of creation is excluded from this worship. The vision is genuinely universal — from the farthest reaches of what was then known to be the inhabited world, all peoples will worship.

word_study.meaning: Families, clans, peoples; the basic social unit smaller than a tribe or nation. Used collectively to describe all peoples.
word_study.significance: Every social grouping, every ethnic identity, every family structure — all will bow. The universality is not abstract but concrete, encompassing the actual diversity of human peoples.

word_study.meaning: They will bow down, prostrate themselves, worship. The root שׁחה (shachah) is the physical gesture of worship, the bending of the body as an expression of submission and reverence.
word_study.significance: This is not intellectual assent to doctrine but bodily submission — the entire person oriented toward God in worship. The physical gesture of bowing expresses the spiritual reality of surrender to God's sovereignty.

cross_references.connection: The Abrahamic promise: 'In you shall all families of the earth be blessed.' This verse asserts that the afflicted one becomes the instrument through which that promise is fulfilled.

The suffering servant passage: 'The Lord hath made bare his holy arm in the eyes of all the nations; and all the ends of the earth shall see the salvation of our God.' The sufferer's vindication is the mechanism of universal revelation.

Paul quotes this theme in relation to Christ: 'That at the name of Jesus every knee should bow, of things in heaven, and things in earth, and things under the earth; And that every tongue should confess that Jesus Christ is Lord, to the glory of God the Father.'

The saints sing the song of Moses and of the Lamb: 'Great and marvellous are thy works, Lord God Almighty; just and true are thy ways, thou King of saints. Who shall not fear thee, O Lord, and glorify thy name? for thou only art holy.'

Joseph Smith taught about the universal gathering: 'Draw near unto me and I will draw near unto you... Therefore, come unto me and hearken to my voice, and I will reason with you... that you may understand.' The gathering of all peoples in the last days fulfills this vision.

commentary.historical_context: In the ancient Near East, the defeat or vindication of a single person could carry cosmic and political significance. The humbling of a king in battle or the exaltation of a righteous ruler was understood to have implications beyond the individual — it revealed the will of the gods and the shape of destiny. However, this psalm's vision is unprecedented in its scope and its mechanism: not through military conquest or political triumph but through one person's dereliction and deliverance does the entire world learn who God is. This reflects a theological insight distinctive to Israelite monotheism: the character of God is revealed not through coercive power but through mercy toward the afflicted. The nations will bow not because they have been conquered but because they have witnessed, in one person's salvation, the God who refuses to despise suffering, who hears the cry of the afflicted, and who vindicates the meek. This is a form of soft power — the conversion of the world through the revelation of divine character.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: The Book of Mormon extensively develops this vision of universal gathering. In 2 Nephi 27, Isaiah's prophecy is quoted about the book of the Lord being brought forth in the last days, and 'the deaf shall hear the words of the book, and the eyes of the blind shall see out of obscurity and out of darkness.' The nations remember God and return to him through the Book of Mormon, which is the record of the afflicted ones (the Nephites, and ultimately Christ) vindicated.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 38:1 teaches Joseph Smith: 'Thus saith the Lord your God, even Jesus Christ... Behold, verily, verily, I say unto you, that the Lord's scourge shall pass over by day and by night, and the report thereof shall vex all people; yea, it shall not be stayed until the Lord comes.' The universal turning of the nations involves judgment and the proclamation of God's word. D&C 110:7-10 describes the appearance of Christ in the Kirtland Temple and the outpouring of the Spirit to prepare the nations for his return.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: In temple symbolism, the gathering of all nations before the throne of God is the ultimate fulfillment of temple worship — when all creation joins in the celestial liturgy and all acknowledge God's sovereignty. The temple is the earthly type of this universal gathering.

commentary.christological_typology: This verse is explicitly messianic. The one whose affliction leads to universal worship must be the Messiah. Psalm 22 is densely quoted in the New Testament accounts of the crucifixion (verse 1 in Matthew 27:46, verse 18 in John 19:24, verse 22 in Hebrews 2:12). The suffering servant of Isaiah 53, who is despised and rejected yet makes an offering for sin, is the fulfillment of this vision. Christ's self-sacrifice becomes the occasion for the world's turning. All nations worship before him because he has borne the universal weight of human sin and affliction. This verse is the messianic promise that Christ's suffering is redemptive for the entire world.
commentary.application: For modern covenant members, this verse transforms our understanding of personal affliction and testimony. Our suffering, faithfully borne and honestly witnessed, is not meaningless but becomes part of a much larger salvation history. When we testify of God's faithfulness in our afflictions, we become instruments through which others encounter the true God. The vision also calls us to a kind of missionary zeal — we are invited to recognize that the nations can and will turn to God, that all the ends of the earth are within God's vision and mercy, and that our role is to witness and testify to God's character, especially as revealed in the faces of the afflicted.

text_kjv: For the kingdom is the LORD'S: and he is the governor among the nations.

commentary.narrative: This brief verse is the theological hinge on which the entire universal vision rests. The reason all the nations will remember and turn, the reason all families will bow down, is stated here with absolute simplicity: the kingdom belongs to God, and he rules among the nations. This is monotheistic affirmation at its most stark and powerful. While earthly kings claim dominion, while nations compete for power and honor, the ultimate sovereignty belongs to God alone. The sufferer's vindication is not merely a personal rescue but a revelation of who actually holds power in the cosmos — not the mockers, not the strong, not the nations, but the Lord. Verse 29 answers the question that haunts the opening of the psalm: if God is truly just and merciful, why does the afflicted one suffer? The answer is not provided in verse 29 directly but through the assertion of God's ultimate kingship: there is a justice that transcends apparent injustice, a sovereignty that encompasses even suffering within a larger redemptive purpose.

word_study.meaning: The kingdom, the royal rule, the reign; from the root מלך (malak), to be king, to rule. Ha-melukhah is the definite, singular monarchy — 'the kingdom,' referring to absolute sovereignty.
word_study.significance: This is not a kingdom among kingdoms but 'the kingdom' — the ultimate, universal rule. All other kingdoms are subordinate to this melukhah.

word_study.meaning: To the Lord, the preposition 'l' (le) indicating possession, belonging, ownership. The kingdom is possessed by and belongs to God alone.
word_study.significance: This is a statement of divine ownership and prerogative. The kingdom is not shared, earned, or competed for — it is the exclusive possession of God.

word_study.meaning: One who rules, governs, holds dominion. The root משל (mishal) means to rule, to govern, to exercise sovereignty. A moshel is one who has active, ongoing authority.
word_study.significance: God is not merely the abstract source of legitimacy for earthly rulers but the active governor, the one who directly rules among the nations. His governance is concrete, present, and absolute.

cross_references.connection: The Lord reigns; he is clothed with majesty and strength. The world is established and cannot be moved. His throne is established from of old.
In Nebuchadnezzar's dream, it is revealed: 'The most High ruleth in the kingdom of men, and giveth it to whomsoever he will.' Earthly kingdoms exist only as God permits.
The final affirmation of this truth: 'The kingdoms of this world are become the kingdoms of our Lord, and of his Christ; and he shall reign for ever and ever.'
Joseph Smith's vision of exaltation: 'Now this is the blessing of the faithful... They are they into whose hands the Father has given all things.'
Captain Moroni raises the title of liberty, proclaiming that God is supreme ruler and that his people are free to worship him. The kingdom belongs to God, not to tyrants.

commentary.historical_context: In the ancient Near East, the theology of divine kingship was common but often understood within a polytheistic framework — different gods ruled different nations, or different gods had delegated authority to earthly kings. Israel's radical claim was monotheistic: not only does God rule, but God rules alone and universally. This was theologically subversive. It meant that earthly kings (even good kings) were only subordinate agents of the true king. It also meant that empires that claimed absolute power were ultimately delusional. When Psalm 22 declares that God rules among all nations, it stakes a claim that would have been heard as politically and religiously revolutionary — whether by Babylonian conquerors or by any imperial power that denied the sovereignty of Israel's God.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: Mosiah 29:25-27 explicitly teaches this principle in a political context: 'But behold, the Spirit hath said this much unto me... if ye support the laws which are just and cheerfully submit to those officers which the Lord hath appointed... ye shall be preserved.' The kingdom belongs to God, and those who rule must rule under his law and authority.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 101:80 teaches about the kingdom of God: 'And it shall come to pass that I, the Lord God, will send one mighty and strong, holding the scepter of power in his hand, clothed with light for a covering, unto all nations.' God's rule is not abstract but will be visibly demonstrated in the last days.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: In the temple, members renew the covenant to sustain the Lord as king and his anointed. The temple is the earthly symbol of God's actual kingdom. In temple language, we move from the telestial (kingdoms of men) through the terrestrial to the celestial (God's kingdom), learning to recognize God's ultimate sovereignty and our place within it.

commentary.christological_typology: This verse proclaims the kingship of Christ. In the Gospels, 'the kingdom of God' is often shorthand for Christ's reign and his rule. The sufferer of Psalm 22 who is vindicated is revealed to be the King — not king of the nations in an earthly sense but King of Kings, to whom all rule and authority ultimately belongs. The cross, which seems to be the moment of the sufferer's greatest defeat, is actually the moment of his deepest victory — the moment when God's kingdom is most fully revealed, when the powers of darkness are conquered, and when Christ begins his eternal reign.
commentary.application: In modern covenant life, this verse calls us to orient ourselves toward God's actual kingship rather than the apparent power of earthly rulers and institutions. When we are afflicted, mocked, or seemingly defeated by worldly powers, this verse asserts that appearances are deceptive — the kingdom belongs to the Lord. We are invited to submit to his rule, not out of fear or coercion, but out of recognition that his is the only rule that is just, eternal, and true. The verse also suggests a kind of serenity in the face of earthly turmoil — the kingdoms of this world are important but ultimately subordinate. Our primary loyalty is to God's kingdom, which cannot be shaken.

text_kjv: All they that be fat upon earth shall eat and worship: all they that go down to the dust shall bow before him: and none can keep alive his own soul.

commentary.narrative:
The final verse of Psalm 22's public proclamation reaches toward the eschatological boundary and perhaps beyond it. The circle of worship expands now to include not just the living but the dead. The 'fat ones' (dishnei-arets) — the prosperous, the well-fed, those with abundance — will eat and bow down. These are not the anavim (humble) of verse 27 but the wealthy and powerful. The logic seems to be: if even the proud and satisfied acknowledge God's kingship, then all categories of humanity are encompassed. Then the verse turns to 'all who descend to the dust' (yordei afar) — the euphemism for death and those who go down to Sheol. And then the final, stunning clause: 'and his soul he cannot keep alive' (ve-nafsho lo chiyyah) — even those who lack the power to preserve their own life will kneel before God.

This verse may be the most theologically daring in the psalm. In typical Old Testament theology, the dead in Sheol are cut off from the living and from worship. Psalm 6:5 asks: 'For in death there is no remembrance of thee: in the grave who shall give thee thanks?' The Psalmist elsewhere acknowledges that the dead praise not the Lord (Psalm 88:10-12). Yet Psalm 22:30 seems to envision something different — a worship that includes even the dead, a kneeling that transcends the boundary of death. This could be read as hyperbolic poetry (universalizing to the point of including the dead to emphasize totality) or as a glimpse of resurrection hope — a conviction that God's kingdom encompasses death and brings all who have ever lived into his presence. The final phrase about those who cannot keep alive their own souls emphasizes human powerlessness before God — and it may hint at a power beyond human autonomy, a keeping-alive that only God can provide.

word_study.meaning: The prosperous ones, those who are fat (well-fed, satisfied). From דשן (dashen), to be fat, to have abundance. These are the wealthy, the satiated, those with resources.
word_study.significance: While the anavim (poor) are fed at the todah meal, these dishnei-arets (fat ones) also bow down. The universality includes not just the needy but the satisfied, not just those who seek but even those who have no need. All bow.

word_study.meaning: They will eat, they will consume. In the context of universal worship, 'eating' may refer again to participation in the sacred meal or more generally to the sustenance of life lived in God's presence.
word_study.significance: Even those with all they need participate in the meal, the blessing, the communion of God's people. Eating is the fundamental act of community and covenant.

word_study.meaning: Those who descend to the dust, a euphemism for death and the grave. Afar (dust) is the biblical symbol for human mortality and the grave.
word_study.significance: The dead are included in the worship. This is extraordinary in Old Testament terms and may suggest a resurrection hope — that even those who have died will participate in God's final worship.

word_study.meaning: They will kneel, bend the knee, bow down; from כרע (kara), to kneel, a gesture of submission and worship.
word_study.significance: Even the dead, if they are included, are not passive observers but active worshippers, bending the knee before God.

word_study.meaning: To keep alive, to preserve life, to make alive. The root חיה (chaya) is the verb of life and vitality. It can mean 'to preserve' but also carries connotations of 'to make alive again' — potentially resurrection.
word_study.significance: The phrase 'his soul he cannot keep alive' (nafsho lo chiyyah) means that human beings lack the power to preserve their own souls in existence. Only God can truly make alive. This may hint at the resurrection — the life that comes from God's power, not human will.

cross_references.connection: Paul writes: 'That at the name of Jesus every knee should bow, of things in heaven, and things in earth, and things under the earth; And that every tongue should confess that Jesus Christ is Lord, to the glory of God the Father.' Paul's vision of universal worship explicitly includes the heavenly, earthly, and subterranean (underworld), encompassing the living and dead.
Paul quotes Isaiah: 'As I live, saith the Lord, every knee shall bow to me, and every tongue shall confess to God.' Universal submission before God is inevitable.

In John's apocalyptic vision: 'And every creature which is in heaven, and on the earth, and under the earth, and such as are in the sea, and all that are in them, heard I saying, Blessing, and honour, and glory, and power, be unto him that sitteth upon the throne, and unto the Lamb for ever and ever.'
Nephi is shown in vision that 'the Lamb of God is the Son of the Eternal Father, and the Savior of the world; and that all men must come unto him, or they cannot be saved.'

Joseph Smith received revelation: 'And now, verily I say unto you, that through you the oracles shall be given to another... And to every one it shall be given, according to their circumstances and their diligence and faithfulness.' The gathering of all dispensations and all peoples before God.

commentary.historical_context: The phrase 'those who go down to the dust' was an unambiguous reference to death and the grave in Hebrew thought. The journey to Sheol was understood as descent into the underworld, into darkness and silence. The ancient Israelite worldview generally held that death was the end of meaningful existence — the dead could not praise God or participate in worship. The famous Hezekiah lament captures this: 'For the grave cannot praise thee, death can not celebrate thee: they that go down into the pit cannot hope for thy truth' (Isaiah 38:18). To include the dead in the worship of God was theologically shocking. Some scholars suggest this verse may reflect a later theological development, influenced by Persian or Greek ideas about the afterlife and immortality, or it may represent an emerging belief in resurrection that would become more explicit in Daniel and the intertestamental period. Regardless of its dating, the verse breaks the boundary between the living and the dead, insisting that God's sovereignty extends beyond death and that all creation — past, present, and future — will ultimately acknowledge his kingship.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: Alma 11:41-45 explicitly teaches the resurrection: 'Now, there is a resurrection, therefore all men shall come forth from the dead and stand before God, and shall be judged according to their works... And those who have done good shall have everlasting life; and those who have done evil shall have everlasting damnation." The Book of Mormon fills in what Psalm 22:30 hints at — that all, living and dead, will stand before God.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 76 presents Joseph Smith's vision of the three kingdoms of glory, describing how all people, after death and resurrection, will be assigned to a kingdom according to their deeds. This is the fulfillment of Psalm 22:30 — all who have lived or will live, including the dead, will kneel before God and receive his judgment.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: In the temple, we perform work for the dead, affirming that death does not end God's covenant reach. The living and the dead are connected in the worship and covenant renewal. The sealing power extends to all generations — binding families not just in mortality but in eternity. The temple is where the boundary between living and dead most visibly dissolves.

commentary.christological_typology: This verse is the final affirmation that the sufferer is the Messiah who will reign over all creation. Christ's resurrection is the event that makes it possible for the dead to participate in worship. Through his victory over death, he opens the way for all the dead to come forth. As the Son of God, he has 'all power... in heaven and in earth' (Matthew 28:18), and before him every knee will bow. The clause about souls that cannot keep themselves alive points to Christ's power to give life — 'I am the resurrection, and the life' (John 11:25). Christ's kingship extends beyond the living into the realm of the dead, making him the ultimate sovereign who can animate, judge, and bless all creation.
commentary.application: For modern covenant members, this verse profoundly transforms our understanding of death and the scope of God's kingdom. First, it asserts that death is not the end — God's kingship and our ultimate accountability extend beyond mortality. Second, it invites us to remember and pray for the dead, recognizing that they are not cut off from God but are part of the ultimate gathering. Third, it humbles us with the recognition that we cannot 'keep ourselves alive' — our very existence depends on God's will and power. Fourth, it gives us faith that whatever we face in mortality, God's justice and mercy will ultimately encompass all, including those we have lost. The verse ends Psalm 22 not with the sufferer's personal vindication but with the universal, cosmic acknowledgment of God's kingship — affirming that our individual stories are part of an infinitely larger redemptive narrative.

text_kjv: A seed shall serve him; it shall be accounted to the Lord for a generation.

commentary.narrative:
This final verse of Psalm 22 provides the resolution to the entire psalm's arc from anguish to vindication. The psalmist moves beyond personal deliverance to envision the eternal significance of his suffering and God's rescue. 'A seed shall serve him' (or more precisely, 'a generation to come will serve him') transforms the psalmist's individual trial into a testimony that will echo through all future generations. This is not merely about biological descendants, but about the perpetual transmission of God's faithfulness across time itself. The sufferer's experience becomes a permanent witness—his story will be retold, his deliverance remembered, and through that remembering, future generations will encounter and serve the God who rescued him.

The verse captures a profound theological truth: suffering that is witnessed by God and answered by God becomes redemptive not only for the sufferer but for all who hear of it. The Hebrew word zera ('seed, offspring, generation') carries temporal weight—it points forward to a succession of generations who will inherit knowledge of God's covenant faithfulness through the telling of this story. This transforms personal pain into communal gospel. What begins in Psalm 22:1 as 'My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me?' ends with the assurance that this very experience of abandonment and rescue will become the foundation of perpetual worship.

word_study.meaning: offspring, descendants, posterity, generation; also used temporally to indicate future generations as a collective entity
word_study.significance: The Covenant Rendering notes that zera introduces 'the temporal dimension'—not just immediate descendants, but the succession of generations across time. In covenant language, one's 'seed' inherits the promises and responsibilities. Here, the psalmist envisions all future generations as inheritors of the testimony of God's deliverance. This term carries forward the Abrahamic promise language where God speaks of descendants who will possess blessing.

word_study.meaning: will serve, will worship, will work for; implies both obedience and religious devotion
word_study.significance: The future tense carries assurance—not a wish but a prophecy. Future generations will not accidentally hear this story and forget it; they will actively serve God because of it. This echoes the covenant pattern where God's deliverance generates obligatory worship and obedience in response.

word_study.meaning: it will be told, recounted, narrated; from the root spr meaning 'to count, recount, narrate'
word_study.significance: The Covenant Rendering emphasizes that yesuppar means 'it will be told, recounted' rather than merely 'accounted to.' This is not an abstract accounting but an active narrative transmission. The story will be spoken, preserved orally and textually, becoming the vehicle through which future generations encounter God's faithfulness. The passive voice ('it will be told') suggests divine providence in the telling—God ensures the story persists.

word_study.meaning: Lord, Master; a reverential substitute for the divine name YHWH
word_study.significance: The psalmist's return to covenantal language ('the Lord') marks the restoration of the relationship that seemed broken at the psalm's opening. By Psalm 22:31, the psalmist no longer cries 'My God, my God' in abandonment, but confidently addresses 'the Lord' as one whose name and deeds will be declared.

cross_references.connection: The opening lament—'My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me?'—finds its answer and completion in verse 31. The suffering endured and the deliverance received become testimony for future generations.

This shall be written for the generation to come: and the people which shall be created shall praise the Lord.' Like Psalm 22:31, this verse envisions suffering and praise being written and transmitted to future generations as permanent testimony.

The servant will see his seed (offspring) and prolong his days; the pleasure of the Lord shall prosper in his hand. This Messianic passage shares with Psalm 22:31 the vision of the suffering servant's experience bearing fruit across generations.

Quoting Psalm 22, the New Testament applies this psalm directly to Christ: 'I will declare thy name unto my brethren.' Christ's redemptive suffering becomes the foundation for all future worship—His 'seed' (His body, the Church) declares His name eternally.

All those who receive the priesthood receive this oath and covenant...that all that he hath shall be given unto him. The covenant promise that faithful service leads to inheritance echoes the psalmist's vision of generations inheriting blessing through transmitted testimony.

commentary.historical_context: In ancient Near Eastern covenant tradition, the transmission of testimony across generations was a central mechanism for covenant renewal and perpetuation. Stories of divine deliverance were told at festivals (like Passover) where each generation heard again how God had acted to save His people. The psalmist assumes this cultural practice—that his suffering and rescue will be integrated into Israel's collective memory and liturgical practice. The idea that personal suffering could have communal, trans-generational significance aligns with how Israel understood the role of the righteous sufferer in the economy of covenant. Ancient Near Eastern texts also reveal that kings and leaders expected their deeds to be 'told' (narrated in inscriptions and oral tradition) so that their names and reputations would live forever. Here, the psalmist's name matters less than the eternal telling of God's name and faithfulness.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: Mosiah 5:13 resonates with Psalm 22:31: 'And now, I would that ye should understand that this is my desire...that this people should be my people.' King Benjamin's prophecy that future generations will inherit covenant identity through the telling of the king's words parallels how the psalmist's deliverance becomes testimony for all generations. Also, the Book of Mormon frequently employs the pattern of individual righteousness and suffering becoming communal blessing (Nephi, Abinadi, Alma)—suffering that generates lasting conversion and spiritual renewal in others.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 76:1-4 presents a pattern where Joseph Smith and Sidney Rigdon receive vision, and then 'it shall be made known' to others—the testimony is transmitted. D&C 88:75-80 emphasizes the role of passing truth from parent to child 'that all may be edified of all.' The Restoration explicitly values the transmission of testimony across generations, making Psalm 22:31 an Old Testament precursor to this restored understanding.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The temple endowment itself is a performance and transmission of sacred narrative meant to be experienced and then transmitted in spirit (though not detail) to future generations. Like the psalmist's suffering becoming eternal testimony, the Atonement of Christ (which the temple ordinances represent) becomes the basis for all future generations' approach to God. The Psalm's movement from individual agony to communal, eternal significance mirrors the movement from personal covenant-making in the temple to the exaltation of one's entire family line.

prophetic_quotes.speaker: President Russell M. Nelson
prophetic_quotes.quote: Your testimony is not just for you. It is for your family, for your community, and for the world. As you share what the Lord has done for you, others will see Him, love Him, and serve Him.
prophetic_quotes.relevance: This statement directly echoes Psalm 22:31—personal experience of God's deliverance becomes testimony transmitted to future generations, generating their commitment to serve.

commentary.christological_typology: Psalm 22 is perhaps the most explicitly Messianic psalm in the Old Testament. Every major element of the psalm—abandonment, mockery by onlookers, piercing of hands and feet, division of garments, casting of lots—appears in the Gospels' account of Christ's crucifixion. Verse 31 completes the typological pattern: just as the righteous sufferer in Psalm 22 experiences vindication and eternal praise, Christ's suffering becomes the eternal foundation of redemption for all generations. His 'seed' (Isaiah 53:10) is not biological but spiritual—all who believe in Him and who will believe until the end of time. The suffering and apparent abandonment in verses 1-24 finds its ultimate meaning in verses 25-31: Christ's agony becomes humanity's salvation testimony, transmitted from generation to generation. Every time the Gospel is proclaimed, Psalm 22:31 is fulfilled—Christ's deliverance is 'told to the Lord,' recounted in preaching and testimony, becoming the ground of faith for the next generation.
commentary.application: This verse invites us to reframe our suffering and trials in covenantal terms. When we experience deep difficulty and God delivers us, that deliverance is not merely private blessing—it becomes testimony. Our children, grandchildren, and spiritual children hear how God was faithful to us, and that hearing becomes the foundation of their faith. In modern Latter-day Saint context, we are invited to bear testimony specifically so that future generations inherit certainty of God's reality and love. Moreover, as we participate in passing along the gospel narrative (through family home evening, family scripture study, written records, missionary work), we are literally fulfilling Psalm 22:31—we are telling to the Lord's name across generations. The suffering of pioneers, the faith of converts, the dedication of leaders become permanent testimony that shapes all who come after. What feels like isolated struggle is actually woven into the eternal fabric of witness. This means our trials matter not only for us but for all who will inherit the blessing of our faithfulness.

text_kjv: A Psalm of David. The LORD is my shepherd; I shall not want.

commentary.narrative:
Psalm 23 opens with one of scripture's most intimate theological declarations. The superscription 'A Psalm of David' is not mere attribution—it grounds the psalm in the experience of one who was himself a shepherd, who fought lions and bears to protect his flocks (1 Samuel 17:34–37). When David says 'The LORD is my shepherd,' he is not employing abstract theological language but drawing on lived experience. The Hebrew term ro'eh (shepherd) in the ancient world meant far more than someone who tends sheep from a distance. A shepherd was simultaneously provider, protector, healer, and guide—roles that demanded constant presence, intimate knowledge of each animal's vulnerabilities, and willingness to put his own life at risk. By claiming 'the LORD is my shepherd,' David is asserting that the God of Israel exhibits all these dimensions of care toward him personally.

The consequence of this claim is radical totality: 'I shall not want' (lo echsar). The verb chasar means 'to lack, to be without, to be deficient.' This is not a statement about material abundance—the psalmist is not claiming he will never experience hunger or want. Rather, it is a proclamation that in the presence of a shepherd-God who knows him intimately and is committed to his welfare, he lacks nothing essential. He is not left orphaned, abandoned, or without guidance. The Covenant Rendering captures this with 'I lack nothing'—a statement of relational security rather than material satiation.

word_study.meaning: One who tends, pastures, or feeds flocks; comes from ra'ah ('to feed, graze, pasture'). In the ancient Near East, the shepherd was the protector against predators, provider of pasture and water, healer of wounds, and guide through terrain. The term was applied to kings throughout Egypt and Mesopotamia as a metaphor for rulership.
word_study.significance: David's choice of this metaphor is personal and embodied. As a former shepherd himself (1 Samuel 16:11), David understood the intimate, tireless, sacrificial nature of shepherd work. Calling God his shepherd claims that divine care is personal, constant, and willing to suffer on the sheep's behalf. This stands in contrast to hierarchical or distant models of divine rule.

word_study.meaning: I will not lack, I will not be deficient, I will not be without. The verb chasar means 'to lack, to be in need, to be deprived.' The negation makes it emphatic: complete absence of lack.
word_study.significance: This is not prosperity theology but relational assurance. The speaker is affirming that in relationship with a shepherd-God, no essential thing is withheld. The focus is on wholeness of relationship, not material accumulation. The Covenant Rendering's 'I lack nothing' emphasizes this as a statement of sufficiency rather than endless supply.

word_study.meaning: The Hebrew possessive suffix on ro'i ('my shepherd') makes this deeply personal—not 'the LORD is a shepherd' (abstract) or 'the LORD is Israel's shepherd' (collective) but 'the LORD is my shepherd' (individual).
word_study.significance: The intimacy is the grammatical point. Each reader/hearer of this psalm is invited to make this claim individually: 'my shepherd.' This transforms a statement about God's character into a personal relationship. In Latter-day Saint theology, this reflects the doctrine that God knows and cares for each of His children individually, not merely collectively.

cross_references.connection: David recounts to Saul how he fought lions and bears as a shepherd, protecting his flock. This personal experience as a shepherd gives embodied weight to his metaphor when he later calls God his shepherd.

Isaiah describes the Lord coming 'as a shepherd: he shall feed his flock like a shepherd: he shall gather the lambs with his arm.' This parallel image of divine shepherding extends David's metaphor into the broader covenant tradition.
Jesus declares 'I am the good shepherd' and explains that a good shepherd lays down his life for the sheep. This is the Christological fulfillment of the shepherd metaphor that David introduces.

Alma asks his people: 'Have ye spiritually been born of God? Have ye received his image in your countenances?' This echoes the intimate personal relationship implied in 'my shepherd'—not a generic divine attribute but a transforming personal encounter.

The Lord states 'he that hath ears to hear, let him hear,' implying a personal, direct relationship. Like David's 'my shepherd,' this assumes individual attentiveness to divine voice rather than merely corporate instruction.

commentary.historical_context: In the ancient Near East, the title 'shepherd' (Hebrew ro'eh, Akkadian re'u) was applied to kings as a standard metaphor for rulership. Egyptian pharaohs called themselves shepherds of their people; Mesopotamian kings bore the title 'shepherd' as formal designation of their responsibility to feed and protect the realm. However, such royal shepherds often ruled from palaces at great distance from their people. David's revolutionary claim is that the God of Israel is a shepherd who does not rule from distance but walks with his flock, knows each sheep by name, and shares in their vulnerability. This was particularly striking in a cultural moment when shepherding was a low-status occupation—kings described themselves as shepherds metaphorically while treating actual shepherds as socially marginal. David reclaims the metaphor as authentically intimate.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: In Mosiah 23:12, Alma leads his people to a promised land and they 'did taste the fruit thereof, and it did satisfy their hunger.' The shepherd metaphor—providing for essential needs in a covenant relationship—appears throughout Book of Mormon descriptions of God's provision for His people (1 Nephi 8, 2 Nephi 25:20).
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 21:4–6 describes the Lord's promise to the Church: 'Wherefore, meaning the church, thou shalt give heed unto all his words and commandments which he shall give unto you as he receiveth them, walking in all holiness before me.' The pattern of shepherding—guiding the sheep through divine word and personal presence—echoes throughout Doctrine and Covenants.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The shepherd metaphor is foundational to temple theology. In temple ordinances, the covenant relationship is described as intimate guidance by divine beings who know the initiate by name and lead them through spiritual progression. The phrase 'my shepherd' anticipates the personal relationship cultivated in temple worship.

commentary.christological_typology: David as shepherd-king points typologically to Christ, the 'Lamb of God' (John 1:29) who himself becomes the Good Shepherd (John 10:11). The intimacy of 'my shepherd' finds its ultimate fulfillment in Jesus's teaching that He knows His sheep by name and they know His voice (John 10:14–16). The willingness of the shepherd to die for the sheep (John 10:15) is foreshadowed in David's willingness to fight lions and bears to protect his flock.
commentary.application: For modern covenant members, Psalm 23:1 invites a foundational reorientation of the self toward divine care. In a culture of endless productivity, anxiety, and self-sufficiency, the declaration 'The LORD is my shepherd; I shall not want' requires deliberate, repeated choice. It means trusting that when you have done what you can do—when you have worked, planned, and exercised stewardship—the ultimate provision and guidance come from relationship with God, not from your own effort alone. This is not passivity but the peace that comes from distinguishing between what you must do and what only God can do. Practically, it invites daily practices of listening for the Shepherd's guidance, examining whether you are fleeing from His presence when danger comes, and asking: In what specific area of my life right now am I not trusting that the Lord is my shepherd?

text_kjv: He maketh me to lie down in green pastures: he leadeth me beside the still waters.

commentary.narrative:
With verse 2, the psalm moves from statement to image—from declaring the shepherd's identity to experiencing the shepherd's care in concrete, sensory detail. 'Green pastures' (neot deshe) is not metaphor for vague blessing but precise provision. In the arid Palestinian landscape, lush green grass is not everywhere or always available. Finding such pasture required knowledge of terrain, seasonal water patterns, and hidden valleys. The shepherd who provides 'tender grass' (neot deshe literally means 'pastures of delicate vegetation') is one who knows the land intimately and leads the flock to hidden abundance.

The verb 'maketh me to lie down' (yarbitseni) carries profound significance. Sheep will not lie down when threatened, hungry, or disturbed. They lie down only when they feel completely safe, when their primary needs are met, when the shepherd is present and watchful. The shepherd cannot force a sheep to rest; he can only create the conditions—safety, food, presence—that allow the sheep to voluntarily choose rest. This is a picture of a God who respects the sheep's nature, who provides rather than coerces, whose care results in genuine peace rather than forced compliance.

The second image completes the provision: 'still waters' (mei menuchot). The Hebrew menuchah means not merely 'quiet' but 'rest, resting place, settled peace.' Sheep fear fast-moving water; they instinctively avoid rushing streams, fearing they will lose footing or be swept away. They require calm, clear water they can drink from without panic. The shepherd who 'leadeth me' (yenahaleni) does not merely point to water; he actively guides the sheep to this place of rest. The verb nahal specifically means 'to lead to water'—it is tender, particular, and responsive to the flock's vulnerability.

word_study.meaning: Pastures of tender grass; literally 'places of delicate vegetation.' Deshe suggests fresh, young, nutritious grass—the kind that nourishes a flock most fully. Binot/neot are the enclosed spaces or pasture-lands where such growth occurs.
word_study.significance: The specificity matters. Not 'pastures' generically but green, tender ones. In the arid ancient Near East, lush pasture was a luxury requiring the shepherd's intimate knowledge and active provision. This grounds the metaphor in real vulnerability—the sheep cannot find good pasture on its own; it needs the shepherd's guidance.

word_study.meaning: He makes me lie down, causes me to recline, brings me to rest. From the root rabats ('to lie down, recline'). The causative form suggests the shepherd creates the conditions in which lying down becomes possible.
word_study.significance: Rest is not something the sheep achieves through effort; it is something the shepherd enables through provision and presence. Theologically, this speaks to grace—divine provision that precedes and enables human response. Rest in God's care is a gift, not an achievement.

word_study.meaning: Beside waters of rest, still/peaceful waters. Menuchah literally means 'rest, resting place, settled peace, security.' The waters are not merely calm but are associated with the divine rest itself.
word_study.significance: Menuchah is the same word used for the Promised Land as Israel's 'rest' (Deuteronomy 12:9) and for the resting place of the ark (Numbers 10:33, 1 Chronicles 28:2). The waters are not just refreshment but participation in divine rest. To drink from these waters is to enter the peace of God's own settled condition. The Covenant Rendering's 'still waters' captures the serenity, while deeper study reveals these are 'waters of rest'—waters that confer divine peace.

word_study.meaning: He leads me, guides me. The root nahal specifically refers to leading flocks to water—it is not generic guidance but the particular, tender work of leading thirsty animals to drink.
word_study.significance: This verb appears in Isaiah 49:10 ('he that hath mercy on them shall lead them, even by the springs of water shall he guide them') and Genesis 33:14 (Jacob adjusting his pace for the children and nursing animals). It is the language of accommodated provision—the leader adjusting to the vulnerability of those being led.

cross_references.connection: The promised land is described as 'the rest and the inheritance which the LORD your God giveth you.' Like the still waters of menuchah, the land itself is a place of rest that God provides—Psalm 23:2 anticipates the theology of covenant rest.
The Servant is promised 'he shall feed them, and lead them beside the springs of water.' The exact pastoral language of Psalm 23:2 appears in prophecy about the Messiah's care for God's people.

Jesus tells the Samaritan woman about 'living water' that becomes 'a well of water springing up into everlasting life.' The still waters of divine provision in Psalm 23 find their ultimate meaning in the life-giving waters Jesus offers.

Nephi leads his people 'that they might pitch their tents in the valley which is northward.' The pattern of the shepherd-leader bringing the flock to provision and rest appears throughout the Book of Mormon narrative of covenant migration.
