word_study.significance: Rachamim is God's felt response to suffering. It is not abstract justice but the moved heart of a parent seeing a child in pain. This is the texture of God's character that the speaker invokes.

word_study.meaning: faithfulness, steadfast love, covenant loyalty, mercy; refers to God's reliable commitment to his people. Not a single act but the pattern of faithful action across time.
word_study.significance: The Covenant Rendering translates chasadim as 'acts of faithful love'—emphasizing that these are concrete demonstrations, not mere sentiment. The plural form (chasadim) suggests the accumulation across history: 'all the times God has been faithful.' The speaker is saying: 'You have acted faithfully countless times before; act faithfully now.'

word_study.meaning: from eternity, from of old, from ancient times, from the beginning; olam can mean the distant past or the indefinite future—it suggests time beyond human reckoning.
word_study.significance: The phrase suggests that God's compassion and faithfulness are not recent innovations or changeable policies. They are ancient, eternal, the foundational pattern of reality itself. This makes the appeal powerful—the speaker is calling God to consistency with eternity itself.

cross_references.connection: A passage from suffering that mirrors verse 6: 'It is of the LORD'S mercies that we are not consumed, because his compassions fail not. They are new every morning: great is thy faithfulness.' Compassion (rachamim) and faithfulness are paired as the grounds for hope in crisis.

God's own description of himself after the golden calf incident: 'The LORD, The LORD, God merciful and gracious, longsuffering, and abundant in goodness and truth.' Rachamim and chesed are the foundational qualities of God's self-revelation.

A prayer asking God to 'pardon the iniquity' of his people, invoking God's ancient mercies and faithfulness: 'He will turn again, he will have compassion upon us.' The appeal to God's character as the basis for hope appears throughout the prophets.

The Doctrine and Covenants describes God's mercy and truth as the foundation of salvation: 'For we beheld, and lo, the glory of the Only Begotten of the Father, which was with him before the world was made.'
Mormon appeals to God's faithfulness: 'O Lord, have mercy upon this people, and as thou hast said that there should be no more Cain, so spare this people and let sin be unto them as a light thing.'

commentary.historical_context: The appeal to God's ancient character and historical faithfulness was a standard form in Israelite prayer. The people of Israel understood themselves as inheritors of a long tradition of God's covenant keeping. The exodus, the wilderness wandering, the possession of the land, the various deliverances from enemies—all were understood as evidence of God's unchanging mercies and faithfulness. When facing new crises, it was appropriate to remind God (metaphorically) of what he had always been. This was not manipulation but theology: the God who was faithful to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob will be faithful to us. The appeal to me-olam (from of old, from eternity) would have resonated with cosmological understanding—the idea that God's attributes are primordial, woven into the structure of reality itself.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: Alma 36:17-20 records Alma's appeal to Christ's mercy: 'And now, behold, when I thought this, I could remember my pains no more; yea, I was harrowed up by the memory of my sins no more. And oh, what joy, and what marvelous light I did behold.' The invocation of God's mercy (rachamim) as the grounds for transformation appears throughout the Book of Mormon.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 109:76-77 (from the Kirtland Temple dedication) invokes God's mercy: 'And we ask thee, Holy Father, that thy servants may go forth from this house armed with thy power, and that thy name may be upon them.' The appeal to God's character and faithfulness as a basis for blessing and protection is echoed.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The temple experience includes moments where the worshiper is reminded of God's covenants and mercies—the endowment tells the story of God's faithfulness and the promises he has made. The invocation of God's ancient mercies is central to the temple's theology.

commentary.christological_typology: In Christ, God's rachamim (compassion) and chesed (faithful love) reach their fullest expression. The incarnation itself is the answer to the prayer of verse 6—God remembering his compassion, acting in accordance with his eternal character. The crucifixion is God's compassion demonstrated at infinite cost; the resurrection is God's faithfulness made undeniable. Those who follow Christ are recipients of the very mercies the psalmist invokes—mercies 'from of old,' now made personal and available through the Savior's atonement.
commentary.application: Verse 6 invites us to recall our own history with God and to appeal to it. What has God's faithfulness looked like in your life? When have you experienced his compassion? The prayer asks us to remember—and then to call on that memory as grounds for trust in the present. This practice of 'remembering God's mercies' is not nostalgia but a deliberate spiritual discipline. It trains the mind to recognize the pattern of God's faithfulness across time and to trust that the pattern will continue. In moments of doubt or darkness, verse 6 invites us to speak to God from the deepest place of faith: 'You have always been merciful. You have always kept your covenants. I am calling on that ancient, eternal part of your character. Be true to yourself—and therefore true to me.'

text_kjv: Remember not the sins of my youth, nor my transgressions: according to thy mercy remember thou me; according to thy lovingkindness remember thou me, for thy goodness' sake, O LORD.

commentary.narrative:
Psalm 25:7 establishes the psalm's central theological tension: the appeal for selective divine memory. The speaker has a documented past—sins of youth (chattot neuray) and deliberate rebellions (peshaim)—but asks God to practice what amounts to holy forgetfulness. This is not naïve denial; it is a sophisticated appeal based entirely on God's character rather than the speaker's merit. The juxtaposition of 'do not remember' and 'remember me' creates the interpretive heart of the psalm: God is asked to forget the failures but remember the person. The speaker acknowledges both accidental transgressions and willful defiance without excuse or minimization.

The basis of this prayer is not reform but grace. The speaker does not say 'remember me because I have changed' or 'because I deserve it.' He says 'remember me according to your faithful love' (al-chesedekha zokhreni) and 'for your goodness' sake' (lemaan tuvkha). God's character—his chesed (covenantal devotion) and tov (goodness)—is larger than the speaker's past. This is the grammar of grace in the Hebrew Bible: the appeal is always to who God is, not who we have become.

word_study.meaning: Chattot (plural of chet) refers to transgressions or failures, literally 'missing the mark' (the root suggests deviation from a target). Neuray means 'of my youth.' Together they denote the immature, uninformed sins of earlier years—failures that may have proceeded from inexperience rather than malice.
word_study.significance: The speaker distinguishes between youthful inadvertence and mature rebellion, yet asks for neither to be held against him. This linguistic honesty—naming the category of sin rather than denying it—is characteristic of penitential prayer in the Psalms. The acknowledgment that youth brings its own sins (without the full moral culpability of willful defiance) is psychologically realistic.

word_study.meaning: Pesha means deliberate rebellion, willful defiance, or breach of covenant. It is a stronger term than chet because it implies intentionality and choice. The speaker confesses not just failure but rebellion.
word_study.significance: By using both chattot ('miss the mark') and peshaim ('willful rebellion'), the psalmist takes full responsibility for both categories of sin. He does not hide behind the 'youth' excuse for his rebellions. This comprehensive confession—claiming both accidental and intentional sin—demonstrates the seriousness of the penitential stance.

word_study.meaning: Zakar means 'to remember, recall, bring to mind.' In Hebrew, remembering is not passive recollection but active engagement—to remember something is to act on it, to let it shape behavior. The phrase 'do not remember' (al-tizkor) asks God to refrain from the active engagement with sin that judgment represents.
word_study.significance: The Covenant Rendering notes the central interplay: 'do not remember' the sins but 'remember me' according to chesed. God is asked to maintain relationship with the person while suspending judgment on the past. This reflects the biblical understanding that forgiveness often means a change in what God 'remembers' or actively engages with. See Genesis 8:1 (God remembered Noah) and Exodus 2:24 (God remembered the covenant)—remembrance as divine action, not mere recollection.

word_study.meaning: Chesed is often translated 'mercy,' 'lovingkindness,' or 'faithful love.' The term denotes God's committed, covenantal devotion—love that is not based on the beloved's merit but on God's binding commitment. Chesed is reliable, enduring, and constitutive of God's character.
word_study.significance: The Covenant Rendering highlights that chesed is 'faithful love'—not sentimental emotion but structured devotion. The speaker asks God to remember him according to this foundational aspect of divine character. Chesed appears throughout Psalms as the ground of hope and the basis of prayer.

word_study.meaning: Tuv means 'goodness, kindness, benefit, well-being.' It describes both the moral excellence of God's character and the positive ordering of creation. God's tuv is his benevolent disposition.
word_study.significance: The final appeal 'for your goodness' sake' (lemaan tuvkha) grounds the prayer not in the speaker's worthiness but in God's essential benevolence. This is the ultimate basis: God is good, and his nature is to act for the good of his creatures, especially those who call upon him.

cross_references.connection: The foundational revelation of God's character: 'The LORD, The LORD, God merciful and gracious, slow to anger, and abounding in steadfast love and faithfulness.' Psalm 25:7 echoes this self-revelation, appealing to the very nature God revealed.

The discretion of a man defers his anger; it is his glory to overlook a transgression.' The concept of selective memory—letting go of offense—is the mark of wisdom and glory. God's 'not remembering' our sins reflects his wisdom.

'I, even I, am he that blotteth out thy transgressions for mine own sake, and will not remember thy sins.' The prophet uses identical language ('I will not remember') to describe God's forgiveness as an act of divine will, not forgetting but refusing to hold sin against the penitent.

Alma's great confession of youthful rebellion and subsequent divine forgiveness parallels the psalmist's stance: acknowledging serious, willful sin while appealing to God's mercy. Both experiences show the transformative power of true repentance grounded in God's character.

Behold, he who has repented of his sins, the same is forgiven, and I, the Lord, remember them no more.' The Restoration clarifies that divine forgiveness means God ceases to hold sin against the person—matching the psalmist's prayer for non-remembrance.

commentary.historical_context: In ancient Near Eastern royal inscriptions, the king often appeals to a god's 'name' and 'goodness' rather than his own achievements. Similarly, this psalm reflects the culture of lament and confession common in Israel and beyond. The language of 'sins of youth' suggests a mature speaker reflecting on earlier failures—a retrospective posture that became characteristic of penitential literature. The appeal to God's chesed reflects the covenant theology central to Israel's understanding of the God-human relationship: the covenant established God's commitment (chesed) to his people, and that commitment could be appealed to even when the human partner had broken covenant obligations.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: The pattern of acknowledging sin and appealing to God's mercy recurs throughout the Book of Mormon. See Alma 36:21-22, where Alma describes his spiritual death and resurrection through the power of Christ's atonement, and Helaman 5:12, which emphasizes building on Christ as the foundation of hope. The Book of Mormon adds the explicit understanding that this forgiveness is made possible through Christ's atoning sacrifice, which the psalmist foreshadows.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 88:68-69 teaches that knowledge comes through light and truth, which concept connects to Psalm 25:8-9's emphasis on God teaching sinners and the humble. Additionally, D&C 58:42 directly parallels the psalmist's request for non-remembrance: 'I, the Lord, remember them no more.' The Restoration makes explicit what the Old Testament prayer only implies: divine forgiveness is complete and not merely pragmatic.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The penitential stance of Psalm 25:7—confessing sin, appealing to God's character, and seeking forgiveness—is foundational to the temple experience. In the temple endowment, participants encounter both the reality of human transgression and God's willingness to forgive and restore those who approach him with sincerity. The prayer for selective memory anticipates the temple's teaching that God can cover and sanctify the penitent.

commentary.christological_typology: The psalmist's appeal to God's chesed (faithful love) and goodness as the basis for forgiveness foreshadows Christ, who is the full embodiment of God's mercy and the means by which forgiveness is accomplished. In the New Testament, Paul teaches that God's grace (charis, the Greek equivalent of chesed) was revealed and made operative through Christ's death (Romans 3:23-26). The prayer 'remember me according to your mercy' receives its ultimate answer in Christ's sacrifice, which makes divine forgiveness both just and gracious.
commentary.application: Modern covenant members who have experienced youthful sin or deliberate rebellion should take comfort in Psalm 25:7's assurance that God's character—not our worthiness—is the basis of forgiveness. Rather than rehearsing past failures or trying to 'earn back' God's favor through improved behavior, we appeal to the covenantal faithfulness God has already established. This psalm teaches that confession, repentance, and reliance on God's character are the path forward. It also invites us to grant the same selective memory to others—to 'remember' people according to their better nature and God's grace, not merely according to their past failures.

text_kjv: Good and upright is the LORD: therefore will he teach sinners in the way.

commentary.narrative:
Verse 8 shifts from petition to affirmation: it declares why the preceding prayer is both reasonable and hopeful. God's goodness (tov) and righteousness (yashar) are not abstract qualities but the active ground of his pedagogy. The logic is countercultural: because God is morally excellent, he teaches sinners rather than casting them away. This verse answers the question posed implicitly by verse 7: Why would a good and upright God care to 'remember' a sinner? The answer is that his goodness manifests precisely in instruction—in reaching out to the morally lost.

The verb yorah ('he teaches, instructs, directs') is the root of Torah, God's instructional law. God's response to sin is not primarily judgment or rejection but pedagogy. The sinner who recognizes his lostness and seeks instruction can expect to find in God not a stern judge but a teacher. This is a profound reframing of God's relationship to those who have failed: the good God is known by his willingness to instruct the wayward. The 'way' (derech) is both the moral path and the practical direction forward, and God teaches both.

word_study.meaning: Tov means 'good,' encompassing moral excellence and benevolence. Yashar means 'straight, upright, just, right.' Together they describe God's moral character: he is both benevolent and just, both kind and righteous.
word_study.significance: This pairing appears throughout the Psalms as shorthand for God's comprehensive moral excellence. The two terms together prevent either sentimentalism (goodness without justice) or harshness (justice without benevolence). God is both—and both motivate his willingness to teach.

word_study.meaning: Yorah is the simple future form of yarah, 'to teach, instruct, direct, show the way.' The root is connected to Torah, divine instruction. The verb carries the sense of pointing out the path, as an experienced guide would direct a lost traveler.
word_study.significance: The use of yorah—the verb from which 'Torah' derives—suggests that God's instruction is not merely advice but authoritative direction. God teaches as one with authority and knowledge. The same word appears in Psalm 25:9 ('he teaches the humble his way') and in Psalm 25:12 ('him shall he teach'), creating a theme of divine pedagogy throughout the psalm.

word_study.meaning: Chattaim is the plural of chatta, 'sinner, one who has missed the mark.' The term is descriptive, not necessarily condemnatory in this context—it simply identifies those who have failed to meet God's standard.
word_study.significance: The striking assertion is that God teaches chattaim—the morally failed, the off-target, those who have deviated from the right way. This opens the possibility that sin is not an absolute disqualifier from God's instruction but rather a condition that makes instruction necessary and available.

word_study.meaning: Derech means 'way, path, journey, manner of living.' The definite article 'the way' suggests not a vague direction but the specific righteous way God has established.
word_study.significance: The 'way' is central to biblical wisdom and covenantal theology: it is the path of life itself, the trajectory toward flourishing. God teaches the way—both the destination and the steps to get there.

cross_references.connection: Wisdom (personified) calls out in the streets to teach the simple and the foolish. Like Psalm 25:8, Proverbs presents divine instruction as available to those aware of their need, with no prerequisite except willingness to learn.
Come, ye children, hearken unto me: I will teach you the fear of the LORD.' This mirrors Psalm 25:8's affirmation that God is actively engaged in teaching and instructing those who draw near.

Thus saith the LORD, thy Redeemer, the Holy One of Israel; I am the LORD thy God which teacheth thee to profit, which leadeth thee by the way that thou shouldest go.' God's goodness (redemption and holiness) is bound up with his role as teacher and guide.

It is written in the prophets, And they shall be all taught of God.' The New Testament applies this Old Testament vision to Christ's redemptive work: those who listen to the Father's instruction are drawn to the Son.

If ye will awake and arouse your faculties, even to an experiment upon my words, and exercise a particle of faith, yea, even if ye can no more than desire to believe... God will make the word swell in your bosom.' Like Psalm 25:8, Alma teaches that divine instruction meets the sincere seeker and nourishes growth.

commentary.historical_context: In the ancient Near East, teaching (especially instruction in the moral and political order) was understood as a function of divine kingship. Egyptian pharaohs and Mesopotamian kings claimed to 'teach' their subjects in the ways of justice and order. This psalm inverts that expectation: it is not the human king who teaches in God's place, but God himself who teaches even sinners—the lowest class, the morally excluded. The verb yorah (teach) occurs frequently in law-code preambles and wisdom literature, where it denotes authoritative instruction from a source of knowledge and power. The original audience would have recognized that a truly good God would not seal himself off from the sinful but would reach out through instruction—a radical claim in any ancient culture.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: Alma's account of his conversion (Alma 36) emphasizes that even in his rebellion, he retained the capacity to hear God's voice and learn God's way. Doctrine and Covenants 6:33 states, 'If thou art faithful and full of the Holy Ghost, the powers of darkness shall have no power over thee,' indicating that God's teaching (through the Holy Ghost) is available even to those who have stumbled. The Book of Mormon repeatedly affirms that God reaches out to teach the wayward.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 64:10 teaches that God delights in the immediate forgiveness of sin, not as soft indulgence but as the foundation for transformation. The teaching aspect of forgiveness is central: God forgives in order that the forgiven may learn and grow. D&C 76:40-42 describes those who receive knowledge of God through the Spirit as being among God's greatest treasures—all of whom are sinners who have responded to divine instruction.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: In the temple, God is presented as the ultimate teacher, revealing sacred instruction to those who covenant with him. The pattern of God teaching sinners (Psalm 25:8) is enacted in the endowment, where participants move through states of relative ignorance toward increasing light and knowledge, guided by heavenly instruction throughout.

commentary.christological_typology: Christ is the ultimate manifestation of God's goodness and righteousness teaching sinners the way. In Matthew 11:28, Jesus invites: 'Come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest.' His entire ministry was one of instruction to sinners, publicans, and the morally excluded. Christ embodies the promise of Psalm 25:8—the good and upright God reaching out to teach and redeem the lost.
commentary.application: For modern believers, Psalm 25:8 means that God's fundamental stance toward us is not condemning but instructional. When we have failed morally and recognize our need, we should expect God to teach us—not to punish us into oblivion but to guide us into righteousness. This should inspire both repentance and hope: repentance because we acknowledge that we need instruction, and hope because the teacher is infinitely patient and good. It also invites us to adopt a similar posture toward others: to see those who have failed not as beyond redemption but as people who need and can receive instruction in the way. A covenant community that truly believes Psalm 25:8 will be characterized by its willingness to instruct and teach rather than merely condemn.

text_kjv: The meek will he guide in judgment: and the meek will he teach his way.

commentary.narrative:
Verse 9 specifies the recipients of divine teaching: anavim, the humble, the meek, the afflicted. The psalm narrows from its general claim that 'God teaches sinners' (v. 8) to the particular condition: those who are humble. This is not inconsistency but clarification. The teaching of God is not automatic or indiscriminate; it flows toward and finds purchase in the hearts of the humble. The 'meek' (anavim) here carries multiple dimensions: it denotes those who are socially lowly, those who have been reduced to dependence on God through suffering, and—most importantly—those who have adopted the spiritual posture of humility, recognizing their need before God.

The verse employs two parallel verbs: yadrek ('he guides, directs, treads') and yelammedu ('he teaches'). The first emphasizes direction through difficulty (guidance in judgment, mishpat), and the second emphasizes the transmission of God's path (derech). Together they describe the comprehensive nature of God's instruction: both the navigation through complex moral situations (judgment) and the long-term formation in God's way. The Covenant Rendering captures the distinction: God guides the humble in justice (the immediate moral decision) and teaches them his way (the larger trajectory). Humility is the prerequisite for this teaching because the humble person has already surrendered the illusion of self-sufficiency and stands ready to learn.

word_study.meaning: Anavim is the plural of anav, 'humble, meek, lowly, afflicted.' The term can denote either social lowliness (the poor, the marginalized) or spiritual humility (the disposition of recognizing dependence on God). The semantic range includes both objective circumstance and subjective stance.
word_study.significance: In biblical thought, the anavim are often identified as God's special concern and the particular recipients of his blessing. The term is central to the prophetic tradition (Isaiah 61:1: 'to bind up the brokenhearted, to proclaim liberty to the captives') and to the Beatitudes of the New Testament ('Blessed are the meek'). The psalm teaches that humility—either through circumstances that reduce one to dependence or through conscious choice to adopt a humble posture—is the condition for receiving God's instruction.

word_study.meaning: Yadrek is the imperfect (future/habitual) form of the verb yarah or nadrak, 'to guide, lead, direct, tread.' The image is of one walking a path and guiding another along it. The verb carries the sense of stepping out onto the way together.
word_study.significance: Unlike yorah (teach, instruct), yadrek emphasizes the relational and physical aspect of guidance—God does not simply tell the way but walks it with the humble, demonstrating the path through his presence and direction.

word_study.meaning: Mishpat encompasses 'judgment, justice, right order, legal decision, decree.' It denotes both the act of discerning what is right and the execution of that discernment. In this context, it refers to the specific moments when the humble must decide what is just.
word_study.significance: God guides not in general abstractions but in the concrete moments when justice must be discerned and practiced. The humble need guidance specifically at the point of decision, where abstract principle meets lived complexity.

word_study.meaning: Yelammedu is the imperfect form of lamad, 'to teach, learn, instruct, train.' The verb carries both the sense of transmission and of practice—teaching involves both telling and showing. Darko ('his way') is possessive: God's own path, his characteristic way of moving through the world.
word_study.significance: To teach someone God's way is not to hand them a rulebook but to form them in a lived pattern of obedience and trust. The repetition of anavim ('the humble') emphasizes that this teaching is covenantal—it happens in the context of relationship between the humble and their God.

cross_references.connection: Blessed are the meek: for they shall inherit the earth.' Jesus appropriates the anav tradition from the Psalms and the prophets, identifying the humble as those upon whom God's future blessings fall.
The fear of the LORD is the instruction of wisdom; and before honour is humility.' The book of Proverbs teaches that humility is the precondition for wisdom—the same teaching as Psalm 25:9.

God resisteth the proud, but giveth grace unto the humble. Humble yourselves therefore under the mighty hand of God, that he may exalt you.' The New Testament adopts the Old Testament principle that God's favor flows toward the humble and his resistance toward the proud.

Great and marvelous are thy works, O Lord God Almighty! ... And by the power of thy Spirit thou wast carried away in the Spirit and beholdest the things which were to come.' The humble, open-hearted recipients of revelation are shown the vision of God's kingdom—a modern application of God teaching his way to the meek.

For the natural man is an enemy to God... But to be spiritually minded is life eternal. The Book of Mormon echoes Psalm 25:9 in teaching that becoming humble—losing the pride of the natural man—is prerequisite to receiving God's instruction and entering his way.

commentary.historical_context: In ancient Israel, the anavim ('humble, afflicted') emerged as a distinctive group, especially following the Assyrian deportations and the Babylonian exile. The term came to identify not just the economically poor but the spiritually oriented poor—those who had been reduced to dependence on God and who found in that dependence a path to righteousness. The Psalter, compiled largely in the post-exilic period, shows deep concern for the anavim and their vindication by God. Psalm 25:9 reflects this concern: those whom the world has humbled are the ones most capable of receiving God's instruction. The ancient context makes clear that anavim is not a counsel of voluntary self-abasement but rather a recognition that those with few other resources must learn to rely on God's guidance.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: Alma 32 presents a discourse on faith that directly parallels Psalm 25:9. Alma teaches the poor in spirit at Antionum, saying that they are 'blessed' because their poverty has prepared them to receive truth. He asks, 'Will ye exercise the faith which ye have even if ye have not, yet if ye believe in Christ ye can be nourished by his word.' The humble (those without earthly substance) become the ideal students of God's way. Similarly, Nephi's contrast between the proud Laman and Lemuel and the humble Nephi and Sam demonstrates that humility is the prerequisite for revelation and guidance.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 112:10 states, 'Be thou humble; and the Lord thy God shall lead thee by the hand, and give thee answer to thy prayers.' This directly affirms Psalm 25:9's promise that the humble will be guided by the Lord. D&C 4:2 teaches that God grants to those who come unto him with sincere hearts (a posture of humility) the desire to serve and the understanding to do so. The Doctrine and Covenants repeatedly affirms that the meek inherit the promises.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The temple ceremony emphasizes the posture of humility before God: participants are clothed in simple garments, adopted into God's covenant family, and taught sacred ordinances. The progression through the temple is one of increasing light and knowledge, available precisely to those who approach in humility and faith. The temple enacts Psalm 25:9's promise: the humble are guided through moral complexity (represented by the endowment's scenarios) and taught God's way (through covenants and ordinances).

commentary.christological_typology: Christ is the embodiment of the anavim—the humble servant who emptied himself and took on human form. In Philippians 2:5-8, Paul describes Christ's fundamental attitude as one of humility: 'Let this mind be in you, which was also in Christ Jesus... he humbled himself, and became obedient.' Jesus teaches his disciples, 'Learn of me; for I am meek and lowly in heart' (Matthew 11:29). The path that Christ both walked and teaches is the way of humility before the Father. Those who follow Christ's way do so by adopting his posture of meekness.
commentary.application: For modern covenant members, Psalm 25:9 is a direct invitation to humility as the gateway to spiritual understanding. When we face moral complexity or spiritual confusion, our first step should be to adopt the stance of the anavim—to lay aside pride in our own judgment and stand ready to be guided. This means approaching scripture, priesthood leaders, and the Holy Ghost not with a posture of superiority or skepticism but with genuine openness. It also means recognizing that life circumstances that humble us—setbacks, losses, trials—can become the very conditions in which God teaches us his way most effectively. A proud person may read Psalm 25:9 intellectually, but only the humble can receive its promise.

text_kjv: All the paths of the LORD are mercy and truth unto such as keep his covenant and his testimonies.

commentary.narrative:
Verse 10 represents the theological summit of Psalm 25. It makes a comprehensive statement about the character of God and the nature of covenant relationship. The speaker asserts that every orach ('path,' 'way,' 'trail') that the LORD walks—every action God takes, every decision he makes, every way he moves through history—is characterized by chesed ve-emet (faithful love and truth, or merciful faithfulness). This is not a claim about one aspect of God's behavior but about his comprehensive character. When God acts, his actions exhibit both devotion (chesed) and reliability (emet). These two terms together form a hendiadys—a single complex reality expressed through two words.

Crucially, verse 10 also introduces a condition: this experience of God's character belongs specifically to those who keep his covenant (berito) and his decrees/testimonies (edotav). The relationship is bilateral. God's chesed ve-emet is not an impersonal force dispensed indiscriminately but a covenantal reality, flowing fully to those who reciprocate with obedience. This moves beyond the universal claim (God is good) to the specific promise (God's goodness pursues those who keep covenant). The Covenant Rendering emphasizes this crucial distinction: chesed ve-emet belongs to those who keep the covenant and decrees—it is the reward and experience of the covenant-keeper, not a blanket universal benediction. The psalm thus binds together the prior affirmations (God teaches sinners, guides the humble) with this condition: the full realization of God's character comes in the covenant relationship.

word_study.meaning: Orchot is the plural of orach, 'path, way, trail, journey, manner of life.' In biblical usage, it often denotes both the literal traveling path and the figurative life-path, the trajectory a person or community follows.
word_study.significance: By speaking of 'all the paths' of God (not just one or some, but all), the psalmist makes a comprehensive claim: every aspect of God's behavior, every decision and action, exhibits the same character. There is no hidden, vindictive God behind the merciful one—all his ways are consistent.

word_study.term_english: mercy and truth / faithful love and truth
word_study.meaning: This is the signature pair in the Hebrew Bible for God's essential character. Chesed (often translated 'mercy,' 'lovingkindness,' 'steadfast love,' or—in The Covenant Rendering—'faithful love') denotes committed, covenantal devotion. Emet ('truth,' 'faithfulness,' 'reliability,' 'what is true') denotes the trustworthiness and constancy of that devotion. Together they mean: God's love is not fickle or sentimental (emet grounds it in reality and reliability), and God's truthfulness is not cold or distant (chesed fills it with warmth and commitment).
word_study.significance: This pair appears first at Sinai in Exodus 34:6, where God reveals his essential nature. It recurs throughout the Psalms and wisdom literature as the bedrock of hope. The source note in The Covenant Rendering emphasizes that this is not two separate qualities but one complex reality: God's reliable, covenantal, devoted love. To know God is to know this pairing.

word_study.meaning: Notserei is the plural of notser, 'keeper, one who keeps watch over, preserves.' Berit is 'covenant, treaty, binding agreement.' To 'keep the covenant' means to maintain fidelity to the bilateral agreement God established, to live within its obligations and blessings.
word_study.significance: The term 'keeper of the covenant' (notser berito) emphasizes active maintenance. Covenant is not static but lived; keeping it requires ongoing faithfulness, commitment, and obedience. Those who keep covenant position themselves to experience God's chesed ve-emet.

word_study.meaning: Edot (plural edotim, edot) refers to 'testimonies,' 'stipulations,' 'laws,' or 'decrees.' The term derives from ed, 'witness,' and carries the sense of God's stipulations standing as witness to the covenant relationship. God's edot are the specifications of how covenant-keepers are to live.
word_study.significance: By speaking of 'his testimonies,' the psalm identifies God's laws not as arbitrary rules but as expressions of the covenant itself. To keep God's edot is to honor the covenant relationship. The parallel structure ('covenant and his testimonies') suggests that testimonies are the practical specification of the covenant.

cross_references.connection: And the LORD passed by before him, and proclaimed, The LORD, The LORD, God merciful and gracious, slow to anger, and abounding in steadfast love and truth.' This is the foundational revelation of God's character (chesed ve-emet), which Psalm 25:10 echoes and applies.

But thou, O Lord, art a God full of compassion, and gracious, long suffering, and plenteous in mercy and truth.' A parallel affirmation of God's comprehensive character of chesed ve-emet, applied to God's dealings with his people.

Justice and judgment are the habitation of thy throne: mercy and truth shall go before thy face.' This verse specifies that God's chesed ve-emet (mercy and truth) are the advance guard of his throne—they characterize his rule.

Know therefore that the LORD thy God, he is God, the faithful God, which keepeth covenant and mercy with them that love him and keep his commandments unto a thousand generations.' The covenantal condition is explicit: God's merciful faithfulness is experienced by those who keep the covenant and commandments.

And it came to pass that I, Nephi, beheld the power of the Lamb of God, that it descended upon the saints of the church of the Lamb, and upon the covenant people of the Lord, who were scattered upon all the face of the earth; and they were armed with righteousness and with the power of God in great glory.' The Book of Mormon applies the covenant promise of Psalm 25:10 to those who accept Christ and keep covenant.

commentary.historical_context: The phrase 'chesed ve-emet' is the theological signature of Israel's covenant tradition, appearing in contexts of God's faithfulness to patriarchal promises (Genesis 24:27), God's revelation at Sinai (Exodus 34:6), and the Davidic covenant (Psalm 89:14). In the post-exilic context, when Psalm 25 was likely composed or compiled, the affirmation that all God's paths exhibit chesed ve-emet would have been both a comfort and a challenge: a comfort to the exiled community (God's character had not changed despite Jerusalem's fall), and a challenge (the people's return to covenant faithfulness was the condition for experiencing that character fully). The bilateral nature of covenant was essential to ancient Near Eastern treaty thinking: the suzerain's benefits flowed to the vassal who maintained his obligations.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: The Book of Mormon repeatedly affirms that God's merciful faithfulness (chesed ve-emet) is bound to the covenant. Alma 7:26-27 teaches that God denieth none who cometh unto him with a broken heart and contrite spirit, 'and he hath promised unto him that he shall take upon him the sins of his people.' The Book of Mormon emphasizes that God's mercy (which could be understood as chesed) is extended through the atonement of Christ to all who keep covenant with him. Helaman 5:9-12 describes the foundation of Christ as one that 'cannot fall,' available to 'the children of men' who 'build upon this foundation' through covenant.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 21:4-5 states that God's paths are straight and his course one eternal round, adding, 'Therefore, prepare thy heart to receive and obey the instructions which I am about to give unto you.' The promise of God's unwavering, covenantal faithfulness is tied to obedience. D&C 132:6 promises eternal increase and exaltation specifically to those who 'keep my covenants.' The Doctrine and Covenants makes explicit that God's chesed ve-emet flows toward covenant-keepers.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The temple ceremony emphasizes the bilateral nature of covenant: God makes promises and offers blessings to those who covenant with him to keep his commandments. The endowment teaching of 'obedience, sacrifice, gospel, virtue, and knowledge' specifies the human obligations within the covenant. Psalm 25:10's affirmation that God's paths are mercy and truth for those who keep covenant is enacted in the temple's progression from ignorance toward light and truth, conditional upon covenant-keeping.

commentary.christological_typology: Christ is the perfect keeper of the covenant between God and humanity. In Matthew 3:15, when baptized by John, Jesus says, 'Suffer it to be so now: for thus it becometh us to fulfill all righteousness'—he keeps the covenant perfectly. Christ's life, death, and resurrection are the ultimate expression of God's chesed ve-emet: his merciful faithfulness shown through the atonement (Romans 3:25-26). Those who enter covenant through Christ's name become participants in God's covenantal faithfulness; their paths too become marked by mercy and truth as they follow his way.
commentary.application: Psalm 25:10 teaches modern covenant members that the full experience of God's merciful faithfulness (chesed ve-emet) is conditional on covenant-keeping. This does not mean that God's character changes or that his love is earned, but rather that covenantal obedience is the channel through which God's character flows fully into our lives. When we keep our temple covenants, honor the Sabbath, sustain Church leaders, keep the law of chastity, and serve others, we position ourselves to experience God's complete character—both his warmth (chesed) and his reliability (emet). Conversely, when we break covenant, we shut ourselves off from the full experience of God's character, like a person who stands in falling rain but holds an umbrella. The promise is that all God's paths—all his dealings with us—will be characterized by devotion and truth if we maintain covenant fidelity.

text_kjv: For thy name's sake, O LORD, pardon mine iniquity; for it is great.

commentary.narrative:
Verse 11 returns from the theological affirmation of verse 10 to direct petition, and it contains perhaps the most striking moment of confession in the entire psalm. The speaker asks for forgiveness with radical honesty: 'pardon mine iniquity; for it is great' (salach leavoni ki rav-hu). Rather than minimizing guilt or offering self-justification, the speaker magnifies it. The iniquity is rav—large, abundant, heavy, overwhelming. This frank admission is remarkable: in most religious contexts, the penitent tries to make his transgression seem smaller or less culpable. This speaker does the opposite. He names his guilt as extensive, beyond excuse.

Yet the basis for the petition is not the speaker's reform or worth. It is lemaan shimkha—'for the sake of your name.' God's reputation, God's glory, God's revealed character is invoked as the reason for forgiveness. The prayer essentially says: 'My iniquity is enormous, and the only thing that can be greater than it is your name and the goodness your name represents. Forgive me—not so that I feel better, but so that your name is glorified. Let the world see that the God who has revealed himself as merciful and faithful does indeed forgive even great transgression.' This is a profound reframing of forgiveness: it is not primarily about the sinner's benefit but about God's honor. To forgive great iniquity is to demonstrate the greatness of God's character. The Covenant Rendering captures this by translating avon not as 'iniquity' (which can sound abstract) but as 'guilt'—the weight and burden of actual wrongdoing.

word_study.meaning: Lemaan means 'for the sake of, for the purpose of, in order that.' Shem ('name') in biblical context denotes not merely a label but the revelation and character of the person. God's shem is the sum of his self-revelation—his covenantal commitments, his demonstrated attributes, his glory. To invoke God's name is to appeal to all that he has revealed himself to be.
word_study.significance: By appealing 'for your name's sake,' the speaker invokes God's honor and reputation. It is as though the prayer says: 'The forgiveness I ask will demonstrate who you are. If you forgive my great iniquity, your name will be glorified.' This kind of appeal—based on God's honor rather than the speaker's desert—is frequent in the Psalms and in Moses' intercessions (Exodus 32:11-14, Numbers 14:13-16).

word_study.meaning: Salach means 'to pardon, forgive, excuse, show clemency.' It is not equivalent to 'cover' or 'atone for' but specifically to 'pardon'—to refuse to hold something against someone, to let it go. In the Hebrew Bible, salach is often used of God's pardoning; humans rarely salach one another.
word_study.significance: The use of salach emphasizes that forgiveness is a divine prerogative. God alone can truly pardon; he chooses not to hold transgression against the guilty party. This makes the petition particularly poignant—the speaker is asking God to exercise the prerogative of the powerful toward the weak.

word_study.meaning: Avon encompasses 'iniquity,' 'guilt,' 'moral wrong,' and 'punishment for wrong.' The term is complex: it can refer to the transgression itself, the moral culpability of the transgressor, and the consequences that follow. The Covenant Rendering translates it 'guilt' to emphasize the moral weight and burden.
word_study.significance: By using avon rather than chet or pesha, the speaker emphasizes the serious, persistent nature of his transgression. Avon is the kind of sin that lingers, that has consequences, that weighs on the conscience. It is not a momentary lapse but a condition of guilt.

word_study.meaning: Rav means 'great, much, abundant, many, large, mighty.' In this context, it modifies the guilt: the guilt is rav—extensive, overwhelming, great in magnitude.
word_study.significance: The honest admission that the guilt is rav (not small, not excusable, but genuinely great) is the psalmist's final acceptance of accountability before God. This makes the petition all the more striking: the speaker simultaneously admits the enormity of his guilt and appeals to God's name for pardon. There is no attempt to minimize or excuse.

cross_references.connection: Moses intercedes for Israel after the golden calf incident, appealing: 'Wherefore should the Egyptians speak, and say, For mischief did he bring them out... Turn from thy fierce wrath.' Like Psalm 25:11, Moses bases his prayer for forgiveness on God's reputation and name.

Moses again intercedes: 'Now if thou shalt kill all this people as one man, then the nations which have heard the fame of thee will speak, saying, Because the LORD was not able to bring this people into the land.' The appeal is for God's name's sake—for the vindication of God's character and power.

I, even I, am he that blotteth out thy transgressions for mine own sake, and will not remember thy sins.' God's forgiveness flows from God's purpose to demonstrate mercy—reminiscent of Psalm 25:11's appeal that forgiveness will glorify God's name.

O Lord, hear; O Lord, forgive; O Lord, hearken and do; defer not, for thine own sake, O my God.' Daniel's confession includes the same appeal: forgive 'for thine own sake,' invoking God's honor as the basis for mercy.

Thus mercy can satisfy the demands of justice, and encircles them in the arms of safety, while he that has no faith to repent is exposed, by himself, to all the power of justice; thus justice exerciseth all his power upon him.' The Book of Mormon teaches that mercy and justice must both be satisfied; God's character (his name) is at stake in how he handles transgression.

commentary.historical_context: In the ancient Near East, a god's 'name' was his reputation and power—what made him honored and feared. To appeal to a god's name was to invoke his self-interest in maintaining his reputation. This is not cynical manipulation but theological honesty: God's own character and glory are at stake in how he responds to transgression. The pattern of intercession based on God's name appears throughout Israel's history—Abraham (Genesis 18), Moses (Exodus 32, Numbers 14), Hezekiah (2 Kings 19)—suggesting that this was a recognized and respected mode of prayer in Israel's tradition.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: Alma's great confession of sin (Alma 36) includes both the frank acknowledgment of his transgression and the recognition that forgiveness comes through Christ. Alma says, 'I was racked with eternal torment... behold, my soul did turn from the wrath of God, and did go no more after the killing of the prophets.' The Book of Mormon pattern is similar to Psalm 25:11: acknowledge the seriousness of guilt, appeal to God's mercy (in the BOM, specifically through Christ), and understand that forgiveness glorifies God's character. Helaman 5:5-6 teaches that redemption comes 'because of the redemption of God, which has been bought with his blood, that hath been shed for the remission of sins.'
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 58:42 states, 'Behold, he who has repented of his sins, the same is forgiven, and I, the Lord, remember them no more.' God's forgiveness is presented not as a reward for good behavior but as a divine act that demonstrates God's merciful character. D&C 88:104 teaches that all things are 'created and made to bear record of me, both things which are temporal, and things which are spiritual; things which are in the heavens above, and things which are on the earth, and things which are in the earth, and things which are under the earth, both visible and invisible'—emphasizing that all creation exists to glorify God's name. Forgiveness, then, is one way God's name is glorified.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: In the temple, the idea that forgiveness glorifies God's name is enacted through the understanding that the atonement of Christ redeems the penitent and demonstrates God's justice, mercy, and love simultaneously. The forgiveness offered in the temple covenant is explicitly tied to Christ's redemptive sacrifice—his blood, shed for the remission of sins. This makes clear that forgiveness is not a soft indulgence but a supreme manifestation of God's name and character.

commentary.christological_typology: Christ is the perfect embodiment of the principle that forgiveness glorifies God's name. His sacrifice is described in Hebrews 10:14 as making perfect those who are sanctified, 'by one offering.' The cross demonstrates simultaneously God's justice (the penalty for sin is real and serious), God's mercy (forgiveness is offered), and God's love (God pays the price). In this way, Christ's atonement is the ultimate act of forgiveness for the sake of God's name—it shows God to be both righteous and merciful, just and gracious. Romans 3:25-26 explains: 'Whom God hath set forth to be a propitiation through faith in his blood, to declare his righteousness... that he might be just, and the justifier of him which believeth in Jesus.'
commentary.application: For modern believers, Psalm 25:11 invites a reframing of how we approach repentance and seek forgiveness. Rather than appealing to God on the basis of our improvement or worthiness (which is always minimal), we should appeal to God's character and reputation. When we confess great sin honestly and ask for forgiveness, we are essentially saying: 'Lord, my transgression is real and serious, but your name—your character as merciful and faithful—is greater still. Forgive me, not because I deserve it, but so that your name is glorified in my redemption.' This shifts the focus from our shame and inadequacy to God's glory. It also means that when we forgive others, we do so 'for God's name's sake'—recognizing that our willingness to pardon, like God's, demonstrates and glorifies God's character. A community characterized by genuine, big-hearted forgiveness testifies to the world about God's nature.

text_kjv: What man is he that feareth the LORD? him shall he teach in the way that he shall choose.

commentary.narrative:
Verse 12 shifts from the first-person petition of verses 7-11 to a rhetorical question that invites the broader community into the psalm's teaching. The question 'What man is he that feareth the LORD?' is not genuine puzzlement but rhetorical affirmation: it is an invitation to readers to identify themselves as those who fear God. Those who do—the question implies—will find that God teaches them 'in the way that he shall choose' (bederekh yivchar). The verb yorah ('teach') reappears for the third time in this psalm (vv. 8, 9, 12), emphasizing that divine pedagogy is the consistent response to the faithful.

The final phrase 'in the way he shall choose' (bederekh yivchar) is particularly rich. It suggests that life presents genuine choices and decisions, and God's instruction enables the discerning of the right path. The phrase could mean either 'in the way he [God] chooses for them' or 'in the way they choose with God's instruction'—the Hebrew is ambiguous and the ambiguity is itself instructive. The point is that those who fear God learn to choose rightly because they are taught by him. The fear of God is not paralyzing dread but the foundation of wisdom (proverbs 1:7), the orientation that makes right choice possible. Verse 12 thus serves as an invitation and a summary: all the prior teaching about God's character, his willingness to teach sinners and guide the humble, and his covenantal faithfulness—all of this is available to 'the one who fears the LORD.'

word_study.meaning: Mi means 'who.' Zeh is the demonstrative 'this, that, the one.' Ha-ish is 'the man, mankind, the person.' Together, the phrase is a rhetorical question: 'Who is this person?' or 'What kind of man is he?'
word_study.significance: The rhetorical question invites the reader to identify himself or herself as the one described: the fearful of God, the one who will be taught. It is a form of address that includes the listener in the promise.

word_study.meaning: Yere is the masculine singular participle of yarah, 'to fear, be afraid, stand in awe.' Yere YHWH is the standing phrase for the fear of God. In biblical usage, this fear is not craven terror but reverent awe—a profound respect for God's power, holiness, and character that shapes one's entire orientation to life.
word_study.significance: The fear of God is presented throughout wisdom literature as the beginning of knowledge (Proverbs 1:7) and understanding (Proverbs 9:10). It is the precondition for receiving divine instruction, just as humility is in verse 9. The fear of God and the love of God are not opposed in biblical thought; they are complementary: one fears God's power and holiness and loves God's character and goodness.

word_study.meaning: Yorenu is the imperfect (future/habitual) form of yarah ('to teach, instruct, direct') with a pronominal suffix ('him'). God will instruct the one who fears him.
word_study.significance: The third appearance of yorah (teach) in this psalm creates a clear theme: divine instruction is available to sinners (v. 8), to the humble (v. 9), and to those who fear God (v. 12). The repetition emphasizes that God's primary response to human need is pedagogical, not punitive.

word_study.term_english: in the way he shall choose
word_study.meaning: Bederekh is 'in/according to the way.' Yivchar is the imperfect form of bachar, 'to choose, select, elect.' The phrase is intentionally ambiguous: it could mean 'in the way [God] chooses [for them]' or 'in the way [the person] chooses [with God's teaching].'
word_study.significance: The Covenant Rendering resolves the ambiguity by translating 'in the way he should choose,' emphasizing that God's instruction enables right choosing. The underlying point is that human decision-making is not autonomous but is shaped by divine instruction. Those taught by God learn to choose the right way. This respects both divine guidance and human responsibility: God teaches, and the person learns to choose accordingly.

cross_references.connection: The fear of the LORD is the beginning of knowledge: but fools despise wisdom and instruction.' Fear of God is presented as the prerequisite for receiving wisdom and instruction, just as in Psalm 25:12.
The fear of the LORD is the beginning of wisdom: and the knowledge of the holy is understanding.' Fear of God is linked explicitly to wisdom and knowledge of God.

Come, ye children, hearken unto me: I will teach you the fear of the LORD.' This verse echoes Psalm 25:12's promise of instruction, specifically on the fear of God. Those who learn fear also receive instruction.
By humility and the fear of the LORD are riches, and honour, and life.' Fear of God (like humility in v. 9) is presented as the path to blessing and life.

Search these commandments, for they are true and faithful, and the prophecies and promises which are in them shall all be fulfilled.' Those who search God's word with fear and reverence receive the instruction God offers.

commentary.historical_context: The phrase 'fear of the LORD' (yirat YHWH or yere YHWH) is central to Hebrew wisdom literature and covenantal theology. It denotes not craven terror but the proper orientation of a creature toward the Creator—a combination of reverence, awe, obedience, and love. In the ancient Near East, the relationship between a god and a worshiper was often described in terms of fear; the biblical innovation was to combine this fear with the covenantal language of love and faithfulness. The wisdom literature, particularly Proverbs and Job, shows that fear of God is not opposed to human learning and discernment but is rather the foundation that enables true understanding. The rhetorical form of verse 12—the question that invites identification—is characteristic of wisdom literature, which often addresses readers directly and invites them to take on particular postures or identities.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: The Book of Mormon repeatedly affirms that the fear of God (understood as reverent awe and obedience) leads to instruction and blessing. 2 Nephi 9:41 teaches that those who trust in the Lord and do good shall be blessed. Alma 32:21-22 emphasizes that faith (which grows from the fear of God) is the foundation for learning from God's word. The Book of Mormon pattern parallels Psalm 25:12: those who approach God with proper reverence receive his instruction.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 38:1 begins: 'Hearken, O ye my people, which belong to the church, who have accepted my covenant and your sins are forgiven you.' The covenant that forgives sin is available to those who accept it with reverent commitment. D&C 89:1 teaches that principles of health are revealed 'in consequence of evils and designs which do and will exist in the hearts of conspiring men in the last days'—emphasizing that divine instruction responds to human need and condition. Those who fear God (respect his wisdom) receive his instruction for their welfare.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: In the temple, the fear of God is enacted through the participant's approach to sacred space with reverence, humility, and obedience. The instruction given in the temple is understood as divine teaching to those who approach with proper fear and respect. The endowment ceremony moves participants from a state of relative darkness (ignorance) toward light (knowledge), with the precondition being reverent participation in the covenantal ordinances.

commentary.christological_typology: Christ embodies the fear of God in its perfection. Hebrews 5:7 describes Jesus in the Garden of Gethsemane: 'Who in the days of his flesh, when he had offered up prayers and supplications with strong crying and tears unto him that was able to save him from death, and was heard in that he feared God.' Christ's reverent fear of the Father is not craven terror but complete alignment with the Father's will. Those who follow Christ learn to adopt his stance of reverent obedience toward the Father. John 8:28-29 records Jesus saying, 'When ye have lifted up the Son of man, then shall ye know that I am he, and that I do nothing of myself; but as my Father hath taught me, I speak these things. And he that sent me is with me: the Father hath not left me alone; for I do always those things that please him.' Christ learns from the Father through reverent obedience and in turn teaches those who follow him.
commentary.application: Psalm 25:12 invites modern members of the Church to embrace the fear of God as the foundation of all learning and choice-making. This fear—understood as reverent awe, respect, and obedience—positions us to receive divine instruction. When we face decisions about education, career, relationships, or spiritual direction, we should approach them not with the presumption that we already know the right choice, but with the reverent openness to God's instruction characteristic of those who fear him. This is the opposite of pride or self-sufficiency. It is also the opposite of paralyzing anxiety; it is the confident trust that if we fear God, he will teach us 'in the way [we] should choose.' For parents and Church leaders, the psalm suggests that the primary goal is not to make all choices for others but to cultivate in them a fear of God—a reverent respect for his wisdom and willingness to be taught by him—so that they learn to choose rightly for themselves.

text_kjv: His soul shall dwell at ease; and his seed shall inherit the earth.

commentary.narrative: Psalm 25 is an acrostic of the Hebrew alphabet, with each verse beginning with the next consecutive letter. Verse 13 is the nun (ן) line, marking the midpoint of the poem and shifting focus from the speaker's personal plea to a promise about the righteous person's ultimate destiny. The verse presents a two-part promise: the fear of the LORD brings present security (the soul dwelling in goodness), and it brings future inheritance (the seed receiving the land). This is not a guarantee of ease or wealth, but rather the assurance that a life lived in God-fearing obedience settles into a profound sense of well-being that no external circumstance can ultimately disturb.
commentary.narrative_continued: The Hebrew word nafsho (נַפְשׁוֹ, 'his soul') encompasses the entire person—not just the spiritual part but the whole self, the seat of desire, emotion, and will. The verb talin (תָּלִין, 'will lodge/spend the night') carries the connotation of seeking shelter and rest. In the ancient Near East, traveling at night without shelter exposed one to danger; to 'lodge' safely meant to find refuge. The soul that dwells with the LORD finds this kind of rest—protected, secure, at ease. The second promise—that the seed will inherit the land—echoes the Abrahamic covenant, where inheritance of the land was the physical sign of God's blessing passed through generations. The righteous person's legacy is not merely personal gain but covenantal blessing that extends forward.
commentary.narrative_continued2: For the Psalmist's original audience, land inheritance had profound theological significance. It represented not just property but God's faithfulness, the fulfillment of promise, and the security of place. Jesus later reframed this promise in Matthew 5:5 ('Blessed are the meek, for they shall inherit the earth'), showing that the inheritance is ultimately redemptive and applies to all who align themselves with God's kingdom, not merely to biological descendants. The verse teaches a principle: alignment with God's fear produces both present peace and future blessing.

cross_references.connection: God's promise to Abraham: 'Unto thy seed will I give this land.' Verse 13 extends this patriarchal promise to all who fear the LORD.
Jesus's Beatitude reframes the inheritance promise: 'Blessed are the meek: for they shall inherit the earth.' The ultimate inheritance transcends physical land.
The connection between fearing God and dwelling safely: 'And now, Israel, what doth the LORD thy God require of thee...but to fear the LORD thy God...for thy good?'
Another expression of the righteous person's stability: 'The righteous shall never be removed: but the wicked shall not inhabit the earth.'

commentary.christological_typology: The Psalmist's promise of rest and inheritance finds its ultimate fulfillment in Christ, who is both the heir of all things (Hebrews 1:2) and the one who grants inheritance to his followers. Those who fear God and follow Christ receive the 'rest' that Jesus promised: 'Come unto me, all ye that are weary...and I will give you rest' (Matthew 11:28). The 'land' becomes the kingdom of God—an eternal inheritance secured through Christ's redemption.

word_study.meaning: The whole person; the seat of life, desire, emotion, and will. In Hebrew anthropology, the soul is not separate from the body but encompasses the entire living being.
word_study.significance: When the Psalmist says 'his soul shall dwell at ease,' he means the entire person—body, mind, spirit—finds lasting security and well-being in covenant relationship with God.

word_study.term_english: dwell at ease / lodge in goodness
word_study.meaning: The verb talin means 'to lodge, to spend the night in safety.' Be-tov means 'in goodness, in well-being.' The image is of finding shelter and rest after danger or travel.
word_study.significance: This is not idle comfort but the security of the protected—the assurance that comes from knowing one is sheltered by God's care. The Covenant Rendering's 'rest in prosperity' captures the sense of settled well-being.

word_study.meaning: To inherit, to possess as an inheritance (yerush); the land (erets) promised to the patriarchs. Inheritance suggests both gift and covenant fulfillment.
word_study.significance: This echoes Genesis 12:7 and other Abrahamic covenant texts. The land is not earned but given—it is the fruit of covenantal faithfulness over generations. The righteous live not for themselves alone but for the continuation and blessing of their seed.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: The Book of Mormon extends the Abrahamic covenant to all faithful believers. Nephi's vision in 1 Nephi 13-14 shows that the inheritance promised to Abraham is ultimately spiritual—the inheritance of God's kingdom through Jesus Christ. The righteous 'rest' promised in Psalm 25:13 parallels the 'rest' spoken of in Moroni 7, where those who endure in faith shall rest in the presence of God.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 59:2-4 promises rest to the righteous: 'Wherefore I say unto you, that ye ought to forgive one another...And I give unto you a commandment, that ye shall observe to keep my law...' The promise of rest and inheritance is tied to faithfulness. D&C 76 describes the inheritance of the righteous in the celestial kingdom, showing that the land inheritance speaks of a greater, eternal inheritance.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The temple represents the place where God's presence dwells and where the faithful 'lodge' in his presence. The promise of the seed inheriting the land connects to the covenant of posterity made in the temple—that the righteous shall be sealed together with their descendants. The temple endowment teaches that adherence to covenant brings both present peace and future exaltation.

commentary.application: For the modern Latter-day Saint, this verse teaches that fidelity to God brings both immediate and long-term blessing. The 'ease' is not the absence of struggle but the deep peace that comes from knowing you are living in alignment with God's will. This peace is not dependent on outward circumstances but on inward orientation toward the LORD. Additionally, the emphasis on 'seed' inheriting the land reminds us that our covenants have generational significance—the choices we make to fear and follow God affect our children and their children. We are stewards not just of our own spiritual life but of a legacy of faith.
commentary.historical_context: In ancient Near Eastern thought, land was not merely real estate but the sign of divine blessing and covenantal security. The Abrahamic promise tied blessing directly to land inheritance—a tangible, visible sign that God had chosen this family and fulfilled his word. For the Psalmist's community in exile or in times of political instability, this promise would have been both a comfort and a hope: even when the present circumstances were uncertain, the promise to the righteous and their seed remained. The imagery of the soul 'lodging' in goodness evokes the security sought by the ancient traveler—a place of rest, protection, and belonging. The verb talin ('to lodge') suggests not a permanent dwelling but a night's safe rest in the midst of a journey, reinforcing that present well-being coexists with future promise.

text_kjv: The secret of the LORD is with them that fear him; and he will shew them his covenant.

commentary.narrative: Verse 14, the samekh (ס) line, presents one of the most profound statements in the Psalter about the nature of divine relationship. The Hebrew word sod (סוֹד), here translated 'secret,' carries multiple layers of meaning: it can mean a secret counsel, an intimate conversation, or an inner circle of confidants. The Psalmist is saying that God does not keep his deepest purposes hidden from those who fear him—rather, he admits them into his confidence. This is a radical statement about God's accessibility and the privilege of the fearful. God shares not merely information but intimacy itself.
commentary.narrative_continued: The verse establishes a direct correlation: those who fear the LORD are granted access to his counsel (sod). This is not a reward earned through works but a relational privilege that flows from reverence and submission. The second line says that God makes his covenant known to them. The word covenant (berit, בְרִית) refers to the binding agreement between God and his people—the terms of relationship, the promises made, the mutual commitments. Those in God's inner circle know not only what he is doing but why he is doing it; they understand the covenant framework within which all his actions operate.
commentary.narrative_continued2: The term 'counsel of the LORD' appears elsewhere in Scripture with the same weight. In Job 15:8, Eliphaz challenges Job: 'Hast thou heard the secret of God?' (yod sod Elohim)—implying that such access is extraordinary and not lightly claimed. In Amos 3:7, the prophet declares: 'Surely the Lord GOD will do nothing, but he revealeth his secret unto his servants the prophets' (ki lo yaaseh YHWH Adonai dabar ki im-galah sodo el-avadav hanevi'im). The righteous, especially those called as prophets, are included in God's inner workings. The Psalmist democratizes this idea: anyone who fears the LORD—not just prophets or kings—is admitted to this circle of divine confidence.

cross_references.connection: The prophet declares that God reveals his counsel (sod) to his servants the prophets. Psalm 25:14 extends this privilege to all who fear God, not just prophets.
Eliphaz challenges Job with the question 'Hast thou heard the secret of God?'—acknowledging that access to divine counsel is extraordinary and not easily claimed.
A parallel statement: 'For the froward is abomination to the LORD: but his secret is with the righteous.' Those in covenant alignment with God know his purposes.
Jesus says to his disciples, 'I have called you friends...for I have told you all things that I have heard of my Father.' Covenant relationship means admission into God's intimate counsel.
Moses distinguishes between 'secret things' that belong to God and 'revealed things' that belong to us and our children forever. The covenant makes the revealed things known.

commentary.christological_typology: Christ is the ultimate embodiment of God's council and covenant. He is the Word through whom God speaks (John 1:1-3), and through his life, death, and resurrection, he reveals and fulfills all of God's purposes. In the Gospel accounts, Jesus admits his disciples into his counsel, teaching them privately the deeper meanings of the parables and kingdom truths (Mark 4:33-34). The Last Supper becomes a covenant meal where Jesus shares his most intimate purpose—his redemptive sacrifice. Those who fear and follow Jesus are admitted into the mystery of the kingdom, just as the Psalmist promises admission to those who fear God.

word_study.meaning: Secret counsel, intimate conversation, or inner circle. The word combines secrecy with intimacy—it refers to what is hidden from outsiders but known to those within the circle.
word_study.significance: The Covenant Rendering translates it as 'counsel,' which better captures the sense of God's plans and purposes, not merely hidden facts but his ongoing guidance and will. Those who fear God are invited into his deliberative circle.

word_study.meaning: Those who fear him. The verb yare (יָרֵא) means to fear, but in the covenant context, it means reverent awe and submission—not terror but respectful acknowledgment of God's greatness and authority.
word_study.significance: In Psalms, the fear of the LORD is the foundation of wisdom and righteousness. It is the posture of the one who recognizes God's sovereignty and responds with allegiance.

word_study.meaning: A binding agreement or bond between parties, involving mutual obligations and promises. In biblical context, God's covenant with his people establishes the framework of relationship.
word_study.significance: The covenant is not abstract doctrine but the lived reality of relationship with God. Those admitted to God's counsel understand the covenant—they know the terms, the promises, and their place within it.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: In Alma 12:9-10, Alma teaches that God reveals his secrets to the humble and faithful: 'And now Alma began to expound these things unto him, saying: It is given unto many to know the mysteries of God; nevertheless they are laid under a strict commandment that they shall not impart only according to the portion of his word which he doth grant unto the children of men...And therefore he that will harden his heart, the same receiveth the lesser portion of the word; and he that will not harden his heart, to him is given the greater portion of the word.' Those who remain teachable and fearful of God receive greater knowledge of divine purposes.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 76:10-12 describes the privilege of receiving revelation: 'And this is the epitome of his law...Wherefore, I say unto you that I have sent my servant Joseph Smith, Jun., with my covenant and my law.' The Restoration teaches that God continues to reveal his counsel through his prophets to all who receive it. D&C 84:19-22 connects the oath and covenant of the priesthood directly to knowledge of God: 'And I have sent my servant Joseph Smith, Jun...And those who receive my law and keep it, are my disciples...And by this you may know if a man repenteth of his sins—behold, he will confess them and forsake them.'
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The temple is the place where God's counsel is most fully revealed. The endowment ceremony itself is structured as an admission into God's inner circle—the secrets and signs of the priesthood are taught only to those who have been found worthy and covenant-faithful. The temple further teaches that God's plan of salvation (his deepest counsel) is made known to those who enter and receive the ordinances. The 'veils' in the temple represent the barriers between the earthly and divine realms; passing through them symbolizes admission into God's inner circle of knowledge and power.

commentary.application: For the modern Latter-day Saint, this verse teaches that God is not distant or withholding of his purposes. If we approach him with genuine reverence and submission, we are invited into his counsel. This happens through prayer, through study of scripture, through the guidance of the Holy Ghost, and through obedience to the covenants we have made. The implication is profound: you are not excluded from understanding God's will for your life. The 'secret of the LORD' that belongs to the fearful includes personal revelation about your own path. Additionally, learning God's covenant—understanding its terms, its promises, and your place within it—is not an academic exercise but a pathway to intimate relationship with God. When you know the covenant deeply, you understand not just what God requires but why he requires it, and you move from obedience born of obligation to obedience born of love.
commentary.historical_context: In ancient Near Eastern royal courts, the 'inner circle' or 'council' (sod) was a place of highest privilege and trust. To be admitted to the king's private counsel was a mark of exceptional favor and access to the king's plans and strategies. The Psalmist applies this courtly imagery to God: the righteous are granted access to God's council. This democratizes divine privilege—it is not reserved for a royal elite but open to anyone who fears God. The concept of covenant (berit) was also deeply rooted in ancient Near Eastern diplomacy and law. A covenant established mutual obligations, promises, and a framework for ongoing relationship. By stating that God 'makes known' his covenant to the fearful, the Psalmist emphasizes that God does not keep his people in ignorance about the terms of their relationship with him.

text_kjv: Mine eyes are ever toward the LORD; for he shall pluck my feet out of the net.

commentary.narrative: Verse 15, the ayin (ע) line, shifts from the promise of verse 14 to the Psalmist's personal response. The ayin is the eye in Hebrew, and the verse opens with 'eyes' (einai)—a wordplay fitting for the Hebrew acrostic. The Psalmist declares that his eyes are 'always' (tamid) toward the LORD. This is not a glance or a periodic check-in but a continuous, unwavering gaze. In the imagery of the psalm, the Psalmist is in a net—he is caught, trapped, ensnared—but rather than staring fixedly at the net (which would induce despair), he keeps his eyes on the LORD.
commentary.narrative_continued: The Hebrew word reshet (רֶשֶׁת, 'net') refers to a hunting trap or snare—an image of being caught in circumstances beyond one's control. The dangers might be literal (enemies, physical threat) or metaphorical (sin, trials, confusion). The verb yotsi (יוֹצִיא, 'will bring out, will extract') means to pull out, to deliver. The logic of the verse is profound: the speaker does not deny being in the net, but he knows that deliverance comes not from studying the net more carefully but from fixing his gaze on the LORD. The orientation of the eyes determines the outcome.
commentary.narrative_continued2: This verse presents a principle of spiritual psychology: what you look at shapes what you believe and what you become. The modern tendency is often to fixate on the problem—to analyze the trap, to understand how we got caught, to measure the depth of the danger. The Psalmist teaches a different way: acknowledge the predicament but train your eyes on the source of deliverance. This requires faith because the deliverance is not yet visible—the eyes are on the LORD in trust that he will act. The verse speaks not of past deliverance ('he plucked') but of future assurance ('he shall pluck'), suggesting that the speaker looks ahead with confidence based on God's character and past faithfulness.
