cross_references.connection: A similar declaration: 'But mine eyes are unto thee, O GOD the Lord: in thee is my trust.' The pattern of keeping eyes on God in the midst of threat appears throughout the Psalms.

Elisha prays that his servant's eyes be opened to see the divine protection surrounding them: 'And Elisha prayed, and said, LORD, I pray thee, open his eyes that he may see.' The orientation of one's sight determines what one perceives.
Wisdom instruction: 'Let thine eyes look right on, and let thine eyelids look straight before thee.' The focused gaze is the path to wisdom and safety.
The New Testament applies this principle Christologically: 'Looking unto Jesus the author and finisher of our faith.' The eyes fixed on Christ rather than on trials lead to endurance.
Peter speaks of being 'kept by the power of God through faith'—the protection comes from trust directed toward God, just as the Psalmist's eyes directed toward the LORD bring deliverance.

commentary.christological_typology: Jesus exemplifies this principle perfectly. In Gethsemane, facing the agony of the Atonement, he kept his gaze and will directed toward God the Father: 'Not my will, but thine, be done' (Luke 22:42). On the cross, he cried out, not to his persecutors but to his Father: 'Father, into thy hands I commend my spirit' (Luke 23:46). The Psalmist's teaching about keeping eyes fixed on God becomes the template for how the Savior himself faced the ultimate 'net'—and found deliverance through perfect alignment with God's will.

word_study.meaning: My eyes [are] always/continually toward. Tamid means 'perpetually, always, without interruption.' The preposition el ('toward') indicates direction and orientation.
word_study.significance: This is a statement of unwavering attention and allegiance. The eyes, in Hebrew thought, are the seat of vision and intention. To have your eyes continually toward the LORD means your gaze, your focus, your intention are fixed on him.

word_study.meaning: To bring out, to extract, to deliver. The verb suggests an active, forceful extraction—not a gentle release but a firm pulling out.
word_study.significance: God does not gradually loosen the net; he actively pulls the trapped person out. The verb conveys both the severity of the trap and the sufficiency of God's intervention.

word_study.meaning: A hunting net or trap; metaphorically, any ensnaring circumstances or dangers from which one cannot easily escape.
word_study.significance: The net is a trap set by hunters—it suggests an active threat from enemies or circumstances, not merely accidental misfortune. The image is of being immobilized and helpless without divine intervention.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: Alma 26:27 uses similar language: 'And my heart doth exceedingly rejoice in the Lord, my God, and my delight is in his works.' The focus of the righteous is continually directed toward God and his works. Moroni 7:26 emphasizes that 'faith is the hope of things not seen which are true'—having eyes fixed on the LORD is a manifestation of faith directed toward things not yet visible.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 38:8 teaches: 'Therefore, verily I say unto you, lift up your voice unto this people; speak the thoughts that I shall put into your hearts, and you shall not be confounded before men.' The promise is that those whose orientation is toward God (whose eyes are on him) will receive the thoughts and words they need. D&C 121:45 promises similar guidance to those whose hearts are centered on God.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The temple is the place where the eyes are most appropriately directed toward the divine presence. The architecture of the temple draws the eye forward toward the altar and the holy of holies, symbolizing that the worshipper's gaze should be directed toward God. The endowment ceremony itself teaches that through proper orientation and obedience, we are 'brought to the presence of God.' The practice of keeping one's eyes fixed on the ordinance worker or the ceremonies represents the principle of keeping attention on divine instruction.

commentary.application: The modern application of this verse is both psychological and spiritual. When you face a difficult situation—a health crisis, a relationship conflict, financial pressure, spiritual confusion—the impulse is often to fixate on the problem, analyzing it endlessly, sometimes falling into despair. The Psalmist teaches a different posture: acknowledge the trap, but deliberately train your eyes elsewhere. Keep your gaze on the character of God, on his past faithfulness to you and his people, on his promises. This is not denial of the problem but a refusal to let the problem be your fixed point. In practical terms, this might mean choosing to read scripture rather than ruminating on your worry; turning to prayer rather than panicked planning; seeking the companionship of the Holy Ghost through meditation rather than anxious analysis. The promise is not that the net will disappear, but that God will extract you from it. Your responsibility is to train your eyes in the right direction and maintain your gaze in faith.
commentary.historical_context: In ancient Israel, hunting nets and snares were literal dangers; the Psalmist's audience would have known the image viscerally. A hunter's snare was designed to immobilize its prey completely. Similarly, enemies used nets in warfare to entangle and capture. The image would have resonated with people who understood both physical danger and the metaphorical sense of being 'caught' by circumstances, illness, or spiritual confusion. The custom of looking toward a king or authority figure for protection is also rooted in ancient Near Eastern court culture—subjects would look to their king or to a deity for deliverance from threats. The Psalmist's practice of keeping his eyes on the LORD is the spiritual analogue to a vassal looking to his king for protection.

text_kjv: Turn thee unto me, and have mercy upon me; for I am desolate and afflicted.

commentary.narrative: Verse 16, the pe (פ) line, represents a turn toward petition. The Psalmist has declared his unwavering gaze toward God (verse 15), and now he calls out explicitly for God's response: 'Turn to me.' In Hebrew thought, God's 'face' (panim) is his presence, his attention, his favor. To ask God to 'turn' toward you is to request that he shift his attention from all else to you, that he look upon your condition. The phrase 'have mercy upon me' (ve-chonen-ni) calls for hesed—unmerited grace, steadfast love, covenant mercy. This is a petition not for reward earned but for grace given.
commentary.narrative_continued: The Psalmist describes himself with two words: yachid (יָחִיד, 'solitary, alone, only') and ani (עָנִי, 'afflicted, poor, humble'). The combination is striking—the suffering has isolated him. He is not merely afflicted but lonely in his affliction. The word yachid often refers to an only child or a solitary individual without support or companionship. This doubles the burden: not only does he suffer, but he suffers without the comfort of community, relationship, or presence. The call for God's mercy is thus directed to the One who can bridge this isolation.
commentary.narrative_continued2: The verse reflects a profound spiritual reality: suffering often isolates us. Grief, shame, fear, or illness can create a sense of solitary confinement, even when surrounded by others. The Psalmist's candor about this isolation is important—he does not hide it or spiritualize it away. Instead, he presents it directly to God: 'I am alone and afflicted; turn your face toward me.' This is not self-pity but radical honesty about the human condition in distress. The call for God to turn toward him acknowledges that relationship itself is part of the healing. Before any external circumstance changes, the Psalmist needs the assurance of God's attention and presence.

cross_references.connection: Similar language: 'Hear, O LORD, when I cry with my voice...When thou saidst, Seek ye my face; my heart said unto thee, Thy face, LORD, will I seek.' The constant theme is seeking God's face and attention.
David cries: 'Hear me, O LORD; for thy lovingkindness is good: turn unto me according to the multitude of thy tender mercies.' The request to turn is grounded in God's covenant character.
The prayer 'Turn thou us unto thee, O LORD' expresses the same longing for God's attention and restoration of relationship after profound loss.

Paul echoes the Psalmist's longing for God's face to shine: 'For God, who commanded the light to shine out of darkness, hath shined in our hearts, to give the light of the knowledge of the glory of God in the face of Jesus Christ.' Christ is the ultimate manifestation of God's turned face.

commentary.christological_typology: Jesus, in his ministry, became the embodiment of God's turned face—his presence meant the experience of divine attention and mercy. To the woman caught in adultery (John 8), to Zacchaeus the tax collector (Luke 19), to the Samaritan woman (John 4), Jesus turned toward them with full attention and grace. On the cross, Jesus experienced the opposite—the apparent hiding of God's face ('My God, why hast thou forsaken me?'), but his cry itself represents the turning of petition toward the Father. His resurrection is the ultimate turning of God's face toward humanity in redemptive love.

word_study.term_english: turn to me / turn your face toward
word_study.meaning: Turn to me; literally, 'turn your face toward me.' Peneh comes from panim ('face'), indicating a shift of attention and presence.
word_study.significance: In biblical thought, God's face represents his presence, his favor, and his engagement. To ask God to turn toward you is to ask for his full attention and the benefit of his presence.

word_study.meaning: And be gracious to me. The verb chanan means to show favor, mercy, or grace—specifically unmerited favor. The noun chen (grace) derives from this root.
word_study.significance: This is a request for hesed (steadfast love) and covenant mercy, not for earned reward. The Psalmist appeals to God's character and covenant commitment, not to personal merit.

word_study.meaning: Alone, solitary, only. Can refer to an only child or a person isolated without companions or support.
word_study.significance: The word emphasizes not just loneliness of feeling but the actual lack of companionship and support. The afflicted person is without human resources to help.

word_study.meaning: Poor, afflicted, humble, brought low. Can refer to economic poverty, physical suffering, or spiritual humility.
word_study.significance: The word encompasses the whole condition of one who has been brought low by circumstances beyond their control. It is not a virtue but a description of desperate need.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: Enos 1:4-5 describes a similar cry for God's turned face: 'And my soul hungered...And I kneeled down before my Maker...Behold, I went to hunt beasts in the forests; and the words which I had often heard my father speak concerning eternal life, and the justice of God, did throng upon my mind.' When Enos turned his face toward God through prayer, God turned his face toward him. Alma 34:38 similarly teaches: 'Therefore, if ye do cast out your sins by repentance, and remain with your sister, I cannot cast you out. For God shall receive you, if ye bring forth fruits meet for repentance.'
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 29:4-5 contains Jesus's promise: 'And now I show unto you a mystery, a thing which is had in secret chambers, to bring to pass your destruction...And inasmuch as ye have received the everlasting covenant, ye are called to bring forth the works thereof.' Those who covenant with God experience his face turned toward them. D&C 76:11-12 emphasizes God's desire to reveal himself: 'Wherefore, I now show unto you before my Father all the glory of my work which my Father hath caused to be wrought through you.'
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The endowment ceremony literally enacts God's turned face toward his covenant people. The progression through the temple represents moving closer to God's presence, culminating in the celestial room, which symbolizes standing before God's face. The practice of looking at the altar and the officiators during the ceremony represents the humble petition for God's attention and presence, mirrored in verse 16's plea for God to 'turn to me.'

commentary.application: This verse permits us to voice the most honest parts of our experience. If you feel isolated, if you are suffering alone, if you sense that God's attention has been withdrawn or was never granted—you can bring this directly to God, just as the Psalmist does. There is no shame in loneliness or affliction; the shame would be in pretending it away. The verse teaches that you can petition God for the most fundamental need: the experience of his presence and attention. In modern terms, this might mean asking not for the problem to disappear but for the assurance that you are not abandoned in the problem. When you feel most alone and most afflicted, the Psalmist's prayer becomes your prayer: God, turn your face toward me. Let me know that I am seen. Show me mercy. This petition is not rejected; it is the language of covenant, and God responds to those who call upon him in truth.
commentary.historical_context: In ancient Near Eastern religion and politics, the 'face' of a deity or ruler was understood as the locus of blessing and favor. To be 'before the face' of a king meant to be in his presence and benefit from his attention. Conversely, to have one's face 'hidden' or turned away meant rejection and loss of favor. The Psalmist's plea for God to 'turn' toward him would have been understood in this courtly and covenantal context as a plea for the restoration of relationship and favor. Additionally, the mention of being yachid ('alone') in ancient Israel would have had legal and social implications. A person without family, without the support of a clan, was profoundly vulnerable in a society where collective identity and protection were paramount. The isolation the Psalmist describes is thus not merely emotional but social and existential.

text_kjv: The troubles of my heart are enlarged: O bring thou me out of my distresses.

commentary.narrative: Verse 17, the tsade (צ) line, shifts the focus inward to the Psalmist's emotional and spiritual state. The opening phrase, 'The troubles of my heart are enlarged,' uses the Hebrew word hirchivu (הִרְחִיבוּ), which means 'have been widened, expanded, or enlarged.' The tsarot (צָרוֹת, troubles) are active forces that are actively expanding—the inner anguish is not static but growing. The heart (levav), in Hebrew anthropology, is the seat of thought, decision, and emotion; it is the core of the person. The image is of inner turmoil that keeps spreading, like a wound that grows rather than heals.
commentary.narrative_continued: The second line provides a contrasting image: 'Bring me out of my distresses' (metsuqotai). The noun tsukah (from tsuq, 'to be narrow, pressed, confined') refers to the state of being in a narrow place, cramped, squeezed. While the troubles enlarge within, the external circumstances feel narrowing and confining. The Psalmist is pulled in opposite directions simultaneously—internally expanding with trouble, externally contracted by pressure. This paradoxical image captures the experience of inner overwhelm coupled with external constraint. The verb 'bring out' (hotsiaeni) is a plea for deliverance from this dual bind.
commentary.narrative_continued2: The verse moves from the declaration of undivided gaze (verse 15) and the petition for God's turned face (verse 16) to the exposure of how internal the struggle is. The Psalmist admits that the problem is not merely external enemies or circumstances but his own expanding inner anguish. This is psychologically astute: the troubles of the heart often outgrow the actual external threats. Fear, shame, guilt, sorrow—these can proliferate within regardless of external reality. By naming this inward enlargement, the Psalmist models honest prayer. He does not pretend to have it together emotionally; he acknowledges that his heart is increasingly troubled and asks for deliverance not just from outward pressure but from inward turmoil.

cross_references.connection: When parents fail or friends abandon, 'the LORD will take me up.' The verse addresses the fear that internal distress might be too much even for God to handle.
God promises to give 'beauty for ashes, the oil of joy for mourning, the garment of praise for the spirit of heaviness.' The promise addresses the enlargement of internal sorrow.

Paul teaches the antidote to multiplying troubles: 'Be careful for nothing; but in every thing by prayer and supplication with thanksgiving let your requests be made known unto God: And the peace of God, which passeth all understanding, shall keep your hearts and minds.'

Jesus's invitation addresses both the internal and external burden: 'Come unto me, all ye that are weary and heavy laden, and I will give you rest.' Rest comes not from the removal of all pressures but from the transformation of one's relationship to them.

commentary.christological_typology: Jesus in Gethsemane experienced the exact condition the Psalmist describes: his internal anguish expanded ('my soul is exceeding sorrowful,' Matthew 26:38) while he was constrained externally by the knowledge of what lay ahead. His cry—'O my Father, if it be possible, let this cup pass from me: nevertheless not as I will, but as thou wilt' (Matthew 26:39)—mirrors the Psalmist's twin experience of internal turmoil and external confinement. Yet Jesus provides the model of how to endure it: by turning to the Father, by petitioning for deliverance, and by submitting to God's will. His resurrection is the ultimate 'bringing out' of distress.

word_study.meaning: Troubles/pressures of my heart have been enlarged/widened. Hirchivu comes from the root rachav, 'to be wide, to spread.' The troubles are actively expanding.
word_study.significance: This suggests not a single, static problem but an ongoing multiplication of inner anguish. The troubles are not being resolved but growing in scope and intensity.

word_study.meaning: The heart; the center of the person encompassing thought, emotion, will, and conscience. The heart is the seat of all inner life.
word_study.significance: When the Psalmist says the troubles of his heart are enlarged, he is speaking of the deepest part of himself being overwhelmed. This is not surface distress but existential turmoil.

word_study.meaning: My distresses, my straits, my confined places. From tsuq, 'to be narrow or confined.' The word suggests a literal narrow place from which one cannot easily escape.
word_study.significance: While the troubles enlarge inwardly, outwardly the Psalmist is confined and constrained. There is no room to move or escape. The word captures both literal siege and metaphorical entrapment.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: Mosiah 4:2-3 describes the effect of the spirit upon those who realize their sin: 'And they had viewed themselves in their own carnal state, even less than the dust of the earth. But this is not all; they had heard the voice of the angel, and he spake unto them; and his voice was as thunder, which shook the earth; and they understood that there was no way that they could stand before God save it were through the merits, and mercy, and grace of the Holy Messiah, who was promised unto them.' The troubles of the heart enlarge when one sees oneself clearly, but God provides the means of deliverance.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 6:35-36 offers the same kind of comfort: 'Do not be troubled, for when ye are brought to see your nakedness without the gospel of Jesus Christ, then ye shall feel a wound also, as the seed of Joseph hath felt, because his heart is grieved...But I am in your midst, and I am the light and the life of the world; wherefore, fear not, but believe in me, and ye shall not be confounded.' The promise is that though troubles enlarge inwardly, God's presence is sufficient.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The temple ordinances are specifically designed to address both internal trouble and external confinement. The progression through the temple represents moving from narrow places (where choices were limited) through the veil into broader expansion (entering fully into covenant and God's presence). The relief and peace experienced in the celestial room represent the answer to this verse—deliverance from internal and external constraint.

commentary.application: This verse validates the experience of feeling emotionally overwhelmed. Sometimes the trouble is not one dramatic crisis but a slow multiplication of worries, fears, hurts, and concerns that gradually expand until they feel larger than you can contain. The Psalmist normalizes this and models the response: acknowledge it directly and bring it to God. Do not pretend your heart is at peace when it is troubled and expanding. Do not minimize your internal anguish as if it is spiritually weak to admit it. Instead, do what the Psalmist does: name the trouble, acknowledge the confinement, and petition God for deliverance. In modern terms, this might involve honest prayer, perhaps journaling or speaking with a trusted counselor or church leader about the expanding troubles of your heart. The promise is that God hears and can 'bring you out' from the double bind of internal and external pressure. Deliverance may not mean the removal of all pain, but it means moving from overwhelming isolation to companionship with God in the midst of pain.
commentary.historical_context: In ancient Israel, both literal and metaphorical siege was a common experience. Besieged cities experienced the exact condition the Psalmist describes: the internal panic (troubles of the heart) enlarging even as external pressure confined them. The Psalmist's language would have resonated with those who had experienced military siege, famine, or exile. Additionally, the concept of the 'troubled heart' appears frequently in ancient Near Eastern wisdom literature, suggesting that the psychological experience of unexplained or expanding anxiety was a recognized human phenomenon even in antiquity. The understanding that inward anguish can exceed external circumstances would have been familiar to the wisdom tradition.

text_kjv: Look upon mine affliction and my pain; and forgive all my sins.

commentary.narrative: Verse 18, the resh (ר) line, completes the Psalmist's petition with a request that brings together two seemingly separate realities: affliction and sin. The verb reeh ('look upon, see') is not a casual glance but a careful attention to—God is asked to observe the Psalmist's state comprehensively. The affliction (onyi, עׇנְיִי) and toil or trouble (amali, עֲמָלִי) are the outward manifestations of suffering. But then the prayer shifts to the inward reality: 'forgive all my sins' (salah le-kol-chattotai). The conjunction is crucial: the Psalmist does not separate these but presents them together. He is asking God to see both his suffering and his sin as interconnected parts of his total condition.
commentary.narrative_continued: The move to forgiveness is theologically significant. Throughout the psalm, the Psalmist has petitioned God to hear, to turn, to deliver. Now he connects his need for material and emotional deliverance with his need for spiritual forgiveness. This acknowledges a biblical principle that appears elsewhere in the Psalter and throughout Scripture: sin and suffering are often intertwined, though not always in a direct causative relationship (as the book of Job makes clear). The Psalmist is not claiming that all his troubles are deserved consequences of sin, but he is acknowledging that as he faces his suffering, he also faces his sin. Both need God's attention.
commentary.narrative_continued2: The verb salah (סָלַח, 'to forgive') literally means 'to lift up, to bear away.' When applied to sin, it means to lift the burden of sin from the sinner. The promise is that God does not hold sin against the one who confesses and seeks reconciliation. The Psalmist asks that all (kol) his sins be forgiven—not just the obvious ones, not just the public ones, but all of them. This is complete forgiveness, not partial restoration. The prayer acknowledges that true wholeness—true deliverance from affliction—requires spiritual forgiveness and restoration. You cannot be fully healed while carrying the weight of unforgiven sin. This verse thus represents the deepest layer of the Psalmist's need and the broadest scope of God's mercy.

cross_references.connection: 'When thou with rebukes dost correct man for iniquity, thou makest his beauty to consume away like a moth.' The psalm acknowledges that affliction and sin are often intertwined in the experience of the righteous.
'He that covereth his sins shall not prosper: but whoso confesseth and forsaketh them shall have mercy.' The sequence of confession and forgiveness leads to true healing.
'Surely he hath borne our griefs, and carried our sorrows...he was bruised for our iniquities.' The Messianic figure addresses both suffering and sin in a single redemptive act.

'He will turn again, he will have compassion upon us; he will subdue our iniquities; and thou wilt cast all their sins into the depths of the sea.' The promise of complete forgiveness parallels the Psalmist's request for all sins to be forgiven.

'If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.' The New Testament affirms the principle the Psalmist articulates: confession and forgiveness are available.

commentary.christological_typology: Jesus Christ is the ultimate answer to this verse. He came to see (in the sense of comprehend and bear) both human affliction and human sin. In his compassion, he addresses both: 'Come unto me, all ye that are weary and heavy laden, and I will give you rest' (Matthew 11:28) speaks to affliction; 'thy sins are forgiven' (Luke 7:48) speaks to sin. The Atonement itself is the mechanism by which God 'lifts' both the burden of suffering and the weight of sin. Jesus's suffering in Gethsemane and on the cross encompassed both—he bore our sicknesses and griefs (Isaiah 53:4) and carried away our sins (1 John 2:2). The resurrection promised that those who believe in him will have both their afflictions healed and their sins forgiven in the ultimate redemption.

word_study.meaning: See, look upon, behold. The imperative form calling God to direct his attention. More than mere casual seeing, it implies careful observation and comprehension.
word_study.significance: The Psalmist asks God not merely to be aware of the situation but to truly see it—to comprehend it fully and acknowledge it. The request is for genuine attention to one's condition.

word_study.meaning: My affliction, my humiliation, my brought-low condition. The state of being reduced, diminished, or subjected to hardship.
word_study.significance: Unlike yachid (solitary) in verse 16, which emphasized isolation, onyi emphasizes the condition of being reduced or subdued. The Psalmist is not merely alone but diminished by circumstances.

word_study.meaning: My toil, my trouble, my labor, my pain. From amal, referring to painful work or distress resulting from exertion.
word_study.significance: This word suggests not just passive suffering but active struggle—the pain of trying to cope, the weariness of ongoing difficulty. It encompasses both the suffering itself and the exhaustion it produces.

word_study.meaning: To forgive, to pardon. Literally, to lift up or bear away. When God forgives, he lifts the burden of sin from the sinner.
word_study.significance: Forgiveness is not merely saying 'it's okay' but an active lifting of the burden. It is the removal of guilt and the restoration of relationship. The Covenant Rendering of this concept emphasizes that forgiveness is a divine action that changes the sinner's standing.

word_study.meaning: My sins, my transgressions. From chata, meaning to miss the mark, to err, to sin against God or another.
word_study.significance: Sin in Hebrew is conceived as missing the mark, stepping out of line, failing to hit the target of righteousness. The Psalmist acknowledges specific failures and transgressions, not merely a general moral impurity.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: In Alma 36, Alma describes his experience of affliction and the connection to sin: 'But I was racked with eternal torment, for my soul was harrowed up to the greatest degree and racked with all my sins. Yea, I did remember all my sins and iniquities' (v. 12-13). His plea for God to see both his affliction and his sin leads to redemption: 'And oh, what joy, and what marvelous light I did behold' (v. 20). The sequence is identical to Psalm 25:18—acknowledgment of suffering and sin together, followed by divine mercy.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 61:2 contains the Lord's instruction to Joseph Smith: 'And now, verily I say unto you, that it is not revealed, and no man knoweth where the city of Zion shall be built, but it shall be given hereafter. Behold, I say unto you that it shall be on the borders by the Lamanites.' More directly, D&C 64:10 teaches the principle of forgiveness: 'I, the Lord, will forgive whom I will forgive, but of you it is required to forgive all men.' The interconnection of affliction and forgiveness is woven throughout the Doctrine and Covenants.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The temple endowment narrative traces the human journey from innocence through sin, then through education and covenant, leading to standing before God. The ordinances of the temple specifically address both the recognition of sin (symbolized in the garden scene and the fall) and the provision for forgiveness and redemption (symbolized through the covenants and the progression toward the celestial room). The temple teaches that we cannot enter God's presence while bearing unresolved sin and unhealed affliction—both must be addressed. The washing and anointing ordinances symbolize cleansing from sin; the subsequent covenants represent alignment with God despite our imperfections.

commentary.application: This verse gives permission to bring both your suffering and your sin to God simultaneously. Often we compartmentalize: we confess our sins in one moment and petition for relief from suffering in another. The Psalmist models an integrated prayer that acknowledges both realities at once. If you are experiencing affliction, do not pretend you are sinless as you ask for God's help; do not let unresolved guilt complicate your petition. Similarly, if you are conscious of sin, do not hide it from God in hopes of a more favorable answer. Instead, lay both before him: 'God, look on my affliction and my pain, and forgive all my sins.' The promise is not that God will shame you for acknowledging both, but that he will address both comprehensively. In practical terms, this might mean: when you are struggling with illness or hardship, also take time for genuine repentance and confession. When you are seeking forgiveness, also be honest about how your sin has caused suffering to yourself and others, and ask for healing of those wounds. The mercy of God is large enough to encompass the whole person—sufferer and sinner—and to bring restoration to both.
commentary.historical_context: In ancient Israel, affliction was often interpreted through the lens of covenant theology: God blessed obedience and afflicted disobedience. When someone experienced significant suffering, a natural question arose: 'What sin caused this?' This is the assumption behind many of the dialogues in the book of Job, and it appears in the interpretations of exile and plague throughout the historical books. However, the biblical tradition also recognizes that this is not a simple equation—the righteous sometimes suffer innocently (Job, various psalms of lament). The Psalmist's approach here acknowledges both: he is suffering, and he also bears the consciousness of sin. Rather than trying to parse which came first, he presents both to God and asks for complete attention to his total condition. This reflects a mature theological understanding that refuses to deny either suffering or responsibility.

text_kjv: Consider mine enemies; for they are many; and they hate me with cruel hatred.

commentary.narrative:
The psalmist shifts from personal prayer to a stark confrontation with reality: enemies surround him, and their hostility is not casual dislike but deliberate, active malice. This verse occurs at the second occurrence of resh in the acrostic structure—a doubling that emphasizes the weight of this petition. The word translated "cruel hatred" in the KJV is the Hebrew phrase *sinat chamas*, which carries the connotation of violent, destructive hatred rooted in wrongdoing. The enemies are *rav* (numerous, overwhelming), suggesting that the threat is not merely personal but feels insurmountable. Yet the psalmist does not ask for vengeance; he asks God to "look" or "see" them—to acknowledge the reality of the threat and, implicitly, to act on behalf of the one who has taken refuge in God.

This candid presentation of the problem is characteristic of the psalms of lament. The psalmist does not minimize suffering or pretend enemies do not exist. Instead, he brings the full weight of his circumstances before God. The structure of the petition—"look at my enemies, for they are many"—invites God to witness the scale of the problem. In the ancient Near Eastern context, calling upon a powerful figure to "see" or "consider" something was a way of activating that person's protective power. The psalmist is not complaining; he is calling God to attention and action.

word_study.meaning: to see, to perceive, to regard with attention. In petitionary contexts, it carries the sense of 'look upon, acknowledge, and act on behalf of.'
word_study.significance: This is not a passive request for information but an active call for God to witness and intervene. The same root appears in Genesis 29:32, where a name is chosen because 'the LORD has seen my affliction.'

word_study.meaning: enemy, adversary, one who opposes. Plural here emphasizes their number and collective threat.
word_study.significance: Throughout the Psalms, oyev refers not merely to personal rivals but to enemies of God's anointed and God's people. The term carries both personal and covenantal weight.

word_study.meaning: many, numerous, great in quantity or power. Can also mean 'much' or 'abundant.'
word_study.significance: The emphasis on multitude suggests the threat is overwhelming by human estimation—yet the psalmist's refuge remains God, not military strength or political alliance.

word_study.meaning: Hatred characterized by violence, cruelty, and wrongdoing. Chamas specifically denotes destructive violence and moral wrong, not mere dislike.
word_study.significance: This phrase elevates the enemies' opposition from personal animosity to a violation of justice and right order. Their hatred is enacted through harmful action, making it a threat not just to the psalmist but to the moral fabric of society.

cross_references.connection: A parallel opening to another psalm of lament: 'Lord, how are they increased that trouble me! Many are they that rise up against me.' The enemies' multitude and opposition are a recurring theme in David's prayers.
Another prayer against false witnesses and violent enemies: 'Deliver me not over unto the will of mine enemies.' The pattern of calling God to witness and protect against numerous adversaries.
Hatred stirs up strife, but love covers all sins. The contrast illuminates that the enemies' *sinat chamas* (violent hatred) stands in direct opposition to the way of wisdom.

The New Testament echoes this ancient concern: the adversary (Satan) as a roaring lion seeks to devour. The psalmist's enemies are typologically understood in the Restoration as spiritual adversaries.
Joseph Smith's revelation to the persecuted Saints echoes the psalmist's cry: 'And if they have persecuted me, they shall also persecute you.' Yet it promises that God's covenant cannot be broken.

commentary.historical_context: In the ancient Near East, a person surrounded by enemies often sought asylum in a sanctuary or under the protection of a powerful patron. The royal psalms, many attributed to David, reflect the political and military context of a kingdom threatened by rival powers. However, this psalm's language suggests a vulnerability that cannot be resolved by military might alone—the psalmist's enemies are numerous beyond counting, and their hatred is virulent and deeply rooted. The psalmist's only recourse is to call upon God as the ultimate guarantor of protection and justice. The acrostic structure, which moves through the Hebrew alphabet with disciplined prayer, suggests that this is a liturgical composition designed for communal use in the temple, where individuals facing persecution could voice their lament within the structured container of Israel's covenantal prayer tradition.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: Alma 5:18 captures a similar sentiment: 'Have ye spiritually been born of God? Have ye received his image in your countenances?' The contrast suggests that the psalmist's enemy is defined not only by their actions but by their moral and spiritual opposition to God's purposes. Similarly, Alma 31:5 describes the Zoramites as enemies characterized by pride and false worship—their hatred is rooted in opposition to God's truth.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 64:2 teaches that 'I, the Lord, will forgive whom I will forgive, but of you it is required to forgive all men.' The psalmist's petition to God to acknowledge his enemies is part of a larger framework in which God judges all hearts and actions. D&C 122:4 directly addresses persecution: 'Know thou, my son, that all these things shall give thee experience, and shall be for thy good.' The enemies' hatred becomes, in God's hands, a means of refining faith.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The psalm's progression from lament to refuge, and its use as a liturgical piece in the temple, anticipates the endowment pattern of seeking God's protection through covenantal prayer. The psalmist's enemies represent the forces of opposition and chaos that the temple ritual symbolically addresses through ordinance and covenant.

commentary.christological_typology: The psalmist's enemies prefigure Christ's adversaries—those who opposed His mission and ultimately sought His death. In the Gospels, Jesus faces a similar multitude of enemies: the religious authorities, the political powers, and the forces of spiritual opposition. Yet like the psalmist, Jesus brings His case before God the Father in prayer. The crucifixion, though it appears to be a victory for the enemies, becomes the occasion of Christ's ultimate triumph. The psalm's language of hatred and violence thus becomes transparent to the suffering Messiah, whose enemies' *sinat chamas* (violent hatred) could not ultimately prevail against God's purposes.
commentary.application: Modern readers face adversaries and opposition—not necessarily in the form of literal enemies seeking physical harm, but in the form of ideologies, pressures, and forces that oppose covenant living. The psalmist's example teaches us that acknowledging the reality and severity of these obstacles is not weakness or lack of faith; it is the honest ground upon which faith is built. We are invited to bring the full weight of our struggle before God, to ask Him to see and acknowledge what we face. The petition does not demand immediate deliverance but asks God to bear witness to our condition. This becomes a foundation for the hope expressed in the following verses: that God's protecting presence, accessed through refuge in Him, is a surer defense than any earthly power.

text_kjv: O keep my soul, and deliver me: let me not be ashamed; for I put my trust in thee.

commentary.narrative:
The psalmist now moves from acknowledging the enemies to petitioning God for protection. This is the shin line of the acrostic, and it contains two parallel requests: "guard my life" (*shomrah nafshi*) and "deliver me" (*hatssileni*). The pairing reflects a complete picture of divine protection—both preservation and rescue. Shame (*evosh*) emerges as a secondary but crucial concern. In ancient Israel, shame was not merely an emotional state but a social reality that signified loss of honor, public disgrace, and disconnection from the community. To be put to shame before one's enemies would compound the physical threat with spiritual and social death. The basis of the petition—"for I put my trust in you"—echoes the opening of the psalm and creates an inclusio (a literary frame) that reinforces the central theme: the life of faith is rooted in trust in God's protection.

The verb *chasah* (to take refuge) deserves careful attention. It describes not a momentary escape but an ongoing state of hiding under divine protection. The same verb appears in Psalm 91:4, where God's wings provide shelter, and throughout the Psalms where the faithful are described as those who "take refuge in the Lord." The psalmist's confidence is not based on the assumption that trouble will disappear, but on the assurance that God is a reliable shelter. This verse pivots from the darkness of verse 19 (enemies are many) to the light of verse 20 (God will guard and deliver). The movement is not from problem to denial, but from problem to trust.

word_study.meaning: to guard, keep, watch over, preserve. Can mean both active vigilance and protective custody.
word_study.significance: This is the verb of the shepherd watching over sheep, and of God watching over His covenant people. It suggests not passive existence but active, attentive protection.

word_study.meaning: soul, life, person, being. In Hebrew thought, the nephesh is the vital essence, the living person in their totality—not a non-physical entity but the animate self.
word_study.significance: The psalmist asks for protection of the whole self, not merely physical survival but the continuation of meaningful life and community belonging.

word_study.meaning: to snatch away, deliver, rescue from danger. Often implies active extraction from a dangerous situation.
word_study.significance: This is the language of dramatic rescue—God as the one who pulls the drowning person from the water, who snatches the victim from the predator's mouth.

word_study.meaning: to be ashamed, confounded, humiliated. In the social context of ancient Israel, shame is loss of honor and standing before the community.
word_study.significance: Shame in biblical thought is not merely psychological but social and covenantal. To be shamed is to be severed from one's place in the community and potentially from covenant relationship with God.

word_study.meaning: to take refuge, seek shelter, hide under protection. Implies a deliberate turning toward someone or something as a shelter.
word_study.significance: The Covenant Rendering emphasizes that this is not passive hope but active taking refuge—a choice to position oneself under divine protection, like a bird sheltering under a wing.

cross_references.connection: Expands on the theme of taking refuge: 'He that dwelleth in the secret place of the most High shall abide under the shadow of the Almighty... He shall cover thee with his feathers, and under his wings shalt thou trust.' The shelter motif reaches full expression.
A parallel from another David psalm: 'Hear, O Lord, when I cry with my voice... my heart said unto thee, Thy face, Lord, will I seek.' The petition for God to hear and protect the one who seeks Him.
God's promise to Israel: 'Fear thou not; for I am with thee: be not dismayed; for I am thy God.' The assurance that undergirds the psalmist's petition.
Nephi's plea: 'O Lord, wilt thou redeem my soul?' The Book of Mormon echoes the psalmist's language of deliverance and divine protection.
The Lord to Oliver Cowdery: 'Look unto me in every thought; doubt not, fear not.' The framework of trust that undergirds protection, echoing the psalmist's foundation of faith.

commentary.historical_context: In the ancient world, shame was a public and familial matter. To be shamed meant one's name was dishonored, one's place in the community was threatened, and one's ability to make binding covenants or conduct business was compromised. A person facing persecution by enemies lived under a double threat: physical danger and the threat of public humiliation if the enemies succeeded. The call to take refuge in God's presence would have been understood in the temple context as a literal, spatial thing—the psalmist or the worshiper who identified with these words would be physically present in the sanctuary, a place believed to be especially inhabited by God's protective presence. The acrostic structure of the psalm ensured that this petition would be remembered and repeated, reinforcing the habit of turning to God rather than to human protectors or military strength.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: Alma 31:37-38 describes Alma's prayer for deliverance from the apostate Zoramites: 'Extend the arms of thy mercy towards them, that they may believe in thee.' The pattern of seeking God's protective and redemptive action on behalf of oneself and others.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 121:7-8 records Joseph Smith's prayer from Liberty Jail, a prayer that echoes the psalmist's language: 'O God, where art thou? And where is the pavilion that covereth thy hiding place?' The prayer for God's protective presence in the midst of persecution. D&C 121:45 promises that those who exercise faith will be endowed with power and authority—a promise that answers the psalmist's petition for protection.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The concept of taking refuge in God is central to temple worship. The temple itself is constructed as a sanctuary—a place of refuge where covenant believers are protected from the chaos and opposition of the world. The endowment ritual walks the participant through threats and opposition, with the assurance that faithful adherence to covenant brings divine protection and guidance.

commentary.christological_typology: Jesus exemplifies the trust expressed in this verse. In Gethsemane, facing the ultimate enemies—death, sin, and separation from His Father—Jesus prays not for escape but for God to guard His soul and see Him through. His resurrection becomes the ultimate answer to the petition for deliverance and freedom from shame. His exaltation vindicates Him completely, proving that trust in God's purposes, even in the face of overwhelming opposition, leads to ultimate glory and honor.
commentary.application: In modern covenant life, we face situations where our integrity and standing in our communities are challenged. The psalmist's petition reminds us that seeking God's protection against shame is not cowardice but wisdom. When we feel threatened—whether by gossip, by pressure to compromise our values, or by hostility from those who oppose our faith—we are invited to petition God as the psalmist does: to ask Him to guard our lives, to rescue us from the power of those who seek to harm us, and to preserve our honor in His sight. The phrase "for I put my trust in thee" is not a condition that must be earned; it is a statement of intention and choice. We choose, in the moment of pressure, to trust God rather than to retaliate, appease, or flee into shame. That choice itself becomes the ground of protection.

text_kjv: Let integrity and uprightness preserve me; for I wait on thee.

commentary.narrative:
This is the final acrostic line, using tav, the last letter of the Hebrew alphabet. The psalm has moved through the full alphabet—from aleph (verse 1) to tav (verse 21)—a structure that signals completeness and totality of prayer. The psalmist now articulates a mature vision of how protection works: not through external power alone, but through the integration of moral character with faithful waiting. The phrase *tom va-yosher* (integrity and uprightness) is striking because these virtues are personified as active guardians: "Let integrity and uprightness preserve me." The verbs *yitseruni* (they will guard me) treats moral qualities as if they are protective agents, standing watch over the one who embodies them.

This is a profoundly biblical insight: righteousness is not merely an internal quality or a source of divine favor; it becomes a visible protection, a shield that repels the attacks of enemies. Those who live with *tom* (integrity, wholeness, the absence of guile) and *yosher* (uprightness, rectitude, the quality of standing straight before God) create around themselves a kind of moral force field. They are less vulnerable to the corrupting influence of their enemies because they are not divided against themselves. The final phrase—"for I wait on thee" (*ki qivvitikha*)—circles back to the opening of the psalm and anchors the whole prayer in patient trust. The verb *qavah* (to wait, to hope, to look forward with expectant patience) suggests that this is not passive inactivity but an active posture of readiness and reliance.

word_study.meaning: integrity, wholeness, completeness, innocence. Describes a person who is not divided or deceitful, who stands in singular alignment with truth.
word_study.significance: Tom is a cornerstone word in wisdom literature and the Psalms. Job is described as having tom (Job 1:1). It represents the state of being undivided in allegiance and undeceptive in character.

word_study.meaning: uprightness, rectitude, straightness. Describes the quality of standing straight, morally and spiritually aligned with what is right.
word_study.significance: Yosher is the opposite of crookedness or deceit. It evokes the image of a tree growing straight, of a path that goes directly toward its destination rather than winding away.

word_study.meaning: to keep, guard, watch, preserve. Similar to shamar but often emphasizes guarding against harm or loss.
word_study.significance: Here, moral qualities are treated as if they are sentries or guards—they protect the one who possesses them by keeping away corruption and vulnerability to enemy influence.

word_study.meaning: to wait, to hope, to look forward with expectancy. Often implies waiting with patient trust rather than anxious desperation.
word_study.significance: This verb appears frequently in the Psalms to describe the proper posture toward God—not passive resignation but active, hopeful waiting. The Psalms often end with the affirmation that those who wait for the Lord will not be put to shame.

cross_references.connection: The opening of the psalm circles back: 'Unto thee, O Lord, do I lift up my soul... Let none that wait on thee be ashamed.' The inclusio is complete—the psalm moves from the opening petition to wait for God to the final assertion that waiting on God, grounded in integrity and uprightness, is the sufficient protection.
He that walketh uprightly walketh surely: but he that perverteth his ways shall be known.' Uprightness provides a kind of moral protection and visibility that deceit cannot.
Better is the poor that walketh in his integrity, than he that is perverse in his lips, and is a fool.' Tom and yosher are presented as more valuable than wealth or status.
Mark the perfect man, and behold the upright: for the end of that man is peace... The Lord saveth the righteous.' Righteousness and uprightness lead to God's protection and peace.

And thus we see that the Lord began to prepare the way for our redemption, according to his merciful plan in the revelation of Jesus Christ.' The Book of Mormon emphasizes that walking uprightly and maintaining integrity are part of the path prepared by God.

commentary.historical_context: In the ancient Near East, a person's character was understood to have practical consequences. The concept of *tom* (integrity, wholeness) carried legal and social weight—a person known for tom could be trusted to keep covenants and conduct business honestly. To be described as lacking *tom* was a serious accusation. The Egyptian concept of *ma'at* (truth, justice, order) is a parallel: living in alignment with *ma'at* brings protection and stability, while deviation from it brings chaos. The acrostic structure of the psalm, reaching its completion with the letter tav, suggests that the prayer is "complete" or "finished"—the psalmist has brought all of his concerns before God in an orderly, comprehensive way. The completion of the alphabet symbolizes that nothing is left out, that the whole of human experience has been addressed through prayer structured by the pattern of creation itself (the Hebrew alphabet being foundational to creation in Jewish mystical thought).

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: Alma 38:12 teaches Corianton: 'Let all thy doings be unto the Lord, and whithersoever thou goest, go with the Lord; yea, let all thy thoughts be directed unto the Lord; yea, let the affections of thy heart be placed upon the Lord forever.' This captures the integration of integrity and uprightness with patient waiting on God that the psalmist articulates.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 121:45-46 describes the power that flows from integrity and uprightness: 'Let virtue garnish thy thoughts unceasingly; then shall thy confidence wax strong in the presence of God.' The principle is the same as the psalmist's: moral character and righteousness become active protective forces.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The temple endowment emphasizes that walking uprightly through the world and maintaining one's covenants provides a kind of spiritual protection. The temple garment symbolizes the protective power of covenant and righteousness. The psalmist's assertion that tom and yosher preserve him is echoed in temple theology—those who live according to covenant are protected by God's power.

commentary.christological_typology: Jesus Christ is the perfect embodiment of tom (integrity) and yosher (uprightness). He is undivided in His allegiance to God's will and perfectly aligned with righteousness. His life demonstrates that perfect integrity does not prevent suffering at the hands of enemies, but it does ensure vindication and ultimate triumph. His resurrection proves that those who wait on God while maintaining perfect integrity will be preserved. The Sermon on the Mount, with its call to authenticity and integrity of heart, echoes the psalmist's teaching that internal moral wholeness matters more than external protection.
commentary.application: The psalmist offers a subtle challenge to the modern idea that protection comes primarily from external means—security systems, legal action, powerful allies. Instead, he suggests that the best protection is the kind we build through our own integrity and uprightness. When we choose honesty in business, consistency in our commitments, and authenticity in our relationships, we create a kind of moral force field that enemies cannot easily penetrate. We become less vulnerable to manipulation, blackmail, or the fear that prompts compromise. More importantly, living with integrity means we can trust our own character and can wait patiently for God to act, knowing that we are aligned with His purposes. In covenant life, this means being the same person in private as in public, keeping promises when no one is watching, and living in a way that God's spirit can confirm. The phrase "for I wait on thee" reminds us that this is not about self-reliance; it is about relying on God's justice and protection while ourselves doing the work of character that allows us to trust His guidance.

text_kjv: Redeem Israel, O God, out of all his troubles.

commentary.narrative:
The psalm concludes with a striking shift from the personal singular ("me," "my") to the communal collective ("Israel," "its troubles"). This final verse stands outside the acrostic structure—there is no Hebrew letter corresponding to it in the alphabetic pattern. Scholars debate whether this is an original part of the psalm or a later addition made to transform a personal lament into a liturgical prayer for communal worship. Either interpretation carries theological weight. If original, it suggests that the psalmist understood his personal deliverance as inseparable from the redemption of God's people. If added later for liturgical use, it demonstrates that the ancient community recognized the principle: no individual's prayer is truly complete until it includes the wider community of faith.

The verb *padah* (redeem) carries the connotation of ransoming or setting free by means of a price or exchange. It is the language of exodus and liberation, of God acting as a kinsman-redeemer to reclaim His people. The address "O God" (*Elohim*) emphasizes God as the mighty power, the one capable of redemption on a cosmic scale. The phrase "out of all his troubles" (*mikol tzarotav*) completes the thought: not deliverance from some troubles, but from all of them. This is an eschatological prayer—a prayer that reaches beyond the psalmist's immediate circumstances to the ultimate redemption of God's people. By ending here, Psalm 25 affirms that the pattern of petitioning God for protection and guidance—the pattern the individual has lived out through twenty-one verses—is meant to be replicated in the life of the covenant community. The psalm moves from the individual lament to corporate hope, suggesting that personal faithfulness is always part of a larger story of communal redemption.

word_study.meaning: to redeem, ransom, set free by payment or exchange. Often implies recovery of what was lost or enslaved.
word_study.significance: This is the language of the exodus—God as the redeemer who buys back Israel from slavery. It carries a sense of both legal transaction (the price is paid) and relational care (God acts as kinsman-redeemer).

word_study.meaning: Israel, the people of God, the nation chosen and covenanted by God. Literally, 'he who strives with God,' based on Jacob's name change.
word_study.significance: The use of Israel's corporate name (not just 'your people') emphasizes the continuity of God's covenant with the nation and the ongoing redemptive story of which individuals are a part.

word_study.meaning: troubles, distresses, hardships, narrow straits. The word conveys both external threat and internal constraint.
word_study.significance: Tzarot encompasses the whole range of difficulties—military, social, spiritual—that afflict a covenant people. The prayer is for complete liberation from the full scope of affliction.

cross_references.connection: The Song of Moses: 'Thou in thy mercy hast led forth the people which thou hast redeemed: thou hast guided them in thy strength unto thy holy habitation.' The exodus redemption sets the pattern for all subsequent redemptive hopes.

Let Israel hope in the Lord: for with the Lord there is mercy, and with him is plenteous redemption. And he shall redeem Israel from all his iniquities.' The individual prayer finds its completion in the communal redemption promised to the whole people.

But now thus saith the Lord that created thee, O Jacob, and he that formed thee, O Israel, Fear not: for I have redeemed thee.' The assurance of redemption extends from past (the exodus) to future (messianic redemption) to the continuous present.

And now it came to pass that when Amlici saw that his design had been frustrated, he fled to the land that was northward... Seek ye the Kingdom of God.' The Book of Mormon mirrors the pattern of individual conversion flowing into communal salvation.

Thus saith the Lord unto you my servants, who have assembled yourselves together to receive my commandments concerning the afflictions which have come upon you.' God's promises of redemption to the covenant community, echoing the pattern of Israel's redemption.

commentary.historical_context: The shift from singular to plural at the end of the psalm suggests its use in communal worship. An individual would come to the temple, perhaps after an experience of persecution or crisis, and voice this psalm. But the psalm was structured (or was received as structured) in such a way that the individual's prayer could be woven into the larger prayer of the community. When the psalm was sung or recited in the assembly, the final verse reminded the gathered people that their own deliverance is bound up with the redemption of the whole covenant community. This reflects a fundamental principle of ancient Israel: there is no purely private salvation. An individual's standing before God is always understood in relation to the covenant people as a whole. The historical troubles of Israel—exile, oppression, exile, foreign domination—gave this verse particular urgency. It became not just a prayer for relief but a prayer for the fulfillment of God's covenant promises, for the restoration of the people to their land and their proper relationship with God.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: 1 Nephi 22:1-2 describes the latter-day redemption of Israel: 'And now it came to pass that after I, Nephi, had read these things, I was desirous to know the things which should come to pass hereafter.' The Book of Mormon itself is structured as the story of individual covenants flowing into communal redemption—the principle that Psalm 25 articulates.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 29:1-3 describes God's redemptive purpose: 'Hearken, O ye people of my church, saith the voice of him whose eyes are upon all men... even Jesus Christ, whom I have sent.' Restoration doctrine emphasizes that communal redemption flows through individual faithfulness and covenant-keeping. D&C 38:1-3 promises that those who endure will be redeemed with their families and communities.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The temple is itself a symbol and type of redemption. Individuals come to the temple to make covenants, but those covenants are always understood in the context of the larger restoration of all things. The endowment narrative walks from the creation through the fall and toward redemption—a pattern that moves from personal to cosmic, from individual to universal.

commentary.christological_typology: Jesus Christ is himself Israel's ultimate redeemer (*go'el*, kinsman-redeemer in Hebrew thought). His atonement is the means by which the redemption prayed for in this verse is accomplished. He redeems not just individuals but all of covenant Israel (and eventually all of God's children) from the bondage of sin and death. The Resurrection and Ascension prove that Jesus has purchased redemption by his own sacrifice. His second coming will accomplish the final redemption of all things, gathering Israel and all the faithful into the presence of God. The psalmic prayer thus becomes, in Christian and Latter-day Saint understanding, a prayer that points toward Christ and is answered through His redemptive work.
commentary.application: The psalmist teaches us that personal prayer and communal concern cannot be separated. As we pray for our own needs and deliverance, we are invited to expand our vision to include the needs of the larger community—our congregation, our nation, and ultimately the entire covenant family. When we face personal trials, we are not meant to become so focused on ourselves that we forget the struggles of others. Instead, we are invited to bring our own petitions to God while also bringing the petitions of our community. This reflects the Latter-day Saint principle of weeping with those who weep and bearing one another's burdens. In the temple, this principle is made concrete: our personal ordinances are part of the larger work of redemption for all God's children. The shift to the communal voice at the close of Psalm 25 reminds us that our individual faithfulness matters because it is part of the larger story of God's redemption of His people. We are invited to pray not just for ourselves but for the redemption of Zion—the covenant community in its fullest sense.

text_kjv: That I may publish with the voice of thanksgiving, and tell of all thy wondrous works.

commentary.narrative: The psalmist moves from internal integrity (verses 1-6) to public declaration. The phrase 'voice of thanksgiving' (qol todah) is not merely personal piety but a specific liturgical act: the public announcement that accompanies the todah offering in Israel's worship system. The speaker has walked in integrity; now he must give voice to it in community. The 'wondrous works' (nifleotekha) are not abstract theological principles but concrete divine interventions in history and personal experience. Hebrew worship is fundamentally narrative—it recounts what God has done. The speaker's intention is not self-promotion but witness. By publishing God's deeds with thanksgiving, he positions himself as a faithful covenant member who testifies to the community about divine faithfulness.
commentary.narrative_continued: This verse reveals the complete arc of Hebrew piety: internal integrity must necessarily overflow into communal testimony. Silence about God's works would be a form of ingratitude. The progression from 'I have washed my hands in innocency' (v. 6) to 'I will publish' (v. 7) shows that personal righteousness is never meant to be private. The assembly is called to witness not the speaker's virtue but God's mighty deeds. The Covenant Rendering's emphasis on 'raising a shout' captures the vocal, physical, communal intensity of Hebrew thanksgiving—not a whisper but a declaration.

word_study.meaning: The vocal component of the todah (thanksgiving) offering; the public declaration that accompanies a sacrifice of gratitude. Qol refers to 'voice' or 'sound,' emphasizing audibility and communal awareness; todah is the thanksgiving offering, which in Israel's sacrificial system was unique in that it was accompanied by bread, wine, and explicit public testimony of what God had done.
word_study.significance: This is not casual praise but a formal, liturgical act embedded in Israel's covenant worship. The speaker is not merely feeling grateful but performing the todah ritual—the most social of all Israel's sacrifices. Modern worship often separates gratitude from testimony, but Hebrew worship integrates them. The 'voice' must be heard; silence would nullify the offering.

word_study.meaning: Your wonders, your extraordinary deeds, your miraculous acts. From the root pala ('to be extraordinary, to be separate from ordinary occurrence'). These are not generic divine attributes but specific, concrete interventions that break ordinary patterns.
word_study.significance: The psalmist is not giving thanks for abstract 'goodness' but for identifiable acts of God. This grounds worship in history and testimony. The speaker's integrity and God's mighty deeds are bound together—the speaker witnesses to what God has done. Nifleotekha appears frequently in the Psalms as a warrant for trust and a call to remember God's pattern of deliverance.

cross_references.connection: The opening of Psalm 107 explicitly connects redemption with the command to tell: 'Let the redeemed of the LORD say so, whom he hath redeemed from the hand of the enemy.' Testimony is the natural response to divine deliverance.

The todah offering is described with specific regulations about bread and grain accompany thanksgiving sacrifices, linking this psalm's 'voice of thanksgiving' to the actual covenant worship system of Israel.
A parallel declaration: 'I have preached righteousness in the great congregation: lo, I have not refrained my lips, O LORD, thou knowest.' Both psalms move from internal integrity to public witness.

Nephi records his family's desire to 'make a record of our proceedings in these days' so that their children would know of the tender mercies of God. Like the psalmist, covenant people are commanded to testify of God's wondrous works to the community.

commentary.historical_context: The todah offering occupied a unique place in Israel's sacrificial system. Unlike the sin offering (brought for transgression) or the peace offering (brought for communion), the todah was explicitly a testimony offering—a public statement of gratitude with witnesses present. Archaeological and textual evidence suggests that the todah ritual included the recitation of a narrative: what God had done, how the worshiper had called upon him, how God had answered. The 'voice of thanksgiving' that the psalmist speaks of would have been accompanied by the actual breaking of bread and the sharing of the sacrificial meal among family and friends, making it a communal meal of witness. The public assembly (qahel) provided the social context where such testimony had weight. In ancient Israel, worship was never a private affair; it was always tied to the remembering community.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: The Book of Mormon covenant people repeatedly command future generations to testify of God's wonders. Lehi's vision becomes testimony (1 Nephi 1); Nephi's experiences become record and witness (1 Nephi 19:23); Mormon explicitly structures his record to cause future readers to 'feel' the reality of God's works (Mormon 8:35). The principle that internal knowledge must become external testimony runs throughout the restoration.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 30:11 commands 'thou shalt declare the things which have been revealed to thee'—the exact pattern of this psalm. Personal experience of God's wonders must flow into public declaration. This is the pattern of covenant membership.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The todah offering was brought to the temple; its recitation of God's mighty deeds mirrors the testimony tradition of Latter-day Saint temple worship, where covenants are made in remembrance of Christ's atonement—God's supreme 'wondrous work.' The speaker's voice in the assembly recalls the communal witness-bearing of the sacrament blessing and testimony meetings in the restored church.

commentary.christological_typology: The todah offering is a type of Christ's offering. Jesus's sacrifice is not only expiation but testimony—his death and resurrection publicly declare the Father's power and love. The psalmist's 'voice of thanksgiving' declaring God's mighty works anticipates the gospel proclamation, which is fundamentally the testimony of what God has done through Christ: redemption, resurrection, and reunion with the Father. Christ's sacrifice encompasses both the internal integrity demanded (living without sin) and the public declaration required (the gospel preached to all nations).
commentary.application: For modern covenant members, this verse challenges the separation between private faith and public testimony. The psalmist does not worship privately and remain silent publicly; he moves necessarily from integrity to declaration. In our cultural moment, when testimony-bearing in the congregation has become less common, this verse calls us to recover the ancient principle: if you have experienced God's mighty works, you are obligated to raise your voice in the assembly and tell of them. This is not self-promotion; it is witness. The integrity that matters most is the integrity to testify even when silence seems safer. Personal righteousness that never becomes testimony is incomplete.

text_kjv: LORD, I have loved the habitation of thy house, and the place where thine honour dwelleth.

commentary.narrative: The psalmist pivots from public declaration to personal confession of love. The verb 'loved' (ahavti) is the same Hebrew word used for marital love, familial affection, and friendship love—it is passionate attachment, not dutiful obligation. The object of this love is not abstract theology but 'the habitation of thy house' and 'the place where thine honour dwelleth'—concrete, localized, physical reality. The speaker loves the temple, the central institution of covenant community, but more precisely, he loves it because God's glory (kavod) dwells there. He is not romanticizing a building but expressing attachment to the place where the transcendent God becomes accessible to his people.
commentary.narrative_continued: This verse addresses a fundamental tension in Hebrew faith: how can finite humans love the infinite God? The answer in the Psalms is that God has made himself localized, accessible, visible. The temple is where 'the place where thine honour dwelleth'—where God's weight, presence, glory becomes palpable. The Covenant Rendering clarifies that 'dwelling place' (mikvash, related to the mishkan) echoes the wilderness tabernacle where God's glory first descended (Exodus 40:34). By loving the temple, the psalmist is loving the continuation of that primal encounter with God's presence. His love is grounded in memory and in the persistence of God's covenant commitment to dwell among his people.

word_study.meaning: First person singular perfect of ahav ('to love'). This verb carries emotional intensity and personal commitment. It is used for romantic love (Genesis 29:18, 'Jacob loved Rachel'), covenant love between friends (1 Samuel 18:1, 'the soul of Jonathan was knit with the soul of David'), and for the love of God (Deuteronomy 6:5, 'thou shalt love the LORD thy God'). The verb encompasses both feeling and commitment.
word_study.significance: The psalmist does not say 'I reverence' or 'I serve' God's house; he says he loves it. This makes his faith personal and passionate. The contrast with verse 9 ('Do not sweep my soul away with sinners') becomes sharper: the speaker's separation from the wicked is not legalistic but flows from passionate attachment to the true God and his house.

word_study.meaning: A dwelling place, a habitation, particularly used of God's residence. The term suggests both the physical structure and the reality of inhabitation—God actually dwells there. Related to the root 'anah ('to dwell, to be at home').
word_study.significance: The speaker loves not an empty building but the place of God's presence. This grounds attachment to the physical sanctuary in theological reality: God is there. The temple is not a symbol; it is the locus of divine presence.

word_study.meaning: Glory, splendor, honor, weight, dignity. The literal root meaning is 'heaviness' or 'weight'—kavod denotes something substantive, weighty, visible, and overwhelming. In biblical usage, the kavod of God is the visible manifestation of his presence, often described as radiant light. The mishkan ('tabernacle') was filled with God's kavod when it was completed (Exodus 40:34); the temple continues as the dwelling place of that kavod.
word_study.significance: The speaker loves the place where God's kavod resides—where the infinite becomes visible, where the transcendent becomes palpable. Kavod is not abstract; it is the overwhelming presence of the holy. The Covenant Rendering preserves this sense of 'glory' as something that 'resides,' making the temple the container of divine presence.

word_study.meaning: To dwell, to inhabit, to settle, to reside. The verb carries the sense of permanence and stability—not a temporary visit but establishment of residence.
word_study.significance: God does not merely visit the temple; he dwells there. His presence is not occasional but permanent, bound by covenant to Israel. This permanence is what the speaker loves.

cross_references.connection: When the tabernacle was completed, 'the glory of the LORD filled the tabernacle.' This is the primal moment of divine habitation that grounds the psalmist's love for God's house—the speaker is loving the continuation of that original covenant presence.

A parallel expression of love for God's house: 'How amiable are thy tabernacles, O LORD of hosts! My soul longeth, yea, even fainteth for the courts of the LORD.' The same passionate attachment to the place of divine presence.

At the dedication of Solomon's temple, 'the glory of the LORD had filled the house of God.' The temple worship system carries forward the tabernacle tradition of God's visible, tangible presence dwelling among his covenant people.

Nephi describes his vision of 'the tree of life, and also the river of water' that give life and sustenance, then asks an angel to interpret, seeking understanding of spiritual reality. Like the psalmist, Nephi loves knowledge of the place where God's presence dwells.

The Lord declares of temples: 'My house is a house of order...a house of God.' The Restoration recovers the principle that God designates specific places as the loci of his presence and covenant-making, just as the ancient temple was.

commentary.historical_context: In ancient Israel, the temple was not merely a religious building but the center of national identity and covenant relationship with God. The Jerusalem temple, which stood from Solomon's era (10th century BCE) through its destruction in 586 BCE, was understood as the dwelling place of the divine name and presence. Archaeological evidence from surrounding ancient Near Eastern cultures shows that temples were conceptualized as the cosmic center where heaven and earth met. The Israelite temple, however, was unique in its emphasis on monotheism and on God's covenant promises to David and to the entire nation. For the psalmist, love of the temple was not aesthetic appreciation of architecture but relational attachment to the place where God had bound himself to his people. The temple was where sacrifices were offered, where festivals were celebrated, where the community experienced God's presence communally. To love the temple was to love being part of the covenant community.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: The Book of Mormon preserves the principle of a sanctified place of God's dwelling. Nephi brings the Liahona (the sacred artifact of divine guidance), the plates, and Laban's sword to the land of promise, establishing a center of covenant life. The temple in Mesoamerica becomes the gathering place of Nephite civilization (2 Nephi 5:16). Later, Alma sanctifies priests 'after the order of the Son of God' (Alma 13:1) and establishes covenant worship centered on remembrance of Christ. The Restoration principle of 'love the temple' is renewed.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 109-110 contain the dedicatory prayer of the Kirtland Temple and the vision of the Savior in that temple. The love of God's house is literally a Latter-day Saint principle: members are commanded to gather in temples to make covenants. D&C 124:26 speaks of the Nauvoo Temple as 'a house of God, a house of prayer, a house of fasting, a house of faith, a house of learning, a house of glory, a house of order, a house of God.' This directly echoes the psalmist's love of the place where God's glory dwells.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: This verse is fundamentally about temple love and temple theology. The psalmist's love for 'the place where thine honour dwelleth' directly parallels the Latter-day Saint principle that temples are the most sacred spaces on earth, where heaven touches earth, where God's presence is particularly accessible, and where eternal covenants are made. Members are taught to love the temple, to serve in it, to approach it with reverence, and to make it central to their covenant life. The principle of personal, passionate love for the temple—not merely dutiful attendance—is central to this verse's meaning.
