word_study.meaning: Heart, mind, will, resolve. In Hebrew thought, the heart is not sentimentality but the seat of will, intention, decision, and moral character. To strengthen the heart means to fortify one's capacity to choose rightly and persevere faithfully.
word_study.significance: The TCR rendering preserves the focus on the heart as the center of resolve. Modern readers often think of the heart as emotion; the Hebrew tradition understands it as the core of personhood—will, mind, and spirit together.

word_study.meaning: The preposition el means 'to, toward, unto'—suggesting movement or orientation. One does not wait in isolation but waits toward someone, for someone. The object is YHWH, the God of covenant and redemption.
word_study.significance: The repetition of this phrase at the beginning and end of the verse (el-YHWH... el-YHWH) creates a bookend that makes orientation toward God the alpha and omega of the waiting posture.

cross_references.connection: But they that wait upon the LORD shall renew their strength... they shall run, and not be weary; and they shall walk, and not faint—connecting waiting for God with the renewal of strength and endurance.

God commands Joshua repeatedly to 'be strong and of a good courage' in the face of the conquest, using the same Hebrew root (chazak) as Psalm 27:14, and grounding courage in the promise of God's presence.

The LORD is good unto them that wait for him, to the soul that seeketh him. It is good that a man should both hope and quietly wait for the salvation of the LORD—expressing the same conviction that waiting for God is both duty and blessing.

And now as I said concerning faith—faith is not to have a perfect knowledge of things; therefore if ye have faith ye hope for things which are not seen, which are true—connecting the principle of faith (belief) with hope (active, expectant waiting for God's provision).

Wherefore, be faithful; stand in the place whereon I have appointed you, and remain faithful and steadfast, always abounding in good works—echoing the call to firmness, resolve, and sustained trust in God's direction.

commentary.historical_context: In ancient Israel, waiting was not a luxury but often a necessity—waiting for deliverance from enemies, waiting for the rains to come, waiting for God to act in history. The military and hunting imagery embedded in qavah ('to wait expectantly') reflects a world in which one literally watched the horizon for approaching threat or relief. The heart (lebab) in Semitic thought was the center of the person—will, intention, memory, and moral choice all located there. To strengthen the heart was to fortify the whole person against despair. The repetition of 'Wait for the LORD' appears in several psalms and prayers of Israel (see Psalm 37:7, 40:1; Lamentations 3:25), suggesting it was a liturgical refrain used in communal worship and private devotion. The psalm likely was sung or chanted, making the repetition even more powerful through musical reinforcement.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: Alma 26:6-12 captures this same spirit of patience and courage in the face of opposition. Alma exhorts the Zoramite converts: 'And I would that ye should be steadfast and immovable, always abounding in good works' (Alma 32:42)—calling for the same qavah-like stance of steadfast faith. Moroni's closing words in Moroni 10:30-31 promise that as saints wait upon God with faith, He will manifest Himself: 'And I would exhort you... that ye receive these things, and that ye search these things diligently... I would exhort you that when ye shall receive these things, ye would exhort all men to repent, that they prepare to come unto me in my Father's kingdom.'
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 121:1-6 presents Joseph Smith in prison waiting for God's deliverance, and the Lord responds with the assurance of His presence and eventual vindication. The entire passage mirrors Psalm 27's structure: distress, plea for help, and the call to trust and wait. D&C 68:6 teaches that 'by small and simple things are great things brought to pass' (Alma 37:6), echoing the principle that faith is maintained through daily, patient waiting and obedience rather than dramatic demonstrations.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The temple covenant is fundamentally a covenant to wait—to wait for exaltation, to wait for the Savior, to remain faithful through the trials of mortality. The endowment ceremony teaches that progression toward God comes through patient obedience and steadfast waiting for His guidance and strength. Each temple recommend renewal symbolizes the renewal of the covenant to strengthen one's heart and remain steadfast in faith.

commentary.christological_typology: Jesus Christ embodies the perfect waiting posture in Gethsemane: 'Nevertheless not as I will, but as thou wilt' (Matthew 26:39). His willingness to wait for the Father's will, to strengthen His heart to endure the cross, to submit to suffering while maintaining perfect faith—all of this is the ultimate expression of qavah. In Hebrews 12:2, Jesus is described as 'the author and finisher of our faith,' and the context is His ability to 'endure the cross, despising the shame.' He waited for the joy set before Him, just as the psalmist waits for the goodness of the LORD. The resurrection is the vindication of His waiting—the proof that trusting in God's character and purpose is justified.
commentary.application: In the modern world, waiting is countercultural. We expect instant results, quick fixes, rapid delivery. Yet this verse calls covenant keepers to a discipline as old as faith itself: to wait with active, taut expectation for the LORD's action. This means holding firm in faith even when circumstances suggest despair. It means refusing to manufacture solutions that bypass God's will and timing. It means strengthening one's heart daily through prayer, scripture study, and community—the spiritual practices that reinforce resolve when doubt threatens. For those facing illness, unemployment, broken relationships, or ministry struggles, this verse offers no promise of immediate relief but something deeper: the assurance that as you wait, looking toward the LORD with steadfast faith, He will strengthen your heart. The waiting itself becomes the proving ground where faith is deepened, character is formed, and the soul is prepared for God's eventual answer. The repetition of the command—'Wait, wait, WAIT'—suggests that this must be not a momentary stance but a sustained posture, renewed daily, supported by conscious acts of courage and faith.

text_kjv: The LORD is my strength and my shield; my heart trusted in him, and I am helped: therefore my heart greatly rejoiceth; and with my song will I praise him.

commentary.narrative: This verse marks the pivot from desperate petition to jubilant thanksgiving—the answer has come. The psalmist who moments before cried out in anguish (verse 1) now declares absolute trust and exultation. The parallelism is intentional: the same heart that trembled in fear now leaps with joy. This is not merely intellectual assent but embodied transformation. The heart does not gradually warm to confidence; it is helped, and the response is spontaneous overflow—the body cannot contain the joy. The verb 'alaz' (leaps for joy) suggests involuntary, uncontainable exultation, the kind that bursts forth in song. The psalmist moves from silence (the terror of not being heard) to song (the proof of being heard). This progression from desperation through trust to praise models the spiritual journey of all believers who have known the distance between unanswered prayer and answered prayer.
commentary.narrative_continued: What makes this verse theologically significant is its insistence that the same God who is strength (military protection, fortification) is also shield (personal, intimate protection). The Covenant Rendering's distinction between these titles—uzzi and maginni—reveals that God's protection operates at multiple registers. The heart's trust (batach) is not tentative or conditional; it is the stance of one who has cast anxieties upon the Lord and found them held. The movement from 'I trusted' to 'I am helped' to 'my heart leaps' traces the actual experience of faith actualized: trust produces the evidence of answered prayer, which produces joy. The final phrase—'with my song will I praise him'—indicates that the psalmist's response is not private. Public testimony through song becomes the natural overflow of private vindication.

word_study.meaning: My strength; literally 'my might' or 'my power.' The root 'oz' conveys fortification, hardness, enduring power. In military contexts, it refers to the strength that cannot be breached. The Covenant Rendering preserves this as 'strength' but the deeper sense is the inexhaustible power that stands firm against all assault.
word_study.significance: For the psalmist, God's strength is not abstract but personal—'my strength.' This is not merely the theoretical power of God but the lived experience of that power as protective resource. In Restoration theology, this echoes D&C 84:88: 'I am in your midst, and I am the good shepherd.'

word_study.meaning: My shield; from the root 'ganan,' meaning to cover, protect, defend. Unlike uzzi (strength), which is the inner fortification, maginni is the external barrier that stands between the threat and the protected one. The shield is held before the face; it is the most intimate protection.
word_study.significance: The parallelism between uzzi and maginni suggests that God's protection is both internal (the strength that keeps us standing) and external (the covering that intercepts attack). This dual protection speaks to the comprehensiveness of divine guardianship.

word_study.meaning: To trust, to rely upon, to place confidence in. The root suggests a sense of security that rests upon something solid—literally, to recline upon or lean against. Batach is not mere intellectual belief but committed reliance.
word_study.significance: The heart's trust (lev batach) is the antithesis of the fearful silence of verse 1. Trust is the posture of faith—the settling of the whole person into God's sufficiency. In Proverbs 3:5, batach appears again: 'Trust in the LORD with all thine heart.'

word_study.meaning: I am helped, assisted, rescued. The verb 'azar' means to give aid or support, to come to one's aid. The niphal form (passive/reflexive) suggests both that help came and that the speaker received it. This is answered prayer made manifest.
word_study.significance: The speaker moves from petition ('hear me') to evidence ('I am helped'). This verb transforms the subjunctive (if you would help me) into the indicative (you have helped me). It is the hinge upon which despair turns toward joy.

word_study.meaning: To exult, to leap, to rejoice with uncontained excitement. The root 'alaz' carries the sense of spontaneous, physical exultation—not the quiet satisfaction of having needs met, but the involuntary overflow of the entire being. Ancient Near Eastern texts use this verb to describe the joy of warriors after victory or the jubilation of harvest celebrations.
word_study.significance: The Covenant Rendering captures what the KJV's 'greatly rejoiceth' only approximates: the heart does not merely feel joy, it leaps. This is embodied religion—the body cannot help but express what the spirit has experienced. In covenant terms, this is the joy of covenant renewal, the exultation that comes when God's faithfulness is known directly.

cross_references.connection: Both affirm trust in the Lord as shepherd/strength. Psalm 28:7 declares 'The LORD is my strength and my shield,' while Psalm 23:1 declares 'The LORD is my shepherd.' Both psalms move from the declaration of God's protection to the consequent peace and joy.

Moses declares, 'The LORD is my strength and song, and he is become my salvation.' The parallelism is exact: strength, song, and salvation converge. Psalm 28:7 echoes this triumphant song of deliverance after crossing the Red Sea.

The Lord promises, 'I am in your midst, and I am the good shepherd, and the stone of Israel.' The language of strength and shepherding protection directly parallels the psalmist's declaration. God's presence is the ground of both strength and safety.

Ammon declares, 'Blessed be the name of our God; let us sing to his praise, yea, let us give thanks to his holy name.' Like Psalm 28:7, the response to God's deliverance is spontaneous song—the natural overflow of gratitude.

Paul writes, 'Rejoice in the Lord always... In every thing by prayer and supplication with thanksgiving let your requests be made known unto God.' The movement from supplication to thanksgiving to joy mirrors the arc of Psalm 28:7.

commentary.historical_context: In ancient Near Eastern royal ideology, the king's personal triumph was understood as the nation's deliverance. When the king speaks of his own rescue and exultation, he is not being purely personal but rather modeling and enacting the people's covenant relationship with their God. The shield and strength language draws on the visual imagery of ancient warfare—God as the fortress, the impregnable wall, the protective covering that stands between the enemies and the protected one. The song of praise (verse 7) would have been performed publicly, possibly at the temple during a ceremony of thanksgiving. The public performance of the king's private experience sanctified and taught the entire covenant community how to respond when their prayers are answered. The shift from individual to national in verses 8-9 makes clear that the king's deliverance is paradigmatic—it teaches the people how to trust and pray.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: In Alma 26:12-16, Ammon's exultation after his successful mission mirrors the psalmist's joy in verse 7. Both testimonies move from the declaration of God's strength to the irrepressible need to share that strength through song. The Book of Mormon emphasizes that true strength comes only through faith in Christ, anticipating the fuller revelation that the 'anointed one' (meshiach) of verse 8 is Christ himself.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 19:38 states, 'I am Alpha and Omega, the beginning and the end... I am in your midst.' This echoes the psalmist's intimate declaration that the LORD is his personal strength and shield. The Doctrine and Covenants teaches that Christ's presence—his strength and protection—is available to every covenant member, not only to kings. D&C 84:88 extends the shepherding language of verse 9 to the Savior, making explicit what Psalm 28 foreshadows: Christ is the ultimate anointed one whose strength and shepherding care embrace the entire covenant people.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The sequence of supplication, reception of help, and joyful song mirrors the temple endowment experience: the seeker approaches in need, receives covenantal promises of divine aid, and exits in exaltation. The 'heart' (lev) that trusts and leaps for joy is the sanctified heart of the covenant participant. The song of praise in verse 7 resonates with the jubilation of those who have passed through the veil and returned transformed. Verse 9's imperative language—'Save your people, bless your inheritance, shepherd them'—reflects the intercessory prayers offered in the temple on behalf of the living and the dead.

commentary.christological_typology: The psalmist's private deliverance and subsequent exultation typify Christ's resurrection. Like the psalmist moving from desperate petition to jubilant thanksgiving, Christ moved through suffering and death to exultation and the pouring out of joy to the disciples. The language of being 'helped' (ne'ezarti) and 'strengthened' points to Christ's experience in Gethsemane when an angel strengthened him (Luke 22:43). The final song of praise—'with my song will I praise him'—finds its ultimate expression in Christ's resurrection hymn and the disciples' recognition that their prayers have been answered through the Atonement. The 'heart' that trusts in God (verse 7) prefigures the heart perfected and unafraid in Christ.
commentary.application: For modern covenant members, Psalm 28:7 teaches that the movement from desperation to joy is not the exception but the expected pattern of faithful prayer. When you find yourself in the silence of unanswered prayer, the psalmist invites you to remember that this is the beginning of the arc, not the end. The verb batach (trust) is not passive waiting but active reliance—the deliberate posture of placing your whole self into God's hands. The exultation that follows is not a luxury or an emotional excess but the natural, necessary response when the heart has trusted and proven God's faithfulness. The psalmist's song is meant to be shared publicly because private deliverance teaches public doctrine: this is how covenant works. When you have been helped, when you have felt the strength and shield of God's protection, you are called to sing—not for your own satisfaction but to teach others that God is as faithful to them as he has been to you.

text_kjv: The LORD is their strength, and he is the saving strength of his anointed.

commentary.narrative: The scope of the psalm expands abruptly from the individual 'I' to the communal 'their' and 'his people.' The personal experience of verses 1-7 becomes the foundation for national intercession. This is the characteristic movement of Davidic psalms: the king's private struggle is never merely private because the king is the focal point of the covenant community. What God does for the king, he does for the people; what the king learns through prayer, he teaches the nation through testimony. The phrase 'saving strength' (maoz yeshuot) introduces a new dimension: the strength that saves, the refuge that delivers. This is not merely protective strength but redemptive strength—the power that snatches from the grip of enemies or from the abyss itself.
commentary.narrative_continued: The introduction of 'his anointed' (meshicho) is theologically freighted. In the original Davidic context, this refers to the reigning king, anointed with oil as God's chosen representative. But the language carries weight beyond any single dynasty. The Jewish and later Christian traditions understood 'the anointed one' as a title laden with messianic expectation—the future king who would embody God's saving purpose definitively. The Covenant Rendering's distinction between 'the strength of his people' (oz-lamo) and 'the saving refuge of his anointed' (maoz yeshuot meshicho) reveals that the anointed one's salvation is not separate from the people's but rather the paradigm and ground of it. The anointed one is saved so that the people might be saved; his deliverance is their deliverance.

word_study.meaning: Strength, might, power. This is the masculine singular of the root uzzi (verse 7). It conveys the sense of power that stands firm, that cannot be shaken. In biblical usage, oz is often paired with malkhut (kingdom)—strength and rule together.
word_study.significance: The use of oz (rather than the possessive uzzi) here makes the statement more universal. The psalmist is not claiming private protection but declaring a truth about God's relationship to his entire people. God's strength belongs to the people as a collective inheritance.

word_study.meaning: Refuge of salvations; the fortified place of deliverance. Maoz is a stronghold or fortress—a place of refuge. Yeshuot (plural of yeshuah) literally means 'salvations'—the plural form suggesting multiple acts of deliverance, multiple instances of God's saving power. The genitive construction makes this a refuge characterized by salvation.
word_study.significance: This phrase moves beyond mere protection to active redemption. It is not just a shield from harm but a source of liberation. The Covenant Rendering captures this well: 'saving refuge'—a place where one is not only protected from enemies but actively delivered from bondage. This is the language of exodus.

word_study.meaning: His anointed one; from the root masach (to anoint with oil). In ancient Near Eastern royal ideology, anointing with oil marked the transfer of divine power and authority. The anointed one is the vessel through whom God's will is enacted in history. In Hebrew, mashiach literally means 'anointed one,' a term that became synonymous with the eschatological deliverer (the Messiah).
word_study.significance: For a Davidic psalm, meshicho refers to the Davidic king. But the language is susceptible to messianic reading—indeed, early Christian interpreters and Jewish messianic thought read this as referring to the ultimate anointed one who would deliver not just politically but cosmically. The singular 'his anointed' (not 'his anointed ones') suggests a unique, irreplaceable figure—a pattern that found its fulfillment in Christian theology as pointing to Christ.

cross_references.connection: The Lord gives grace and glory; no good thing will he withhold from those that walk uprightly. Like verse 8, this affirms God's comprehensive provision—the shield, the fortress, and the salvation all flow from the same source.

Hannah prophesies, 'The LORD shall judge the ends of the earth; and he shall give strength unto his king, and exalt the horn of his anointed.' The pairing of strength with the anointed one's exaltation directly parallels Psalm 28:8's structure.

The Davidic covenant promises that God will establish the throne of David's offspring forever. Psalm 28:8 reflects this covenant theology—the king stands as the focal point of God's saving purpose for the entire nation.

The psalmist declares, 'I have found David my servant; with my holy oil have I anointed him.' This foundational anointing is what verse 8 refers to—the anointing that makes the king the conduit of God's strength to the people.

Jesus quotes Isaiah 61:1 in the synagogue: 'The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because he hath anointed me.' Jesus claims to be the ultimate meshiach ('anointed one'), fulfilling the messianic hope embedded in this verse.

The Doctrine and Covenants identifies Jesus as 'the Only Begotten Son, who is in the bosom of the Father... the Lord and Savior of all people.' Christ is the ultimate meshiach, in whom all salvation is concentrated and through whom all deliverance flows.

commentary.historical_context: In ancient Near Eastern royal ideology, the king was understood as the mediator between the divine and human realms. The king's strength was not personal but derived—he stood between God and the people as the conduit through which divine blessing flowed. The anointing with oil was a public ceremony that transferred divine authorization to the chosen one. The people's welfare was understood to be inseparable from the king's fidelity to God's covenant. Thus, when the psalmist prays for the king's salvation (as in verse 8), he is praying for the salvation of the entire nation. The language of 'saving strength' (maoz yeshuot) draws on the exodus narrative—God's refuge in the wilderness, his saving acts against Egypt. The Jewish people understood their covenant relationship through the lens of exodus: God had saved them once and would save them again through whatever anointed figure he raised up. This eschatological expectation grew more pronounced during periods of exile and foreign domination, when the need for a true anointed deliverer became acute.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: In 2 Nephi 6:8-13, Nephi teaches that the anointed one will bring salvation to the people: 'Wherefore, all those who are broken off must come unto him, and they must bow down before him, or they cannot be saved.' The Book of Mormon interprets the meshiach (anointed one) of verse 8 as Christ himself, and demonstrates that the people's salvation flows through the anointed one's saving power. The scope of verse 8—from individual king to the anointed one to the entire people—is the very movement that the Book of Mormon makes explicit when it identifies Christ as the anointed one and all covenant believers as the beneficiaries of his anointing.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 21:4-5 teaches that the Lord will stand by his servants, and 'him that receiveth my word and my covenant... unto him will I grant all things whatsoever he hath asked.' This resonates with verse 8's promise that the anointed one receives the saving strength of God. More profoundly, D&C 110 reveals that Christ himself comes to the Kirtland Temple, confirming that Jesus is the ultimate meshiach whose saving power extends to all who accept his covenant. The Doctrine and Covenants makes explicit what Psalm 28:8 foreshadows: there is an anointed one through whom all salvation flows.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: In Latter-day Saint temple theology, every member who receives the holy anointing in the temple becomes, in a derivative sense, 'anointed.' The words spoken to each covenant member—'As the hair of the head of the Son is never touched with scissors, so shall the hair of the head of one faithful in this covenant be preserved'—echo the sacred anointing of the king. But the ultimate anointing belongs to Christ. The ritual anointing of the faithful is participation in and anticipation of the perfect anointing of Christ. The temple thus teaches that the saving strength promised to the anointed one (verse 8) flows to all who enter into his covenant.

commentary.christological_typology: The anointed one of Psalm 28:8 is the primary OT type of Christ. The anointing with oil prefigures the anointing of Jesus as the Messiah—literally, the 'Anointed One.' His saving strength is the power by which all deliverance flows. The Covenant Rendering's phrase 'saving refuge' (maoz yeshuot) finds its ultimate fulfillment in the Atonement, where Christ becomes the place of refuge for all humanity and the source of salvation. Just as the Davidic king's deliverance was meant to encompass the nation's deliverance, Christ's resurrection and glorification opened the way of salvation for all people. The movement from the individual king (verse 7) to the anointed one (verse 8) to the entire people (verse 9) prefigures the redemptive structure of the Atonement: Christ's individual triumph becomes the ground of collective salvation.
commentary.application: For modern members, Psalm 28:8 challenges the notion that faith is purely personal. Your salvation is not isolated but part of a covenantal chain: Christ is the anointed one whose saving strength grounds the salvation of all who believe. When you declare, with the psalmist, that 'The LORD is their strength,' you are acknowledging that your strength comes not from private achievement but from participation in Christ's redemptive power. This verse teaches that leadership, whether in families, wards, or communities, is not about personal prominence but about being a channel through which God's saving power flows to others. If you are called to any position of stewardship or teaching, the psalmist reminds you that your role is not to be the source of strength but to direct your people toward the ultimate anointed one—Christ himself. Your own deliverance (verse 7) equips you to intercede for others (verses 8-9) and to teach them that they, too, are under the care of the anointed one whose strength is sufficient for all.

text_kjv: Save thy people, and bless thine inheritance: feed them also, and lift them up for ever.

commentary.narrative: The psalm reaches its climax in a torrent of imperatives—four commands directed to God on behalf of the nation. After the personal thanksgiving of verse 7 and the declaration of the anointed one's universal role in verse 8, the psalmist turns entirely to intercession. This is the mark of genuine spiritual maturity: having received help, the one who prayed now prays for others. The four verbs—hoshiah (save), barekh (bless), ureem (shepherd), nasseem (carry)—are not four separate actions but four dimensions of the one saving care that God extends to his covenant people. The parallel phrases 'your people' (ammekha) and 'your inheritance' (nachalatekha) both emphasize the intimate relationship between God and his people. They are not God's subjects (whom he rules) but his people and his inheritance—terms of covenant belonging.
commentary.narrative_continued: The verb 'shepherd' (raah) is the pastoral verb of Psalm 23, suggesting that the same intimate care that protects the individual heart (verses 1-7) also embraces the entire flock. The final verb—'carry them' (nasseem)—introduces the image of a parent carrying a child or a shepherd carrying a lamb. This is not strength displayed in battle but strength expressed in tenderness, in bearing the weight of others. The final phrase—'forever' (ad ha-olam, literally 'to eternity')—extends God's shepherding care beyond any historical moment into the eternal. The psalmist prays not for temporary relief but for permanent transformation. The progression of the four verbs suggests a deepening intimacy: save (from external threat), bless (with spiritual abundance), shepherd (with daily care), carry (with intimate protection). By verse 9, the psalmist has moved from personal deliverance to the vision of God's people forever held in divine arms.

word_study.meaning: Save, deliver, rescue. The imperative form (a command or urgent request) of the root yasha, meaning to make safe, to deliver from danger or bondage. Yasha carries the sense of liberation—to make wide, to bring into spacious places. Salvation in Hebrew is not merely rescue from punishment but deliverance into freedom and abundance.
word_study.significance: The same root appears in the name 'Jesus'/'Yeshua,' meaning 'God saves.' The verb hoshiah places the psalmist's request squarely in the salvation tradition—God's repeated, covenantal acts of liberation. Each use of this verb invokes the memory of the exodus.

word_study.meaning: Bless, make prosperous, cause to prosper. The root brk literally means to kneel, and blessing is understood as the flowing forth of divine favor from one who stands in a position of power and authority. A blessing is not merely kind words but effective word—it carries power and results in actual flourishing.
word_study.significance: God's blessing in Abrahamic covenant (Genesis 12:2-3) is the template: 'I will bless thee... and thou shalt be a blessing.' Blessing is the inheritance—the permanent condition of those in covenant with God. The psalmist prays that God will make the people prosper and flourish in every dimension.

word_study.meaning: Shepherd them, feed them, tend them as a flock. From the root raah, to pasture, to shepherd. The shepherd's role is to lead the flock to pasture, to protect from predators, to gather the wandering, to know each sheep by name. The Covenant Rendering renders this 'shepherd' (rather than 'feed'), which captures the comprehensive nature of pastoral care.
word_study.significance: This verb appears in Psalm 23:1 ('The LORD is my shepherd') and in Jeremiah 23:4 where God promises to raise up shepherds to shepherd the people with knowledge. The imagery of shepherding suggests intimate knowledge, daily care, and the constant protection of the weak. In Latter-day Saint theology, this becomes the pattern for all leadership.

word_study.meaning: Carry them, lift them up, bear them. From the root nasa, to lift, to carry, to bear a burden. When God 'carries' his people, the image is not of dragging or driving but of bearing them up—the way a parent carries a sleeping child or a shepherd carries a lamb that cannot keep pace.
word_study.significance: This verb appears in Exodus 19:4, where God tells Israel at Sinai, 'I bare you on eagles' wings, and brought you unto myself.' The carrying of the people is not a sign of weakness but of intimate love and complete devotion. It suggests that God carries the weight of his people's burdens as his own concern.

word_study.meaning: Your inheritance; from the root nachal, to inherit, to take possession of an inheritance as a permanent holding. An inheritance is not earned or purchased but received as a birthright, something that belongs to you by covenant, by family relationship.
word_study.significance: The use of 'inheritance' rather than 'subjects' or 'servants' emphasizes the covenant relationship. The people are not the Lord's possessions to be disposed of but his inheritance—the permanent, cherished holding of the one who made covenant. This language of inheritance carries all the weight of Abrahamic promise.

word_study.meaning: Until eternity, forever, unto the age. Ha-olam literally means 'the age,' and 'ad ha-olam' means 'to the age'—extending forward without terminus, into the indefinite future and ultimately into eternity.
word_study.significance: The Covenant Rendering's rendering 'forever' captures the ultimate extension of God's care. The shepherding and carrying are not temporary accommodations but permanent conditions. This points to the eternal covenant—the everlasting bond between God and his people.

cross_references.connection: The shepherd language of verse 9 ('shepherd them') directly parallels Psalm 23's intimate portrait of God as shepherd. Both psalms move from personal comfort to the assurance of permanent care and the promise of dwelling in God's house forever.

God tells Israel, 'I bare you on eagles' wings, and brought you unto myself.' The carrying language of verse 9 ('carry them forever') echoes this foundational covenant moment, suggesting that the eternal carrying of the people is God's permanent commitment since the exodus.

Isaiah writes, 'He shall feed his flock like a shepherd: he shall gather the lambs with his arm, and carry them in his bosom.' This passage elaborates the shepherd and carrying imagery of verse 9 into a vision of God's tenderness toward the weak and vulnerable.

Nephi teaches that Christ 'inviteth them all to come unto him and partake of his goodness; and he denieth none that come unto him, black and white, bond and free, male and female.' This reflects verse 9's imperative that God save and bless his entire people—the comprehensive nature of covenant inclusion.

Christ teaches about the nature of redemption: 'Therefore I command you to repent, and keep the commandments which you have received.' Verse 9's imperatives to save, bless, shepherd, and carry find their fulfillment in Christ's work as described in the Doctrine and Covenants.

Alma asks, 'Have ye experienced a change of heart?' and speaks of the shepherd gathering his people. The pastoral imagery of verse 9 becomes the pattern for spiritual leadership in the Book of Mormon.

commentary.historical_context: Verse 9 represents the culmination of the Davidic psalm form—the point at which the king's personal deliverance becomes the occasion for national prayer and intercession. In the ancient Near Eastern royal context, the king was the intercessor—the one who stood between God and the people, bringing their prayers and needs before the divine. The four imperatives of verse 9 would have been the formulaic conclusion to a royal prayer, likely offered in the sanctuary after a public victory or during a festival. The terms 'your people' (ammekha) and 'your inheritance' (nachalatekha) echo the language of the Abrahamic covenant, reminding the listener that God's relationship to Israel is permanent and characterized by absolute commitment. The shepherding language reflects the central metaphor of ancient Near Eastern kingship: the king, too, was expected to be a shepherd of his people. The final phrase—'forever'—extends the prayer beyond any particular crisis into the eternal, suggesting that God's care is not episodic but permanent. This verse functions as a transition from the particular to the universal, from the king's deliverance to the people's eternal salvation.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: In Mosiah 23:10-14, King Limhi prays for his people with language that echoes verse 9: 'Strengthen us, O God, that we may be delivered from the bondage of our enemies.' The Book of Mormon pattern of leadership is defined by the kind of intercession modeled in verse 9—the leader prays for the people, not for personal aggrandizement. Similarly, in 3 Nephi 17:6-10, Christ performs miracles of healing and shepherding his people, and the text notes, 'Jesus wept.' This tender compassion—the God who carries his people—is the fulfillment of verse 9's vision. The Book of Mormon interprets the shepherd language of verse 9 as descriptive of Christ's actual ministry among the Nephites.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 29:1-2 contains Christ's voice: 'Hearken, O ye people of my church, saith the voice of him whose eyes are upon all men, and whose desire is to bring to pass the immortality and eternal life of man.' The divine commitment to save, bless, shepherd, and carry the people expressed in verse 9 is fulfilled in the ongoing work of salvation described in the Doctrine and Covenants. D&C 11:28 teaches, 'Now, as thou hast asked, thou mayest receive this blessing, that thou shalt be faithful over many things.' The theme of shepherding stewardship—a participation in God's shepherding of verse 9—appears throughout the Doctrine and Covenants.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: In the temple, the liturgy of verse 9 is enacted. The temple ceremony itself is the great intercessory work—members come to pray for the living and the dead, asking God to save and bless them. The shepherding language resonates with the intimate covenants made in the temple. The endowment, particularly, teaches that God cares for and carries each covenant member through the journey of mortality and beyond. The temple is the place where the promises of verse 9—eternal saving, blessing, shepherding, and carrying—are ritualized and made available to all who enter into covenant. The temple represents the fulfillment of the psalmist's prayer: God does save, does bless, does shepherd, and does carry his people.

commentary.christological_typology: Psalm 28:9's imperatives are all answered in Christ. Christ is the one who 'saves thy people' (Matthew 1:21: 'He shall save his people from their sins'). Christ is the one who 'blesses' the people (Matthew 5 begins with the Beatitudes, Christ's pronouncements of blessing). Christ is the one who 'shepherds them' (John 10:11: 'I am the good shepherd'). And Christ is the one who 'carries them'—both in the sense of bearing their infirmities and suffering, and ultimately in the sense of gathering them into eternal life. The vision of verse 9—comprehensive, eternal care—finds its complete fulfillment in the person and work of Christ. Just as the Davidic king was the type, Christ is the antitype in whom all the saving, blessing, shepherding, and carrying are eternally secured.
commentary.application: Psalm 28:9 calls you to understand that your own salvation is inseparable from your responsibility to pray and work for the salvation of others. Having received the Lord's help (verse 7), you are not to rest in private comfort but to become an intercessor, as the psalmist becomes. The imperatives of verse 9—save, bless, shepherd, carry—are not your commands to give, but they are patterns for your prayer life and your service. When you pray for family members, friends, ward members, you are praying in the mode of verse 9. When you serve in any position of leadership or stewardship, these four verbs define your role: you are to work to save people from sin and error, to pronounce and cultivate blessing in their lives, to tend their spiritual growth with the care of a shepherd, and to bear their burdens with you. The word 'forever' (ad ha-olam) teaches that commitment to the people is not temporary or seasonal but eternal. Your covenant is not with persons for a season but with God's people forever. This requires a shift from seeing your religious life as private to understanding it as part of the great intercessory work of bringing all God's children to salvation and eternal glory with him.

text_kjv: The voice of the LORD divideth the flames of fire.

commentary.narrative: We now enter the middle movement of the psalm, where the divine voice moves from the cosmic heavens down to the terrestrial landscape. Verse 7 marks the first of seven consecutive statements beginning with "the voice of the LORD" (qol-YHWH), a structural anchor that drives the entire middle section. Here, the voice does not merely make sound—it *splits* or *hews* fire itself, as a mason cuts stone. The Hebrew verb חצב (chatzav) means to quarry, to hew, to shape stone with intentional craft. Applied to lightning, this is not random electrical discharge in a storm, but the *deliberate craftsmanship* of divine speech shaping fire into bolts. The Covenant Rendering captures this better than the KJV's "divideth": the LORD *splits* flames of fire—a sharp, active, purposeful division. Lightning becomes a metaphor for how God's word operates: it cuts through the darkness of the sky the way a stonecutter's chisel cuts through rock. Power and precision are inseparable in God's voice.
commentary.narrative_continued: The placement of this verse in the storm sequence is significant. We have just heard of the voice breaking cedars and stripping forests (v. 5-6). Now we see that same voice commanding the very lightning that illuminates and energizes the storm. The psalmist is not describing meteorology; he is describing a theophany—a visible manifestation of God's presence and power. Every element of the storm becomes a medium through which the divine voice operates. There is an economy to this imagery: God does not *create* new lightning and then *use* it. Rather, his voice *becomes* the lightning, or more precisely, his voice *shapes* the fire into lightning. This reflects the ancient Near Eastern understanding that words are not mere sound but are forces that accomplish things in the physical world.

word_study.meaning: to hew, cut, quarry, shape with a cutting tool; to divide or split with force and precision
word_study.significance: The verb typically describes the work of a mason or stonecutter. By applying it to God's action upon fire, the psalmist portrays divine speech as *deliberate craftsmanship*, not random power. The KJV 'divideth' is accurate but softer than the Hebrew sense of cutting or hewing. The Covenant Rendering's 'splits' is closer to the active, violent sense of the original verb. This verb elevates God's power from mere force to *purposeful shaping*.

word_study.meaning: flames of fire; literally, the bright, licking tongues of fire; collectively, the lightning or fiery bolts of the storm
word_study.significance: Lahavot (plural of lahav) refers to the visible, flickering flames—the appearance of fire. In the context of a storm, this unmistakably refers to lightning. The pairing of lahavot ('flames') with esh ('fire') creates intensity and redundancy for effect: not just fire, but the *flaming appearance* of fire—the brightness and heat that command attention. This is how lightning would be understood in an ancient context: as divine fire descending from heaven.

cross_references.connection: The theophany at Sinai features thunder, lightning, and fire—God's voice manifesting as natural forces. Both passages present God's speech as simultaneously audible and visible, mediated through storm phenomena.
Elihu describes God's voice in the thunder and the lightning that follows his word. Like Psalm 29, this passage identifies the voice of God with the thunder and electric manifestations of the storm.
The LORD comes with fire and flame, his voice riding on the storm. The connection between God's voice and fire is a consistent image of divine judgment and power throughout the prophetic literature.
The LORD's way is in the whirlwind and the storm, and the mountains quake at his presence. This passage echoes Psalm 29's image of nature convulsing at the voice of God.

commentary.historical_context: The verb חצב (chatzav) is the same word used in ancient Near Eastern inscriptions and the Bible for quarrying, including the quarrying of stone for temple construction. By using this term for God's action on fire, the psalmist draws on the imagery of a master craftsman. In the ancient Levantine world, masonry and stonecutting were marks of civilization and divine order—they represented the imposition of human (and divine) will upon raw materials. Lightning, in this metaphor, is the raw material of fire being shaped by the divine will into a weapon or tool. The Canaanite storm-god Baal was portrayed in mythological texts as a wielder of lightning and a shaper of nature; the psalmist may be deliberately reframing Baal's attributes as belonging exclusively to YHWH, the God of Israel.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: Nephi describes the voice of the LORD in terms of natural power: 'the voice of the Lord caused the earth to shake' (1 Nephi 19:11). The Book of Mormon consistently presents God's voice as a creative and destructive force manifesting through natural phenomena, paralleling the Psalmic imagery.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: Doctrine and Covenants 29:16 describes how God's voice causes the earth to shake and the heavens to quake. The principle that God's word is creative and transformative power is foundational to Restoration theology.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: In temple worship, the endowment includes imagery of God's power and voice manifesting through nature. The lightning that splits fire mirrors the divine manifestations associated with heavenly power and divine presence in sacred space.

commentary.christological_typology: The voice of God that shapes fire prefigures Christ as the Word (Logos) through whom all things are made and sustained. Hebrews 1:3 describes the Son as 'the brightness of his glory, and the express image of his person.' The lightning split by the voice mirrors Christ as the medium through which divine power operates in creation and providence.
commentary.application: This verse invites us to recognize that God's word is not merely informational but transformative. When the psalmist portrays God's voice as deliberately splitting fire, he challenges us to move beyond thinking of prayer and scripture as passive reception. God's word *accomplishes* things. In our own lives, recognizing the power of God's voice—whether in scripture, in prophetic testimony, or in the Spirit's whisper—should inspire both reverence and confidence. The same precision that splits lightning can shape the circumstances and character of our lives if we align ourselves with his word.

text_kjv: The voice of the LORD shaketh the wilderness; the LORD shaketh the wilderness of Kadesh.

commentary.narrative: The storm has now tracked south from the heights of Lebanon (v. 5-6) to the barren wilderness. The repetition of the verb יחיל (yachil) — 'shakes' or 'writhes' — twice in this verse creates a rhythmic emphasis. The wilderness is shaken, and specifically the wilderness of Kadesh is shaken. This is the second appearance of 'the voice of the LORD' as a structural refrain, and it marks a crucial transition: the storm moves from the inhabited and cultivated north to the uninhabited desert south. The theological implication is profound: God's power does not require an audience. The wilderness—the midbar—is deserted, empty of human witnesses. Yet it trembles before God's voice. This speaks to the absolute and independent reality of God's dominion. He does not need spectators to be powerful; his word accomplishes its effects whether anyone observes or not.
commentary.narrative_continued: The specific mention of 'the wilderness of Kadesh' is geographically and theologically weighted. Kadesh-barnea was the place where Israel was tested in the wilderness wanderings (Numbers 13-14), where the nation failed to trust God and was sentenced to forty years of wandering. Or, if this refers to a northern Kadesh, it still carries the sense of a place of testing and covenant. Either way, Kadesh is associated with covenant failure and divine judgment. By declaring that God's voice shakes Kadesh, the psalmist is reminding Israel that the same God who once judged them in the wilderness retains absolute power over that place. The wilderness that seemed so vast and threatening during the wilderness wandering is convulsed like a laboring woman at the mere sound of God's voice. Time has not diminished his power; the years have not altered his dominion.

word_study.meaning: to shake, tremble, writhe, be in labor, convulse, be agitated; to be in the throes of pain or fear
word_study.significance: This verb is far richer than 'shaketh' or 'shakes' alone. Yachil is used of labor pains (Job 15:20), of fear that grips the body, of the earth convulsing. The wilderness is not merely vibrating or oscillating—it is *writhing*, as though in labor, as though possessed by a force from within. The Covenant Rendering's choice to render verse 9 with 'the LORD makes the deer writhe in labor' makes clear that yachil carries this connotation of birth pangs or involuntary convulsion. The wilderness responds to God's voice the way a woman's body responds to labor—with involuntary, all-consuming movement.

word_study.meaning: wilderness, desert, uncultivated open land; the place beyond human settlement and control
word_study.significance: The midbar in Hebrew thought is not merely a geographical zone but a symbolic space—the place where God tests his people, where divine power is most starkly visible because human structures and civilization cannot hide it. By shaking the midbar, God demonstrates his sovereignty in the one place where human power has no purchase. This is theologically significant: God does not rule only over cities and temples where people have built altars to worship him. He rules over the empty places too.

word_study.meaning: Kadesh; likely Kadesh-barnea in the Negev desert, or possibly a northern Kadesh in Syria; the name carries associations with holiness (from qadosh, 'holy') but also with the covenant-testing events of Israel's wilderness period
word_study.significance: The place name itself deserves attention. Qadesh comes from the root qadosh ('holy'), yet it is the wilderness—the unholy, undomesticated space. This irony—a holy place in the wilderness, where Israel was tested and nearly destroyed—makes the location theologically charged. God's voice shaking Kadesh is thus not merely a geographical detail but a statement about his power to reclaim even the spaces of Israel's deepest trial and failure.

cross_references.connection: Kadesh-barnea is the location where the Israelite spies returned with a report that caused the congregation to rebel and lose faith in God's promise. The shaking of Kadesh in Psalm 29 reframes that place of faithlessness as subject to God's undiminished power.

Isaiah marvels that the nations and wilderness are as nothing before God, easily swept away like dust. Psalm 29:8 echoes this sense of cosmic indifference to human perspective—the wilderness shakes not because anyone watches, but because God speaks.

Jeremiah's vision of the earth returning to chaos and wilderness when God judges. The shaking of the wilderness in Psalm 29 demonstrates God's ability to unmake civilization and order by reverting to primordial desolation.

Alma describes being racked with torment and tormented as though by a burning fire. The language of the wilderness convulsing parallels the internal dissolution that Alma experiences—the self writhing as though in labor when confronted by God's voice.

commentary.historical_context: Kadesh-barnea lay on the southern frontier of Canaan, about 80 kilometers south of Beersheba, in the Negev desert. Archaeological surveys identify it as the site of 'Ain Qudeirat or a nearby spring. In the ancient world, the wilderness (midbar) was understood as a thin place—a location where the barrier between the divine and human realms grew permeable. It was not a place to be conquered or settled (though Bedouin tribes inhabited it seasonally) but a place where one encountered the raw presence of God. The storm imagery in Psalm 29 may reflect actual weather patterns: Mediterranean storms can track southeastward from the coast toward the Negev, moving from the green hills of Lebanon down to the bare desert. The psalmist's eye follows this storm path, using natural phenomena to articulate theological truth about God's sovereignty over both cultivation and wildness.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: The Book of Mormon repeatedly emphasizes God's power in the wilderness and over wild nature. Lehi and his family are led through the wilderness of Arabia; Alma's people find safety in the wilderness from their enemies. The wilderness is the place where divine covenant is renewed and tested, just as Kadesh was for ancient Israel. See 1 Nephi 2:1-4 and Alma 22:29.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: Doctrine and Covenants 1:14 describes the voice of God as coming forth unto the earth, accomplishing his purposes. The principle that God's word is not merely declarative but performative—it *does* things—is central to Restoration theology of divine speech.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The wilderness can symbolize the trials of mortality and the absence of the divine presence in ordinary life. The temple, by contrast, is the place where God's voice is closest and most clearly heard. Verse 8's image of the wilderness shaking at God's distant voice may contrast implicitly with the temple space where his voice is immediately present and peace is given (see v. 11).

commentary.christological_typology: Christ is described as the Word (John 1:1-3) through whom all things were made and are upheld. The wilderness, which seems to exist beyond God's concern or attention, is subject to the same Word that sustains all creation. This prefigures the truth that no part of creation—no wilderness, no failure, no trial—lies outside Christ's dominion or his power to redeem.
commentary.application: This verse speaks powerfully to those who feel lost or abandoned in their own wilderness seasons. The image of Kadesh—the very place of Israel's covenant failure and loss of faith—being shaken at God's voice assures us that God has not abandoned the wilderness places in our lives. The trials, the deserts, the seasons of wandering all remain under God's dominion. His power is not limited to the places where we gather to worship or where others observe our faith. In the hidden, desolate places of our experience, God's voice remains effective and creative. This should inspire both humility (our trials are not hidden from God) and hope (our wilderness is not abandoned to chaos).

text_kjv: The voice of the LORD maketh the hinds to calve, and discovereth the forests: and in his temple doth every one speak of his glory.

commentary.narrative: This is the pivotal verse of Psalm 29, where the focus shifts from the external natural world to the internal sacred space—from the physical storm to the worshipping community. The verse presents two parallel effects of God's voice: (1) the hinds (female deer) writhe in premature labor, and (2) the forests are stripped bare. Then the psalmist pivots sharply: 'And in his temple, all cry: Glory!' The theological arc is now complete. The storm that convulsed the natural world—breaking cedars, shaking the wilderness, causing deer to writhe in labor—corresponds to and culminates in the single unified cry of the temple community: Kavod ('Glory!'). The compression is extraordinary. While nature exhibits violent, diverse responses to God's voice, the temple exhibits singular, unified worship. The word kavod that opened the psalm (v. 1: 'Ascribe to the LORD...glory') now echoes in the mouths of all the temple worshippers.
commentary.narrative_continued: The image of the hinds in labor is particularly striking. The storm's power is so tremendous that it induces premature labor in pregnant deer. This is not mere poetic exaggeration but a way of expressing the overwhelming totality of God's voice—it penetrates even to the deepest animal instinct, the generative power of creatures. Nature is simultaneously creating and destroying under the force of God's voice. The forests that once stood proud are stripped bare (yechesof yearot—the trees are denuded, their protective canopy torn away). Yet this nakedness, this exposure of the forests, reveals their fundamental vulnerability and God's absolute power. The forests do not resist; they submit. And then, suddenly, the scene shifts to the temple. The storm outside and the worship inside are not two separate events but a single coordinated testimony to God's power. The temple response is not elaborate liturgy or explanation—it is one word: Kavod. Everything the storm displays—power, majesty, dominion over nature, the ability to command creation—is captured in and named by this single word. The brevity is the point: when you have witnessed what God's voice can do, no elaborate speech is needed.

word_study.transliteration: yecholel (Piel imperfect 3rd person masculine singular, from חוּל chul)
word_study.meaning: to cause to writhe, twist, be in labor; to induce the pangs of childbirth; to cause severe pain or agitation
word_study.significance: The Piel form indicates that God's voice actively *causes* the writhing, not that the deer happen to be in labor. The verb חוּל (chul) is used of labor pains, of fear that grips the body, of the earth convulsing. By using yecholel, the psalmist portrays God's voice as so physically overwhelming that it induces birth pangs in the does. This is a profound image of God's power penetrating to the deepest biological and instinctual levels of creation. The KJV's 'maketh...to calve' is technically accurate—birth is the result—but misses the sense of involuntary convulsion and pain. The Covenant Rendering's 'makes the deer writhe in labor' captures the visceral agony.

word_study.transliteration: vayechesof (Qal imperfect vav-consecutive 3rd person masculine singular, from חשׁף chasaf)
word_study.meaning: to strip, expose, uncover, make bare; to tear away covering or protection
word_study.significance: The verb חשׁף (chasaf) means to uncover or expose—to strip away what conceals or protects. Applied to forests, it means to denude them of their leaves, branches, and protective canopy. The storm tears away the forest's protective covering, leaving it bare and exposed. The KJV 'discovereth' is archaic but accurate in its sense of 'uncover' or 'reveal'; the Covenant Rendering's 'strips...bare' is more immediately vivid. The image is not of destruction in the sense of annihilation, but of exposure—the forcing of the forests into a state of nakedness and vulnerability before God.

word_study.meaning: female deer, does; creatures of grace and natural beauty
word_study.significance: The psalmist chooses not to mention stags or male deer, but specifically hinds—pregnant females. This emphasizes the vulnerability of creation and the penetrating power of God's voice. The hind in biblical poetry often symbolizes grace, beauty, and gentleness (Proverbs 5:19; Song of Solomon 2:7). By showing the hinds wracked with labor pains at God's voice, the psalmist emphasizes that even the most graceful and beautiful of creatures cannot resist the power of God's speech. There is no hiding place in nature; even the most vulnerable are subject to God's dominion.

word_study.meaning: forests, groves, dense woodlands; places of darkness and shelter
word_study.significance: Forests in ancient Near Eastern thought were both beautiful and threatening—places of abundance and danger. The Lebanese forests mentioned in verse 5-6 were the greatest timber resource in the ancient Near Eastern world. By stripping the forests bare, God's voice demonstrates power over the very resource that ancient powers coveted and relied upon for shipbuilding and construction. The forests cannot hide or protect themselves; they are exposed and made vulnerable.

word_study.meaning: palace, temple, shrine; the dwelling place of the divine or a king; the inner sanctum
word_study.significance: The hekal is not merely a building but a sacred space where divine presence is concentrated and where humanity approaches the divine. The shift from the wildness of the storm to the ordered space of the temple marks a theological move: the chaos of nature is gathered into the peace and order of worship. The hekal represents the point where human and divine meet, where the divine voice that tears forests is encountered and responded to with ordered ritual and unified voice.

word_study.meaning: to speak, say, utter; in this context, to cry out, declare, proclaim
word_study.significance: The participle form suggests a continuous or habitual action—the temple community does not speak once but speaks continuously, their utterance becoming the defining activity of the sacred space. All the temple worshippers are united in this single utterance. Their speaking is a response-action to the power they have witnessed in the storm. Omer is simple speech, but when unified by all the temple, it becomes a powerful declaration.

word_study.meaning: glory, splendor, majesty, honor, weightiness; the manifestation of divine presence and power; the visible expression of who and what God is
word_study.significance: Kavod closes the psalm's worship arc. It opened in verse 1 ('Ascribe to the LORD...glory'). The divine voice that caused the heavenly beings to ascribe glory (v. 1) and the God of glory who thundered (v. 3) now has that same glory proclaimed in the temple. Kavod is the name given to everything the storm displays—the breaking of cedars, the shaking of wilderness, the stripping of forests—all is gathered under the single word kavod. The word is extraordinarily compressed: when you have witnessed what God's voice can do, one word suffices. Kavod is the summary statement, the synthesis of all the storm displays. It names the reality: this is what God's glory looks like when it is unveiled in the natural world.

cross_references.connection: The opening command to ascribe glory to the LORD is now answered by the temple community in verse 9. The heavenly beings were commanded to give glory; now the earthly worshippers join that heavenly chorus.

Isaiah's temple vision features seraphim proclaiming 'Holy, holy, holy' while the temple is filled with smoke and the doorposts shake. Like Psalm 29:9, the temple becomes the place where divine power is experienced and worshipped.
The glory (kavod) of the LORD appears on Mount Sinai like a devouring fire. The connection between God's glory and natural power—fire, storm, thunder—is a consistent biblical association.
The creatures in heaven worship saying 'Worthy is the Lamb...to receive glory and honor and power.' Like Psalm 29:9, worship is the appropriate response to witnessing divine glory and power.
Alma addresses the people by reminding them of the power of God's voice in their lives. The experience of God's word cutting through and transforming leads to unified testimony.

commentary.historical_context: The temple in Psalm 29 is likely the Jerusalem temple, though the poem may predate Solomon's temple and could have originally referred to any cultic shrine where God's presence was experienced. The image of the temple community responding with unified voice to the storm outside suggests an actual liturgical practice: the worshippers would have gathered in the temple during storms or at times of covenant renewal, and the storm itself would have been understood as the presence of God. The juxtaposition of violent natural power and peaceful unified worship reflects an ancient Near Eastern cosmology in which temples served as microcosms of divine order—places where chaos was ordered and brought into harmony through ritual and worship. The progression of the psalm from cosmic heavens to mountain to wilderness to temple creates a geographical and theological journey that would have been familiar to ancient Israelite worshippers: God's dominion is universal, but his relationship with his people is centered in the temple.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: The temple in Book of Mormon theology is the place where God's voice is most clearly heard and where the community gathers to worship in unified voice. 2 Nephi 4:15-35 presents a prayer uttered in the temple setting that echoes the kind of unified worship described in Psalm 29:9. The connection between witnessing God's power (through revelation or experience) and responding with unified testimony pervades Book of Mormon narrative.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: Doctrine and Covenants 109, the dedicatory prayer of the Kirtland Temple, repeatedly asks that God's glory be revealed in the temple and that the people gathered there will be able to hear his voice. The temple is presented as the place where God's voice becomes particularly accessible and where the community responds with united faith and worship.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: This verse is foundational to understanding the temple in LDS theology. The temple is the place where God's voice—whether in revelation, ordinance, or spiritual experience—is encountered and where the covenant community responds with unified heart and voice. The progression from storm (God's power over chaos) to temple (God's power ordered in covenant) reflects the temple's role as the place where chaos is ordered and brought into harmony through sacred ritual. The single word 'Glory!' uttered by all the temple is analogous to the united testimony and covenant-keeping of the Latter-day Saint community.

commentary.christological_typology: Christ is the Word (Logos) through whom all things were made and are sustained (John 1:1-3, Hebrews 1:1-3). The voice of God that convulses nature is the voice of Christ. The shift from the violent manifestation of God's power in nature to the peaceful proclamation of 'Glory!' in the temple prefigures Christ's dual role as both the thundering power of judgment and the gentle presence of peace. The temple itself, in Christian theology, is fulfilled in Christ's body (John 2:21), and the unified worship of the temple community is gathered into the worship of the risen Christ.
commentary.application: This verse reminds us that authentic worship is a response to encountering God's reality and power. The temple community does not worship because they have been commanded to perform ritual, but because they have witnessed God's power. Their one word—'Glory!'—is the appropriate and sufficient response. In our own lives, this suggests that our worship and testimony are most authentic when they arise from genuine encounter with God's power and presence. Whether that encounter comes through scripture, revelation, answered prayer, or spiritual experience, our response should be like the temple community's: simple, unified, and focused on naming who God is. We also gather strength from the image of the entire temple speaking with one voice. Our individual testimony becomes part of a larger community witness. When we speak 'Glory!' we do not speak alone, but join with all the saints who have ever encountered God's power and responded with praise.

text_kjv: The LORD sitteth upon the flood; yea, the LORD sitteth King for ever.

commentary.narrative: The storm imagery abruptly shifts to cosmic mythology. The word מַבּוּל (mabbul, 'flood') appears in only two places in the Hebrew Bible: the Genesis deluge narrative and this verse. The appearance of mabbul here is not accidental but deliberately loaded. The psalmist is invoking the primordial flood—the time when God unmade creation itself, when the chaos waters covered the earth, when divine judgment obliterated humanity except for the one family in the ark. That flood was the ultimate demonstration of God's power over chaos. Now the psalmist declares: the LORD who sent that flood sits enthroned over those same waters permanently. The flood was not a one-time catastrophe whose waters have since receded into insignificance. Rather, the flood revealed a permanent reality: God reigns over chaos. The waters of chaos (in ancient Near Eastern cosmology, the primordial waters represented ultimate disorder and threat) are not independent or autonomous. They do not pose a threat to God's throne. Rather, God sits enthroned *upon* those very waters. His throne is established upon the thing that most threatens human order and security.
commentary.narrative_continued: The verb יָשַׁב (yashav, 'to sit, dwell, be enthroned') is repeated twice in this verse, creating an emphatic statement: YHWH la-mabbul yashav ('the LORD upon the flood sits') and vayyeshev YHWH melekh le-olam ('the LORD sits as king forever'). The double sitting emphasizes not motion or strain but *stability* and *settlement*. God is not pacing, not anxious, not straining to maintain control. He is seated, settled, at ease upon the chaos waters. This conveys complete confidence and absolute dominion. The phrase melekh le-olam ('king forever') places no time limit on this sovereignty. The storm that just shook the earth is now revealed as merely an exhibition of the permanent ordering principle: God reigns. His throne predates the flood; it survives the flood; it will endure when all things pass away. The seven-fold repetition of 'the voice of the LORD' (vv. 3-9) has demonstrated the power of God in the natural world. Now verse 10 reveals the cosmic principle undergirding all that power: God's kingship is not conditional or temporary. It is eternal and unshakeable.

word_study.meaning: to sit, dwell, settle, be enthroned; to be seated in a position of authority or rest
word_study.significance: The verb yashav suggests not active straining but restful settlement. A king who sits on his throne is not fighting to maintain it; he is at rest in his authority. The psalmist uses yashav twice in this verse, creating an almost monotone repetition that emphasizes the stability and unchanging nature of God's throne. This is not 'the LORD stands firm upon the flood' (suggesting tension or bracing) but 'the LORD sits enthroned'—suggesting ease and confidence. The repetition of yashav is a stylistic choice that underscores the settled, permanent nature of God's dominion.

word_study.meaning: flood, deluge, the waters of chaos; specifically, the Genesis flood or flood-like waters in general
word_study.significance: This word is extraordinarily rare in biblical Hebrew. It appears in Genesis 6-9 (the flood narrative) and here in Psalm 29:10. No other instances exist. This rarity makes the word weighty and deliberate. Every Hebrew reader, upon encountering mabbul, would immediately think of the Genesis flood—the moment when God's judgment unmade creation and returned the world to chaos. By declaring that God sits enthroned upon the mabbul, the psalmist is making a stunning theological claim: the waters that God used to judge the world now serve as God's throne. The chaos that once threatened all creation has become the very foundation of God's eternal rule. There is no power more ultimate than God's; even the primordial chaos is subject to him.

word_study.meaning: king, ruler, monarch; one who holds absolute authority
word_study.significance: The word melekh connects this verse to verse 1, where the heavenly beings are commanded to ascribe glory to the LORD 'in the beauty of holiness' (בְנוֹעַם קֹדֶשׁ be-noam kodesh). The heavenly court recognizes the LORD as melekh—as sovereign. Now, having witnessed the display of God's power in the storm (vv. 3-9), the earthly temple community understands why he is melekh. His kingship is not ceremonial or decorative; it is based on absolute dominion over all things, even the primordial chaos.

word_study.meaning: forever, eternally, to the end of time; a duration with no limit
word_study.significance: The phrase melekh le-olam is a compressed statement of God's eternality. His kingship is not temporary or contingent on circumstances. It is permanent and unchanging. The storm will pass, the thunder will fade, but God's throne remains unmoved. This phrase is comfort to those who experience the terror of the storm: the God whose voice shakes the earth is also the God whose rule is forever stable and trustworthy.

cross_references.connection: The Genesis flood narrative describes the mabbul ('flood') that covers the earth. Psalm 29:10 invokes this same flood, declaring that God sits enthroned over the very waters that once seemed to threaten all existence.

John's vision declares that there will be 'no more sea'—the water of chaos will be absent from the new creation. Psalm 29:10 shows that even before the eschaton, God's throne rests upon and masters the chaotic waters.
Daniel's vision of the Eternal God shows his throne like fiery flames and the wheels ablaze with fire. Both passages use images of cosmic power and fire to convey God's eternal kingship.
Psalm 93 declares that 'the LORD reigns' and that his throne is established from of old. Like Psalm 29:10, this psalm emphasizes the eternality and stability of God's rule despite chaotic forces.
Nephi reminds his brothers that the God who brought them through the Red Sea is the same God who brought their ancestors through the waters. The mastery of waters is a sign of God's eternal kingship.

commentary.historical_context: Ancient Near Eastern cosmology, especially in Mesopotamian and Canaanite traditions, presented the universe as emerging from or being constantly threatened by primordial chaos waters. The storm-god Baal was celebrated as the one who defeated chaos. By invoking the Genesis flood (which in the source tradition may have drawn on common ancient Near Eastern flood mythology) and declaring that YHWH sits enthroned over those waters, the psalmist is making a distinctly Israelite theological claim: the God of Israel is not merely the storm-god of local weather; he is the Master of chaos itself. The concept of God's throne (kisseh) sitting above and over the waters appears in ancient Mesopotamian texts as well, but the connection to the specific historical flood event (whether understood as a memory of an actual catastrophic flood or as a theological myth) is what gives the psalmist's statement its weight. The 'flood' is both a natural phenomenon (the waters of the earth) and a cosmic principle (the chaos that threatens order).

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: The Book of Mormon contains a passage where Nephi is led across the Red Sea, and he reflects on how God's hand has guided his people 'through the waters and the wilderness' (1 Nephi 4:18). The mastery of waters is a consistent sign of God's power and kingship in Book of Mormon thought. Also, 2 Nephi 27:29-30 presents God's dominion as eternal and unshakeable, echoing the principle of Psalm 29:10.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: Doctrine and Covenants 29:25-29 presents God's command over all things, including the elements. The principle that God sits enthroned over all creation, including the chaotic forces, is foundational to Restoration theology. Also, D&C 88:6-13 presents Jesus Christ as the light and power that sustains all things, echoing the principle that God's rule is eternal and comprehensive.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The temple is the place where God's throne is made present and accessible to his people. By sitting in the temple, worshippers are brought into contact with God's eternal throne and given assurance that God's kingship is absolute. The imagery of verse 10 transforms the temple from a merely religious building into a cosmic statement: in the temple, we encounter the God who sits enthroned over all creation and all chaos.

commentary.christological_typology: Christ, as the eternal Word through whom all things are made and sustained (Hebrews 1:1-3, Colossians 1:15-17), sits at the right hand of God and participates in God's eternal kingship. Revelation 1:8 describes Christ as the Almighty, and Revelation 21:5-7 shows Christ on the throne making all things new. The image of sitting enthroned is particularly relevant to Christ, who is seated at God's right hand (Romans 8:34) and is therefore sharing in God's eternal rule.
commentary.application: This verse offers extraordinary comfort in times of chaos and crisis. The psalmist has just described the terrifying power of God's voice—breaking cedars, shaking wilderness, inducing labor pains in does, stripping forests bare. It would be natural to feel fear in the face of such overwhelming power. But verse 10 reframes the terror: this God whose voice is so powerful is not erratic or threatening to his covenant people. He *sits* on his throne. He is settled and confident. His rule is *forever*—permanent and reliable. When we experience storms in our lives—whether literal or metaphorical—this verse assures us that the God who allowed the storm is the same God whose throne is eternal and whose rule is just. We do not fear that God will lose control or that chaos will overcome his kingdom. His throne is stable, his power is settled, his reign is forever. This transforms fear into trust: we are in the hands of a God who has mastered not just today's crisis but all chaos that has ever been or ever will be.

text_kjv: The LORD will give strength unto his people; the LORD will bless his people with peace.

commentary.narrative: The psalm concludes with a stunning theological pivot that transforms everything that came before. The same power that splits lightning, breaks cedars, shakes wilderness, and induces labor pains in does is now given as a gift to God's people. The Hebrew עֹז (oz, 'strength') is not given in a diluted or diminished form; it is shared without loss. God's strength is not like a finite resource that, when distributed, becomes exhausted or weakened. Rather, God gives his strength to his people and it remains undiminished in him. This is one of the most concise statements of the paradox of divine power in all of scripture. The God whose voice convulses nature now uses that same voice to bless his people with peace. The progression is remarkable: from terror (the storm), to unified worship (the temple speaking 'Glory!'), to cosmic stability (God sitting enthroned forever), to intimate blessing (God giving strength to his covenant people). The final image is not of God's dominance over his people but of his willingness to share his power with them, to empower them, and to grant them not merely strength but also the peace that comes from knowing they are upheld by a God whose throne is eternal.
commentary.narrative_continued: The two statements of verse 11 are parallel but not identical. 'The LORD will give strength unto his people' emphasizes the transfer of power from God to his covenant community. 'The LORD will bless his people with peace' emphasizes the emotional and relational outcome: peace (שָׁלוֹם shalom). Shalom is far more than the absence of conflict; it is wholeness, completeness, well-being, right relationship. The people who receive God's strength are not hardened into weapons or made into instruments of violence. They are blessed with peace. The paradox deepens: the strength of the storm-God becomes, when given to his people, the basis for peace. This is the culmination of the psalm's entire theological arc. It began with a command to the heavenly beings to ascribe glory to God (v. 1-2). It moved through a sevenfold display of divine power in the natural world (vv. 3-9). It affirmed God's eternal kingship (v. 10). And it ends with the personal, intimate blessing: strength and peace to those who bear God's name.
