He will rejoice specifically "in thy mercy"—but here the word is chesed, which the Covenant Rendering translates as "faithful love." This is not sentimental affection but covenantal commitment. Chesed is the backbone of the God-Israel relationship; it is the reason God does not abandon His people in crisis. David's joy is not naive happiness that pretends suffering doesn't exist; it is grounded in the sober recognition that God has turned His face toward the affliction and knows it intimately.
commentary.narrative_continued: The phrase "thou hast considered my trouble" translates ra'itah et-onyi—literally, "you have seen my affliction." But in Hebrew, "seeing" in the context of divine awareness is not passive observation from a distance. When God "sees," He sees with the intention to respond. Abraham "sees" that the ram is caught in the thicket (Genesis 22:13), and he immediately acts. Moses asks God to "see" the affliction of Israel (Exodus 3:7), and God's "seeing" becomes the trigger for the entire exodus. David trusts that God's seeing of his trouble is already a partial answer to his trouble.
commentary.narrative_continued2: The second clause deepens this: "thou hast known my soul in adversities." The verb yada (to know) in Scripture means far more than intellectual awareness; it means intimate, relational knowledge. When God "knows" His people, He knows them the way a shepherd knows each sheep by name, the way a parent knows the specific contours of a child's pain. This is not forensic knowledge (cataloging facts) but covenantal knowledge (recognizing relationship and responsibility). David's joy flows from the conviction that his suffering is not invisible to God, not peripheral to God's attention, but central to it. The very thing that breaks him is the thing that calls forth God's chesed.

word_study.meaning: Covenant loyalty, faithful love, steadfast mercy. The term describes the committed, obligated love that binds covenant partners together. It is not conditioned on the worthiness of the recipient but on the binding nature of the covenant itself. Chesed persists even when the covenant partner fails.
word_study.significance: Chesed is the central theological category of the Old Testament understanding of God. It explains why God does not abandon Israel despite repeated apostasy. David's rejoicing in chesed is not rejoicing in God's niceness but in God's committed obligation to the covenant relationship. This is why he can be confident even in affliction—God is bound by covenant to respond.

word_study.meaning: To see, to look upon, to regard with attention. In the context of divine action, seeing implies awareness that leads to intervention. The covenant God 'sees' suffering as a trigger to action, not as a mere fact to observe.
word_study.significance: The Covenant Rendering notes that this is not passive observation but 'attentive care.' God sees the way a parent sees a child's pain—with intent to alleviate it. David's confidence in this divine seeing is the foundation of his joy in affliction.

word_study.meaning: To know; to be acquainted with; to recognize; to have relationship with. In covenant language, it implies intimate, relational knowledge rather than detached information.
word_study.significance: God's 'knowing' of David's distress is not forensic investigation but covenantal recognition. The Creator knows His creature not as an outsider studying a problem but as a covenant partner bound to respond. This intimacy is the grounds of David's joy.

word_study.meaning: Soul, life force, breath. The term refers to the whole person—emotional, volitional, physical. It is not separate from the body but the animating principle of the whole being.
word_study.significance: When David says God has 'known my soul in adversities,' he means God knows the deepest center of his being, his most vulnerable interior. The fact that God has this intimate knowledge of his suffering, rather than being comforting in an abstract way, is concrete comfort: someone who matters sees, knows, and cares.

cross_references.connection: YHWH says: 'I have surely seen the affliction of my people...and I am come down to deliver them.' God's 'seeing' of suffering is always the prelude to rescue. David's confidence that he will rejoice rests on this pattern.

David expands the theme of God's intimate knowledge: 'O LORD, thou hast searched me, and known me...thou knowest my downsitting and mine uprising.' God's knowledge is comprehensive and inescapable—a fact that in Psalm 139 becomes comfort rather than threat.

Peter writes: 'Humble yourselves therefore under the mighty hand of God...Casting all your care upon him; for he careth for you.' The New Testament echoes the idea that God's seeing and knowing of our trouble is the ground of our peace.

Alma tells the people oppressed by King Noah: 'The Lord will ease the burdens which are put upon your shoulders, that even you cannot feel them upon your backs.' The Book of Mormon reiterates that God's seeing and knowing leads to concrete relief.

The Lord declares: 'He that ascended up on high...received all things...that he might be in all and through all things, the light of truth.' God's omniscience (His knowing of all things) is presented as foundation for His redemptive power.

commentary.historical_context: In the Ancient Near East, the concept of a king-god relationship often involved the king bringing offerings and performing rituals to appease an otherwise distant deity. The innovation of Israel's covenant theology was that the God of Israel was bound to His people by oath, not by transaction. A God who 'sees' and 'knows' your affliction is not a distant force requiring propitiation but a committed partner. Archaeological evidence from lament psalms found in other Near Eastern contexts shows that lament to other gods often expresses fear that the god has abandoned or forgotten the suppliant. The Israelite psalmist, by contrast, expresses absolute confidence that God has not forgotten because God is covenantally bound to remember. The emotional texture of David's 'gladness' in verse 8 would have struck ancient readers as remarkable: how can one rejoice in affliction? The answer: because the God whose seeing and knowing you trust is different from the distant, capricious gods of surrounding nations.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: Alma 31:26-27 captures the same principle: Alma prays for his missionary sons, saying, 'O that I were an angel, that I could cry out and wake the voice of every people...that they might be brought to belief in thee, the only true God.' Alma's confidence rests on the same covenantal knowledge: God sees and knows the condition of His people and will respond.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 121:4-6 presents Joseph Smith in affliction, crying out: 'O God, where art thou?...Remember the suffererings of thy people.' The Lord's response in verse 7 affirms: 'My son, peace be unto thy soul; thine adversity and thine afflictions shall be but a small moment.' The divine seeing and knowing transforms the meaning of suffering.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The temple is the place where God is understood to 'see' and 'know' His people in their innermost covenants. Endowment worship enacts the principle that God, in the highest, looks upon His people making vows. This intimate divine seeing is what makes temple worship powerful: to be seen and known by God in the making of covenant is to experience the chesed described in this verse.

commentary.christological_typology: Christ's crucifixion enacts this verse in its ultimate form. Jesus cries out, 'My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me?' (Psalm 22:1), expressing the depth of abandonment. Yet the very fact that He cries out to God presupposes that God sees and knows. Hebrews 12:2 captures the reality: Christ 'endured the cross, despising the shame, for the joy that was set before him.' Christ's joy in suffering is grounded in His knowing that the Father sees, knows, and has bound Himself to redeem. The Father's seeing of Christ's affliction becomes the trigger for the redemption of all who trust in Him.
commentary.application: In modern covenant life, this verse addresses the question: Does God see my specific suffering? Not generically, but my affliction? My particular distress? The answer is yes—and not because I have been especially righteous or because God is feeling generous. God sees because He is covenantally bound to see. He knows because He has sworn to know His people by name. When a member struggles with grief, addiction, loneliness, or spiritual darkness, verse 8 calls them to the conviction that their suffering is not lost in the noise of history but is known to the God who bound Himself to them. The text invites not passive acceptance but active rejoicing: to declare, as David does, that I will be glad and rejoice in this covenant faithfulness, precisely because it is the one thing that cannot be taken from me, even in affliction.

text_kjv: And hast not shut me up into the hand of the enemy: thou hast set my feet in a large room.

commentary.narrative: Verse 9 completes David's declaration of confidence with two parallel statements, each expressing the antithesis of what he feared. The first—'And hast not shut me up into the hand of the enemy'—uses language of extradition or imprisonment. To be "shut up into the hand of" an enemy is the worst possible fate: to be handed over, delivered up, imprisoned without recourse. David's prayer opened with the plea to be delivered from the hand of the enemy (v. 15 will return to this); now he declares that despite his affliction, God has not made that final abandonment. He has not been extradited to his enemy.
commentary.narrative_continued: The second statement provides the positive reversal: 'thou hast set my feet in a large room.' The Hebrew word merchav (broad, open space) is the antonym of everything constricting. Throughout the Psalter, spatial imagery carries theological weight: tightness represents danger, enclosure, captivity; spaciousness represents safety, freedom, room to move. Psalm 18:19 uses the identical image when describing deliverance: 'He brought me forth also into a broad place' (merchav). The verb used here—'you have set my feet'—suggests that the LORD Himself has positioned David in safety, actively providing the spaciousness where he can breathe and move freely.
commentary.narrative_continued2: The structure of verses 8 and 9 reveals David's movement from inner assurance (God sees and knows me) to outer confirmation (God has actually protected me and is protecting me). This is not magical thinking. David has experienced real enemies, real threat, real danger. Yet he declares that despite these objective threats, the LORD has not handed him over. His feet stand in open ground. The use of the present tense ('hast not shut...hast set') treats these salvations as accomplished facts, even as verse 10 will return to acknowledge that the affliction persists. David holds both truths: I am genuinely afflicted, yet I am genuinely protected.

word_study.term_english: shut me up / handed me over
word_study.meaning: To shut up, to close, to deliver over, to hand over as a prisoner to an enemy power. The root sagir means literally 'to close' or 'to lock'; in the context of persons, it means to imprison or extradite.
word_study.significance: The Covenant Rendering notes this is 'the language of extradition.' To not be 'shut up into the hand of the enemy' means to not be delivered to the enemy's custody, to not be abandoned to the enemy's power. This was David's deepest fear, the opposite of covenant commitment.

word_study.term_english: set my feet in a large room
word_study.meaning: A wide, open, spacious place. From the root rachav, meaning 'to be wide, to be spacious.' The noun refers to any broad, open space—a plain, a plaza, a room with space to move freely.
word_study.significance: The Covenant Rendering notes that merchav is the opposite of the net and the trap. Throughout Hebrew Scripture, spatial theology equates constriction with danger and openness with safety. That God 'sets my feet' in a merchav means He actively provides the space where David is no longer trapped, no longer constricted by circumstance or enemy.

word_study.meaning: Foot; leg. Used metonymically for the whole person in movement, action, and direction.
word_study.significance: That God has 'set my feet' in spaciousness means David is not merely theoretically safe but actively mobile, able to move, able to act. His feet—the instruments of his movement—are planted on solid, open ground. This is not passive shelter but active freedom.

cross_references.connection: David uses the identical image: 'He brought me forth also into a broad place: he delivered me, because he delighted in me.' The merchav (broad place) is the sign and seal of deliverance.

David prays: 'Hear me when I call, O God of my righteousness: thou hast enlarged me when I was in distress.' The theme of God providing spaciousness (merchav) as relief from affliction runs through David's psalms.

When David has Saul trapped in a cave and could kill him, he refuses, saying the LORD will judge. Later, Saul blesses him: 'The LORD reward thee good for that thou hast done unto me this day.' David's trust that God will not 'shut him up into the hand of the enemy' is vindicated when his enemy himself becomes his refuge-giver.

Isaiah prophesies: 'Enlarge the place of thy tent...for thou shalt break forth on the right hand and on the left.' The imagery of spaciousness as salvation extends into the prophetic promise of restoration.

The Lord tells Joseph Smith in affliction: 'It is the nature and disposition of almost all men, as soon as they get a little authority...they will immediately begin to exercise unrighteous dominion.' God warns against those who would 'shut up' others; by contrast, God gives His servants scope and space to act.

commentary.historical_context: In the ancient world, to be 'handed over into the hand of an enemy' was the ultimate catastrophe—worse than death in many cases, because it meant losing autonomy, losing identity, becoming a possession of the enemy. The fear of being 'shut in' captures the literal experience of siege warfare, where cities were surrounded and their inhabitants confined until surrender. Archaeological evidence from siege narratives in Assyrian records shows the psychological terror of confinement: the goal of siege warfare was not merely military conquest but the breaking of will through enforced tightness and inability to escape. David's declaration that he has not been 'shut up' and that his 'feet stand in a broad place' would have resonated powerfully for an ancient audience who knew the terror of siege, confinement, and extradition to enemy power. The spatial language is not metaphorical for them but evocative of actual, visceral freedom.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: Nephi describes his experience in the dungeon (1 Nephi 16:29-32), where he is physically confined, yet he declares that the Lord has given him 'strength like unto the sinews of a man of might...and also my God hath commanded me that I should make tools.' Nephi's spiritual spaciousness persists even in physical confinement. The principle is that true 'shutting up into the hand of the enemy' is spiritual; physical confinement cannot accomplish it if the spirit is free.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 109:27, in the Kirtland Temple dedication, prays: 'Let the mouth of thy servants be opened...that they may proclaim thy truths, the signs and the wonders, the mighty works and the doings of thy hands.' The Lord provides 'room' for His servants to speak and act, even in hostile circumstances.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The temple is the place of ultimate spiritual spaciousness—the holy of holies where the covenant member stands in the widest spiritual room to encounter God. Conversely, spiritual apostasy is confinement: being 'shut up' from the presence of God and from covenant community. The temple experience enacts verse 9's promise of being set in a broad place where one can stand before God.

commentary.christological_typology: Christ's experience inverts this verse in order to fulfill it for others. Jesus enters into absolute confinement: the tomb is the ultimate 'shutting up.' Yet the Resurrection breaks that confinement and opens a broad place—not just for Christ but for all who trust in Him. Hebrews 9:24 describes Christ entering 'into heaven itself, now to appear in the presence of God for us.' His entry into the heavenly merchav, the broad place of the Father's presence, becomes the opening of that space to all who follow. Through Christ, even those bound by sin and death are set 'in a large room' of grace and freedom.
commentary.application: For modern believers, verse 9 addresses both the reality of being pressured (by circumstance, by enemies, by hostile forces) and the reality of protection that persists despite pressure. The text does not deny that David has enemies or that he faces constraint. Rather, it declares that the ultimate power—the power to 'hand over' completely, to definitively shut him up—is not in the enemy's hands but in God's. And God has used that power to set him in spaciousness. In modern covenant life, this verse challenges us to distinguish between tactical pressure (which may be real and ongoing) and strategic outcome (which belongs to God). A believer may face opposition, limitation, and real constraints; but if God has not 'shut him up' into the enemy's final power, he remains free. The application invites believers in difficult circumstances—those experiencing pressure from work, from hostile relationships, from systemic opposition—to declare with David: 'Despite my present confinement, my feet are set in a broad place. The enemy does not have ultimate authority over me. God has positioned me in freedom.' This is not denial of affliction but refusal to allow present pressure to define ultimate reality.

text_kjv: Have mercy upon me, O LORD, for I am in trouble: mine eye is consumed with grief, yea, my soul and my belly.

commentary.narrative: Abruptly, the psalm reverses. From the confident declarations of verses 8-9, David pivots back to desperate, raw lament. This is neither contradiction nor weakness; it is the structural honesty of psalmic prayer. David has declared his trust and God's protection, yet the affliction persists. His eye is literally wasted away with weeping. His soul is still in distress. His body is still collapsing. The grammar of verse 10 is not "will be" or "may become" but states present reality: I am in trouble now. The verb tsar (to be narrow, to be in straits) describes the condition of being pressed, confined, without room to breathe.
commentary.narrative_continued: The physical symptoms listed—consumed eye, failing soul, wasted belly—trace the ravages of prolonged grief from surface to interior. The eye is the gateway of the soul; when it 'wastes away' (ashshab), it registers the soul's interior breakdown on the body's surface. The belly (beten) in Hebrew thought is the seat of emotion and instinct; its involvement signals that David's distress is total, affecting the rational, emotional, and instinctual centers. He is not describing a spiritual problem while remaining physically functional; he is describing a person whose entire being—outer, inner, deep—is collapsing from grief.
commentary.narrative_continued2: What is striking is that this rawness comes after verses 8-9. David does not move from lament to confidence and stay there. He moves from lament (1-6) to confidence (7-9) to lament again (10-14). This is theologically crucial: it means that confidence does not erase grief, that trust does not make the eye stop weeping. The psalm refuses the false comfort that faith should eliminate pain. Instead, it holds both truths simultaneously: I trust in God's mercy AND I am being consumed by grief. The plea "Have mercy upon me, O LORD" is not abandonment of verse 8's joy but its intensification: Lord, the very faithfulness you have already shown me is the ground on which I appeal for fresh mercy now.

word_study.meaning: To be narrow, to be in straits, to be pressed, to be constricted. The noun tsarah means 'distress, trouble, adversity.' The root carries literal spatial meaning (narrow) and transferred emotional meaning (troubled).
word_study.significance: As the Covenant Rendering notes, tsar is the opposite of merchav (broad place). David has declared his feet stand in spaciousness (v. 9), yet he simultaneously acknowledges that he is in tsarah. This is not contradiction but the reality of living in affliction while trusting God: the inner condition (tsar) and the outer condition (merchav) both exist.

word_study.meaning: To waste away, to grow dim, to fail, to deteriorate. Used of eyes failing from age, weeping, or disease. The Covenant Rendering translates this as 'wastes away.'
word_study.significance: The verb describes not a sudden wound but a gradual, relentless deterioration. Eyes 'waste away' from sustained weeping. The image suggests that David's sorrow is not a momentary crisis but chronic, consuming his very capacity to see.

word_study.meaning: To be gracious, to show favor, to have compassion. The verb is often paired with chesed (covenant faithfulness) but emphasizes the gratuitous nature of grace—favor that is given, not earned.
word_study.significance: David's plea for chanan (grace) in verse 10 follows his declaration of chesed (covenant loyalty) in verse 8. The distinction matters: chesed is what God owes by covenant; chanan is what God gives freely beyond obligation. David appeals to both—the covenant commitment and the discretionary grace that flows from a generous heart.

cross_references.connection: David again describes physical breakdown from grief: 'I am weary with my groaning; all the night make I my bed to swim; I water my couch with my tears.' The wasting of the eyes from weeping is a recurring image in his laments.

The prophet describes the desolation of Jerusalem: 'Mine eyes do fail with tears...my bowels are troubled, my liver is poured upon the earth, for the destruction of the daughter of my people.' The same three-part breakdown (eyes, soul/bowels, liver/belly) appears in ancient lament.

Hezekiah in sickness describes his physical deterioration: 'My life is cut off like a weaver's loom: he will cut me off with pining sickness.' The theme of the body collapsing under spiritual/physical crisis runs through Old Testament lament.
At Lazarus's tomb, Jesus 'groaned in the spirit' and 'wept.' Jesus enters into the physical reality of grief, showing that deep sorrow is not incompatible with divine power.

commentary.historical_context: In the Ancient Near Eastern world, physical deterioration was understood not merely as medical fact but as spiritual sign. When a person's body wasted away—eyes failing, strength sinking—it was interpreted as a sign that the gods had abandoned them or were punishing them. Babylonian lament psalms similarly describe the wasting away of the body as evidence of divine disfavor. What David does here, strikingly, is reverse the interpretation: his body is failing not because God has abandoned him but because the affliction is real, and he is appealing to God to see it and respond. He trusts (v. 8) that God has seen his suffering, yet he still must appeal for relief. The cultural context shows that making one's physical deterioration visible to God was a standard form of lament-based persuasion: the suffering body itself becomes the argument for divine intervention.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: Jacob's wrestling in 2 Nephi 2:1-2 describes a man who has endured deep sorrow: 'Thou knowest the greatness of God; and he shall consecrate thine afflictions for thy gain.' The Book of Mormon acknowledges that the body and soul do suffer in affliction, even for those God loves.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 121:7-8 records Joseph Smith in Liberty Jail: 'My son, peace be unto thy soul; thine adversity and thine afflictions shall be but a small moment; And then, if thou endure it well, God shall exalt thee on high.' The revelation acknowledges Joseph's actual suffering (not dismissing it) while promising its consecration.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The temple includes spaces for both joy and profound seriousness. The psalm's movement from confidence to grief to confidence again mirrors the temple experience, which moves through multiple emotional and spiritual registers, acknowledging the full spectrum of human experience before God.

commentary.christological_typology: Christ's cry from the cross ('My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me?') enacts verse 10 in its most extreme form. Christ's eyes, soul, and body are being consumed in the cross's agony. Yet His cry is itself a prayer, a plea to the Father who He trusts (verse 9) has set Him in a broad place of cosmic significance. Christ refuses to separate His trust from His anguish; the cry and the trust are one act of covenant prayer.
commentary.application: Verse 10 gives permission to the modern believer to acknowledge the real reality of suffering, even while maintaining trust in God. This is crucial in a Church context where the pressure to 'be positive' or to 'have faith' can silence necessary lamentation. A member experiencing grief, depression, chronic illness, or despair can pray this verse and declare the truth: I am in trouble. My strength is failing. My eye is wasted from weeping. AND—in the very same breath—Lord, have mercy on me. The verse refuses the false dichotomy between faith and suffering. It insists that the most sophisticated faith is the faith that can name the pain in full detail and still appeal to God's mercy. This is not weak faith; it is the strongest faith, because it does not depend on denying reality in order to maintain confidence.

text_kjv: For my life is spent with grief, and my years with sighing: my strength faileth because of mine iniquity, and my bones are consumed.

commentary.narrative: David deepens the description of his affliction across all temporal and existential dimensions. His entire life—not just a moment, not just a season—has been "spent" in grief. The verb kalah (to be completed, to be finished, to be exhausted) suggests that grief has used up his life's substance the way an account spends money. His years are not merely marked by sorrow but are animated by groaning and sighing (anachah). Every breath is a sigh. This is not acute pain but chronic desolation that has become the substance of existence itself.
commentary.narrative_continued: The second half pivots from the description of his suffering to an interpretive question: "my strength faileth because of mine iniquity." The Covenant Rendering translates this carefully, noting the ambiguity: the Hebrew avoni can mean either 'my iniquity' (sin) or 'my affliction/punishment.' The context strongly suggests 'affliction,' since the psalm insists throughout on David's innocence and God's justice. David is not confessing guilt; he is describing the way his affliction has drained his strength. He is weakened by the punishment of others' hatred, by the calamity that has befallen him, not by his own moral failure. The bones wasting away (atsamai asheshu) echoes verse 10's physical breakdown: the bone is the deepest structural element, suggesting that the deterioration has reached to his foundation.
commentary.narrative_continued2: Verses 10-11 form a unit of unrelenting description. There is no reprieve, no moment of relief. David is not describing what happened in the past or what might happen in the future; he is describing his present condition as total exhaustion. The temporal scope ('my life,' 'my years,' 'my strength') and the physical scope (eyes, soul, belly in v. 10; bones, strength in v. 11) together create a comprehensive portrait of devastation. Yet the structure is crucial: verses 12-14 will extend this portrait into the social realm. David's affliction is not merely personal but relational; his suffering has effects beyond himself.

word_study.meaning: To be completed, to be finished, to be used up, to be exhausted. Often used of food being consumed, time being fulfilled, or resources being depleted.
word_study.significance: That David's life is 'spent' in grief suggests that grief is not an interruption of life but has become the substance of his life. Time itself has been consumed by sorrow. This is the language of profound chronic depression or despair.

word_study.meaning: A groan, a sigh, a lament. The breath that escapes from deep grief. Anachah is the involuntary sound of sorrow.
word_study.significance: Years spent 'with sighing' suggests that every moment is accompanied by the sound of distress. David's very breath is groaning. This is not occasional lament but the texture of continuous existence.

word_study.meaning: Kashal means 'to stumble, to fail, to be weak.' Avoni can mean 'my iniquity' (moral guilt) or 'my affliction/punishment' (calamity). The Covenant Rendering prefers 'affliction' based on context.
word_study.significance: The phrase describes strength failing under the weight of calamity. David's weakness is not moral culpability but the physical/spiritual exhaustion that affliction produces. His bones are wasting because the burden is too heavy, not because he is guilty.

cross_references.connection: Another psalm of David records: 'O LORD God of my salvation, I have cried day and night before thee.' Psalm 88, like this verse, insists on the totality of suffering across all dimensions of life.

Job similarly describes existence consumed by affliction: 'So am I made to possess months of vanity, and wearisome nights are appointed to me. When I lie down, I say, When shall I arise?' The theme of life being spent in pain is fundamental to biblical lament.

Peter writes: 'Wherein ye greatly rejoice, though now for a season, if need be, ye are in heaviness through manifold temptations; That the trial of your faith, being much more precious than of gold.' Peter acknowledges that suffering can be 'the substance of seasons' while maintaining that it is temporary and transformative.

Alma describes his former sinful state: 'Yea, I was racked with eternal torment, for my soul was harrowed up to the greatest degree and racked with all my sins.' Alma uses similar language of comprehensive, existential torment.

commentary.historical_context: The complaint of the body wasting away was a standard feature of ancient Near Eastern lament. Both Mesopotamian and Egyptian texts describe petitioners whose bones are consumed, whose strength fails, whose very existence is being drained by affliction. The physician papyri of ancient Egypt describe exactly the symptoms David enumerates—wasting, weakness, exhaustion—as signs of divine disfavor or demonic oppression. The cultural expectation was that when a person's body wasted away visibly, it was evidence of spiritual catastrophe and would appeal to the gods for intervention. David is using culturally recognizable language of affliction, which would have been immediately understood by his audience as describing extremity.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: Alma 36:12-13 describes Alma's spiritual crisis: 'But I was racked with eternal torment, for my soul was harrowed up to the greatest degree and racked with all my sins...I knew that I had rebelled against my God.' While Alma's distress stems from guilt and David's does not, both describe the consumption of the entire being.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 127:2, in Joseph Smith's reflections on his persecutions, records: 'It would be a vain attempt for me to describe the invisible power which has sustained me during my pilgrimage...it would require the riches of eternity to acknowledge all the favors which I have received.' Joseph acknowledges sustenance even in the midst of the wasting away that persecution caused.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The temple includes covenants that address the reality that the body will suffer and return to dust. The language of verse 11 (bones consumed) is part of human reality that the temple acknowledges and redeems through covenant.

commentary.christological_typology: In Gethsemane and on the cross, Christ experiences the exhaustion described in verse 11. Luke 22:44 records that 'his sweat was as it were great drops of blood.' Matthew 27:46 records His cry of dereliction. Christ's entire being—body, soul, spirit—is engaged in the work of suffering for sin. Yet unlike David, whose strength fails 'because of affliction,' Christ's strength is spent in bearing the affliction of others. His exhaustion is vicarious; it is the price of redemption. The strength consumed at Golgotha becomes the power of resurrection.
commentary.application: For modern believers experiencing chronic depression, serious illness, ongoing persecution, or long-term trauma, verse 11 offers the permission to name the totality of suffering. It refuses the fragmentation that tries to isolate pain to one dimension of life: 'This is just a spiritual problem' or 'This is just physical' or 'This is just emotional.' Verse 11 insists that authentic human suffering is comprehensive—it touches life, years, strength, bones. A believer who is experiencing this totality should not try to pray around it or minimize it. Instead, the verse calls for the full acknowledgment: My entire being is affected. My years are consumed. My strength is gone. Only when suffering is named in its full reality can the appeal to God's mercy (verse 10) and the confidence in His salvation (verses 8-9, 14) have authentic weight. The verse teaches that spiritual maturity includes the capacity to hold despair and trust simultaneously—to say 'my life is spent in grief' and then to say 'God have mercy on me' without feeling like the second statement negates the first.

text_kjv: I was a reproach among all mine enemies, but especially among my neighbours, and a fear to mine acquaintance: they that did see me without fled from me.

commentary.narrative: The psalmist now extends the scope of his affliction from the personal and physical (verses 10-11) to the social and relational. He is not only suffering internally but is being treated as a social contagion. The word cherpah (reproach, disgrace, shame) in Scripture does not merely describe disapproval; it describes the reduction of a person to an object of mockery and contempt. David has become a reproach "among all mine enemies" (expected, painful) but more woundingly "especially among my neighbours." Those he lived alongside, those he had relationships with, those who knew him intimately—they have withdrawn.
commentary.narrative_continued: Worse still, he has become "a fear to mine acquaintance." The Hebrew word pahad (fear, dread) can mean either that he inspires fear in others or that he is an object of fear and avoidance. The context suggests the latter: people are afraid of him, as though his affliction is contagious or his disgrace might attach to them. The final image is devastating: "they that did see me without fled from me." The phrase "without" (outside, in public, in the street) suggests that David's former friends and acquaintances would actually cross the street to avoid him. They don't approach to offer comfort; they retreat in embarrassment or disgust.
commentary.narrative_continued2: This verse describes what scholars call 'secondary suffering'—the pain that comes not from the original affliction but from the social response to it. David is suffering from whatever circumstance oppresses him (verses 10-11), and this suffering has made him socially unacceptable. The worst of this is not the shame in itself but that it reveals the shallowness of human relationship: in his moment of greatest need, those closest to him disappear. The movement from enemies to neighbors to acquaintances to random strangers in the street traces an expanding circle of rejection. Verse 12 completes the picture of total social isolation that accompany David's physical and emotional devastation.

word_study.meaning: Reproach, disgrace, shame, insult. The term describes public shame, the reduction of a person's status and dignity. To be a cherpah is to be an object of contempt and mockery.
word_study.significance: David is not merely experiencing hardship; he is experiencing public humiliation. His suffering is not private but is being used as material for social judgment. In covenant language, shame is the opposite of honor; to be a cherpah is to be stripped of the dignity that comes from standing in right relationship.

word_study.meaning: Fear, dread, terror. In some contexts, the object feared (something that inspires fear). Here it describes David as someone who has become fearful or feared.
word_study.significance: The Covenant Rendering notes that David has become 'a terror to my friends.' His presence now triggers fear rather than comfort. This is a terrible inversion: the person who should receive support has become someone people flee from.

word_study.meaning: To wander away, to flee, to scatter. The verb suggests not merely a conscious choice but an unconscious scattering or retreat.
word_study.significance: The verb nadedu ('they wandered away') suggests an almost involuntary response. People see David and instinctively retreat. His former acquaintances are not making a deliberate choice to reject him; they are reacting as though his presence is itself a problem to be escaped.

cross_references.connection: David again describes social isolation: 'My lovers and my friends stand aloof from my sore; and my kinsmen stand afar off.' The theme of friends abandoning in affliction haunts David's psalms.

The prophet describes Jerusalem's devastation: 'Jerusalem hath grievously sinned; therefore she is removed: all that honoured her despise her, because they have seen her nakedness.' The language of being a reproach extends to cities and nations experiencing divine judgment.

Job similarly describes total social abandonment: 'All my inward friends abhorred me: and they whom I loved are turned against me...My bone cleaveth to my skin and to my flesh, and I am escaped with the skin of my teeth.' Job's experience parallels David's.

The Prodigal Son's story includes: 'And he would fain have filled his belly with the husks that the swine did eat: and no man gave unto him.' The condition of being utterly abandoned by all is a feature of the extremity of ruin.
Corianton has brought 'much sorrow to thy mother, and he hath also caused me to suffer much sorrow.' Sin and affliction alike damage social bonds and create reproach within family and community.

commentary.historical_context: In the Ancient Near East, where identity and social standing were deeply communal, to become a reproach was a form of social death that could be as devastating as physical death. Honor and shame cultures (which the ancient Mediterranean and Near East certainly were) operated on the principle that a person's identity was constructed by social recognition. To lose that recognition was to lose the very thing that made one human. Archaeological and textual evidence from lament psalms in Mesopotamian sources shows that the complaint of social abandonment—family members fleeing, former friends avoiding—was a standard feature of afflicted persons describing their plight. Babylonian laments describe the afflicted person sitting alone while others pass by and do not greet them. The cultural understanding was that such abandonment was a sign of divine disfavor and made the affliction exponentially worse. David's description would have resonated viscerally with an ancient audience for whom social isolation was equivalent to being cut off from existence itself.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: Alma 36:18 describes his conversion and deliverance, yet earlier texts show how his sin caused him to be cut off: his father 'cast him out and he wandered about from place to place' (Alma 36:11). The Book of Mormon traces both the shame that comes from failing God and the restoration that comes through repentance. The social rejection Alma experienced is temporary and reversible; the text holds the possibility of restoration through change.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: The early members of the Church experienced precisely this social abandonment. D&C 19:18 records that many members were 'driven away from their lands' and made strangers in their own communities. The Church taught that such suffering, like David's, has redemptive potential when borne in faith.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The temple is the place where the isolated, shamed person is restored to dignity and community. The temple covenant restores what social rejection has stripped away: recognition, honor, belonging. The temple oath makes the individual a member of an eternal community that will not abandon them. This is why temple worship is particularly powerful for those experiencing social ostracism: it re-establishes the fundamental human need for community and recognition before God.

commentary.christological_typology: Christ's Passion enacts verse 12 in its fullest form. Christ is made 'a reproach' (Luke 23:35: 'And the people stood beholding. And the rulers also with them derided him'). His closest followers 'fled from him' (Mark 14:50: 'And they all forsook him, and fled'). Peter, His intimate companion, becomes afraid and denies knowing Him (Luke 22:54-62). Even the criminal next to Him joins in mocking (Luke 23:39). Yet uniquely, Christ's social abandonment is not evidence of God's disfavor but of God's identification with the forsaken. By becoming reproach itself, Jesus sanctifies reproach and transforms it into redemptive power. The person who is abandoned becomes, through Christ's precedent, the vehicle of God's compassion for all who are abandoned.
commentary.application: For modern believers experiencing social rejection—whether due to illness that makes others uncomfortable, mental health struggles that frighten people away, past mistakes that create shame, or simply difference that makes one culturally unacceptable—verse 12 gives voice to the specific pain that comes from being alone in a crowd. Many forms of affliction are made exponentially worse when coupled with social abandonment: the person struggling with addiction faces judgment from those who should offer support; the person with mental illness is avoided by friends uncomfortable with emotional struggle; the person with sexual abuse trauma may find that community retreats from their pain. Verse 12 says plainly: this secondary suffering is real. You are not imagining the rejection. Your neighbors and acquaintances have indeed fled. And this devastation—being a reproach, a terror, someone people flee from—this is real suffering that deserves acknowledgment. The verse does not attempt to minimize the pain of social isolation or to reframe it as something bearable. Rather, it names it as one of the deepest forms of human anguish and brings that anguish before God. For Church members, the application includes a call to examine whether they are the ones fleeing from the afflicted. Verse 12 indicts not just David's circumstance but the response of his community. Are we becoming people who, when someone is suffering, 'flee from them'? Or are we becoming the rare people who remain present to the reproached and abandoned?

text_kjv: Let the lying lips be put to silence; which speak grievous things proudly and contemptuously against the righteous.

commentary.narrative: David calls for divine silencing of the liars and mockers who have attacked him. This verse marks a shift in the psalm from personal lament toward a call for justice. The psalmist does not seek the death of his enemies—only their silencing. There is a specific cruelty David names here: these are not honest opponents but people who speak 'grievous things' with deliberate arrogance and contempt. They compound the injury of their falsehood with the contempt of their manner. The KJV's 'put to silence' captures the sense of divine intervention that closes their mouths; they are not merely silenced by shame but stopped by God's action.
commentary.narrative_continued: The Hebrew ataq (arrogant, insolent) describes a particularly brazen kind of speech—words that overstep, that are too bold and dismissive. Combined with ga'avah (pride) and buz (contempt), the picture is of people who mock David while he suffers, who add insult to injury. This is not the silencing of honest disagreement but the stopping of cruel mockery. David appeals to God's justice to vindicate the righteous by muting the voices that defame them. In the ancient Near Eastern context, one's name and reputation were not separate from one's self—to speak grievous lies against someone was to damage their very being, their place in the community.
commentary.narrative_continued_2: What makes this prayer significant is that David does not curse his enemies with death or defeat but with silence. To be silenced in an oral culture is a form of social death, a removal from the sphere of influence. Yet even this is framed as something God accomplishes, not something David takes into his own hands. The prayer for silence is, paradoxically, a prayer for divine protection of truth and the righteous name.

word_study.meaning: The Hebrew shéker means falsehood, deception, or lying. Sifté carries the sense of lips as the instrument that speaks. The pairing emphasizes that the problem is not merely false ideas but false speech—words designed to deceive and harm.
word_study.significance: In Hebrew thought, speech is not merely expressive but creative and performative. Lying lips do not simply convey false information; they actively corrupt reality and damage the one spoken against. This is why David calls for their silencing—they are not neutral voices but instruments of destruction.

word_study.meaning: The adjective ataq describes speech or behavior that is overreaching, brazen, and dismissively confident. It suggests words spoken with unwarranted boldness and contempt for the target.
word_study.significance: The Covenant Rendering notes that ataq describes words that 'overreach'—speech that assumes a right to speak down to or mock the righteous. This is not mere disagreement but presumption combined with cruelty. The word choice indicates that the lying is compounded by arrogance; the liars not only speak falsehood but do so with a swagger that shows contempt for truth and for the righteous person.

word_study.meaning: Ga'avah is pride or arrogance; buz is contempt, scorn, or disdain. Together they describe the emotional stance of the speakers—not merely wrong but dismissive.
word_study.significance: The Covenant Rendering notes that this combination 'describes the particular cruelty of those who mock the suffering of the faithful.' The liars are not just mistaken; they are cruel. They speak with pride (elevating themselves) and contempt (lowering the righteous). This is a deliberate stance of mockery.

cross_references.connection: Another prayer against those who 'whet their tongue like a sword' and who 'shoot at him suddenly, without fear.' David repeatedly cries out against those who weaponize speech against the innocent.
The wicked are said to 'make their tongue sharp as a serpent's.' In both psalms, the tongue is portrayed as a weapon more dangerous than physical violence.
A wisdom parallel: 'In the multitude of words there wanteth not sin: but he that refraineth his lips is wise.' Contrast—the wise restrain lying lips; the fools multiply them.

Joseph Smith received revelation on the nature of priesthood influence: 'No power or influence can or ought to be maintained by virtue of the priesthood, only by persuasion, by long-suffering, by gentleness and meekness, and by love unfeigned.' True power does not coerce through lying or contempt but through truth and love.

commentary.historical_context: In ancient Near Eastern societies, honor and shame were currency. A person's reputation was tied to their family, their standing in the community, and their name. To speak false grievous things against someone was to strip them of honor publicly. The psalmist lives in a shame culture where words can destroy social standing. David's call for the silencing of liars is not merely a request for personal vindication but a prayer for the restoration of justice in a community where the liars hold rhetorical power. The fact that he appeals to God suggests that human justice has failed—the lies have gained credence, and only divine intervention can restore the truth.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: Alma 31:26-27 depicts Zoramite priests who are 'lifted up in the pride of their hearts' and speak against the poor and faithful. Like David's mockers, their speech combines arrogance with contempt for the righteous. Both passages show that covenant communities must guard against those who weaponize speech to oppress.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 64:8 teaches that those who are not justified by the law of God shall be cursed by the law. The Doctrine and Covenants frames justice as belonging to God, not to human vengeance. David's prayer for the silencing of liars is aligned with this principle—he leaves judgment to the Lord.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The temple is a place where truth is taught and false speech is not permitted to reign. The silencing of lying lips in the temple context reflects God's sanctification of speech and the covenant commitment to truth.

commentary.christological_typology: Jesus's enemies also attacked him with lying speech. Matthew 26:59-61 records that false witnesses brought accusations against Jesus at his trial. Yet Jesus did not return curse for curse but entrusted himself to God who judges justly (1 Peter 2:23). The silencing of lying lips ultimately applies to the final vindication of Christ, when all false speech against Him is exposed and truth reigns. At His return, all who opposed Him must account for every careless word (Matthew 12:36).
commentary.application: When we are attacked with false speech and mockery, David's example teaches us to cry out to God rather than to silence our enemies ourselves. We are to trust God's justice to vindicate truth. In our own age of social media and public speech, the temptation is to fight lies with louder rhetoric. But the psalmist teaches a different way: to bring the matter before God and to rest in the confidence that lying lips, in the end, do not prevail. This requires faith that God guards truth and the righteous.

text_kjv: Oh how great is thy goodness, which thou hast laid up for them that fear thee; which thou hast wrought for them that trust in thee before the sons of men!

commentary.narrative: The psalm suddenly shifts from anger at enemies to amazement at God's goodness. This tonal transformation is one of the psalm's most striking features. After calling for the silencing of liars, David pauses and exclaims—not in rage but in wonder. He realizes that while he suffered under the mockery of his enemies, God was storing up goodness for him all along. The exclamation 'Oh how great is thy goodness!' (mah rav tuvkha) is not an intellectual statement but an emotional eruption. David is overwhelmed by the realization that God's benevolence toward him has not diminished during his time of trouble.
commentary.narrative_continued: The Hebrew verb tsafanta ('you have stored up, you have hidden') paints a picture of divine goodness as treasure laid away in reserve. It is not dispensed casually or carelessly but saved, accumulated, held in trust for those who fear God. The Covenant Rendering notes that this 'pictures God's goodness as a treasure laid away in reserve—not dispensed casually but saved for those who fear Him.' David cannot see this treasure yet; he is in the midst of crisis. But the promise is that a hidden stockpile of divine kindness exists, waiting to be revealed. God's goodness is not diminished by the delay in its appearance but accumulates, like wealth in a vault.
commentary.narrative_continued_2: The second half of the verse introduces a crucial shift: pa'alta ('you have worked, you have done') moves from hidden reserve to public display. God's goodness toward the faithful is not only stored in secret but performed 'before the sons of men.' The very people who witnessed David's shame will also witness his deliverance. His vindication will be public. This turns the verse into a theology of witness—God acts not only for the private comfort of the faithful but for the public vindication of truth. When David is restored, everyone will see that those who trust in God are vindicated, while those who mock are confounded.

word_study.meaning: Mah is an exclamation expressing wonder or amazement. Rav means 'great, abundant, many.' Tov (here tovekha, 'your goodness') refers to God's intrinsic goodness, kindness, and benevolence. The phrase is an exclamation of wonder.
word_study.significance: This is not a question but an exclamation—a moment of spiritual breakthrough where David's despair gives way to amazement. The use of mah signals a profound emotional shift, moving from lament to praise. David is not gradually reasoning toward gratitude; he is suddenly struck by the reality of God's goodness.

word_study.transliteration: you have hidden, treasured up, stored
word_study.meaning: The root tsafan means 'to hide, conceal, treasure up, or store away.' It implies intentional preservation and reservation. In Proverbs 2:7, God 'stores up' wisdom for the upright. The verb carries connotations of safety and preservation.
word_study.significance: The Covenant Rendering emphasizes that this verb suggests 'that God's goodness is not diminished by the delay in its appearance—it accumulates, like treasure in a vault, waiting for the right moment.' The image is not of scarcity but of abundance held in trust. David's goodness is not a small mercy dispensed grudgingly but a vast treasure reserved for him. This transforms the meaning of his present suffering—it is not an indication that God has abandoned him but rather a time when his true reward remains hidden from view.

word_study.transliteration: you have worked, you have done, you have accomplished
word_study.meaning: The verb pa'al means 'to do, to work, to accomplish, or to perform.' It carries the sense of active, intentional action—not passive or accidental goodness but deliberate works of deliverance.
word_study.significance: The shift from tsafan (store up, hidden) to pa'al (work, do, perform) indicates a movement from the hidden to the manifest. God's goodness is not merely stored; it is actively worked out in the lives of the faithful. This verb suggests that God is not a distant observer but an active agent in the deliverance of His people.

word_study.meaning: Yirah (fear) in Hebrew wisdom refers not to terror but to awe, reverence, and covenantal respect. 'The fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom' (Proverbs 9:10). Those who fear God are those bound to Him by respect and loyalty.
word_study.significance: Fear of God is the condition for receiving His stored goodness. It is not fear in the sense of being terrorized but the reverent acknowledgment of God's supremacy and the commitment to follow His way. The stored goodness is reserved specifically for this community of the God-fearing.

word_study.transliteration: those who take refuge in you, those who trust in you
word_study.meaning: The root chasa means 'to take refuge, to flee for safety, to trust.' The noun chosim (those who take refuge) describes people who run to God as a fortress or shelter in time of danger.
word_study.significance: Trust here is not intellectual belief but active reliance—fleeing to God as one flees to a city of refuge. The parallelism between 'those who fear you' and 'those who trust in you' shows that these are overlapping descriptions of the covenant faithful. Both fear and trust characterize the relationship with God.

word_study.transliteration: in the sight of, before, in the presence of all people
word_study.meaning: Neged means 'opposite, before, in front of.' Bene adam are 'children/sons of humanity.' The phrase emphasizes public visibility and witness.
word_study.significance: God's work of deliverance is not private or hidden but performed in the sight of all. This has profound implications for testimony and witness. When God vindicates the faithful, the vindication is public, meant to be seen and known by the community. The enemies who mocked publicly will see the public vindication.

cross_references.connection: God 'layeth up sound wisdom for the righteous.' The same metaphor of storing up goodness appears in wisdom literature, emphasizing that divine blessing is preserved and accumulated for the faithful.
Thou preparest a table before me in the presence of mine enemies.' Like verse 20, this shows God's goodness displayed publicly, before witnesses, as a vindication of the righteous.

Believers are 'kept by the power of God through faith unto salvation ready to be revealed in the last time.' The idea of goodness stored and kept until the time of revelation parallels New Testament teaching on inheritance reserved in heaven.

There is a law, irrevocably decreed before the foundation of the world, upon which all blessings are predicated. God's stored goodness operates according to covenant law—it is not random but the fruit of faithfulness and obedience.

Ammon declares that the missionaries have labored in faith, and the Lord is preparing 'to bring forth his word unto the Lamanites...in his own time.' The principle of God's goodness being stored and reserved for the appointed time appears in Book of Mormon theology.

commentary.historical_context: In the ancient Near East, goodness (tov) was understood not as an abstract quality but as concrete blessing—fertility, abundance, protection, and reputation. The Psalmist's world is one where goodness is visible and tangible. The idea that God 'stores up' goodness suggests a theologically sophisticated understanding: even in times when the faithful cannot perceive God's blessing, the blessing is accumulating and will eventually be manifest. This reflects a worldview in which God's providential care is hidden but sure. The public display of God's goodness 'before the sons of men' is crucial to ancient honor-shame cultures, where vindication is not merely private comfort but public restoration of one's name and standing.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: 1 Nephi 11:4-6 records Nephi's spiritual experience where he is shown 'things which no one has seen except it be with an eye of faith.' Like the psalmist, Nephi learns that the goodness of God is reserved for those who approach with spiritual vision and covenant loyalty. The stored goodness of God is revealed to the faithful in their time.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 76:5-10 describes the opening of the heavens and the vision of the degrees of glory—a kind of revelation of God's stored goodness that had been hidden from the foundation of the world. Joseph Smith's restoration brought to light things that had been 'kept hid from the foundation of the world.' God's goodness accumulates and is eventually revealed according to His timing.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The temple is a place where God's stored goodness is made manifest to the faithful. The ordinances performed in the temple are the working out of God's work on behalf of His people. They are performed in a sacred space where the sight of 'the sons of men' is restricted, yet they represent God's public work that will ultimately be revealed.

commentary.christological_typology: Jesus is the ultimate display of God's stored goodness. From the foundation of the world, God had prepared the redemption through Christ. The cross and resurrection reveal publicly—before all creation—the fullness of God's love and mercy. As verse 20 says goodness is worked 'before the sons of men,' so Christ's work of redemption is performed in history, in time, before witnesses. The stored goodness of God becomes manifest in the life, death, and resurrection of Christ.
commentary.application: In seasons of suffering and mockery, this verse invites us to remember that God's goodness toward us is not diminished by our present circumstances. Like a treasure in a vault, His care for the faithful accumulates and is preserved. We are called to trust that what we cannot see now will eventually be revealed. Practically, this means we can continue to fear God and take refuge in Him even when His goodness seems hidden. Our vindication may not come immediately, but it will come publicly, in the sight of all—and that public display will bear witness to the power of God and the foolishness of those who mocked His faithful.

text_kjv: Thou shalt hide them in the secret of thy presence from the pride of man: thou shalt keep them secretly in a pavilion from the strife of tongues.

commentary.narrative: David continues his thanksgiving by describing the two ways God protects the faithful: through His presence and through His sanctuary. The verse employs the language of protection and hiddenness, but with a paradox at its center. God's face, which David asked in verse 17 to 'shine upon' him, now becomes a hiding place. The divine radiance that seemed necessary for deliverance is here redefined as a place of concealment. This is not contradiction but deepening insight: God's presence protects by both illuminating truth and hiding the righteous from their enemies' schemes.
commentary.narrative_continued: The first protection is from 'the pride of man' (ruksei ish). The Hebrew rukis refers to schemes, plots, or conspiracies—the hateful plans that proud enemies devise. God's secret presence (seter panekhа) shields the faithful from these schemes. The parallel second protection is from 'the strife of tongues' (riv leshonot)—the quarrels, accusations, and insults that the wicked use as weapons. David frames the primary threat not as physical violence but as words and plots. The tongue is the enemy's main instrument; mockery and accusation are what he fears.
commentary.narrative_continued_2: The second line shifts slightly: 'Thou shalt keep them secretly in a pavilion' suggests a more active guardianship. The 'pavilion' (sukkah) is a shelter, a booth, a protected space. The language is covenantal—it echoes the sukkot (booths) of Sukkot and the idea of God's protection as tent-like and encompassing. David is describing a multi-layered defense: God's presence hides; God's shelter guards. The righteous are not left exposed but are actively kept safe from the weapons of the wicked—particularly from the 'strife of tongues,' which David identifies as the chief form of persecution he faces.

word_study.term_english: hide them in the secret of thy presence
word_study.transliteration: you will hide them in the hiding place of your face/presence
word_study.meaning: Tastirem is causative of satar (to hide, conceal). Seter is a noun meaning 'hiding place, secret, concealment.' Panekhа is 'your face/presence.' The phrase creates an image of God's face as a refuge where enemies cannot penetrate.
word_study.significance: The Covenant Rendering notes the paradox: 'God's face, which David asked to shine (v. 17), now becomes a hiding place for the faithful. The divine presence is simultaneously radiance for the beloved and concealment from enemies.' This is a profound theological insight. God's presence is not one-dimensional; it simultaneously exposes truth and hides the righteous from harm. Being in God's presence means being both seen by Him and hidden from the sight of the wicked.

word_study.meaning: Rukis (plural rukse) comes from a root meaning 'to arrange, to plot, or to conspire.' It refers to schemes, machinations, or carefully laid plans. Ish is simply 'man.' The phrase refers to the plotted schemes of the wicked.
word_study.significance: David does not say 'the pride of man' directly but 'the plots of man.' The Covenant Rendering translates this as 'schemes of men.' These are not idle thoughts but deliberate, arranged conspiracies. The enemies are not just arrogant but actively plotting. The protection David seeks is from these calculated schemes.

word_study.term_english: keep them secretly in a pavilion
word_study.transliteration: you will hide/keep them safe in a shelter/booth
word_study.meaning: Titzpennem is from tzafan (to hide, to treasure up, to keep safe). Sukkah is a shelter, booth, or pavilion—it can be temporary (as in the Feast of Tabernacles) or more permanent. The verb suggests active keeping safe; the noun suggests a physical or spiritual shelter.
word_study.significance: The verb tatzpennem is the same root used in verse 20 for God's 'stored up' goodness. Here it is applied to keeping the faithful safe in a shelter. The sukkah is covenantal language, evoking God's protection in the wilderness and the Feast of Tabernacles, where God's presence is commemorated through temporary shelters. The faithful are kept safe in a booth-like sanctuary.

word_study.meaning: Riv means quarrel, strife, contention, or lawsuit. Leshonot is the plural of lashon (tongue). The phrase 'strife of tongues' refers to conflicts driven by speech—accusations, insults, slander.
word_study.significance: The Covenant Rendering emphasizes that 'the 'strife of tongues' (riv leshonot) identifies the primary weapon: not swords but words—slander, accusation, gossip.' For David, the chief persecution is linguistic. His enemies do not threaten his life with swords but his reputation with words. The protection he needs is from the power of slanderous speech to destroy him.

cross_references.connection: Keep me as the apple of the eye, hide me under the shadow of thy wings.' This earlier psalm uses similar language of God's protective hiding, emphasizing the intimacy of divine protection.

In the time of trouble he shall hide me in his pavilion: in the secret of his tabernacle shall he hide me.' The exact imagery of hiding in God's pavilion and tabernacle appears here, suggesting a consistent theme in the Psalter.
The Servant of the Lord is described: 'He hath made my mouth like a sharp sword...and hid me in the shadow of his hand.' God hides His anointed in His hand and makes them instruments of His word.

God promises to put Moses in 'a clift of the rock' and hide him 'in the clift of the rock' while the Lord's glory passes by. God's protection is consistently described as providing a sheltered place where the faithful are hidden from harm.

Those who keep the Lord's commandments are promised that 'I will prepare a way before you, if it so be that you will keep my commandments and walk humbly before me.' God actively prepares and protects the path of the faithful.

commentary.historical_context: In ancient Near Eastern contexts, the tent or pavilion (sukkah) was a real and concrete form of protection. It provided shelter from sun, rain, and enemies. For a nomadic or semi-nomadic people, the concept of being hidden in God's tent would evoke powerful images of safety and belonging. The 'strife of tongues' in the ancient world was particularly damaging because oral culture depended on reputation and word-of-mouth communication. False speech in such societies could destroy one's entire standing in the community. A curse, a false accusation, or a well-spread rumor could exile a person socially even if they were physically unharmed. David's concern with protection from 'the strife of tongues' reflects the real power of speech in his world.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: Alma 37:40-41 teaches that those who keep the commandments 'shall be guided to do all things whatsoever the Lord their God shall command them.' The guidance described—being led and protected in hidden ways—parallels the psalmist's confidence in divine hiddenness and protection.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 76:8 describes the visions Joseph Smith received: 'For thus saith the Lord—I the Lord am merciful and gracious unto those who fear me, and delight to honor those who serve me in righteousness and in truth unto the end.' The righteous are honored and protected by God. D&C 109:22 (Kirtland Temple dedication) asks that the Lord 'hide [the Saints] beneath the shadow of thy hand.' The language of hidden protection is central to Restoration theology.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The temple is itself a 'pavilion'—a sacred space where the faithful are hidden from the world and where the 'strife of tongues' cannot penetrate. The temple ordinances are performed in secret, away from mockery and profane disturbance. The veil that separates the temple from the world creates a literal and spiritual hiding place where the covenant faithful are protected and taught.

commentary.christological_typology: Jesus withdrew to secret places to pray and was sometimes hidden from His enemies (John 8:59, Luke 4:30). His transfiguration occurred on a mount, hidden from the multitudes. His greatest protection and exaltation occurred through His submission to God's will, not through physical escape. The cross itself became a kind of pavilion—a place where Jesus was physically vulnerable but spiritually protected by God's presence. His resurrection revealed that this hiding in God's presence was the ultimate victory.
commentary.application: In an age when our words, actions, and reputation are constantly exposed to public scrutiny—through social media, review sites, and public discourse—this verse invites us to understand a different kind of protection. We do not need to defend our reputation obsessively if we trust that God hides the faithful in His presence. The 'strife of tongues' in our time takes new forms: online criticism, character assassination, spreading of false narratives. But the principle remains: those who seek refuge in God's presence and remain covenant faithful are protected from the ultimate power of slander. Public vindication may come later, but in the meantime, our souls are kept safe in God's pavilion. This requires faith that extends beyond our ability to control the narrative.

text_kjv: Blessed be the LORD: for he hath shewed me his marvellous kindness in a strong city.

commentary.narrative: David utters a blessing, praising God for showing him 'marvellous kindness' (hesed) in a strong city. The verse is brief but laden with meaning. The shift to blessing marks another emotional turning point in the psalm—from prayer and plea to praise and thanksgiving. What has changed? Not necessarily David's external circumstances, but his interior perspective. He has come to recognize God's kindness displayed in his very trial. The phrase 'in a strong city' has been much debated by scholars. It could mean David experienced God's kindness while he was besieged in a fortified city, or it could be a poetic way of saying that God's kindness is itself like a fortress—strong, protective, impregnable.
commentary.narrative_continued: The verb 'hath shewed' (hiflia) comes from the root pala, which means 'to be extraordinary, to do wonders, to be difficult or impossible.' The word pele (wonder) derives from this same root. David is saying that God has done something extraordinary, something that transcends the ordinary course of events. God's kindness (hesed) is not merely adequate or functional but remarkable—it is wondrously displayed. The KJV's 'marvellous' captures this sense of the extraordinary. In the ancient Near East, the gods might show favor to their chosen ones, but it was noteworthy when such favor was demonstrated clearly and unambiguously. David recognizes that in the midst of his distress, God has shown him unmistakable signs of extraordinary care.
commentary.narrative_continued_2: The 'strong city' (ir matsor) likely refers to a fortified place where David took refuge during his persecution. Many scholars connect this to David's time hiding from Saul, possibly in cities like Ziklag or other strongholds. But there is theological significance beyond the historical detail: a 'strong city' is a place of human strength and military might. Yet it is in such a place—where human resources are most evident—that David recognizes God's divine kindness. This suggests that David's deliverance is not merely the result of the city's fortifications or his own military cunning but of God's extraordinary intervention. The strong city becomes the venue where God's wonders are displayed.

word_study.meaning: Baruch is the passive participle of barak (to bless, to praise, to kneel before). When applied to God, it means 'praised, blessed, worthy of praise.' It is a declarative statement affirming God's worthiness and goodness.
word_study.significance: This benediction marks a shift to doxology. David moves from petition to praise. The blessing is not a request but a declaration—God is blessed, worthy of praise. This is a crucial turning point in the psalm where David's faith has been transformed from desperation to thanksgiving.

word_study.transliteration: he has made wonderful, he has shown wondrously
word_study.meaning: Hiflia is the hiphil (causative) form of pala (to be extraordinary, to be difficult, to do wonders). The verb means 'to make wonderful, to do something extraordinary, to display wonders.' It is the verb from which pele (wonder, miracle) derives.
word_study.significance: The Covenant Rendering notes: 'The verb hifli ('He made wonderful, He showed wondrously') from the root pala ('to be extraordinary, to do wonders') — the same root that gives us the noun pele ('wonder').' God has not merely been kind but has demonstrated His kindness in a way that is extraordinary, unmistakable, and worthy of wonder. This is not mundane protection but miraculous deliverance.

word_study.transliteration: his faithful love, his covenant kindness
word_study.meaning: Hesed is one of the richest words in Hebrew theology. It means kindness, mercy, loyal love, faithful covenant-keeping. It describes God's enduring commitment to His covenant people, not based on their merit but flowing from His nature.
word_study.significance: Hesed is the primary word used to describe God's covenant relationship with Israel. It is kindness that persists even when undeserved, loyalty that endures through betrayal. David's recognition that God has shown him hesed is an affirmation that God remains faithful to the covenant despite David's present trial. God's kindness is not conditional on David's circumstances but rooted in God's eternal nature and covenant commitment.

word_study.transliteration: in a city of siege, in a fortified city
word_study.meaning: Ir means 'city.' Matsor can mean 'siege' or 'siege-works,' referring either to the city's defensive structures or to a siege laid against it. The phrase could mean 'in a city under siege' or simply 'in a fortified city.'
word_study.significance: The Covenant Rendering notes the ambiguity: 'The phrase be-ir matsor ('in a city of siege/fortress') is debated: it may mean God showed love while David was besieged, or it may mean God's love was itself like a fortified city. Both readings are theologically rich.' The strong city could represent David's refuge or the siege against him. In either case, David is saying that God's extraordinary kindness was displayed precisely in the context of danger, siege, or military threat. God's wonders are shown not in safety but in the midst of peril.

cross_references.connection: David declares 'I will go unto the altar of God, unto God my exceeding joy: yea, upon the harp will I praise thee, O God my God.' The move from crisis to praise by way of the altar is thematic in David's psalms.

O give thanks unto the LORD, for he is good: for his mercy endureth for ever. Let the redeemed of the LORD say so...This psalm begins with thanksgiving for God's hesed and calls others to declare it publicly.

While David abode in the wilderness, Saul sought him daily: but God delivered him not into his hand.' Many scholars connect Psalm 31 to David's wilderness years when he hid from Saul in desert strongholds. This historical parallel illuminates the context of 'a strong city.'

Abraham looked for a city which hath foundations, whose builder and maker is God.' The 'strong city' in Psalm 31 foreshadows the heavenly city—a refuge whose strength comes from God, not human engineering.

In the Latter-day revelation on Zion: 'Inasmuch as this generation hath rejected me, I will leave them alone, and will take away the privileges of my house.' Yet God's hesed toward the righteous endures—He shows wonders to those who seek Him.

commentary.historical_context: The 'strong city' likely refers to a real historical situation in David's life, possibly Ziklag, Mahanaim, or another fortified city where David took refuge during his persecution by Saul. First Samuel 23:14 indicates that 'God delivered him not into his hand'—meaning that despite being hunted in strongholds, David was protected. In the ancient Near East, cities were centers of human power and strength. When David recognizes God's wonders displayed in a strong city, he is acknowledging that God's power supersedes human military strength. The verse reflects the ancient belief that the gods could display their superiority by acting within the sphere of human power—that is, by showing their might where human might is most evident.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: 1 Nephi 17:50 records Nephi's deliverance: 'And I did smile upon them in their anger, for their anger was not against me, but against the Lord; for they would that I should transgress the commandments of the Lord.' Like David, Nephi experienced God's wondrous kindness in a context of persecution. The faithful recognize divine protection precisely in moments of human danger.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 121:7-9 records Joseph Smith in Liberty Jail: 'My son, peace be unto thy soul; thine adversity and thine afflictions shall be but a small moment; And then, if thou endure it well, God shall exalt thee on high.' The principle is consistent: God shows His wondrous kindness precisely in affliction, and the affliction becomes the context for demonstrating His power.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The temple is a strong city—a place of strength built by human hands yet dedicated to God. The Kirtland Temple, the Nauvoo Temple, each temple has been built as a strong city of refuge for the faithful. Within it, God shows His wondrous kindness through ordinances and covenants.

commentary.christological_typology: Jesus's ministry was centered in Palestine, a land occupied by Rome—an imperial power represented by strong cities. Yet Jesus's power was not displayed through military strength but through miracles, teachings, and ultimately through the cross and resurrection. Like David in the strong city, Jesus demonstrated God's wondrous kindness not by overthrowing human military power but by demonstrating divine authority that transcends earthly power structures. His death in Jerusalem (itself a 'strong city') became the place where God's greatest wonder—resurrection and redemption—was displayed.
commentary.application: When we find ourselves in circumstances that seem to require human strength and resources—facing opposition in the workplace, struggling within a difficult family structure, living in a context of hostility to the gospel—this verse invites us to recognize that God's wondrous kindness can be displayed precisely in these strong cities of human power.
