word_study.significance: The sha'on adds an auditory dimension to the pit's horror: it is not silent entombment but roaring chaos, the sound of one's own terror or the sound of chaos itself. The image suggests the psalmist was engulfed not just in darkness but in the tumult of dissolution.

word_study.meaning: The mire or sticky mud of a pit or bog. The adjective yaven may relate to moisture, sogginess, or the unstable, shifty nature of mud that offers no foothold. One sinks in miry clay; it swallows the unwary.
word_study.significance: As The Covenant Rendering notes, the sela ('rock') is the opposite of tit hayaven ('miry mud') — one swallows you, the other supports you. The rescue involves a complete reversal of the ground beneath the psalmist's feet, from something that pulls him down to something that holds him up.

word_study.meaning: A rock, cliff, or crag — the most stable and unshakeable element in nature. Often used metaphorically for God Himself (Psalms 18:2, 31:3, 61:2) or for the security and foundation God provides.
word_study.significance: Setting feet upon the sela is the opposite of sinking in mud. The rock is God's gift of stable foundation. In theological terms, it represents the covenant relationship itself — the grounds on which one stands secure before God.

word_study.meaning: From kunah (to establish, make firm, set in place) and ashurah (steps, ways, paths, or 'goings'). Together: to make one's steps or life path firm and secure, to stabilize the future.
word_study.significance: The rescue is not momentary salvation but lasting restoration. The ashuray (goings) are the person's future steps, life direction, and destiny. To establish them is to secure not just survival but flourishing, not just the present but the future.

cross_references.connection: God will 'hide me in his pavilion' and 'set me up upon a rock,' using the same language of rock-foundation to describe divine protection and stability during distress.

'Thou, which hast shewed me great and sore troubles, shalt quicken me again... thou shalt bring me up again from the depths of the earth.' This echoes Psalm 40:3's recovery from the pit and ascent to new life.
References being 'hid in the pit' as a place of divine judgment and refuge — the pit as a location from which the Lord acts to save or conceal His people.

Describes the narrow way as a path set by the Savior, and those on it are protected from the mist of darkness. The establishment of the ashuray (goings/steps) parallels the Book of Mormon's image of the strait and narrow way leading to eternal life.

Promises that those who receive the priesthood will have their 'goings' established — their steps and life direction secured by covenant power, directly echoing Psalm 40:3's language of established ashuray.

commentary.historical_context: The 'pit' metaphor in ancient Near Eastern literature often referred to actual tombs, cisterns, or siege pits used to imprison enemies. In Israel's context, the bor was both a real danger (Joseph cast into a pit, Jeremiah imprisoned in a cistern) and a metaphorical emblem of Sheol, the undifferentiated realm of the dead. The image of sinking in mud was vivid to desert and Mediterranean cultures familiar with quicksand, unstable lakebeds, and the despair of being trapped in a location from which human effort alone could not extract you. The rock (sela), by contrast, was the sure foundation of the land itself — immovable, eternal, and the basis of all building. When a psalmist spoke of being set on a sela, the image would have resonated as both literal (the psalmist's feet were back on solid earth) and theological (the psalmist was restored to covenant standing).

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: 2 Nephi 15:19-20 describes those who 'stumble in darkness' and 'grope after the wall' — the image of darkness, confusion, and unable movement parallels the pit of Psalm 40:3. The Book of Mormon consistently uses this language of being lost and then found, sinking and then lifted, to describe the redemptive pattern of the gospel.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 128:22-23 describes those who are saved as being 'lifted up' and 'redeemed' — the language of exaltation in latter-day scripture directly parallels the lifting up from the pit in Psalm 40:3. The establishment of one's goings is the security of eternal life, not temporary rescue.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The ascent from the pit to the rock parallels the progression through temple ordinances, which move the participant from a state of separation and darkness to a place of light and divine presence. The rock upon which feet are set may also represent the temple itself as the Lord's foundation stone (Isaiah 28:16).

commentary.christological_typology: Jesus' descent into the grave (the pit of death) and His resurrection (lifting up to eternal life) are the ultimate fulfillment of Psalm 40:3. Christ entered the deepest pit — actual death — and was lifted up by the Father's power to stand on the rock of resurrection, securing not just His own steps but the steps of all who believe in Him. His ascension establishes the way (ashuray) for all believers to ascend to the Father. Hebrews 12:2 describes Jesus as seated at the right hand of God, His goings established eternally.
commentary.application: When believers experience profound despair, illness, loss, or spiritual darkness (the 'pit'), Psalm 40:3 promises that rescue is possible and that it comes not through our own effort but through God's intervention. The verse also teaches that rescue has two dimensions: the rescue itself (being lifted out) and the restoration (being set on stable ground with established future). Modern believers should recognize that recovery from deep crisis is not instantaneous emotional healing but a process of restoration that includes reestablishing a solid foundation for daily living and life direction. The prayer teaches us to believe that God can lift us from any pit and that our feet can again stand on secure ground.

text_kjv: And he hath put a new song in my mouth, even praise unto our God: many shall see it, and fear, and shall trust in the LORD.

commentary.narrative: The personal rescue becomes public testimony. The rescued psalmist overflows with spontaneous praise, but this is not his composition — God Himself has placed a 'new song' (shir chadash) in the psalmist's mouth. The phrase 'new song' does not refer to a recently composed melody but to a song that responds to an unprecedented act of God. The old categories of praise are insufficient; the rescue demands new music. Critically, God is the songwriter, not merely the one being sung about. The psalmist becomes a vessel through which God's own praise emerges. The result is evangelistic and communal: 'many will see and fear and put their trust in the LORD.' The psalmist's deliverance becomes a sign and wonder visible to the community, a testimony that draws others into covenantal trust. The private experience of waiting and rescue issues in corporate witness.

word_study.meaning: A song that is new not in time but in kind — one that arises in response to a new or unprecedented act of God. The adjective chadash (new) suggests something recently made or never before seen, often implying that the old resources are inadequate to the new circumstance.
word_study.significance: As The Covenant Rendering notes, the 'new song' is 'not merely a recently composed song but a song that responds to a new act of God — unprecedented mercy demands unprecedented music.' The phrase appears elsewhere in scripture to mark cosmic redemption (Psalms 96:1, 98:1; Isaiah 42:10; Revelation 5:9, 14:3), suggesting that whenever God acts decisively, new worship emerges.

word_study.meaning: God placed or deposited the song into the psalmist's mouth. The verb natan (to give, put, place) indicates a divine gift, not human composition. The mouth (pi) is the instrument through which the song is voiced.
word_study.significance: The psalmist does not compose; he becomes the mouthpiece. This echoes the prophetic calling (cf. Jeremiah 1:9, where God puts words in the prophet's mouth). The rescue itself generates the worship; the psalmist's response is not planned but spontaneous and divinely enabled.

word_study.meaning: Praise, song of praise, hymn. The root hallal means to shine, be bright, or be praiseworthy. Tehillah is the vocal expression of God's praiseworthiness, often sung in community.
word_study.significance: The entire book of Psalms is called 'Tehillim' (Psalms) — the songs of praise. To offer tehillah is the primary function of the worshipping community. It is not petition but acclamation — the acknowledgment that God is worthy of glory.

word_study.meaning: Third-person plural future: 'they will see.' In Hebrew, seeing often implies understanding, witnessing, or recognizing. To see God's acts is to grasp their meaning.
word_study.significance: The psalmist's rescue is not private; it is visible. The community will witness it and interpret its meaning. The sight of the deliverance moves the observers from fear to faith.

word_study.meaning: Both verbs are third-person plural future. Fear (yirah) in this context means reverential awe or fear of the Lord (yirat YHWH) — the beginning of wisdom. Trust (batach) means to put one's confidence in, to rely upon, to be secure in. The two are linked: fear leads to trust.
word_study.significance: As The Covenant Rendering notes, 'David's rescue becomes a public testimony that draws others to faith.' The witnessed deliverance awakens in observers a reverent fear of God's power, which in turn generates trust (batach) in God's character and faithfulness. This is the evangelistic dynamic: one person's miracle becomes many people's conversion.

cross_references.connection: Another call to sing a 'new song' to the Lord and to 'declare his glory among the heathen.' The new song emerges from God's redemptive work and serves as public testimony.

The redeemed in heaven sing 'a new song,' saying 'Thou art worthy... for thou wast slain, and hast redeemed us to God by thy blood.' The new song is the response to Christ's redemptive work and invites others to join.
'Sing unto the LORD a new song,' anticipating God's redemptive acts of covenant restoration. The new song signals the breaking in of God's eschatological salvation.
Nephi prophesies of a day when those brought out of captivity 'shall sing with the voice of joy,' expressing the same pattern of rescue issuing in spontaneous praise and testimony.

The Lord tells Emma Smith to 'make a selection of sacred hymns' and that 'the song of the righteous is a prayer unto me.' The pattern of the new song in Psalm 40 is incorporated into Restoration theology as a mode of divine communion.

commentary.historical_context: In ancient Israel's cultic practice, the composition of new hymns was understood as a charismatic act — when God rescued someone miraculously, the rescued person (often with the help of temple musicians) would commission or compose a new song to be sung in the sanctuary. These songs became part of the temple's repertoire and were sung by subsequent worshippers, transmitting the story of the original rescue to new generations. The 'new song' was sometimes inscribed in the temple (cf. Psalm 30, inscribed as the dedication song of David's house) and became a permanent part of Israel's liturgy. The fact that 'many will see and fear and trust' indicates that the psalm's primary function was public testimony — it was meant to be sung before the congregation, each singing it to remember God's deliverance and to invite others into faith.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: Alma 26:35 shows Ammon's joy: 'Yea, and he caused a great feast... and they had joy and gladness, and their hearts were swollen with joy.' The overflowing praise of Psalm 40:4 parallels the emotional and spiritual exuberance of those who have witnessed God's mighty works in the Book of Mormon.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 84:88 promises that the Holy Ghost 'shall be in your hearts; and in your hearts shall ye feel the comforting influence of the Holy Ghost.' The 'new song' placed in the mouth by God is connected to the gift of the Holy Ghost, which enables believers to testify of redemptive work and to draw others to faith. D&C 64:34 teaches that song and music are modes of communication with heaven.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: In Latter-day Saint temple worship, the singing of hymns is a covenant act. The 'new song' placed in the psalmist's mouth by God parallels the instruction given to temple worshippers — to arise and offer praise and to testify of God's works. The temple is the place where the community gathers to sing together, making visible and audible the redemptive work of God.

commentary.christological_typology: Jesus Christ is the ultimate source of the 'new song.' His redemptive work — His death and resurrection — generates the new song of all redeemed humanity. Revelation 5:9-10 describes the heavenly chorus singing a new song in response to Christ's work of redemption. Christ Himself is the tune and the lyric of all true praise. Moreover, Christ's ministry was characterized by word and sign working together — His words (the teaching) and His deeds (the miracles and resurrection) combined to awaken faith in others (John 10:37-38). The pattern of Psalm 40:4 is fulfilled in Christ's public ministry, where His rescue of sinners through His own redemptive work causes many to see and believe.
commentary.application: When believers experience deliverance from sin, sickness, despair, or spiritual bondage, Psalm 40:4 teaches that gratitude does not remain private. The recovery itself becomes a testimony that draws others to faith. Modern followers are invited to share their stories of divine intervention, not for self-aggrandizement but as a witness that awakens others to God's power and goodness. The verse also teaches that the believer is not the author of his own testimony — the 'new song' is placed in his mouth by God. This means our testimonies are most powerful when they are not calculated performances but spontaneous expressions of genuine encounter with God. Finally, the verse suggests that public witness has redemptive power: when one person's recovery becomes public knowledge, it becomes an occasion for many others to fear God (reverence Him) and trust in Him.

text_kjv: Blessed is that man that maketh the LORD his trust, and respecteth not the proud, nor such as turn aside to lies.

commentary.narrative: The psalm shifts from narrating personal experience to pronouncing blessing on the paradigm that experience reveals. This is a wisdom-psalm moment — after telling the story of waiting, rescue, and praise, the psalmist now articulates the principle: blessedness belongs to the person whose 'trust' (mivtach) is placed in the LORD and who refuses allegiance to the proud and those who chase after falsehood. The ashrei (blessed) formula is an ancient form of wisdom instruction, appearing frequently in the Psalms and Proverbs (Psalms 1:1, 2:12, 32:1-2; Proverbs 3:13, 8:34). It is not a mere pious wish but a pronouncement rooted in the order of creation itself: those whose trust is anchored in God flourish, while those who trust in human arrogance or deceptive powers doom themselves to instability. The 'proud' (rehabim) and 'liars' (satei khazav) represent the two primary alternatives to trusting in God: self-trust (pride) and trust in false powers or false systems (lies).

word_study.meaning: Blessedness, happiness, the state of flourishing. The root ashr suggests straightness, happiness, or the blessing that comes from being on the right path. Ashrei is not mere emotional happiness but the deep wellbeing that comes from right alignment with God.
word_study.significance: The ashrei formula is a declaration of which way of living produces genuine flourishing. It is not subjective preference but theological anthropology: the human person is designed to flourish when trust is anchored in God.

word_study.meaning: To place, set, or make (sam) one's trust or confidence (mivtach). The root batach means to rely upon, feel secure in, or put one's weight upon. Mivtach is the concrete object of trust — the thing or person one relies on.
word_study.significance: Trust in biblical theology is not abstract belief but concrete reliance. To 'make the LORD your trust' is to treat God as your sole foundation, the one upon whom you stake your security and future. It is the opposite of hedging your bets with multiple sources of confidence.

word_study.meaning: The proud, the arrogant, the boastful. From the root rabah (to swell, be great, boast). The rehabim are those who trust in their own greatness and power.
word_study.significance: Some scholars suggest rehabim may also allude to Rahab, the chaos-sea monster of ancient Near Eastern mythology — suggesting that trusting in the proud is like trusting in chaotic, destructive forces. Either way, the rehabim represent reliance on human power, status, or self-sufficiency rather than on God.

word_study.meaning: Those who turn aside, deviate, or defect toward falsehood or deception. The root sut means to turn aside or go astray. Khazav is falsehood, lies, or deceptive systems.
word_study.significance: The phrase suggests not merely speaking lies but turning one's whole allegiance toward false gods, false systems, or idolatrous religions. To turn aside to lies is to stake your spiritual security on something fundamentally untrue.

cross_references.connection: Another ashrei formula pronouncing blessing on those who walk not in counsel of the wicked (proud) but delight in God's law. Both psalms establish the same binary: trust in God versus trust in human counsel or power.
Pronounces blessed all those who 'put their trust in him' (God). Again, the ashrei formula connects blessedness to exclusive trust in God.
Declares blessed the one who 'trusteth in the LORD.' The wisdom tradition across Israel's scriptures consistently links well-being to trusting God rather than human schemes.
Contrasts the one who trusts in human strength (cursed) with the one who trusts in the LORD (blessed), directly expanding the binary set up in Psalm 40:5.
Alma teaches that those who counsel with the Lord, trust in Him, and heed His commandments shall prosper — the Book of Mormon's restatement of the principle that trust in God generates blessing.

commentary.historical_context: The ashrei formula appears to be one of Israel's oldest wisdom forms, used in teaching contexts to inculcate proper values in the young and in the community. By pronouncing blessing on certain behaviors (trust in God, rejection of pride and falsehood), the community was reinforcing its own identity and the criteria by which members could evaluate their conduct. The psalm's warning against the proud and those who 'turn aside to lies' may reflect actual historical temptations: the temptation to align with powerful neighboring kingdoms (Assyria, Egypt) who promised security, or the temptation to adopt foreign religions with their own systems of belief and ritual. For Israel as a vassal state, the political meaning of the verse was clear: trust in the LORD rather than in foreign alliances or great powers. For individuals, the meaning was equally clear: stake your security on God rather than on your own power or on deceptive systems.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: Helaman 12:1-2 articulates the same principle: 'Thus we can behold how false, and also the unsteadiness of the hearts of the children of men; thus we see that they are subject unto all manner of iniquities; but behold, God is faithful unto all those who are faithful unto him.' The Book of Mormon repeatedly teaches that blessing follows from exclusive trust in God rather than in human power or deceptive teachings.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 21:4-5 warns Church members against trusting in those who turn aside to lies and promises blessing to those who give heed to the Lord's voice. The Restoration scripture updates the ancient warning to address the false teachings and false systems that arise in latter days.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The temple covenant requires the participant to covenant 'to hearken to the voice of the Lord thy God... and to be obedient to his commandments' — placing exclusive trust in God's word and rejecting the counsel of those who teach contrary doctrines. The temple is the place where this covenant of exclusive trust is formally entered and renewed.

commentary.christological_typology: Jesus Christ is the one in whom all true trust culminates. He does not trust in His own power (the pride from which the proud fall) but in the Father: 'Father, all things are possible unto thee; nevertheless not what I will, but what thou wilt' (Mark 14:36). Similarly, Christ rejects all false systems and lies, repeatedly challenging the false traditions and deceptive teachings of the Pharisees. To 'make the LORD your trust' is ultimately to trust in Jesus, who perfectly exemplified such trust and who is God's ultimate revelation of faithfulness. Proverbs 3:5-6 teaches trust in the Lord, and this is fulfilled when believers place their trust in Christ, who is God's wisdom incarnate.
commentary.application: Psalm 40:5 invites believers to examine where they place their confidence. In modern life, the 'proud' may be represented by reliance on wealth, status, degrees, connections, or personal competence — good things in themselves but dangerous when they become the foundation of one's security. The 'liars' may be represented by false philosophies, ideologies, therapies, or religions that promise fulfillment without requiring submission to God. The verse does not forbid prudent planning or utilizing talents; rather, it demands that the ultimate trust be placed in God alone. The blessing promised is not automatically happiness but genuine flourishing — the deep wellbeing that comes from being aligned with reality, truthfully understood as God-centered. Those who refuse this alignment doom themselves to instability, no matter how much earthly success they may temporarily achieve.

text_kjv: Many, O LORD my God, are thy wonderful works which thou hast done, and thy thoughts which are to us-ward: they cannot be reckoned up in order unto thee: if I would declare and speak of them, they are more than can be numbered.

commentary.narrative: The psalm expands its scope from the personal to the cosmic. After narrating his own rescue, the psalmist contemplates God's vast inventory of wonders toward Israel and toward him. The nifle'otekha ('your wonders, your extraordinary deeds') and machshevotekha ('your plans, your thoughts') directed toward us are so numerous that they exceed all human capacity to catalog or comprehend. The phrase 'nothing can compare to you' (ein arokh elekha) declares God's incomparability — every attempt to measure, enumerate, or compare falls short. The final admission — 'they would be too many to count' (atsemu mi-sapper) — is not despair but wonder-struck acknowledgment of infinity. The psalmist has tried to tell his own story of rescue, to offer praise, to pronounce wisdom, but finds that the story is only one thread in a tapestry so vast that it cannot be surveyed. The personal testimony opens onto cosmic theology: God's rescue of David is part of an endless continuum of divine mercies. The verse thus reaches toward doxology — the praise of God's majesty — and acknowledges that all human speech is finally inadequate to express the reality of God.

word_study.meaning: Your wonders, marvels, or extraordinary deeds. From the root palah (to be wonderful, marvelous, extraordinary). Nifle'ot are divine acts that exceed natural explanation and reveal God's power.
word_study.significance: The term is used throughout the Psalms to describe God's mighty acts in creation (Psalms 19:1) and in history (Psalms 77:11-12, 78:4-12). A nifle'ah is inherently revelatory — it shows God's nature and power. The psalmist is saying that God's wonders toward his people are countless.

word_study.meaning: Your thoughts, purposes, designs, or plans. From the root chashav (to think, devise, plan, or account). Machshevot are God's intentions and strategic designs.
word_study.significance: The parallelism of 'wonderful works' and 'thoughts' suggests that God's deeds spring from purposeful intention — His works are not random but express His purposes. That these are directed 'toward us' (eleinu) means they are expressions of God's covenantal intention toward His people.

word_study.term_english: cannot be reckoned up in order
word_study.meaning: There is no order, comparison, or arrangement that can be made of you. The word arokh means to arrange, set in order, or compare. The phrase means God cannot be measured, categorized, or compared to anything.
word_study.significance: As The Covenant Rendering notes, 'nothing can compare to you' conveys 'God is incomparable — every attempt to measure Him fails.' The metaphor shifts from the personal rescue to the cosmic scale: God's nature and works transcend all human categories of understanding.

word_study.meaning: I would declare and I would speak — two verbs for utterance. Aggidah suggests narrating or recounting; adabberah suggests speaking or declaring. The parallelism emphasizes the attempt to make God's works known.
word_study.significance: The psalmist has been doing exactly this throughout the psalm — declaring his experience, pronouncing wisdom, inviting others to praise. But verse 6 acknowledges the insufficiency of even his best efforts. Speech reaches its limit when confronted with the infinite.

word_study.meaning: They are too strong/too great to count. From atsem (to be mighty, be strong) and sapper (to count, number). The phrase literally means God's works are 'too strong for numbering' — they exceed numerical measure.
word_study.significance: This is a recognition that infinity cannot be contained in finitude. The psalmist admits that no speech, no matter how eloquent or extensive, can adequately express the scope and significance of God's works. This is the language of apophatic theology — what can be said only by acknowledging what cannot be said.

cross_references.connection: The heavens declare God's glory, and His works are too numerous to describe. Like Psalm 40:6, this verse celebrates the inexhaustible inventory of God's creative and redemptive acts.

The psalmist meditates on God's wonders and mighty acts, recounting His deeds in the Old Testament history. The acknowledgment that God's works are innumerable is rooted in Israel's memory of redemptive history.
Isaiah teaches that God's understanding is unsearchable and His ways are past finding out — the same acknowledgment of divine incomparability and the inadequacy of human categories.
Ammon overflows with praise, acknowledging that he cannot 'say the smallest part which I feel.' The Book of Mormon echoes Psalm 40:6's recognition that experience of God exceeds speech.
Joseph Smith describes the heavenly vision where he saw things 'which eye hath not seen, and ear hath not heard,' echoing the theme that God's works and thoughts exceed human comprehension.

commentary.historical_context: In ancient Israel's liturgical tradition, the catalog of God's mighty deeds was central to covenant renewal and worship. During festivals, especially Passover and Succoth, the community would recite or sing the magnalia Dei — the great works of God — recounting deliverance from Egypt, the giving of Torah, the entry into the land, and the election of David. Psalm 40:6 stands at the intersection of personal testimony and cosmic theology: the personal rescue is recontextualized as one instance of God's perpetual faithfulness. The recognition that God's works are innumerable served a liturgical function: it taught the community that God is not exhausted by any single manifestation of power and that they could confidently expect God's future intervention. The apophatic moment (recognizing what cannot be said) was not a statement of defeat but of reverent awe and confidence: a God too great to be fully comprehended is a God who cannot fail.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: 2 Nephi 27:26-31 describes the Lord's scriptural works coming forth in abundance, with the Lord saying 'my works cannot be finished.' The concept of God's works exceeding human capacity to encompass them appears throughout the Book of Mormon, emphasizing divine infinity and human finitude.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 88:40-50 teaches that light and truth are the principles on which all things exist and that these are inseparable from God's being. The verse's recognition of God's incomparable nature and infinite works is developed in Restoration theology as the foundation of cosmology itself. All created things depend on God's continuous creative power.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The temple is the place where believers encounter the infinite through finite forms — receiving covenants, ordinances, and endowments that open consciousness to realities that exceed ordinary comprehension. The temple experience echoes Psalm 40:6's acknowledgment that God and His purposes transcend the categories available to the natural mind.

commentary.christological_typology: Jesus Christ is God's most incomparable work, the culmination of all God's wonderful works and thoughts toward us. Colossians 1:15-17 describes Christ as 'the image of the invisible God' in whom 'all things consist.' In Christ, God's infinite wisdom and power are concentrated in human form, making the divine accessible while remaining infinite. The Cross and Resurrection are the supreme manifestation of the 'nifle'otekha' (wonderful works) — an act of redemption so great that it generates the 'new song' that all creation will ultimately sing. John 1:1-3 teaches that through Christ (the Word), 'all things were made,' and in Him is the comprehensive expression of all God's thoughts and works.
commentary.application: Psalm 40:6 serves multiple functions for modern believers. First, it humbles us before the magnitude of God's reality: our theology, our understanding of God, our personal experiences, and our testimonies are all partial glimpses of an infinite reality. This should make us both confident (God is inexhaustible) and humble (we never comprehend fully). Second, it teaches us to trust beyond what we can explain: we may not understand why God allows certain sufferings, or when deliverance will come, but we can trust in the inexhaustibility of His resources and purposes. Third, it invites us to participate in an endless discovery of God: each life stage, each generation, and each individual will discover dimensions of God's nature and works previously unknown to them. Finally, it positions personal testimony (the 'new song' of verse 4) within cosmic perspective: my rescue is meaningful not because it is about me but because it reveals something of God's character and invites others to join an endless chorus of those discovering His wonders.

text_kjv: Sacrifice and offering thou didst not desire; mine ears hast thou opened: burnt offering and sin offering hast thou not required.

commentary.narrative:
This verse stands at the theological heart of Psalm 40 and represents one of the most radical reframings of worship in all of Scripture. David names four categories of sacrifice—zevach (peace/fellowship offering), minchah (grain offering), olah (burnt offering), and chata'ah (sin offering)—which together encompass virtually the entire sacrificial system prescribed in Leviticus. Yet God did not desire them and did not require them. This is not a rejection of the sacrificial system itself, but a declaration of its true purpose: sacrifice without obedience is empty theater.

The heart of the verse lies in the stunning image: 'ears hast thou opened' (oznayim karita li). The verb karah means 'to dig, to excavate, to bore'—the same word used for digging a well or cistern. God did not carve out an animal's throat; He carved out David's ears. He excavated the channels through which hearing occurs, creating in David the capacity to listen and obey. The opened ear replaces the slaughtered animal as the true offering. This is David's central insight: God wants not your possessions but your obedience; not your animals but your availability to hear His word.

The Covenant Rendering's translation of oznayim karita li as 'ears you dug for me' preserves the archaeological metaphor: God has performed an act of creation or restoration in David's inner being. Some scholars have suggested a secondary allusion to Exodus 21:5-6, where a slave who chooses permanent servitude to his master has his ear pierced against a doorpost—an act of voluntary, binding commitment. Whether or not that echo is intentional, the result is the same: the opened ear signifies a person who has chosen to hear and obey.

word_study.meaning: To dig, to excavate, to bore, to hew out. Used for digging wells, cisterns, and graves. Applied metaphorically to ears, it suggests God has physically excavated or hollowed out the channels of hearing—creating the capacity for obedience.
word_study.significance: This is the verse's most powerful image. Rather than animal sacrifice, God desires the opened ear—the organ of obedience. The verb karah transforms the ear from a passive receptor into a newly excavated instrument of divine hearing.

word_study.meaning: To desire, to delight in, to take pleasure in, to will. Expresses preference or pleasure in something. Used both negatively (God does not desire sacrifice) and positively (David desires obedience, v. 9).
word_study.significance: This verb creates the theological pivot of the entire psalm: God does not delight in sacrifice; David delights in obedience. The word choice reveals that worship is fundamentally about desire and pleasure—God's preference and David's alignment with it.

word_study.meaning: A sacrifice, an offering, specifically a peace offering or fellowship offering—an animal killed at the altar, partly burned and partly eaten in communal celebration.
word_study.significance: Zevach was the most social of the sacrifices, involving shared meals. Yet David declares God does not desire it—not because it is wrong in itself, but because it cannot substitute for obedience.

word_study.meaning: A gift offering, grain offering, or tribute. Originally meant any gift brought to a superior; in the sacrificial system, it referred to grain, bread, or oil offerings presented at the altar.
word_study.significance: Minchah represents the non-blood offerings. The fact that God rejects both blood sacrifices (zevach) and grain offerings (minchah) underscores that the problem is not the material offered but the substitution of ritual for righteousness.

word_study.meaning: A burnt offering or whole offering, the most solemn of sacrifices. The entire animal was consumed by fire on the altar, making it the most complete and costly offering.
word_study.significance: Olah represents total surrender and atonement. Yet even this most sacred sacrifice, if offered without obedience, is valueless in God's sight.

word_study.meaning: A sin offering, a sacrifice for unintentional sins or ceremonial uncleanness. The blood was sprinkled in the Holy Place, and the offering was meant to restore covenant relationship after transgression.
word_study.significance: Chata'ah represents confession and restoration. By rejecting it alongside the other offerings, David makes clear that mechanical ritual—even the ritual of repentance—cannot replace genuine obedience.

cross_references.connection: Samuel tells Saul, 'Behold, to obey is better than sacrifice, and to hearken than the fat of rams.' This is the prophetic precedent for Psalm 40:7's rejection of sacrifice without obedience.

God declares through Isaiah that He hates Israel's sacrifices and will not accept burnt offerings, demanding instead that they 'cease to do evil; learn to do well.' The same prophetic principle: obedience over ritual.
God declares, 'I desired mercy, and not sacrifice; and the knowledge of God more than burnt offerings.' Mercy (hesed) and knowledge (da'at) of God replace animal offerings as the true worship.

Hebrews applies Psalm 40:7-8 to Christ's incarnation: 'Wherefore when he cometh into the world, he saith, Sacrifice and offering thou wouldest not, but a body hast thou prepared me.' The opened ear becomes the incarnate body—total obedience to the Father's will.

Micah asks what offering will please God—thousands of rams or rivers of oil?—and answers: 'He hath shewed thee, O man, what is good; and what doth the LORD require of thee, but to do justly, and to love mercy, and to walk humbly with thy God?' Obedience, mercy, and humility replace sacrifice.

commentary.historical_context: In ancient Near Eastern religion, sacrifice was the primary language of worship and the means by which humans maintained their relationship with deity. The sacrificial system in Leviticus was not unique to Israel; comparable systems existed throughout Mesopotamia, Egypt, Syria, and the Hittite empire. However, the Hebrew prophets progressively critiqued the assumption that ritual could substitute for righteousness. This critique reaches its apex in Psalm 40:7, which directly confronts the sacrificial system not by abolishing it but by unveiling its purpose: sacrifice was always meant to express obedience, not to replace it. The 'opened ear' metaphor resonates with ancient Near Eastern imagery of the receptive king or servant who inclines his ear to divine instruction. The dug-out or opened ear becomes the symbol of the truly obedient person—one who has been transformed by God to hear and respond to His voice.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: Alma 34:14-15 presents a similar principle: the Atonement will fulfill the law of Moses, and after Christ's coming, 'ye shall no more offer up your sacrifices and your burnt offerings; but ye shall offer up unto me a broken heart and a contrite spirit.' The opened ear of Psalm 40 finds its fullness in the Restoration's teaching that obedience and covenant-keeping matter infinitely more than external performance.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 97:8 echoes this principle: 'Verily I say unto you, let him who is without sin among you throw a stone at her; and let him who is without sin cast the first stone.' More directly, D&C 64:34-35 teaches that willingness to forgive and obey matters more than any outward work: 'Wherefore, I say unto you, that ye ought to forgive one another; for he that forgiveth his brother the most shall be forgiven of his Father which is in heaven.'
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The opened ear in Psalm 40:7 prefigures the temple experience, where one enters with ears sanctified to hear God's voice. In temple covenant-making, the ear—the capacity to hear and obey—is paramount. The temple is where external ritual (sacrifice and offering) finds its true meaning: the making of binding covenants to hearken to God's voice and obey His commandments.

commentary.christological_typology: Hebrews 10:5-7 explicitly applies Psalm 40:7-8 to Christ's entry into mortality: 'Wherefore when he cometh into the world, he saith, Sacrifice and offering thou wouldest not, but a body hast thou prepared me.' Christ is the perfect embodiment of the opened ear—His entire life is an act of listening and obeying the Father. He comes not to be served by sacrifice but to become the final and sufficient sacrifice through His willing obedience. The transformation of 'ears' into 'body' in Hebrews suggests that Christ's entire incarnate person is the 'opened ear'—the ultimate instrument of divine obedience. Where animal sacrifice was external and temporary, Christ's obedience is internal and eternal.
commentary.application: This verse challenges modern covenant members to examine what we offer God. Do we believe that church attendance, tithing, or calling fulfillment can substitute for genuine obedience and listening to the Spirit? The 'opened ear' demands that we cultivate the capacity to hear God's voice—in personal revelation, in prophetic counsel, in quiet promptings—and then act on what we hear. This is not a rejection of the forms of covenant life (temple worship, sacrament, service) but a clarification of their purpose: they exist to create in us the opened ear, the capacity to hear and obey. The question for each member is: Have I allowed God to dig out my ears? Am I truly listening?

text_kjv: Then said I, Lo, I come: in the volume of the book it is written of me,

commentary.narrative:
David responds to the revelation of verse 7 with total availability and acceptance. The phrase 'Lo, I come' (hinneh ba'ti) is an utterance of complete surrender—the same formula used by Abraham ('Here am I'), by Samuel ('Speak; for thy servant heareth'), and ultimately by the prophets when they accept their divine commission. David has heard God's voice through the opened ear, and his immediate response is: I am here, I am ready, I will come to fulfill whatever You have written for me.

The second half of the verse introduces the crucial image of the book: 'in the volume of the book it is written of me' (bi-megillat sefer katuv alai). This refers to a written document—but which one? Scholars have proposed several referents: the Torah scroll, a specific prophetic oracle concerning David, a heavenly register in which lives are inscribed, or a divine commissioning decree. What matters is not the specific identity of the book but David's conviction that his life has a script, a predetermined pattern written by God, and that he has now come to fulfill it. This is not fatalism—David has made a choice—but rather a confession that his life belongs to the divine narrative, not to his own autonomous will.

word_study.meaning: To come, to go, to enter, to arrive. In covenant contexts, often signals acceptance of a divine call or willingness to participate in God's plan.
word_study.significance: The simple, direct verb ba' ('I come') is David's entire answer to the opened ear. No conditions, no negotiation—only arrival and readiness. This is the covenant language of obedience.

word_study.meaning: Written, inscribed, recorded. The passive participle suggests the action is complete and binding—something has already been determined and set down.
word_study.significance: The use of the passive voice ('it is written') rather than the active ('I will write') emphasizes that this is not David's composition but God's. His role is not to author but to fulfill.

word_study.meaning: A scroll, a roll of parchment, a written document. In biblical usage, refers to sacred or official texts that contain important records.
word_study.significance: The megillah suggests an official, authoritative document—not casual writing but something prepared with care and significance. David's life is not improvised; it is part of a larger narrative text.

word_study.meaning: A book, a scroll, a written record, a document. Can refer to the Torah, prophetic writings, genealogies, divine decrees, or heavenly registries.
word_study.significance: The combination of megillah sefer ('scroll of the book') emphasizes the textual, written nature of God's plan. David's life is inscribed, recorded, part of a narrative arc that began before his awareness.

cross_references.connection: Moses responds to God's call with hesitation, but when God promises 'Certainly I will be with thee,' Moses implicitly accepts. Psalm 40:8's 'Lo, I come' is the opposite posture—David accepts without hesitation because he trusts the opened ear has prepared him.
Samuel responds to God's call with the words, 'Speak; for thy servant heareth.' Like David in Psalm 40:8, Samuel's acceptance is immediate and unconditional upon receiving the opened ear of verse 7.

Isaiah responds to his commissioning vision: 'Here am I; send me.' The same willingness to fulfill a predetermined divine role appears throughout the prophetic tradition—the opened ear leads to immediate availability.

Hebrews applies Psalm 40:8 to Christ: 'Then said I, Lo, I come (in the volume of the book it is written of me,) to do thy will, O God.' Christ's incarnation is His 'I come'—His willingness to fulfill what is written about Him in the law and the prophets.

Mary's response to Gabriel: 'Behold the handmaid of the Lord; be it unto me according to thy word.' She, too, has received the opened ear and responds with 'Lo, I come'—willingness to fulfill what God has written for her life.

commentary.historical_context: In ancient Near Eastern royal ideology, kings were understood as agents of the gods' will, and their reign was sometimes understood as fulfilling a divine script. The image of a king's life being written in a celestial book appears in Mesopotamian sources. In Israel, this concept takes on distinctive theological meaning: the king (and later, any faithful servant) is not merely an instrument but a willing participant in God's narrative. The 'book' may allude to the royal archives or divine registry in which important decrees were recorded. Alternatively, if the 'book' refers to Torah (as some scholars suggest), David is declaring his willingness to embody and fulfill the law. The historical David, who ruled around 1000 BCE, was remembered as the ideal king precisely because he was understood as one whose life aligned with God's written purposes.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: Alma 29:17 captures this same spirit of acceptance: 'Now I do not say this with boasting, but this is my desire, and the desire of all the children of Asa Ahed, which are in the church, that the kingdom of God may be built up in this land.' David's 'I come' is the same willingness to participate in God's unfolding plan that characterizes Nephite prophets. More directly, 1 Nephi 3:7 records Nephi's response when asked to do the impossible: 'I will go and do the things which the Lord hath commanded.' The opened ear leads to this kind of acceptance.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 40:2 records Christ's promise: 'And I now give unto you a commandment, that you shall both preach my gospel.' More broadly, D&C 64:29-34 teaches that the fullness of the gospel is found in covenant-keeping, in aligning one's life with what God has written. The concept of the 'book' in Psalm 40:8 echoes the Doctrine and Covenants itself—a written record of God's will that members accept at baptism and throughout temple covenants.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: In the endowment, the initiate enters at the veil and says 'I come'—literally entering the sacred space and the covenant narrative written there. The endowment is the modern fulfillment of Psalm 40:8: the scroll of the book (the covenant drama) is enacted, and the participant accepts the role written for them. Each participant enters saying, in effect, 'Lo, I come. What is written for me?'

commentary.christological_typology: Hebrews 10:5-7 makes explicit what is implicit in Psalm 40:8: these words describe Christ's advent and mission. 'When he cometh into the world, he saith... Lo, I come... in the volume of the book it is written of me, to do thy will, O God.' Christ's incarnation is His 'I come'—His entry into a pre-written narrative of redemption. Everything in the law and the prophets pointed to Him (Luke 24:27, 44), and His entire ministry was the fulfillment of what was written. Psalm 40:8 thus becomes a Messianic statement: the Messiah is the one whose entire life fulfills the divine script, whose obedience matches perfectly with what was written.
commentary.application: For a modern covenant member, Psalm 40:8 asks: Have you said 'Lo, I come' to God? Have you accepted that your life is meant to fulfill a divine purpose already written? This is not determinism that removes choice, but rather the recognition that God has purposes for us that existed before we were born. The covenants we make—baptism, confirmation, priesthood ordination, temple sealing—are invitations to enter into the 'volume of the book' written for us. The question becomes: Do you live as though your life has a divine narrative, or do you treat it as your own autonomous project? The opened ear prepares us to recognize and accept what is written.

text_kjv: I delight to do thy will, O my God: yea, thy law is within my heart.

commentary.narrative:
David now deepens his commitment beyond mere acceptance to active delight. The verb chafatsti ('I delight, I desire') is the same verb that appeared in verse 7 describing what God does not delight in regarding sacrifice. The reversal is now complete: God does not delight in sacrifice; David delights in obedience. This is not obedience out of fear or obligation, but out of genuine desire and pleasure. David wants to do God's will—not reluctantly, but with the whole force of his affection.

The second line reveals the internal transformation that makes such delight possible: 'thy law is within my heart' (toratekha be-tokh libbi). The word toratekha ('your Torah, your instruction') describes not merely external law but God's complete revelation and guidance. More strikingly, it is 'within my heart' (be-tokh libbi)—the heart being the seat of desire, will, and emotion in Hebrew anthropology. God's instruction has not been imposed externally; it has been internalized, incorporated into David's deepest self. The law is no longer written on stone tablets outside him but on the tablets of his heart, to use Jeremiah's later imagery (31:33). This is the fulfillment of the opened ear in verse 7: the capacity to hear has resulted in the capacity to desire, and the law has been written on David's inmost being.

word_study.meaning: To delight in, to desire, to take pleasure in, to will, to prefer. Expresses emotional and volitional preference.
word_study.significance: The repetition of chafatz from verse 7 (where God does not delight in sacrifice) to verse 9 (where David delights in obedience) marks the thematic pivot. David has internalized God's preference: what God desires, David now desires.

word_study.meaning: Teaching, instruction, revelation, law. Can refer to the Torah scroll, God's revealed will, or instruction in general. Literally means 'to throw' or 'to direct,' suggesting guidance and direction.
word_study.significance: Torah is not merely rules but divine instruction and guidance. The Covenant Rendering translates it as 'instruction' to preserve this broader sense. David's commitment is not to abstract law but to God's living instruction for his life.

word_study.meaning: Within, in the midst of, in the interior of. Indicates location deep inside rather than on the surface.
word_study.significance: The law is not merely memorized or obeyed externally; it has penetrated to the interior of David's being. This prefigures the new covenant promise in Jeremiah 31:33 and the fulfillment of that promise in Hebrews 8:10.

word_study.meaning: Heart, mind, will, center of emotion and decision-making. In Hebrew thought, the heart (not the brain) is the seat of understanding, emotion, and volition.
word_study.significance: The law written on the heart means it has become part of David's deepest self, his core desires and decisions. This is a transformation of the whole person—not mere intellectual assent but integration into one's very being.

cross_references.connection: God promises: 'I will put my law in their inward parts, and write it in their hearts; and will be their God, and they shall be my people.' Psalm 40:9 describes the already-realized condition that Jeremiah's new covenant promises for the future.

Hebrews applies Jeremiah 31:33 to the new covenant in Christ: 'I will put my laws into their mind, and write them in their hearts.' The opened ear and internalized law of Psalm 40:7-9 find their ultimate fulfillment in Christ's covenant.
A later psalm declares: 'O how love I thy law! it is my meditation all the day.' This echoes David's delight in God's law and the internalization of instruction as the pathway to love.

The Shema demands: 'Thou shalt love the LORD thy God with all thine heart... And these words, which I command thee this day, shall be in thine heart.' Psalm 40:9 shows this commandment fulfilled—the law is indeed written on David's heart.

The Lord tells Oliver Cowdery: 'Therefore, fear not to do good, for whatsoever ye sow, that shall ye also reap; therefore, if ye sow good ye shall also reap good for yourselves.' The principle of internal alignment—doing good because you delight in it—is the Restoration's echo of Psalm 40:9.

commentary.historical_context: In ancient Israelite thought, the heart (lev) was understood as the seat of all mental, emotional, and volitional activity—equivalent to what moderns might call the mind, will, and conscience combined. To have God's law written on the heart was thus understood as the deepest possible form of internalization: not external compliance but internal transformation. This contrasts sharply with the critique of the prophets, who often condemned Israel for having only external religion—lips honoring God while the heart remained distant (Isaiah 29:13, cited by Jesus in Matthew 15:8). Psalm 40:9 represents the ideal: perfect alignment between external action and internal desire. The transformed heart becomes the sign of genuine covenant relationship. In the ancient Near Eastern context, a subject who found delight in serving a king was considered truly loyal; similarly, the servant of God who delights in His law demonstrates perfect covenant fidelity.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: Alma 36:24 records Alma's similar transformation: 'And now behold, I have received a remission of my sins, and I am in the spirit; nevertheless, my limbs are weary, for I have suffered the pains of all manner of iniquities.' More directly, Alma 29:3-4 shows the desire for obedience: 'Yea, and I do not glory in my own strength, nor in my own wisdom; but behold, my joy is full, so that I bow down in sorrow before the Father that I am permitted to hallow his holy name.' The Nephite concept of the internalized law is fully articulated in the Book of Mormon.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 93:28 teaches: 'He that keepeth his commandments receiveth truth and light, until he is glorified in truth and knoweth all things.' The internalization of God's word is the pathway to knowledge and light. More directly, D&C 88:63-64 teaches that light dwells in those who obey God's law: the law written on the heart produces light.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: In the temple endowment, covenants are not merely administered but internalized. The participant accepts them, makes them their own, and writes them on their heart. The temple experience is precisely the transformation described in Psalm 40:9: the law of God becomes internal desire rather than external obligation. The covenant to obey God's law in the temple is a covenant to have that law written on one's heart.

commentary.christological_typology: Christ perfectly embodies Psalm 40:9. In John 4:34, Jesus declares: 'My meat is to do the will of him that sent me.' This is the ultimate expression of delight in God's will—obedience is sustenance itself. In John 5:30, He says: 'I seek not mine own will, but the will of the Father which hath sent me.' Christ's entire being is devoted to the Father's will, not as external constraint but as His deepest nature. Thus Christ is the one whose law is perfectly written on His heart, whose every action flows from perfect alignment with the Father's instruction.
commentary.application: Psalm 40:9 confronts modern disciples with a searching question: Do you delight in God's law, or do you merely comply with it? The distinction matters immensely. Compliance can come from fear, habit, or social pressure. Delight comes only from transformation—from allowing God's instruction to move from your head to your heart, from external rule to internal desire. This suggests a path: First, practice obedience (verse 8: 'Lo, I come'). But do not stop there. Reflect on why God's commandments exist. Meditate on their wisdom. See how they protect and enrich life. Gradually, obedience shifts from duty to delight. This is the work of the Holy Ghost—to write the law on your heart so that keeping commandments becomes not a burden but a joy. The question for each member is: Is my covenant-keeping moving in this direction? Am I finding increasing delight in God's will?

text_kjv: I have preached righteousness in the great congregation: lo, I have not refrained my lips, O LORD, thou knowest.

commentary.narrative:
From internal transformation (verses 7-9), David now moves to public testimony. The verb bissarti ('I proclaimed good news, I bore tidings') derives from basar—the very root behind the Greek euangelion ('gospel, good news'). David has been an evangelist of righteousness. He has not kept the opened ear, the internalized law, and the delight in God's will as private treasures but has broadcast them publicly in the great assembly.

The second part of the verse reinforces this commitment: 'lo, I have not refrained my lips' (hinneh sfatai lo ekhla). The word ekhal means 'to restrain, to withhold, to seal.' David's lips have not been sealed. This is particularly meaningful in light of Psalm 39, which immediately precedes this one, where David says: 'I said, I will keep my mouth with a bridle, while the wicked is before me' (39:1). In Psalm 39, silence was the posture of restraint. But here in Psalm 40, after the experience of the opened ear and the internalized law, David breaks that silence. The phrase 'O LORD, thou knowest' (YHWH atta yadata) calls God as witness to his faithfulness—not boastfully, but with the confidence that God understands his heart and sees his testimony.

This verse establishes a crucial principle: private transformation demands public witness. The opened ear is not meant for personal holiness alone but for testimony that draws others toward righteousness. David's proclamation in the great congregation is the fruit of his internal alignment with God's will.

word_study.meaning: To bear tidings, to announce good news, to preach, to evangelize. The causative form of yasa' ('to go out'). This is the root of the Greek euangelion (gospel) and English evangelist.
word_study.significance: The use of basar rather than a generic word for 'speak' indicates that David's proclamation is not mere speech but the bearing of good news—gospel proclamation. His testimony is not self-centered but good-news-centered, announcing the righteousness and faithfulness of God.

word_study.meaning: Righteousness, justice, rightness, vindication. In Hebrew, tsedeq encompasses both moral rightness and the vindication that comes from being right with God. Can mean righteousness as a practice or righteousness as a status.
word_study.significance: David proclaims not his own righteousness but God's—tsedeq as the divine attribute of justice and faithfulness. His testimony is theocentric, not anthropocentric.

word_study.meaning: To restrain, to withhold, to keep back, to seal. Can be used for holding back words, emotions, or actions.
word_study.significance: The negative form 'I have not refrained' emphasizes the commitment to openness and testimony. David has chosen speaking over silence, proclamation over concealment. This is a deliberate choice to break the silence of Psalm 39.

word_study.meaning: Lips, the mouth, the opening of the mouth. Metaphorically, lips represent speech and testimony. Also can mean the banks of a body of water.
word_study.significance: The lips are the instrument of testimony. David's commitment is not merely internal but oral and public—his lips speak what his heart believes.

word_study.meaning: A gathering, an assembly, a congregation, a community. In religious contexts, refers to the assembled people of God gathered for worship or judgment.
word_study.significance: The 'great congregation' (qahal rav) is not a private or elite group but the full assembly of God's people. David testifies before the whole community, not to selected listeners.

cross_references.connection: Psalm 39 ends with David's refusal to speak: 'I was dumb, I opened not my mouth; because thou didst it.' Psalm 40:10 shows David's shift: no longer silent, but speaking freely about God's righteousness. The two psalms form a narrative sequence.

Jesus teaches: 'Whosoever therefore shall confess me before men, him will I confess also before my Father which is in heaven.' David's public testimony in the congregation prefigures the New Testament call to openly confess one's faith.

Paul writes: 'If thou shalt confess with thy mouth the Lord Jesus, and shalt believe in thine heart that God hath raised him from the dead, thou shalt be saved. For with the heart man believeth unto righteousness; and with the mouth confession is made unto salvation.' David's model—internal faith externally proclaimed—is the apostolic pattern.

Peter commands: 'But sanctify the Lord God in your hearts: and be ready always to give an answer to every man that asketh you a reason of the hope that is in you.' David's proclamation of righteousness exemplifies the readiness to give witness that Peter demands.

Alma, after his spiritual transformation, declares: 'I labored hard that I might bring souls unto repentance, that I might bring them to taste of the exceeding joy of which I did taste.' Like David, Alma's internal transformation leads to public testimony and gospel proclamation.

commentary.historical_context: In ancient Israel, the 'great congregation' likely refers to formal gatherings of the people for worship at the temple or at major feasts. Psalm 40 is labeled a psalm 'to the chief musician,' suggesting it was used in temple worship, possibly sung by the king or a priest before the assembled people. The practice of giving public testimony was central to Israelite worship: individuals would recount God's mighty acts and faithfulness before the congregation as a way of strengthening communal faith (cf. Psalm 107, where individuals are called to give thanks in the congregation). David's proclamation of righteousness would have been understood as a public recounting of God's faithfulness and his own alignment with God's will. In ancient Near Eastern royal ideology, a king was expected to make regular public declarations of his piety and alignment with divine will—this was essential to his legitimacy as a ruler under the gods. Psalm 40:10 shows David fulfilling this role, but in the service of testifying to Israel's God, not to promote himself.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: Mosiah 18:8-9 describes Alma's covenant: 'And it came to pass that he said unto them: Behold, here are the waters of Mormon (for thus were they called) and now, as ye are desirous to come into the fold of God, and to be called his people, and are willing to bear one another's burdens, that they may be light... now I say unto you, if this be the desire of your hearts, what have you against being baptized in the name of the Lord, as a witness before him that ye have entered into a covenant with him, to keep his commandments?' The public baptismal covenant in the Book of Mormon parallels David's public testimony—the covenant is not private but witnessed by the congregation.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 33:8-12 commands: 'And thou shalt go forth in the power of my Spirit, preaching my gospel, two by two, in my name, lifting up thy voice as the sound of a trump, both day and night. And I will give unto thee another Comforter, that it may abide with you forever.' The Restoration teaches that testimony and proclamation of the gospel are not optional but central to covenant faithfulness. Those with the opened ear are called to bear witness.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: In the temple endowment, after making covenants, participants are taught that they will become 'saviors on Mount Zion' (D&C 103:9)—they will bear testimony and witness to others. Like David, the temple-covenanted member makes private covenants (in the temple) and then goes into the world to proclaim righteousness publicly. The temple experience itself is designed to produce testifying disciples.

commentary.christological_typology: Christ embodies Psalm 40:10 completely. In John 7:16-17, Jesus says: 'My doctrine is not mine, but his that sent me... If any man will do his will, he shall know of the doctrine, whether it be of God.' Christ's entire public ministry was a proclamation of righteousness—God's justice and mercy revealed. He testified before the great congregation of Israel, and ultimately before all nations. In Acts 1:8, the risen Christ tells the disciples: 'Ye shall receive power... and ye shall be witnesses unto me both in Jerusalem, and in all Judaea, and in Samaria, and unto the uttermost part of the earth.' The proclamation of righteousness that David began reaches its fullness in Christ and the apostolic witness to Him.
commentary.application: This verse challenges modern covenant members about the relationship between private faith and public witness. Have you made the shift from Psalm 39 (sealed lips) to Psalm 40 (open lips)? Does your internal relationship with God find expression in public testimony and proclamation? This does not necessarily mean public speaking or formal testimony meetings—though those are valuable. It means being willing to speak about your faith to friends, family, colleagues, and strangers. It means not being ashamed of your covenant relationship when the opportunity arises. It means proclaiming—in whatever forums are natural to you—the goodness and righteousness of God. For many members, the sealed lips of Psalm 39 feel safer. But Psalm 40:10 suggests that the mark of genuine spiritual transformation is the willingness to break silence and proclaim. The question for each member is: Are you still in Psalm 39, restraining your lips about your faith? Or have you moved into Psalm 40, proclaiming freely?

text_kjv: I have not hid thy righteousness within my heart; I have declared thy faithfulness and thy salvation: I have not concealed thy lovingkindness and thy truth from the great congregation.
text_kjv_alt: Alternative Reading: I have not hid thy righteousness within my heart; I have declared thy faithfulness and thy salvation: I have not concealed thy loving-kindness and thy truth from the great congregation.

commentary.narrative:
This verse expands and deepens verse 10, providing the specific content of David's proclamation. Where verse 10 announced his general commitment to speak, verse 11 catalogs what he has proclaimed: five divine attributes that represent God's complete self-revelation and covenant faithfulness. The structure is doubled negation emphasizing positive proclamation: 'I have not hid... I have not concealed' means 'I have openly proclaimed.'

The five attributes are: (1) tsidqatekha ('your righteousness')—God's justice and moral rightness; (2) emunatekha ('your faithfulness')—God's reliability and covenant-keeping; (3) teshu'atekha ('your salvation')—God's saving power and deliverance; (4) chasdekha ('your faithful love' or 'lovingkindness')—God's covenantal mercy and hesitation to punish; and (5) amittekha ('your truth' or 'reliability')—God's absolute truthfulness and consistency. These five attributes form the complete portrait of who God is for His people: just yet merciful, faithful yet saving, loving yet truthful. David has proclaimed all of them—not selectively, not emphasizing only the merciful God while hiding the just God, but proclaiming the whole counsel of God.

The repetition of 'great congregation' from verse 10 underscores that this is not private sharing but public, corporate proclamation. By refusing to conceal God's attributes from the congregation, David is saying: this belongs to the community, not to me privately. God's righteousness, faithfulness, salvation, love, and truth are communal treasures that must be shared. To conceal them would be a form of embezzlement—stealing from the congregation something that belongs to it.

word_study.meaning: To hide, to conceal, to cover, to keep secret. Often used for hiding something of value or shame. In theological contexts, can mean God hiding His face (displeasure) or hiding treasures.
word_study.significance: David refuses to hide God's righteousness the way one might hide something precious to keep it for oneself. The negative form emphasizes openness and transparency—God's character is meant to be visible, not concealed.

word_study.meaning: Righteousness, justice, vindication, right relationship. Refers to God's just character and His vindication of the righteous.
word_study.significance: The first attribute David proclaims is God's justice. This is not the weak sentimentality that conceals God's moral demands but the full picture of a God who judges righteously.

word_study.meaning: Faithfulness, trustworthiness, reliability, truth, firmness. Refers to God's unwavering commitment to His covenants and His people.
word_study.significance: Emunahis the foundation of covenantal relationship—God can be trusted to keep His word. This is what makes the opened ear safe: God is faithful to guide those who listen.

word_study.meaning: Salvation, deliverance, saving help, rescue. Refers to God's active intervention to save and deliver His people from danger.
word_study.significance: Teshu'ah emphasizes God's dynamic, saving action. It is not mere forgiveness but active rescue. David proclaims that God saves—He does not merely offer mercy from a distance but acts decisively to deliver.

word_study.meaning: Lovingkindness, loyal love, mercy, grace, covenantal love. One of the richest Hebrew words, referring to God's steadfast, covenant-based love that persists despite human unfaithfulness.
word_study.significance: Hesed is the heart of God's character—His love is not sentimental but covenantal and faithful. It is unearned and undeserved, yet God bestows it consistently. The Covenant Rendering's 'faithful love' captures both the love and the faithfulness elements.

word_study.meaning: Truth, reliability, faithfulness, firmness, stability. Related to emunahbut with emphasis on truthfulness and the solidity of God's word.
word_study.significance: Emet is what makes God's other attributes trustworthy—His righteousness is true justice, His faithfulness is authentic commitment, His love is genuine. God's truth is the ground of all reality.

cross_references.connection: God reveals His name and attributes to Moses: 'The LORD, The LORD, God merciful and gracious, longsuffering, and abundant in goodness and truth.' The five attributes David proclaims in Psalm 40:11 are rooted in God's self-revelation to Moses.

Another psalm declares: 'I will sing of the mercies of the LORD for ever: with my mouth will I make known thy faithfulness to all generations.' David's commitment to proclaim God's attributes continues the psalmists' central mission.
The psalmist calls: 'Declare his glory among the heathen, his wonders among all people.' Public proclamation of God's character is not David's private decision but the calling of all God's people.

God declares: 'Let not the wise man glory in his wisdom... But let him that glorieth glory in this, that he understandeth and knoweth me, that I am the LORD which exercise lovingkindness, judgment, and righteousness, in the earth.' David's proclamation aligns with the prophetic call to make God's character the focus of human understanding.

John writes: 'This then is the message which we have heard of him, and declare unto you, That God is light: and in him is no darkness at all.' The apostolic task echoes David's: to proclaim the complete character of God, hiding nothing of what God is.

commentary.historical_context: The practice of publicly proclaiming God's attributes was central to Israelite worship and testimony. In the psalms and in historical narratives, individuals regularly recount God's faithfulness, justice, and saving acts before the assembled people. This was not merely a matter of personal piety but a crucial function in maintaining communal faith and covenant identity. The 'great congregation' would have included representatives from across Israel, making public proclamation a way of strengthening the entire covenantal community. In ancient Near Eastern religion more broadly, priests and prophets were understood as intermediaries who communicated divine will and character to the people. Psalm 40:11 shows David functioning in such a role—not as a priest in the technical sense, but as one through whom God's attributes are made known to the community. The emphasis on proclaiming all five attributes without concealment suggests a critique of partial or selective revelation: true faith requires proclaiming the whole character of God, including the challenging aspects (righteousness and judgment) alongside the comforting aspects (mercy and love).

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: Jacob 1:8 records Jacob's commitment: 'For we labored diligently among our people, that we might persuade them to come unto Christ, and partake of the goodness of God, that they might enter into his rest.' Like David, Jacob proclaims multiple divine attributes to draw his people toward covenantal faithfulness. More directly, 2 Nephi 31:20 expresses the commitment to enduring in proclaiming: 'Wherefore, ye must press forward with a steadfastness in Christ, having a perfect brightness of hope, and a love of God and of all men.'
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 42:12 commands: 'And let them journey together, or singly, taking the highway which I, the Lord, shall point out unto them.' More directly, D&C 133:36-37 speaks of proclaiming the attributes of God: 'And let every man choose for himself what he will do; and those who have kept my commandments shall be called blessed; for they shall escape all things which are of the world, and shall have eternal life.' The Doctrine and Covenants emphasizes that faithful disciples become witnesses and proclaimers of God's character.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: In the temple endowment, divine attributes are revealed and emphasized throughout: the endowment is a dramatic proclaiming of God's character, purposes, and relationship with humanity. As temple-covenanted members, participants learn God's attributes not to keep them secret but to internalize them and ultimately to proclaim them as modern Israel.

commentary.christological_typology: Christ is the perfect proclaimer of God's attributes. In John 1:18, John writes: 'No man hath seen God at any time; the only begotten Son, which is in the bosom of the Father, he hath declared him.' Christ 'declared' (literally, 'expounded') the Father—He revealed God's complete character through His teaching and example. The five attributes David proclaims—righteousness, faithfulness, salvation, love, and truth—are embodied in Christ. He is God's righteousness, He faithfully completes the Father's will, He brings salvation, He shows perfect love even to the point of laying down His life, and He is the truth incarnate (John 14:6). Christ's entire ministry is an open proclamation of God's character, concealing nothing.
commentary.application: This verse challenges modern disciples to examine what they proclaim about God. Do you present a balanced picture of God's character, or do you emphasize only the aspects that are comfortable? Many modern believers want to proclaim God's love (hesed) and mercy (rachamim) while concealing or downplaying God's righteousness (tsedeq) and truth (emet). But Psalm 40:11 insists: proclaim all five attributes. This means teaching others about God's justice as well as His mercy, His demands for righteousness as well as His offer of forgiveness, His truthfulness (which sometimes means facing hard truths) as well as His love. It also means examining whether you are living in a way that allows these attributes to be visible in your life. Your righteousness, faithfulness, salvation of others, loyal love, and truthfulness should characterize your actions, making God's attributes visible to those around you. The question for each member is: Am I proclaiming the whole character of God, or only the comfortable parts? Am I living in a way that displays all these attributes, or am I hiding some of them?

text_kjv: Withhold not thou thy tender mercies from me, O LORD: let thy lovingkindness and thy truth continually preserve me.

commentary.narrative:
After verses of testimony and proclamation, David now shifts to petition. The logic of the verse is crucial: because he has not withheld God's attributes from the congregation (verse 11), he appeals to God not to withhold His compassion from him. This is not quid pro quo—David is not claiming that his faithfulness earns God's favor—but rather a statement of covenant logic. One who has taken God's character seriously enough to proclaim it to others can confidently ask for God's protective care.

The verse draws a verbal parallel: David did not 'conceal' (lo khichadti) God's attributes; therefore God will not 'withhold' (lo tikhla) His mercies from David. The similarity in verbs (both meaning 'not to hold back') creates a resonance: those who do not hide God's character receive freely the flow of God's protecting care. The phrase 'tender mercies' (rachamekha) derives from rechem, meaning 'womb,' suggesting the most intimate, maternal form of compassion. God's compassion is not distant or conditional but womb-like, embodied and nurturing.

The final phrase is the heart of the petition: 'let thy lovingkindness and thy truth continually preserve me' (chasdekha va-amittekha tamid yitseruni). The word natsar ('to preserve, to guard, to watch over') transforms the abstract attributes of verses 11 into active agents protecting David. God's hesed (faithful love) and emet (truth) become bodyguards, surrounding and defending him. The word tamid ('continually, always, forever') emphasizes that this protection is not episodic but constant. David does not ask for mercy once but for continuous preservation by God's covenant love and faithfulness. This is the psalm's resolution: the one whose ear is opened, whose law is internalized, who delights in obedience, and who proclaims God's character publicly can trust in God's constant, covenant-based protection.

word_study.meaning: To withhold, to restrain, to keep back, to hold in. Can be used for holding back water, words, mercies, or any benefits.
word_study.significance: This is the opposite of the opened flow of God's attributes. David asks that the stream of God's mercy continue to flow—unwithheld and unrestrained toward him.

word_study.meaning: Mercies, compassion, pity, tender care. The noun form derives from rechem ('womb'), suggesting the most intimate, protective form of care.
word_study.significance: Rachamim is not abstract forgiveness but embodied, emotional, maternal compassion. God's tender mercies are like the care of a mother for her child. This is the most intimate form of God's care.

word_study.meaning: Covenantal love, faithful love, mercy, grace, loving-kindness. Refers to God's steadfast commitment to His covenant partners.
word_study.significance: As in verse 11, hesed is the covenant-based love of God. Here it is personified as an active guardian—God's love does not remain abstract but surrounds and protects.

word_study.meaning: Truth, reliability, firmness, faithfulness. Refers to God's absolute truthfulness and consistency.
